meta.textbook: Potter & Perry, Fundamentals of Nursing, 12th ed.
meta.notes: Exam 2 set 2. Each section: base questions (ids -v, -hd, -g; no difficulty field), NCLEX level questions (ids -nx, "difficulty": "nclex"), and 15 specification questions (ids -sp01 to -sp15, "difficulty": "difficult") where an exact device, rate, setting or technique decides the answer. Temperatures are Celsius only. The 225 specification questions carry the daily set flag for 2026-10-03.

optionStrategies.name: Eliminate absolutes
optionStrategies.cue: always, never, all, none, only, every
optionStrategies.note: Absolutes are usually wrong because medicine rarely deals in certainties.

optionStrategies.name: Favor qualifiers
optionStrategies.cue: usually, generally, often, may, approximately, most
optionStrategies.note: Qualifiers make a statement realistic. Not automatically right, but worth a second look against an absolute.

optionStrategies.name: Opposite pair, look closely
optionStrategies.cue: increase vs decrease, before vs after
optionStrategies.note: Often one of the pair is correct. Sometimes both are distractors, so treat it as a flag for attention.

optionStrategies.name: Global or umbrella option
optionStrategies.cue: one option covers two or more others
optionStrategies.note: If one option encompasses the others it is often the most complete answer.

optionStrategies.name: Patient-centered option
optionStrategies.cue: asks, involves, or respects the patient
optionStrategies.note: Options that involve the patient beat options that decide for them.

optionStrategies.name: Duplicate facts
optionStrategies.cue: a wrong fact shared by two or more options
optionStrategies.note: One shared wrong fact eliminates several options at once.

optionStrategies.name: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings
optionStrategies.cue: don't worry, it's nothing, most people are fine
optionStrategies.note: Therapeutic communication reflects feelings and invites more.

optionStrategies.name: Odd man wins
optionStrategies.cue: three options share an idea, one stands apart
optionStrategies.note: When most options point one way, the different one is often correct.

optionStrategies.name: Negative polarity
optionStrategies.cue: avoid, except, not, least, contraindicated, requires further teaching
optionStrategies.note: You are hunting the wrong option. Identify polarity before reading the choices.

optionStrategies.name: Priority key word
optionStrategies.cue: priority, immediate, first, best, most, least
optionStrategies.note: More than one option may be true. The key word decides how to choose among them.

optionStrategies.name: Apply the ABCs
optionStrategies.note: In ordering and priority questions, airway, breathing, and circulation come first, then safety, then comfort.

optionStrategies.name: Assessment before intervention
optionStrategies.cue: assess, check, determine versus administer, apply, notify
optionStrategies.note: When the stem asks what comes first and an assessment option is present, assessment usually precedes action.

optionStrategies.name: Treat each option as true or false
optionStrategies.note: Work each option independently. Partial credit means a wrong selection costs you, so only select what the scenario supports.

questions.stem: An 81-year-old slipped to the floor. The nurse stayed, called for help, found no injury and stable vital signs, then assisted her back to bed. Which action does the nurse take next?

options.text: Complete the occurrence report
options.rationale: Required, and tempting because it feels urgent. It comes after the provider knows about the fall.

options.text: Notify the health care provider
options.rationale: The assessment is done. The provider must be told so hidden injury can be evaluated and orders written.

options.text: Reassess her for injury a second time
options.rationale: The stem already gives a complete assessment with no change since.

options.text: Hold the post-fall huddle with the team
options.rationale: Valuable for prevention, and it waits until the client's immediate care is finished.

questions.takeaway: After a fall: call for help, stay, assess, notify the provider, follow policy, reassess the plan, then document and report.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: The stem tells you assessment is finished. Find the next step in the sequence instead of assessing again.

steps.detail: Help called, nurse stayed, injury assessed.
Nothing new has happened to assess.

steps.action: Rank the paperwork and the huddle
steps.detail: Both follow provider notification.

elimination.verdict: Notify the provider. Assessment is complete, so communication is due.

questions.stem: A confused 84-year-old kept pulling at his feeding tube. The nurse taped the tube out of sight and asked his daughter to sit with him. Which finding indicates the plan is effective?

options.text: He is asleep 20 minutes after a dose of lorazepam
options.rationale: A drug given to control behavior is a chemical restraint, so this does not show the alternatives worked.

options.text: His hands are resting quietly inside secured mitts
options.rationale: Mitts are a restraint. Quiet hands in mitts say nothing about the alternatives.

options.text: He has left the tube alone all shift while awake
options.rationale: The goal behavior is met without any restriction, during the time he was able to pull.

options.text: His daughter says he seems more like himself today
options.rationale: Encouraging, and it is an impression. The tube staying untouched is the measured outcome.

questions.takeaway: Judge a restraint alternative by the target behavior stopping while the client is free and awake.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Ask what the plan was meant to change. Then pick the finding that shows that change without a restraint doing the work.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Tube left in place with no restraint.

steps.action: Remove options where something else did the work
steps.detail: Lorazepam and mitts are restraints.
An awake client leaving the tube alone beats a general impression.

elimination.verdict: Tube untouched all shift while awake.

questions.stem: A post-fall huddle reviews a client's 0300 fall on the way to the bathroom. Universal fall precautions were in place and he had voided with staff at 0230. Zolpidem, a sleep medication, was started that evening. Which change does the team make?

options.text: Add a bed exit alarm at night
options.rationale: An alarm tells staff he is already up. It does not remove what contributed to the fall.

options.text: Move him to a room near the station
options.rationale: Closer observation is reasonable, and it still leaves the new cause in place.

options.text: Add scheduled toileting overnight
options.rationale: Tempting because he fell going to the bathroom. He had voided with staff half an hour earlier, so toileting was already covered.

options.text: Have the sleep medication reviewed
options.rationale: The zolpidem is the one new factor the huddle found. Medication dizziness is managed by monitoring and adjusting the drug or its timing.

questions.takeaway: In a huddle, ask what happened, what contributed and whether interventions were in place. When they were in place, change the thing that is new.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Three options add watching or help. Ask which one removes the cause the huddle found.

steps.action: List what was already in place
steps.detail: Universal fall precautions and a toileting visit at 0230.
Overnight toileting duplicates care he already received.
An alarm and a room move watch him more closely. Only the medication review addresses the new factor.

elimination.verdict: Review the sleep medication. Fix the cause, not only the surveillance.

questions.stem: A client receiving maintenance IV fluid says his hand tingles each time he touches the infusion pump. The nurse sees a frayed power cord. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Unplug the pump and take it out of use
options.rationale: The hazard is live now. Removing the source protects the client and the staff before anything else.

options.text: Call clinical engineering to inspect the pump
options.rationale: Needed, after the pump is unplugged and tagged.

options.text: Plug the pump into a different outlet
options.rationale: The fault is in the cord, so a new outlet leaves the same hazard at the bedside.

options.text: Assess the hand for burns and sensation
options.rationale: Tempting as an assessment, but the nurse already knows the cause and the client is still exposed while the pump stays plugged in.

questions.takeaway: Faulty electrical equipment is unplugged and removed from service first, then tagged and reported.
questions.coverage: Not in Lecture PPT. Covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Assessment usually leads. Here the cause is already seen, so ask which action ends the exposure.

steps.detail: Tingling plus a frayed cord. The cause is identified.

steps.action: Cut the option that keeps the hazard
steps.detail: A different outlet still powers a damaged cord.
Unplug first. Then assess the hand and call engineering.

elimination.verdict: Unplug and remove the pump. Stop the exposure, then assess and report.

questions.stem: The nurse plans first rounds on a medical unit. Which client does the nurse visit before the others?

options.text: A client in wrist restraints who reports numb, tingling fingers
options.rationale: An actual neurovascular change from the restraint. It needs a nurse's assessment and release now.

options.text: A high fall risk client asking for help to the bathroom
options.rationale: Urgent and tempting. Assisting with toileting can be delegated to assistive personnel, so it does not need the nurse's first visit.

options.text: A client whose restraint order expires in one hour
options.rationale: Needs reassessment within the hour, and nothing is wrong yet.

options.text: A client stable after a fall, waiting for a hip x-ray
options.rationale: Already assessed and stable.

questions.takeaway: Actual harm outranks potential harm. A need that can be delegated does not have to take the nurse's first visit.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Two clients cannot wait. Ask which one needs the nurse's own judgment and which one can be met by assistive personnel.

steps.detail: The x-ray client and the expiring order can wait.
Numb fingers are actual injury. The bathroom trip is a risk.
Toileting help can be delegated to assistive personnel.

elimination.verdict: The restrained client with numb, tingling fingers.

questions.stem: A client receiving oxygen by nasal cannula is in bed when a wastebasket in the room catches fire. The client cannot walk alone. Place the nurse's actions in order.

options.text: Close the room door and shut off the oxygen supply
options.rationale: Third. Confining the fire and removing oxygen slows its spread.

options.text: Move the client out of the room
options.rationale: First. This client is in immediate danger and cannot leave alone.

options.text: Use the extinguisher if the fire is still small
options.rationale: Last, and only if it can be done safely.

options.text: Activate the fire alarm
options.rationale: Second. Help is called once the client is out of danger.

questions.takeaway: RACE with a client in the room: rescue, alarm, confine, extinguish. Oxygen is shut off as part of confining the fire.
questions.coverage: Not in Lecture PPT. Covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Compare with a fire where no one is in danger. Here the client is beside the fire and cannot walk, so rescue applies.

steps.detail: The client is in the room and dependent.
The alarm brings help while you confine.
Only for a small fire with an exit behind you.

elimination.verdict: Rescue, alarm, confine, extinguish.

questions.stem: Before giving a medication, a nurse scans it and finds pharmacy stocked the wrong strength in the client's drawer. Nothing was given. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Return it to pharmacy and give the correct dose
options.rationale: Fixes this one dose, and the system problem stays hidden for the next nurse.

options.text: Give the correct dose and file an occurrence report
options.rationale: A near miss is a hazard. Reporting it lets the organization learn from it before a client is harmed.

options.text: Tell the charge nurse so the pharmacist is counseled
options.rationale: This aims at blame. A culture of safety looks at the process that let the error through.

options.text: Record the near miss in the client's chart
options.rationale: Nothing reached the client. Hazard reports go through the occurrence system, not the health record.

questions.takeaway: A culture of safety is blame-free and reports hazards and near misses, not only errors that cause harm.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Every option gets the client the right dose. Ask which one also protects the next client.

steps.action: Separate the client from the system
steps.detail: The client is safe once the right dose is given. The stocking problem remains.
Counseling one person does not fix a process.
Near misses go on an occurrence report, not in the chart.

elimination.verdict: Give the correct dose and report the near miss.

questions.stem: A confused client who was calm all morning now keeps trying to climb out of bed and tugs at her gown. She last voided six hours ago. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Turn on the bed alarm and lower the bed
options.rationale: Reasonable precautions that respond to the behavior without asking what is driving it.

options.text: Ask her daughter to come sit with her
options.rationale: Family presence is a good alternative, but it does not meet the need she has right now.

options.text: Move her to a room near the station
options.rationale: More observation, and the cause of the restlessness is still there.

options.text: Take her to the bathroom with help
options.rationale: New restlessness is treated as an unmet need. Six hours without voiding points to toileting.

questions.takeaway: Before any restraint or alarm, ask why. Pain, toileting, hunger, thirst and fear show up as unsafe behavior in a confused client.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: All four are restraint alternatives. The stem gives one detail that explains the behavior, so use it.

steps.detail: Calm this morning, restless now, six hours since she voided.
An alarm, a room move and a sitter watch the behavior.
Toileting addresses the likely cause and can be done now.

elimination.verdict: Take her to the bathroom. Treat the cause of the behavior first.

questions.stem: A nurse sees small flames in a linen cart in the hallway. The nearby clients are in their rooms with doors closed. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Move the nearest clients to another wing
options.rationale: Rescue comes first only when someone is in immediate danger. These clients are behind closed doors.

options.text: Close the remaining open doors on the unit
options.rationale: Confining follows the alarm.

options.text: Activate the fire alarm
options.rationale: No one needs rescue, so the next step is to get help coming.

options.text: Get the extinguisher and put out the flames
options.rationale: Tempting because the fire is small. Fighting it alone before the alarm risks losing control with no help on the way.

questions.takeaway: RACE: rescue, alarm, confine, extinguish. When no one is in immediate danger, the alarm is the first action.
questions.coverage: Not in Lecture PPT. Covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Check whether the rescue step applies. The closed doors tell you it does not, so move to the next letter.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: No client is near the flames.
It is the last step.
Alarm, then confine.

elimination.verdict: Activate the alarm.

questions.stem: A woman weak after a long illness has a fall plan that includes assisted walking. Which finding at the end of the shift indicates the plan is working?

options.text: Walked to the bathroom three times with staff
options.rationale: She moved, with the help the plan called for. That is safe mobility.

options.text: Used the bedpan all shift and had no falls
options.rationale: No falls, but she did not move. Immobility deepens the weakness that put her at risk.

options.text: Walked to the bathroom alone and did not fall
options.rationale: Tempting because nothing happened. She walked without the assistance the plan requires, so the risk was only lucky.

options.text: Called each time and waited in bed for staff
options.rationale: Calling is good. The finding does not show that she walked at all.

questions.takeaway: Fall prevention is safe mobility. Success is movement with the right help, and a shift in bed is not success.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: No option reports a fall. Ask which one shows both parts of the goal: moving and assisted.

steps.detail: Safe mobility, which means walking with assistance.

steps.action: Cut the options with no walking
steps.detail: Bedpan use and waiting in bed do not show movement.
Alone is outside the plan. With staff is the plan working.

elimination.verdict: Three assisted trips to the bathroom. Mobile and safe.

questions.scenario: A client has had bilateral soft wrist restraints for 2 hours after pulling out a central line. The nurse releases one wrist at a time for the scheduled check.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it shows the restraint care is effective or requires the nurse to act. Choose requires action for any finding that means the nurse must change the care, including removing the restraints.

rows.text: Fingers warm with brisk capillary refill
rows.rationale: Circulation is intact below the cuff.

rows.text: Reddened skin under the left cuff that does not blanch
rows.rationale: Early skin injury. The cuff needs padding or repositioning and the need is reassessed.

rows.text: Moves each wrist and elbow through full range when released
rows.rationale: Mobility is being maintained.

rows.text: Last offered fluids and the urinal 4 hours ago
rows.rationale: Hydration and elimination needs are overdue for a client who cannot meet them alone.

rows.text: More agitated and straining against the cuffs than at application
rows.rationale: Increased agitation is a restraint complication and raises the risk of injury from escape attempts.

rows.text: Calm, follows directions and leaves the new line alone during release
rows.rationale: The reason for the restraint is gone, so the nurse acts to have it removed as early as possible.

questions.takeaway: Each restraint check covers skin, circulation, range of motion, hydration, elimination, comfort and mental status, and asks whether the restraint is still needed.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: A good finding can still require action. A calm client who leaves the line alone means the restraint should come off.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Warm fingers and full range are fine. Nonblanching redness is injury.
Four hours without fluids or toileting is overdue.

steps.action: Check the need for the restraint
steps.detail: Worse agitation and a calm cooperative client both call for a change.

elimination.verdict: Effective, action, effective, action, action, action.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews how assistive personnel secured a client's wrist restraint. Which observation requires the nurse to intervene?

options.text: The strap is tied to the raised side rail
options.rationale: Moving the rail pulls the limb and can injure the client. Straps go on the bed frame.

options.text: The strap is secured with a quick-release tie
options.rationale: Correct. It allows fast removal in an emergency.

options.text: Two fingers fit under the cuff
options.rationale: Correct fit that protects circulation and skin.

options.text: The call light is placed in the client's hand
options.rationale: Correct. A restrained client must be able to call.

questions.takeaway: Restraint straps attach to the part of the bed frame that moves with the client, with a quick-release tie and two fingers of space.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: You are hunting the unsafe one. Picture the side rail being lowered with the strap attached.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the error.
Quick release, two fingers, call light.
The arm goes with it.

elimination.verdict: The strap tied to the side rail.

questions.stem: Assistive personnel report that a client on fall precautions seems much more unsteady walking than this morning. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Have assistive personnel check her blood pressure first
options.rationale: Vital signs are useful data, but judging a new change in gait cannot be handed back to the person who reported it.

options.text: Go assess the client's gait and condition
options.rationale: A new change was reported. Assessing fall risk and deciding what it means belong to the nurse.

options.text: Ask physical therapy to evaluate her gait today
options.rationale: A consult may follow. It comes after the nurse knows what has changed and why.

options.text: Notify the provider of the change in her gait
options.rationale: The nurse has nothing to report yet beyond a secondhand observation.

questions.takeaway: Assistive personnel report concerning behavior. Assessing fall risk, setting the plan and evaluating it stay with the nurse.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Three options pass the change to someone else. Ask who is responsible for assessing it first.

steps.detail: A secondhand report of a new change.
Assistive personnel, therapy and the provider all come after the nurse has looked.
Only one option has the nurse see the client.

elimination.verdict: Go assess her. A reported change needs the nurse's eyes before anyone is called.

questions.stem: A client in bed begins a tonic-clonic seizure, lying supine with gurgling secretions. The teeth are clenched. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Suction the mouth with an oral catheter
options.rationale: Aims at the airway, so it tempts. Nothing is forced between clenched teeth.

options.text: Note the time and page the provider
options.rationale: Timing matters and takes a glance. Leaving the airway to make a call does not protect him.

options.text: Turn the client onto his side
options.rationale: Lets secretions drain and keeps the airway clear without entering the mouth.

options.text: Pad the side rails with blankets
options.rationale: Protects from injury after the airway is secured.

questions.takeaway: In a seizure, airway comes first and it is protected by positioning. Nothing goes in the mouth.
questions.coverage: Not in Lecture PPT. Covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Two options address the airway. The clenched teeth rule one of them out.

steps.detail: Suction and side lying.
Suction through the mouth is out.
Timing and padding follow.

elimination.verdict: Turn him onto his side.

questions.stem: A client at high fall risk was taught to call before getting up. Which finding indicates the teaching was effective?

options.text: He says he understands why he should call
options.rationale: Stated understanding is not behavior.

options.text: He correctly repeats the steps for using the call light
options.rationale: Better, and tempting. It still shows knowledge and not use.

options.text: His wife says she will remind him to call
options.rationale: Family support helps. It does not show what he does.

options.text: He presses the call light and waits before standing
options.rationale: He used the device and waited, which is the outcome the teaching aimed for.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate safety teaching by what the client does. Have the client demonstrate call light use.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Line the options up from saying to doing. The strongest evidence is the behavior itself.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Calls and waits.
Understanding and repeating steps.
The wife's reminder.

elimination.verdict: He presses the light and waits.

questions.stem: A nurse cares for a client who is weak, at high fall risk and able to follow directions. Which tasks can the nurse assign to assistive personnel? Select all that apply.

options.text: Walk the client to the bathroom with a gait belt per the plan
options.rationale: Assisting with mobility according to the plan can be delegated.

options.text: Decide whether the client is ready to walk without the belt
options.rationale: Judging readiness is evaluation, which stays with the nurse.

options.text: Keep the floor dry and the path to the bathroom clear
options.rationale: Maintaining a safe environment can be delegated.

options.text: Offer toileting on the schedule the nurse set
options.rationale: Assisting with toileting on a set schedule can be delegated.

options.text: Report if the client tries to get up without calling
options.rationale: Reporting concerning behavior is expected of assistive personnel.

options.text: Complete the fall risk score after the new sedative is started
options.rationale: Fall risk assessment is the nurse's responsibility, especially after a change.

questions.takeaway: The nurse assesses, plans and evaluates. Assistive personnel assist with toileting and mobility, keep the environment safe and report.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Test each option for a judgment word such as decide or score. Doing and reporting can go; judging cannot.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Deciding readiness and scoring risk.
Walking, toileting and clearing the floor.
Telling the nurse about unsafe attempts.

elimination.verdict: A, C, D, E.

questions.stem: A client is found on the floor, alert, reporting severe hip pain. One leg is shorter and turned outward. A coworker offers to help lift him to bed. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Lift him to bed with the coworker, then assess
options.rationale: Comfortable and tempting. Moving a likely fracture before assessment can worsen the injury.

options.text: Keep him still on the floor and complete the injury assessment
options.rationale: The leg findings suggest a fracture, so he is not moved until he is assessed and can be moved safely.

options.text: Help him to a chair and take vital signs
options.rationale: Sitting him up puts weight and motion through the injured hip.

options.text: Leave the coworker with him and call the provider
options.rationale: Notification comes after the nurse has assessment findings to report.

questions.takeaway: After a fall, stay and assess for injury before moving the client. Signs of fracture mean he stays where he is.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: The shortened, rotated leg is the detail that decides it. Any option that moves him first is out.

steps.detail: Shorter and turned outward suggests a hip fracture.
Bed and chair both move the hip.
Assess, then notify.

elimination.verdict: Keep him still and assess.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old insists on walking to the bathroom alone at night as she does at home. She is steady by day but has new nighttime dizziness. Which plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Agree on a night light and staff help at night
options.rationale: It keeps her daytime independence, targets the one new limitation and is made with her.

options.text: Require staff assistance for all walking
options.rationale: More restriction than her risk calls for. She is steady by day.

options.text: Turn on the bed exit alarm at night
options.rationale: Tempting because it covers the risky hours. It is decided for her and only signals after she is already standing.

options.text: Place a commode at the bedside for night use
options.rationale: Shortens the trip, and she still stands up dizzy and alone in the dark.

questions.takeaway: See safety through the client's eyes: learn the home routine, separate normal abilities from new limitations and plan with the client.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Two options target the night. Pick the one she is part of and that puts a person beside her when she stands.

steps.detail: Dizziness at night only.
Assistance for all walking ignores that she is steady by day.
An alarm and a commode leave her standing alone. An agreed plan gives light and help.

elimination.verdict: Agree on a night light and staff help at night. Targeted and shared.

questions.stem: A client in wrist restraints for pulling at his tracheostomy has been quiet for an hour. He no longer pulls at the tube and does not open his eyes to his name. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Release one wrist as a trial of removal
options.rationale: Tempting because calm behavior is the cue to remove restraints early. This quiet is not calm; he is not responding, so the cause comes first.

options.text: Check his breathing and level of consciousness
options.rationale: He does not rouse to his name. Quiet with a drop in responsiveness is a change in mental status, and with a tracheostomy the airway is checked first.

options.text: Continue the restraints and recheck on schedule
options.rationale: Tempting because the pulling stopped. Waiting leaves an unresponsive client unassessed.

options.text: Ask the provider to discontinue the order
options.rationale: The right goal once he is calm and safe. It skips the finding that he will not open his eyes.

questions.takeaway: A restrained client who goes quiet is not automatically better. Mental status is part of every restraint check.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Ask what changed: the behavior stopped, and so did his response to his name. One is good news and one is not.

steps.detail: He no longer pulls, and he does not rouse.

steps.action: Cut the options that assume improvement
steps.detail: Trial release and discontinuing both treat this as calm.
A scheduled recheck leaves a new change unassessed.

elimination.verdict: Assess breathing and responsiveness first.

questions.stem: After report, the nurse has four clients. Which client does the nurse see first?

options.text: In a vest restraint, shouting that he needs the toilet
options.rationale: A real unmet need that should be answered soon, and the likely cause of his agitation. He is alert and voicing it, so he is not deteriorating.

options.text: Had a seizure ten minutes ago, sleepy and slow to answer
options.rationale: Looks alarming, and drowsiness after a seizure is expected. The client still answers when spoken to.

options.text: Fell an hour ago uninjured, now repeats the same question
options.rationale: New repetitive questioning after a fall is a change in mental status and suggests a head injury that the first check missed. It is the only unexpected finding.

options.text: Confused, sitting at the bed edge with assistive personnel beside her
options.rationale: A fall waiting to happen, which makes it tempting. Staff are at her side, so the risk is controlled for now.

questions.takeaway: After a fall, a new change in thinking outranks louder problems. Unexpected beats expected.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: All four need you. Ask which finding is new and not explained by what you already know about the client.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sleepiness after a seizure is the postictal state.
The confused client has staff beside her.
A toileting need is voiced by an alert client. Repeating questions after a fall is a new brain cue.

elimination.verdict: The client who fell and is now repeating the same question.

questions.stem: A client with delirium has pulled out two IV lines despite reorientation, a covered site and a sitter at the bedside. He is now gripping his chest tube. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Apply mitts and obtain a restraint order
options.rationale: Alternatives were tried and failed, and pulling a chest tube is immediate serious harm. Mitts are the least restrictive device that stops the grip.

options.text: Have the sitter reorient him more often
options.rationale: Least restrictive, which is usually the right rule. The stem shows it already failed twice and the harm is now immediate.

options.text: Request a sedative to calm him
options.rationale: Tempting as a quick fix. A drug given to control behavior is a chemical restraint and is more restrictive than mitts.

options.text: Move him to a room near the station
options.rationale: A reasonable alternative for observation. He already has a sitter within reach and still pulled lines.

questions.takeaway: Least restrictive means the least that works. When alternatives have failed and harm is immediate, a restraint is indicated.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Two rules compete: least restrictive and prevent immediate harm. Check whether the stem says alternatives were already tried.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Reorientation, covering the site and a sitter all failed.
A pulled chest tube is serious and immediate.

steps.action: Pick the least restrictive thing that works
steps.detail: Mitts restrict less than wrist ties or a sedative.

elimination.verdict: Mitts with an order.

questions.stem: After a client's night fall, a bed alarm and two-hour toileting rounds were added. Three nights later he has not fallen, and the alarm sounds five times nightly as he gets up to urinate. What does the nurse conclude?

options.text: The plan is effective and should continue
options.rationale: No falls looks like success. The alarm is catching him each time, so the cause of the falls is still there.

options.text: The toileting schedule is not meeting his urgency
options.rationale: He still gets up alone five times a night. The rounds are not matched to when he needs to go, so the risk is unchanged.

options.text: He needs a sitter at night to stay safe
options.rationale: A defensible safety step. It watches the behavior without fixing the urgency that drives it.

options.text: The alarm should be changed to a quieter setting
options.rationale: Sleep disruption is a real concern. It does nothing about the unsafe attempts.

questions.takeaway: No falls is not the same as no risk. Evaluate whether the intervention removed the cause.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Look past the outcome to the behavior. If the alarm is doing all the work, the targeted intervention is failing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Zero falls in three nights.
Five unassisted attempts each night to urinate.
Urgency was the target, and urgency is still getting him up.

elimination.verdict: The toileting schedule needs revising.

questions.stem: A tonic-clonic seizure has just ended. The client lies on his side, drowsy and confused, with noisy snoring breaths and an oxygen saturation of 96%. His wife asks the nurse to wake him. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Suction his mouth and throat right away
options.rationale: Noisy breathing points to the airway, so this tempts. He is side-lying with a saturation of 96%, so the airway is open and draining.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed and offer water
options.rationale: Comforting to the family. A drowsy client can aspirate.

options.text: Rouse him fully to check his orientation
options.rationale: Assessment sounds right. Confusion and sleep are expected now, and the airway data are already in hand.

options.text: Keep him side-lying and stay while he rests
options.rationale: Drowsiness and confusion are expected after a seizure. Side-lying protects the airway, and 96% shows it is working.

questions.takeaway: After a seizure, sleepiness is expected. Protect the airway by position, stay, and let the client recover.
questions.coverage: Not in Lecture PPT. Covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Airway comes first, so ask whether the airway is actually threatened. The saturation answers that.

steps.detail: Noisy breaths, side-lying, saturation 96%.
Drowsy and confused is the postictal state.
Water and sitting up are unsafe for a drowsy client.

elimination.verdict: Side-lying, stay with him, let him rest.

questions.stem: Assistive personnel diluting a disinfectant splashes it into both eyes and reports burning. An eyewash station is in the utility room next door. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Flush both eyes with water at the eyewash station
options.rationale: Correct. The chemical keeps injuring tissue until it is diluted, so flushing starts at once.

options.text: Look up the product on its safety data sheet
options.rationale: Tempting because the sheet gives the exact first aid. Reading it comes while the eyes are already being flushed, not before.

options.text: Send her to the emergency department for an eye exam
options.rationale: She may need this, but travel time without flushing lets the burn deepen.

options.text: Call poison control for instructions on the product
options.rationale: A reasonable resource, but the call delays the one step that limits injury.

questions.takeaway: Chemical in the eyes or on the skin: flush with water first. The safety data sheet, the exam and the report follow.
questions.coverage: Not in Lecture PPT. Covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: All four belong in the response. Ask which one stops the injury while the others only describe or record it.

steps.action: Ask what is still causing harm
steps.detail: The chemical is still in contact with the eyes.
Three options gather information or move her. One removes the chemical.

elimination.verdict: Flush the eyes first.

questions.nursesNote: 2100: 77-year-old admitted from home with pneumonia. Alert and oriented to person, place and time. Reports getting up to urinate four or five times each night. Wears bifocals, which were left at home. Walks with a shuffling gait and steadies herself on furniture. First dose of a sedating cough medicine given this evening. Demonstrates call light use correctly. Wearing nonslip socks.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that raise this client's risk of falling tonight.

segments.text: Alert and oriented to person, place and time
segments.rationale: Intact thinking lowers her risk. She can learn and use the call light.

segments.text: Reports getting up to urinate four or five times each night
segments.rationale: Urgency and frequency mean repeated trips in the dark, often in a hurry.

segments.text: Wears bifocals, which were left at home
segments.rationale: A sensory change with the aid unavailable. She will misjudge an unfamiliar room.

segments.text: Walks with a shuffling gait and steadies herself on furniture
segments.rationale: Altered gait. The hospital furniture she reaches for may roll.

segments.text: First dose of a sedating cough medicine given this evening
segments.rationale: A new medication effect that peaks during the night.

segments.text: Demonstrates call light use correctly
segments.rationale: A universal fall precaution already met.

segments.text: Wearing nonslip socks
segments.rationale: Safe footwear is protective.

questions.takeaway: Intrinsic fall risks are the client's own: weakness, dizziness, altered gait, confusion, sensory change, urgency and medication effects. Each one gets its own targeted intervention.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Separate what the client brings from what staff have already put in place. The precautions that are done are not risks.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Oriented, call light demonstrated, nonslip socks.
Nocturia, missing glasses, shuffling gait, new sedating drug.

elimination.verdict: Nocturia, no glasses, gait and the new medication.

questions.stem: A confused 83-year-old who can walk keeps scooting toward the foot of her bed. Assistive personnel raised all four side rails to keep her in. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Keep the rails up and round on her every 30 minutes
options.rationale: Rounding does not change that the rails are confining her.

options.text: Keep all four rails up and add a bed alarm
options.rationale: Tempting because an alarm is an alternative. With the rails still up she climbs over them and falls from a greater height.

options.text: Lower the bed and one rail and add a bed alarm
options.rationale: Correct. Rails raised to stop a client from getting out are a restraint. A low bed with an exit and an alarm is less restrictive and safer.

options.text: Request an order for a vest restraint overnight
options.rationale: Moves to more restriction before any alternative has been tried.

questions.takeaway: Side rails raised to keep a client in bed count as a restraint and invite injury from escape attempts. Use the least restrictive setup first.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Three options leave her confined or add confinement. One changes the setup so that getting up is less dangerous.

steps.action: Name what four rails are doing
steps.detail: They restrict her movement, so they are a restraint.

steps.action: Drop the options that keep or add restriction
steps.detail: Two keep the rails and one adds a vest.
Low bed, a way out and an alarm.

elimination.verdict: Lower the bed and a rail and use an alarm.

questions.stem: A provider writes for soft wrist restraints as needed for agitation. The client, who has delirium, is calm and has not touched his lines. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Keep the restraints at the bedside until he becomes agitated
options.rationale: Tempting because it seems to delay their use. It still accepts an order that lets anyone apply them later without a new assessment.

options.text: Apply them at night when fewer staff are available
options.rationale: Restraints are never used for staff convenience.

options.text: Have assistive personnel apply them if agitation begins
options.rationale: The decision to restrain needs the nurse's assessment at that moment.

options.text: Contact the provider to question the as-needed order
options.rationale: Correct. A restraint order answers a specific, current behavior and is time limited. It cannot be written as needed.

questions.takeaway: Restraints require a current assessment and a time-limited order for a specific behavior. An as-needed restraint order is not acceptable.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Look at what he is doing now. Nothing in the stem justifies a restraint, so the problem is the order itself.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Check for an immediate risk of harm
steps.detail: He is calm and leaving his lines alone.
Three options plan to use the order as written.
Question it with the provider.

elimination.verdict: Question the as-needed order.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old is found on the floor beside her bed, drowsy and confused, incontinent of urine, with a bitten tongue. No one saw her go down. Which cause does the nurse suspect?

options.text: An unwitnessed seizure
options.rationale: Correct. Drowsiness and confusion afterward, incontinence and a bitten tongue together point to a seizure.

options.text: A drop in blood pressure on standing
options.rationale: Explains going down. It does not explain the bitten tongue, and a faint clears quickly once she is flat.

options.text: A slip while hurrying to the toilet
options.rationale: Tempting because of the urine. A slip leaves her alert and does not injure the tongue.

options.text: Oversedation from a night medication
options.rationale: Fits the drowsiness alone and leaves the tongue and incontinence unexplained.

questions.takeaway: When a client is found down, look for a cause that explains every cue. A seizure changes the plan to airway protection and seizure precautions.
questions.coverage: Not in Lecture PPT. Covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Test each cause against all three findings. Only one accounts for the tongue.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Drowsy and confused, incontinent, bitten tongue.

steps.action: Check each cause against the list
steps.detail: Low pressure, a slip and sedation each explain one cue.

steps.action: Keep the cause that explains all three
steps.detail: Seizure.

elimination.verdict: An unwitnessed seizure.

questions.stem: A client is found sitting on the floor by his bed, uninjured, saying he slipped. The provider was notified and an occurrence report completed. Which entry does the nurse write in the chart?

options.text: "Client fell because he did not call for help as instructed."
options.rationale: States a cause and assigns blame. The chart records what was observed.

options.text: "Found sitting on floor by bed. States, 'I slipped.' No injury noted."
options.rationale: Correct. It gives what the nurse saw, what the client said and what the assessment found.

options.text: "Client fell at bedside. Occurrence report completed and sent to manager."
options.rationale: Tempting because the report was done. The occurrence report is a separate safety document and is not mentioned in the chart.

options.text: "Client slipped on a floor that housekeeping had left wet."
options.rationale: The nurse did not see the fall, and this blames another department.

questions.takeaway: Chart a fall with objective facts: what you found, the client's words, your assessment and who was notified. The occurrence report stays out of the chart.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Read each note for opinion, blame or mention of the report. One note has none of the three.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Two notes blame the client or housekeeping.

steps.action: Remove the note that cites the report
steps.detail: The report is filed separately.
Position, his words, the injury check.

elimination.verdict: The objective note with his own words.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old who uses a wheelchair after a stroke was taught to transfer from the chair to his bed. Which observation shows the teaching was effective?

options.text: Parks the chair close to the bed, then stands
options.rationale: Good placement, but an unlocked chair still rolls away as he pushes off.

options.text: Stands quickly so his legs do not tire
options.rationale: Speed adds to the risk of losing balance.

options.text: Asks his wife to hold the chair as he stands
options.rationale: Tempting because he is using help. A person cannot hold a chair as reliably as its brakes.

options.text: Locks both wheels before he starts to rise
options.rationale: Correct. Wheels are locked whenever the chair is stationary, and that is the step that keeps it under him.

questions.takeaway: Wheelchair wheels are locked whenever the chair is not moving. Check for that behavior before any transfer.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Ask what would make the chair move when he pushes off. Only one option prevents it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Find the hazard in a transfer
steps.detail: The chair rolling as he pushes up.
Close parking, speed and a helper leave the wheels free.

elimination.verdict: He locks both wheels first.

questions.stem: On his first hospital night, a 71-year-old who is oriented by day and takes only his usual medications is found in the hall, unsure where his bathroom is. He reorients quickly. Which factor best explains this?

options.text: Early dementia that was missed on admission
options.rationale: He is oriented by day and reorients at once, which does not fit a lasting cognitive change.

options.text: An adverse effect of a newly started medication
options.rationale: A common cause in the hospital, but the stem rules it out. He has no new drugs.

options.text: Unfamiliar surroundings and interrupted sleep
options.rationale: Correct. Waking in a strange room at night disorients a person who is fine at home. Orienting him to the room and lighting the way answer it.

options.text: Urinary urgency that made him hurry
options.rationale: Tempting since he was looking for the bathroom. Needing to void is normal. The hazard was not knowing the way.

questions.takeaway: Hospitalization itself raises injury risk: unfamiliar surroundings, changed routines and broken sleep. Familiarize the client with the room and the route to the bathroom.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Use the stem to cross off causes. It tells you his daytime thinking and his medication list for a reason.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Use oriented by day and reorients quickly
steps.detail: That removes dementia.
That removes a drug effect.
Urgency is ordinary. The new element is the place.

elimination.verdict: Unfamiliar surroundings and broken sleep.

questions.stem: The wife of a client who is weak and unsteady after surgery will stay overnight. Which statements by the wife show the fall teaching was effective? Select all that apply.

options.text: "He is at risk because his legs are weak right now."
options.rationale: She can state the reason for his risk, which is the first teaching point.

options.text: "I will press the call light before he gets out of bed."
options.rationale: She knows what help is needed and how to get it.

options.text: "I will keep his glasses and water where he can reach them."
options.rationale: Keeping possessions within reach removes a reason to lean or get up.

options.text: "I will tell the nurse if he seems more unsteady."
options.rationale: Family reports changes, and the nurse reassesses.

options.text: "I will put all the rails up so he stays in bed."
options.rationale: Rails used to keep him in are a restraint and lead to climbing injuries.

options.text: "I can walk him to the bathroom myself to save you a trip."
options.rationale: Well meant, but a client who is weak and unsteady walks with staff assistance. She calls for help instead of walking him alone.

questions.takeaway: Fall teaching for family: explain the reason for the risk, specify what help is needed, reinforce the safety measures and make the family part of the plan.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Judge each statement alone. The two wrong ones sound helpful, so ask whether each keeps him moving safely with trained help.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Keep statements that match the four teaching points
steps.detail: Reason, assistance, safety measures, family involvement.
All rails up.
Walking him alone.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D.

questions.stem: At 0200 a woman with dementia calls out over and over but stays in bed. A coworker suggests her as-needed lorazepam so the unit can settle. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Check her for pain, thirst or a need to void
options.rationale: The behavior is a message. Finding the unmet need comes before any drug or device.

options.text: Give the lorazepam at the lowest ordered dose
options.rationale: A sedative given to quiet her for the staff is a chemical restraint, and it raises her fall risk.

options.text: Move her bed to a room beside the station
options.rationale: A fair alternative for observation, but it does not answer why she is calling out.

options.text: Close her door so other clients can sleep
options.rationale: Helps the unit, leaves her need unmet and puts her out of sight.

questions.takeaway: A sedative given for staff convenience is a chemical restraint. Ask why the behavior is happening before you reach for it.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: The coworker's reason is the cue: 'so the unit can settle' is convenience, not client need.

steps.action: Read the reason for the drug
steps.detail: It is for the unit, not for her.
Moving her watches the behavior. Checking her needs explains it.
The stem reports no check for a cause yet.

elimination.verdict: Look for the unmet need first.

questions.stem: The daughter of an unsteady, forgetful 88-year-old asks for a vest restraint at night, as the nursing home used, so her mother cannot fall. Which response does the nurse give?

options.text: "I will ask the provider for an order tonight."
options.rationale: Family consent does not make routine fall prevention a reason for restraint.

options.text: "We will keep all four side rails up instead."
options.rationale: Rails used to keep her in are also a restraint, and climbing over them worsens a fall.

options.text: "Could you stay with her each night she is here?"
options.rationale: Family presence helps, but it cannot be the whole plan or be required of her.

options.text: "Restraints cause injuries. Let me show you what we use."
options.rationale: Restraints are not used for routine fall prevention. The nurse explains and offers the low bed, alarm and toileting rounds.

questions.takeaway: Restraints are never routine fall prevention, even when the family asks. Explain the harm and offer the alternatives.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Three options restrict her or shift the work to the daughter. One teaches and offers a plan.

steps.action: Test the request against the rule
steps.detail: Fall prevention alone is not an indication.
Four rails up is still a restraint.
Explaining and showing the plan answers her fear.

elimination.verdict: Explain the risk and show the alternatives.

questions.stem: A client with epilepsy walking in the hall stops and says she smells burning rubber and feels strange. The nearest chair is across the hall. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Walk her quickly back to her bed
options.rationale: A seizure may start within seconds. Walking her risks a fall from standing height.

options.text: Leave to bring a wheelchair from the alcove
options.rationale: She should not be left standing alone with a warning sign.

options.text: Help her lie down on the floor and cushion her head
options.rationale: The odd smell is an aura. Getting her down safely now prevents the fall and head injury.

options.text: Ask her to describe the smell in more detail
options.rationale: More description delays the one protective step.

questions.takeaway: An aura is a warning. Use those seconds to get the client down safely and protect the head.
questions.coverage: Not in Lecture PPT. Covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: The smell with no source, in a client with epilepsy, is the cue. Choose the option that removes the fall.

steps.detail: A smell that is not there is an aura.
There may be seconds, not minutes.
The floor cannot be fallen from.

elimination.verdict: Ease her to the floor and protect her head.

questions.stem: Twenty minutes after the morning medications, the nurse realizes she gave a client twice the prescribed dose of metoprolol. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Complete an occurrence report
options.rationale: Required, and it comes after the client is safe.

options.text: Tell the charge nurse what happened
options.rationale: Appropriate, but the client's status comes first.

options.text: Call the provider to report the medication error
options.rationale: The provider will ask for the pulse and blood pressure, so get them first.

options.text: Check the client's pulse and blood pressure
options.rationale: An error that reached the client is handled by assessing the client before anything else.

questions.takeaway: When an error reaches the client, assess the client first, then notify, then report. Reporting is for learning, not blame.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: All four happen. The question is order, and nothing has been assessed yet.

steps.detail: Three options protect the record or the team. One protects the client.
The provider needs the findings.
The occurrence report follows care.

elimination.verdict: Pulse and blood pressure first.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old woman who lives alone and fell twice this year was taught home safety before discharge. Which statement shows the teaching was effective?

options.text: "I will take up the hallway rugs and add a night light."
options.rationale: She removes a trip hazard and fixes poor lighting, two extrinsic risks she controls.

options.text: "I will hold on to the furniture as I go room to room."
options.rationale: Furniture walking is unstable support and a sign she needs a device.

options.text: "I will wear my soft slippers so I do not slip on tile."
options.rationale: Soft slippers give poor grip and support. Sturdy nonskid shoes are the safe choice.

options.text: "I will stay in my chair most of the day to be safe."
options.rationale: Inactivity weakens her and raises her fall risk.

questions.takeaway: Home fall prevention fixes the environment and keeps the person moving. It does not trade falls for immobility.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Ask which statement changes the house rather than limiting or propping up the person.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sitting all day weakens her.
Furniture and slippers are hazards.
Rugs and lighting.

elimination.verdict: Rugs up and a night light.

questions.stem: A clear liquid has leaked from an unlabeled bottle on a cleaning cart and is spreading across the hall. A client with a walker is approaching. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Wipe it up at once with bath towels
options.rationale: Prompt spill cleanup is right for water. An unknown chemical is not handled until it is identified.

options.text: Keep people away, then identify the liquid
options.rationale: Blocking the area removes the fall and the exposure. The safety data sheet then guides cleanup.

options.text: Pour water over it to dilute the liquid
options.rationale: Water spreads the spill and can react with some chemicals.

options.text: Call housekeeping and return to the station
options.rationale: Leaving the spill unguarded exposes the approaching client to a fall and to the chemical.

questions.takeaway: For a chemical spill, protect people first, then identify the substance and follow its safety data sheet.
questions.coverage: Not in Lecture PPT. Covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Wiping a spill promptly is a fall rule. The unlabeled bottle changes which rule applies.

steps.action: Find the detail that changes the rule
steps.detail: The bottle is unlabeled.
Keep the client away from the area.
The data sheet says how.

elimination.verdict: Block the area and identify the liquid.

questions.stem: A client scored low fall risk on admission yesterday. Since surgery he has received IV hydromorphone, an opioid, and has a urinary catheter and an IV pole. How does the nurse interpret the admission score?

options.text: It stands until the scheduled weekly reassessment is due
options.rationale: Scores are repeated when condition changes, not only on a calendar.

options.text: It still applies because he is alert and oriented
options.rationale: Orientation is one factor. Opioids and tethering equipment are others.

options.text: It no longer reflects his risk and needs repeating
options.rationale: New medication, a procedure and attached equipment each change fall risk.

options.text: It applies only after the catheter is removed
options.rationale: The catheter is one of the reasons his risk is higher now.

questions.takeaway: A fall risk score describes one moment. Reassess after surgery, new medications, a change in condition or a fall.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Count what is new since the score was taken.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Surgery, an opioid, a catheter, an IV pole.
Medication effects and equipment are both on the list.

steps.action: Decide if the score is current
steps.detail: It is not.

elimination.verdict: Repeat the assessment now.

questions.stem: The nurse checks the room of a client who walks steadily only with a walker. Which finding requires the nurse to act?

options.text: The bed is in its lowest position
options.rationale: This is a universal fall precaution, already correct.

options.text: He is wearing nonslip socks in bed
options.rationale: Appropriate footwear for getting up.

options.text: The overbed table holds his water and phone
options.rationale: Possessions within reach are a fall precaution.

options.text: His walker is folded against the far wall
options.rationale: He is steady only with the device. Out of reach, he will walk without it.

questions.takeaway: An assistive device the client cannot reach is an extrinsic fall risk. Keep it at the bedside.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Three findings are precautions in place. Look for the one that takes away what makes him steady.

steps.action: Check each against universal fall precautions
steps.detail: Low bed, footwear and possessions in reach all pass.
The walker.
Across the room.

elimination.verdict: Bring the walker to the bedside.

questions.stem: A 104 kg client who cannot assist must move from bed to a stretcher for a scan. Three staff are available. Which plan does the nurse choose?

options.text: Three staff lift him across together on the draw sheet
options.rationale: A manual lift of a dependent client this size injures staff and risks dropping him.

options.text: Use a lateral transfer device with the three staff
options.rationale: A slide board or air-assisted device removes the lifting. This protects client and staff.

options.text: Have him roll and scoot himself across
options.rationale: He cannot assist, so this will not work and risks a fall between surfaces.

options.text: Wait for two more staff to join the lift
options.rationale: More hands still means a manual lift. Equipment is the answer, not numbers.

questions.takeaway: Safe patient handling means equipment replaces manual lifting when the client cannot help.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Two options are the same manual lift with different head counts.

steps.detail: He cannot assist.
Three staff or five, it is still lifting.
A lateral transfer aid.

elimination.verdict: Lateral transfer device.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A client has had soft wrist restraints for 2 hours after pulling out his breathing tube, which was replaced. At this check the nurse releases [[1]].

While the limb is free, the nurse offers fluids and toileting and [[2]].

That evening his wife arrives and he settles while she holds his hand. She will stay for 3 hours. The nurse [[3]].

options.text: one wrist at a time
options.rationale: He stays protected while each limb is checked and moved.

options.text: both wrists together
options.rationale: Both hands free at once gives him the chance to pull the tube.

options.text: neither wrist while he is asleep
options.rationale: Checks and release happen on schedule whether or not he is asleep.

options.text: both wrists once a family member arrives
options.rationale: Release is not tied to visitors.

options.text: moves the joints through range of motion
options.rationale: Restraint causes loss of mobility. Range of motion and a skin and circulation check are part of every release.

options.text: reties the strap to the side rail
options.rationale: Straps go on the bed frame, which moves with him.

options.text: asks whether he promises to leave the tube alone
options.rationale: A promise is not an assessment of his behavior.

options.text: shortens the strap for a closer fit
options.rationale: A tighter restraint raises skin and nerve injury risk.

options.text: tries him without the restraints while she sits with him
options.rationale: Family presence is a restraint alternative. The nurse steps down to the least restrictive measure and keeps checking him.

options.text: keeps the restraints on because the tube is critical
options.rationale: The need is reassessed continually. A calm client with someone at the bedside may not need them.

options.text: lengthens both straps so he can reach his wife
options.rationale: Longer straps let him reach the tube while still restricting him.

options.text: asks her to untie him whenever he seems calm
options.rationale: Deciding when a restraint comes off is the nurse's assessment, not the family's.

questions.takeaway: Restraint care: release one limb at a time, do range of motion, offer fluids and toileting, and step down to an alternative such as family presence as soon as it is safe.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: In each blank, choose the least restriction that still keeps him safe.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: One limb at a time.
Movement, fluids and toileting.

steps.action: Step down when an alternative appears
steps.detail: His wife at the bedside lets the nurse try him without restraints.

elimination.verdict: One wrist at a time; range of motion; trial without restraints while his wife stays.

questions.scenario: A 78-year-old with heart failure is alert, oriented and steady when walking with staff by day. Furosemide, a diuretic, was scheduled at 2000 starting two nights ago. On both nights staff found her hurrying to the bathroom alone, and she says she could not wait.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 problem the client is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Toilet her at bedtime and on a set schedule overnight
options.rationale: Planned trips remove the rush that makes her go alone.

options.text: Ask the provider and pharmacist about an earlier dose time
options.rationale: A morning diuretic moves the urgency to hours when she is awake and staff are near.

options.text: Keep her on bed rest with a bedpan at night
options.rationale: Restricting mobility weakens her and does not stop the urge.

options.text: Request an indwelling urinary catheter
options.rationale: A catheter for convenience adds infection risk and a tether to trip on.

options.text: Fall risk from medication-related urinary urgency
options.rationale: The unsafe trips began with the evening diuretic and happen only at night.

options.text: Fall risk from confusion
options.rationale: She is alert and oriented and explains why she got up.

options.text: Fall risk from leg weakness
options.rationale: She walks steadily by day.

options.text: Fall risk from an unfamiliar room
options.rationale: She finds the bathroom. The problem is the rush.

options.text: Number of unassisted trips to the bathroom at night
options.rationale: This is the unsafe behavior the plan is meant to stop.

options.text: How often she voids overnight
options.rationale: Shows whether the dose time change moved the urgency.

options.text: Orientation to person, place and time
options.rationale: Not the factor driving her risk.

options.text: Grip strength in both hands
options.rationale: Unrelated to why she is getting up.

questions.takeaway: Match the fall intervention to the risk factor. Urgency from an evening diuretic is fixed with timing and scheduled toileting, not with restriction.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Ask what changed two nights ago. The answer names the problem and both actions.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The 2000 diuretic.
Bed rest and a catheter treat the staff's worry, not her urgency.

steps.action: Monitor the behavior and its cause
steps.detail: Unassisted trips and overnight voids.

elimination.verdict: Urgency from the diuretic; scheduled toileting and a dose time review; unassisted trips and overnight voiding.

questions.stem: Assistive personnel tell the nurse they found a 68-year-old on the floor beside his bed and helped him back into bed. He says he feels fine. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Notify the health care provider of the fall
options.rationale: The provider is notified after every fall, but the nurse has no findings to report yet.

options.text: Assess him for injury
options.rationale: No one has assessed him since the fall, and feeling fine does not rule out an injury. Assessment comes before every other step.

options.text: Complete the occurrence report
options.rationale: The report is required, but it comes after the client is assessed and the provider is told.

options.text: Ask the assistive personnel how he was lying when found
options.rationale: This is useful information about the fall, but it describes the event. His own condition has not been checked and comes first.

questions.takeaway: After a fall the order is assess for injury, notify the provider, then document and reassess the plan. Being moved back to bed does not replace the assessment.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Two options gather data. Choose the one about the client's condition now, because no one has checked him since the fall.

steps.detail: Only his statement that he feels fine. No injury assessment was done.
How he was lying explains the fall. Assessing him finds an injury that needs care now.

steps.action: Place the rest in the sequence
steps.detail: Notifying and reporting both follow the assessment.

elimination.verdict: Assess him for injury. Nothing can be reported until he is assessed.

questions.stem: At 1410 the nurse applies restraints in an emergency to a 45-year-old who is hitting staff. By what time must a provider assess the client in person?

options.rationale: A provider must assess a client restrained for violent behavior within 60 minutes of application.
Two hours is too late. The in-person assessment is due within 60 minutes.
Four hours is the length of an adult order for violent behavior. It is the wrong clock for the in-person assessment.

options.text: 1410 the next day
options.rationale: Twenty-four hours is the cap on renewals. The assessment cannot wait a day.

questions.takeaway: When restraints are applied for violent or self-destructive behavior, a provider assesses the client face to face within 60 minutes.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Two clocks start when the restraint goes on. Pick the one for the provider's in-person assessment, which is the short one.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Violent behavior, hitting staff.
The in-person assessment is due within 60 minutes.
1410 plus 60 minutes is 1510.

elimination.verdict: 1510. Sixty minutes for the face-to-face assessment.

questions.stem: Four clients were admitted this shift. Which client does the nurse identify as at greatest risk for a fall?

options.text: An 82-year-old who wears glasses and walks steadily
options.rationale: Tempting because she is the oldest, but the sensory change is corrected and the gait is steady.

options.text: A 50-year-old with an IV pole who walks steadily
options.rationale: Equipment is an extrinsic risk, but no intrinsic factor is added.

options.text: A 36-year-old on bed rest who calls for the bedpan
options.rationale: This client stays in bed and asks for help, so exposure is low.

options.text: A 61-year-old who is newly confused and has urinary urgency
options.rationale: Confusion leads to unsafe attempts to get up, and urgency makes the client rush to the bathroom. Two intrinsic factors act together in one client.

questions.takeaway: Count the risk factors in each client, not the years. Confusion plus urgency outweighs age with a steady gait.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Do not pick by age alone. Look for the client with more than one intrinsic risk factor and a reason to get up in a hurry.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The client on bed rest calls for help.
Glasses in place or an IV pole, each with a steady gait.
Confusion and urgency in the same client.

elimination.verdict: The newly confused client with urinary urgency.

questions.stem: A client in soft wrist restraints has a right hand that is cool and pale with a weak radial pulse. The left hand is warm and pink. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Release the right restraint
options.rationale: The findings show impaired circulation below the restraint. The assessment is complete, so the nurse removes the cause at once and stays with the client.

options.text: Notify the health care provider
options.rationale: The provider is told right away, but after the restraint is off. Calling first leaves the hand without blood flow.

options.text: Add padding under the right restraint
options.rationale: Padding protects skin. It does not restore circulation.

options.text: Recheck the right hand in 15 minutes
options.rationale: Waiting lets the injury progress when the cause is already clear.

questions.takeaway: Cool, pale skin and a weak pulse below a restraint mean neurovascular impairment: release it immediately, stay with the client, then notify the provider.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: The data are already complete, so this is an act item. Choose the action that removes the cause.

steps.detail: One hand cool, pale, weak pulse. The other normal.

steps.action: Ask if more data are needed
steps.detail: No. The comparison is done.
Release, then notify.

elimination.verdict: Release the right restraint first.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old walks steadily except for about an hour after his morning blood pressure medication, when he becomes dizzy on standing. Which plan does the nurse choose?

options.text: Keep him in bed through the morning with the rails up
options.rationale: Restricting him for hours treats a one hour problem with immobility, which weakens him.

options.text: Assist him with walking after the dose and ask the pharmacist about its timing
options.rationale: The risk is medication dizziness in a known window, so the plan is help during that window and a review of timing.

options.text: Turn on a bed alarm for the whole day
options.rationale: An alarm all day ignores that he is steady outside the hour after the dose.

options.text: Ask the provider to stop the medication
options.rationale: Tempting because the drug causes the dizziness, but timing and assistance are tried before giving up a needed treatment.

questions.takeaway: For medication dizziness the targeted plan is to monitor symptoms, adjust timing and assist with mobility, with the pharmacist involved.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Find when the risk happens. The best plan covers that window and leaves him free to move the rest of the day.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Dizzy for about an hour after the morning dose.
Bed all morning and an all-day alarm go beyond the window.
Stopping the drug skips the simpler fix of timing and help.

elimination.verdict: Assist after the dose and review timing with the pharmacist.

questions.stem: A client at high fall risk started a diuretic this morning. The nurse is working with assistive personnel. Which activity does the nurse keep?

options.text: Taking him to the bathroom on the toileting schedule
options.rationale: Assisting with toileting may be delegated.

options.text: Walking him in the hall as the plan directs
options.rationale: Assisting with mobility according to the plan may be delegated.

options.text: Keeping his room free of clutter and spills
options.rationale: Maintaining a safe environment may be delegated.

options.text: Deciding whether his prevention plan still fits
options.rationale: A new medication changes his risk. Assessing fall risk, determining the plan and evaluating it stay with the nurse.

questions.takeaway: The nurse assesses fall risk, determines the plan and evaluates it. Assistive personnel carry out toileting, mobility and a safe environment, and report concerns.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Three options carry out a plan. One judges the plan. The judging stays with the nurse.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Find the tasks that follow a plan
steps.detail: Toileting, walking and tidying are done as directed.

steps.action: Find the task that needs judgment
steps.detail: Deciding if the plan still fits after a new diuretic.
Assessment and evaluation are not delegated.

elimination.verdict: Deciding whether his prevention plan still fits.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old with a steady gait fell while leaning out of bed to reach her phone on the windowsill. She was not injured. Which change to her fall plan best fits this fall?

options.text: Add a bed alarm
options.rationale: An alarm signals that she is leaving the bed. She fell reaching from the bed, so the cause stays in place.

options.text: Schedule toileting every 2 hours
options.rationale: This targets urgency, and nothing in this fall involved the bathroom.

options.text: Keep her belongings within reach
options.rationale: The fall happened because she reached for an item placed too far away. Removing that cause is the targeted change.

options.text: Have staff walk with her on every trip
options.rationale: Tempting because it sounds safest, but her gait is steady and she did not fall while walking.

questions.takeaway: Reassess the plan after a fall by matching the change to what caused this fall, not by adding every precaution.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Name the cause of this fall in a few words, then pick the option that removes that cause.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Reaching for a phone that was out of reach.
