Alarm, toileting and walking help do not change where her things are.
A steady gait rules out walking assistance as the fix.

elimination.verdict: Keep her belongings within reach. It is the only option aimed at the cause.

questions.stem: A client was placed in wrist restraints 3 hours ago for pulling at his central line. Since then he has become more agitated and more confused. His hands are warm and pink. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Add ankle restraints to protect the line
options.rationale: More restriction is likely to worsen agitation that the restraint itself may be causing.

options.text: Continue the restraints, because agitation is the reason they were applied
options.rationale: Tempting, but the stem says the agitation and confusion grew after the restraints went on. That is a known harm of restraints, not proof they are needed.

options.text: Loosen both restraints and recheck him in an hour
options.rationale: His circulation is intact, so tightness is not the problem, and an hour of waiting leaves the cause in place.

options.text: Reassess the need for the restraints and try alternatives
options.rationale: Increased agitation and confusion are complications of restraints. The need is reassessed continually and the least restrictive option is used.

questions.takeaway: Restraints can cause the agitation and confusion they were meant to control. When a client worsens after application, reassess the need and use the least restrictive option.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Look at the timing in the stem. The behavior got worse after the restraints, so ask whether the restraints are the cause.

steps.detail: More agitated and confused since the restraints were applied.
Hands are warm and pink, so loosening does not address it.
More restraint feeds the problem. Reassessing and using alternatives addresses it.

elimination.verdict: Reassess the need for the restraints and try alternatives.

questions.stem: The fire alarm is sounding for a fire in the room next to a client on a mechanical ventilator. Which action does the nurse take for this client?

options.text: Close his door and stay with him until firefighters arrive
options.rationale: Closing doors contains a fire, but a client this close to it is at risk and needs to be moved.

options.text: Direct the walking clients to safety, then return for him
options.rationale: Walking clients can go by themselves. The client beside the fire who cannot move is the one who needs the nurse.

options.text: Ventilate him with a bag-valve-mask while moving him in his bed
options.rationale: A client near a fire is moved, and a client on life support is ventilated by hand until away from the fire.

options.text: Carry him to the hall with a coworker
options.rationale: Carrying is avoided. A bed, stretcher or wheelchair is used, and this leaves him without ventilation.

questions.takeaway: Clients close to a fire are moved regardless of its size. A client on life support is ventilated manually with a bag-valve-mask during the move.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Two needs compete: get away from the fire and keep breathing. Pick the option that meets both.

steps.detail: Next to the fire, so he must be moved.
He depends on the ventilator, so someone must ventilate by hand.
Bag-valve-mask while moving the bed.

elimination.verdict: Ventilate with a bag-valve-mask while moving him in his bed.

questions.stem: A 73-year-old at high fall risk has stayed in bed with an alarm for 4 days and has not fallen. Today her knees buckle when she stands with one staff member. What does the nurse conclude?

options.text: The plan is working and continues unchanged
options.rationale: No falls looks like success, but her new weakness shows the plan is causing harm.

options.text: She needs a sitter at the bedside
options.rationale: A sitter adds watching. It does not rebuild the strength she is losing.

options.text: Bed rest is weakening her, so assisted walking is added
options.rationale: Four days in bed followed by buckling knees means immobility has made her weaker. The goal is safe mobility.

options.text: She needs two staff for standing and fewer trips out of bed
options.rationale: Two staff for standing is reasonable, but fewer trips deepens the weakness that now raises her risk.

questions.takeaway: Zero falls does not prove a fall plan works. Fall prevention means safe mobility, and immobility worsens weakness.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Judge the plan by both outcomes in the stem: no falls, and legs that now buckle.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: No falls, but new weakness after 4 days in bed.
Staying in bed is the reason she is weaker.
Fewer trips out of bed adds more of the cause.

elimination.verdict: Bed rest is weakening her. Add assisted walking.

questions.stem: The nurse has timed a client's tonic-clonic seizure from its start. Which observation means the nurse calls for emergency treatment?

options.text: Jerking still continues 6 minutes after it began
options.rationale: A tonic-clonic seizure lasts about 1 to 3 minutes and no longer than 5. A prolonged seizure signals status epilepticus, a medical emergency.

options.text: He loses urine during the jerking
options.rationale: Incontinence is an expected part of a tonic-clonic seizure.

options.text: He cried out and stiffened at the start
options.rationale: A cry and stiffening are the expected opening of a tonic-clonic seizure.

options.text: He is drowsy and confused when jerking stops at 2 minutes
options.rationale: Two minutes is within the usual length, and confusion afterward is expected.

questions.takeaway: A tonic-clonic seizure lasts about 1 to 3 minutes and no longer than 5. Longer than that is treated as status epilepticus.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Sort expected from unexpected. The number on the watch is what separates an ordinary seizure from an emergency.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Cry, stiffening, incontinence and confusion afterward all belong to the seizure.
Two minutes is usual. Six minutes is past the 5 minute limit.

elimination.verdict: Jerking at 6 minutes. Past 5 minutes is an emergency.

questions.stem: A client has worn wrist restraints for 2 days for pulling at his endotracheal tube. The provider removed the tube this morning, and he is calm. The order runs until evening. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Keep the restraints on until the order ends
options.rationale: An order sets the longest time allowed. It does not require the restraint to stay on once the need is gone.

options.text: Remove the restraints and observe him
options.rationale: The tube he was pulling at is out and he is calm, so the reason for the restraint no longer exists. Restraints come off as early as possible.

options.text: Change to mitts as a less restrictive device
options.rationale: Tempting as least restrictive, but mitts are still a restraint and nothing remains for them to protect.

options.text: Release one wrist at a time every 2 hours
options.rationale: This is care for a restraint that is still needed.

questions.takeaway: Keep reassessing the need and remove restraints as early as possible. When the reason is gone, the restraint goes, whatever time is left on the order.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Ask why the restraint was applied, then check whether that reason still exists in the stem.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pulling at the endotracheal tube.
The tube is out and he is calm.
Waiting, mitts and timed release all keep him restrained.

elimination.verdict: Remove the restraints and observe him.

questions.stem: A client with delirium was toileted and given his analgesic 30 minutes ago. He is restless and picking at his IV dressing while the television plays and several visitors talk. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Apply hand mitts and request a restraint order
options.rationale: Restraints are for immediate harm when less restrictive options are not enough. No alternative has been tried for this behavior yet.

options.text: Turn off the television and ask one visitor to stay quietly
options.rationale: Excess stimulation is a cause of this behavior, and his toileting and pain needs were just met. Changing the environment and keeping a family presence are restraint alternatives.

options.text: Offer the urinal and another dose of analgesic
options.rationale: Unmet needs are checked first, but both were met 30 minutes ago. The stem points to the noise in the room.

options.text: Move him to a chair at the nurses' station for closer observation
options.rationale: Tempting because observation is a restraint alternative. The station adds more noise and activity, which is what is driving the behavior.

questions.takeaway: Before a restraint, ask why the behavior is happening: pain, toileting, hunger, thirst, delirium, medication effects, fear, excess stimulation or an unfamiliar environment. Match the alternative to the cause.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two options are restraint alternatives. Use the cause named in the stem to choose between less stimulation and more.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Rule out the needs already met
steps.detail: Toileted and medicated for pain 30 minutes ago.

steps.action: Name the cause left in the stem
steps.detail: Television and several visitors talking.
A quiet room with one visitor lowers stimulation. The nurses' station raises it.

elimination.verdict: Turn off the television and ask one visitor to stay quietly.

questions.stem: A client fell in the bathroom. The nurse stayed with her, called for help, found no injury, returned her to bed and notified the provider. Which actions complete the nurse's response? Select all that apply.

options.text: Document the fall and the assessment findings in her record
options.rationale: The event is documented in the record even when no injury is found.

options.text: Complete an occurrence report
options.rationale: A fall is reported through an occurrence report per agency policy.

options.text: Keep her on bed rest with all rails raised
options.rationale: She has no injury, and restricting her to bed weakens her. Rails raised to keep a client in act as a restraint.

options.text: Review the event with the team and revise her fall plan
options.rationale: A post-fall huddle asks what happened, what contributed and what needs to change.

options.text: Wait for the next scheduled assessment to rescore her fall risk
options.rationale: A fall is itself a reason to reassess the prevention plan now.

questions.takeaway: After a fall: call for help, stay, assess, notify the provider, follow policy, reassess the plan, document and complete the occurrence report, then huddle.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: The stem lists the steps already done. Check each option against the steps that remain, and reject any that restrict her or delay the review.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Stayed, called for help, assessed, returned to bed, notified the provider.
Document, report, review and revise the plan.
Bed rest with rails up, and waiting to rescore.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D.

questions.stem: Assistive personnel give the nurse four reports at the same time. Which client does the nurse go to first?

options.text: A confused client who is climbing out of bed without help
options.rationale: Confusion leads to unsafe attempts to get up, and this client is in the act of doing it. This is the only report with harm seconds away.

options.text: A client in wrist restraints who is shouting and pulling against them
options.rationale: Rising agitation in restraints needs the nurse soon, but this client is contained for the moment. The client climbing out of bed can fall in seconds.

options.text: A client who fell yesterday and wants medication for a bruised elbow
options.rationale: Pain after a known injury is expected and can wait briefly.

options.text: A weak client sitting in a chair who wants help back to bed
options.rationale: This client is seated and asking for help, so is safe for a few minutes.

questions.takeaway: Go first to the client whose harm is happening now. A worsening but contained problem is next, then comfort needs and requests.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Sort each report as about to cause injury now, worsening but contained, or able to wait.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Mark the requests that can wait
steps.detail: Pain from a bruise and a seated client asking for help.
The restrained client is agitated but held. The confused client is already leaving the bed.
A fall is seconds away.

elimination.verdict: The confused client climbing out of bed.

questions.stem: At a post-fall huddle, a staff member says the fall happened because assistive personnel were slow to answer the call light. Which response by the nurse leading the huddle is best?

options.text: "I will note in the client's chart who was assigned to that light."
options.rationale: The chart records the event and the client's condition. It is not used to assign fault.

options.text: "That needs to go to the manager before we continue."
options.rationale: This turns the review toward discipline and stops the team from finding causes.

options.text: "What made the light hard to answer then, and what should we change?"
options.rationale: A huddle asks what happened, what contributed, whether interventions were in place and what needs to change, in a blame-free way.

options.text: "Let us wait and review this when everyone is calmer."
options.rationale: A delay loses details. The huddle is held soon after the fall.

questions.takeaway: A post-fall huddle looks for contributing factors and what to change. A culture of safety is blame-free so that staff keep reporting hazards and errors.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Pick the response that keeps the review on causes and changes, not on a person.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Charting a name and sending it to the manager both assign fault.
Waiting loses information.
What contributed and what needs to change.

elimination.verdict: Ask what made the light hard to answer and what should change.

questions.stem: The nurse hears a thud and finds a 70-year-old on the bathroom floor, awake and trying to stand. The nurse is alone, and the bathroom call cord is within reach. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Help her up onto the toilet seat
options.rationale: She has not been assessed for injury, and one person lifting risks a second injury.

options.text: Go to the hall to find a second staff member
options.rationale: Help is needed, but leaving lets her keep trying to stand alone.

options.text: Leave to get the equipment for vital signs
options.rationale: Vital signs are part of the assessment, but leaving her alone on the floor comes at the cost of her safety.

options.text: Pull the call cord and stay beside her
options.rationale: The first steps after a fall are to call for assistance and stay with the client. The cord lets the nurse do both, then assess for injury.

questions.takeaway: When a client falls: call for assistance, stay with the client, assess for injury, then notify the provider. Do not leave and do not lift before assessing.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Two options bring help. Choose the one that brings help without leaving her.

steps.detail: Going to the hall and going for equipment.
She is not yet assessed for injury.
The call cord is within reach.

elimination.verdict: Pull the call cord and stay beside her.

questions.stem: The nurse enters the room of a client at high fall risk. He is standing unsteadily at the bedside in a puddle of urine with IV tubing looped around his ankle. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Wipe up the urine
options.rationale: The wet floor is a hazard, but he could fall while the nurse is cleaning.

options.text: Unloop the tubing from his ankle
options.rationale: The tubing only trips him if he steps, and bending to free it leaves him unsupported.

options.text: Press the call light and wait for help
options.rationale: Calling for help is right, but waiting without supporting him leaves him standing unsteadily.

options.text: Steady him and help him sit on the bed
options.rationale: He is unsteady now. Sitting him down removes the immediate risk, then the floor and tubing are dealt with.

questions.takeaway: When several hazards are present, secure the client first, then fix the environment.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Ask which hazard can hurt him in the next few seconds. It is his unsteady standing, not the floor or the tubing.

steps.detail: Unsteady standing, wet floor, tubing at the ankle.
He is already unsteady on his feet.
Seat him, then call for help, clear the tubing and the floor.

elimination.verdict: Steady him and help him sit on the bed.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old one day after surgery sits unsupported at the bedside and shakes the nurse's hand across midline. She cannot straighten either knee. Which plan does the nurse choose for moving her to the chair?

options.text: Stand her with a gait belt and a walker
options.rationale: Tempting because she sits so well. Legs that cannot extend at the knee will not hold her in standing.

options.text: Use a mechanical lift for the transfer
options.rationale: She passed sitting balance and failed leg strength, so she cannot help stand. Equipment does the lifting.

options.text: Have two assistive personnel pivot her to the chair
options.rationale: More hands still means lifting her weight, which injures staff and can drop her.

options.text: Keep her in bed until her legs are stronger
options.rationale: Safe today, and it adds a day of immobility she does not need. She can sit, so she can be up in a chair.

questions.takeaway: Each bedside mobility test she fails sets the equipment. Good sitting balance with no leg strength means a lift, not a walker and not bed rest.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Two options feel safe: the lift and staying in bed. The stem says she can sit, so she can be up in a chair; it also says her knees will not extend, so she cannot stand.

steps.detail: Knees will not straighten, so standing options are out.
Two people lifting is not safe handling.
She can sit, so the chair is still the goal.

elimination.verdict: Mechanical lift. Out of bed, without asking her legs to do what they cannot.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old on bed rest for 9 days walks in the hall for the first time. Which findings mean the nurse stops the walk and sits him down? Select all that apply.

options.text: He says the hallway is starting to spin
options.rationale: Dizziness during activity signals poor brain perfusion and a fall about to happen.

options.text: His face is pale and wet with sweat
options.rationale: Diaphoresis and pallor show the heart is not keeping up with the demand.

options.text: Heart rate rises from 76 to 92
options.rationale: A modest rise is the expected response to walking.

options.text: He reports new pressure in his chest
options.rationale: Chest pain with exertion means the heart muscle is short of oxygen. Stop the demand.

options.text: Respirations rise from 16 to 20 with easy speech
options.rationale: A small rise with comfortable talking is normal exertion, not dyspnea.

options.text: He says his legs feel a little tired
options.rationale: Mild fatigue after 9 days in bed is expected. Shorten the distance, but it is not a stop sign.

questions.takeaway: Activity tolerance is judged by the response. Dizziness, diaphoresis, chest pain and dyspnea end the walk. A modest rise in rate that recovers does not.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Sort each finding into the body working harder, which is expected, or the body failing to keep up.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Small rises in heart rate and breathing with easy speech, plus mild leg fatigue.
Spinning, pale and sweaty, chest pressure.

elimination.verdict: Dizziness, diaphoresis and chest pressure stop the walk.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with left leg weakness is taught to walk with a straight cane. Which observation shows the teaching was effective?

options.text: Cane in the right hand, moved forward before the left leg
options.rationale: The cane goes on the strong side and leads, so it shares the load when the weak leg steps.

options.text: Cane in the left hand, moved forward with the left leg
options.rationale: Feels natural to put support beside the weak leg, but it shifts weight toward that side and narrows the base.

options.text: Cane in the right hand, moved forward after the right leg
options.rationale: Right side is correct, but stepping strong leg first leaves the weak leg bearing weight alone.

options.text: Cane in the left hand, kept a full stride ahead
options.rationale: Wrong side, and a long reach pulls him off balance.

questions.takeaway: Cane on the stronger side. Cane, then weak leg, then strong leg, so two points of support stay on the floor.
questions.coverage: Not in Lecture PPT. Covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Two things have to be right: which hand and which order. Check the hand against the stem first, then the order.

steps.detail: Weak leg is the left, so the cane is in the right hand. Two options drop out.
The cane must be down before the weak leg takes weight.

elimination.verdict: Right hand, cane first, then the left leg.

questions.stem: A nurse walks a patient with a gait belt. Ten feet from the nearest chair his knees buckle and he starts to go down. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Hold him upright by the belt and call for help
options.rationale: She cannot hold his full weight. Both of them are injured this way.

options.text: Support him under the arm and hurry to the chair
options.rationale: Ten feet is too far for a patient whose knees have already given way, and pulling on an arm can injure the shoulder.

options.text: Widen her stance and ease him to the floor
options.rationale: A wide base keeps her stable, and a controlled slide protects his head and her back.

options.text: Brace him against the wall until a wheelchair arrives
options.rationale: Tempting because it avoids the floor. He cannot bear weight, so he will slide down the wall uncontrolled.

questions.takeaway: Once a patient is going down, you do not stop the fall. You guide it: wide base, slide him down your leg, protect the head.
questions.coverage: Not in Lecture PPT. Covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Three options try to keep him upright. Ask whether that is possible once the knees have buckled.

steps.detail: Knees buckled and he is already going down.

steps.action: Cut the options that fight the fall
steps.detail: Holding, hurrying and bracing all depend on legs that have failed.
Only one option accepts the fall and makes it safe.

elimination.verdict: Wide stance, ease him to the floor. Guide the fall.

questions.stem: A thin patient kept with the head of the bed at 60 degrees slides down the bed each hour, and staff drag him back up by the arms. Which change addresses the cause of his skin risk?

options.text: Float both heels on a pillow
options.rationale: Good heel care. The damage here comes from sliding and dragging at the sacrum.

options.text: Massage the sacrum after each move
options.rationale: Rubbing skin that is already stressed adds friction and can injure the tissue.

options.text: Turn him side to side every two hours
options.rationale: Tempting because turning is standard care. It relieves pressure and leaves the sliding and dragging unchanged.

options.text: Lift him with a draw sheet, knees slightly flexed
options.rationale: Lifting removes friction, and flexed knees keep him from sliding, which is what causes shear.

questions.takeaway: Pressure, friction and shear are separate threats. Sliding down is shear and dragging is friction, so lift the patient and stop the slide.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Name the force in the stem before picking the fix. Sliding and dragging are not the same problem as lying still.

steps.detail: Sliding down the bed is shear. Being dragged up is friction.
Massage rubs skin that is already at risk.

steps.action: Separate pressure care from the cause
steps.detail: Heel floating and turning treat pressure. Only the lift with flexed knees stops the slide and the drag.

elimination.verdict: Draw sheet lift with knees slightly flexed. Remove the friction and the shear.

questions.stem: A patient with right-sided weakness after a stroke can lift her right arm halfway to shoulder height but no farther. Which exercise plan fits her right shoulder?

options.text: She lifts as far as she can, then the nurse completes the range
options.rationale: Active-assistive range of motion uses the muscle she has and still takes the joint through its full range.

options.text: The nurse moves the arm through the full range while she relaxes
options.rationale: Protects the joint, and tempting because the arm is weak. It leaves the strength she has unused, and unused muscle weakens.

options.text: She lifts the arm halfway ten times each hour on her own
options.rationale: Keeps the muscle working, but the top half of the range is never reached and will stiffen.

options.text: She presses the arm against the mattress and holds
options.rationale: Isometric work builds static strength without moving the joint, so range is not maintained.

questions.takeaway: Match range of motion to what the patient can do: active if she can do it all, active-assistive if partway, passive only if not at all.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Passive and active-assistive both protect the joint. Halfway on her own is the detail that says use her muscle.

steps.detail: Half the range, actively.

steps.action: Cut options that skip full range
steps.detail: Halfway only, and isometric holds.
Only one keeps both the muscle and the joint.

elimination.verdict: She moves it, the nurse finishes it.

questions.stem: A patient on bed rest for a week had fluids increased and now uses a bedside commode in place of the bedpan. Which finding shows these measures are working?

options.text: Bowel sounds are heard in all four quadrants
options.rationale: Sounds can be present while stool sits hard in the colon, so this does not show the outcome.

options.text: Small liquid stools pass several times a day
options.rationale: Tempting because stool is moving. Frequent liquid leakage after immobility can be seepage around hard stool.

options.text: A soft formed stool passes every day or two
options.rationale: The measures aimed at slowed motility. Regular soft stool is the outcome itself.

options.text: He drinks every glass of water offered
options.rationale: That shows the intervention was done. It does not show the result.

questions.takeaway: Immobility slows the bowel. Judge fluids and upright toileting by regular, soft, formed stool.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Separate what was done from what changed in the patient, then check that the change is the healthy one.

steps.detail: Decreased motility and constipation from immobility.
Drinking the water is the intervention.
Liquid leakage can mean hard stool higher up. Soft formed stool is the goal.

elimination.verdict: Soft formed stool every day or two. The bowel is moving normally.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old in a long leg cast for 6 weeks wants to keep his thigh strong. The knee cannot bend inside the cast. Which exercise does the nurse teach?

options.text: Passive hip range of motion twice a day
options.rationale: Passive movement keeps a joint flexible. It does not make a muscle work.

options.text: Tighten the thigh, hold, then relax
options.rationale: An isometric contraction works the muscle without moving the joint, which is safe around a healing limb.

options.text: Leg lifts with a weight on the other leg
options.rationale: Isotonic work for the wrong thigh.

options.text: Wiggle the toes of the casted leg hourly
options.rationale: Useful for circulation checks and it does not load the thigh.

questions.takeaway: Isotonic exercise moves the joint. Isometric exercise contracts the muscle with no joint movement, so it fits a casted or painful joint.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy and Potter).
questions.strategy: Two conditions have to be met: the thigh muscle works and the knee stays still.

steps.detail: Thigh contraction, no knee movement.
Toe movement and the other leg do not work this thigh.
Passive motion does not build or keep strength.

elimination.verdict: Tighten, hold, relax. Strength without joint movement.

questions.scenario: A 79-year-old woman is admitted for a urinary tract infection. The nurse completes a musculoskeletal assessment and compares both sides.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is expected with aging or requires follow-up.

rows.text: Lost 1.5 inches of height over 10 years
rows.rationale: Gradual bone loss and disk thinning shorten the spine slowly.

rows.text: Walks more slowly than she did at 60
rows.rationale: Movement slows as muscle mass declines.

rows.text: Right knee swollen and warm since yesterday
rows.rationale: One-sided, new and inflamed. Aging is gradual and symmetric.

rows.text: Both shoulders reach slightly less overhead
rows.rationale: Cartilage is less elastic, so range drops on both sides equally.

rows.text: Left foot has dragged for the past 3 days
rows.rationale: New one-sided loss of movement points to nerve injury or stroke.

rows.text: Thighs slightly thinner on both sides
rows.rationale: Muscle tissue atrophies with age. Symmetry is the reassuring detail.

questions.takeaway: Aging changes are gradual and equal on both sides. Sudden or one-sided findings are not aging.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Ask two questions of each row: did it come on slowly, and is it the same on both sides? Two yes answers mean aging.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Yesterday and 3 days are sudden. Ten years is gradual.
Right knee and left foot are one-sided.

elimination.verdict: The swollen knee and the dragging foot need follow-up. The rest is aging.

questions.stem: A patient straightens each knee at the bedside, then lifts his buttocks off the bed but drops back after 2 seconds. He needs the bathroom. Which plan does the nurse choose?

options.text: Walk him with a walker and standby assist
options.rationale: A walker helps balance. It does not supply the leg strength he just showed he lacks.

options.text: Walk him with a gait belt and one staff member
options.rationale: A gait belt steadies a patient who can stand; it cannot hold him up.

options.text: Offer a urinal in bed until he can stand longer
options.rationale: Safe, and tempting after a failed stand. It skips the weight bearing he can do and adds immobility.

options.text: Use a sit-to-stand lift to take him to the toilet
options.rationale: He has some leg strength but could not hold the stand; he dropped back after 2 seconds. The lift lets him bear weight safely.

questions.takeaway: A patient who can start a stand but not hold it is moderate assist. Use equipment that lets him use his legs without relying on them.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: The urinal and the lift are both safe. He has usable leg strength, so pick the safe option that keeps him moving.

steps.detail: He could not hold the stand past 2 seconds, so walking is out.
Both prevent a fall. Only one preserves function.

elimination.verdict: Sit-to-stand lift.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old who cannot bear weight on the left foot is taught to use axillary crutches. Which observation shows the teaching was effective?

options.text: Crutch pads sit snug in the axillae as he swings through
options.rationale: Feels stable, and it puts body weight on the axillary nerves.

options.text: Weight rests on his hands with a gap below each axilla
options.rationale: Hands carry the weight. Space under the arm keeps pressure off the nerves in the axilla.

options.text: Elbows stay locked straight while he bears down
options.rationale: A slight bend lets the arms absorb load. Locked elbows mean the crutches are too short or the grips too low.

options.text: Crutch tips land directly beside his toes
options.rationale: Tips belong ahead and to the side to form a wide tripod base.

questions.takeaway: With axillary crutches the hands bear the weight, never the armpits.
questions.coverage: Not in Lecture PPT. Covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: The snug option sounds secure. Ask where his weight is going in each picture.

steps.detail: Snug in the axilla versus a gap below it.
Axilla pressure injures nerves. Hands are built for it.

elimination.verdict: Weight on the hands with a gap under the arms.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old who takes insulin for diabetes plans to start brisk 40-minute walks after work. Which instruction does the nurse include?

options.text: Check glucose first and carry glucose tablets
options.rationale: Exercise lowers glucose. A check before and a fast carbohydrate on hand make the walk safe.

options.text: Lower the insulin dose himself on walking days
options.rationale: Dose changes come from the provider. Self-adjusting risks both high and low glucose.

options.text: Inject into the thigh so the insulin lasts the walk
options.rationale: A working muscle absorbs insulin faster, which raises the risk of a low during the walk.

options.text: Eat a larger dinner afterward to replace calories
options.rationale: This comes after the risk has passed. The low happens during or soon after the walk.

questions.takeaway: Chronic illness changes the exercise plan; it does not remove it. For insulin users the change is glucose checks and a carbohydrate on hand.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Ask when the danger occurs. The instruction has to protect him during the walk.

steps.detail: Hypoglycemia during exercise.

steps.action: Cut what is outside his role
steps.detail: Changing the dose is the provider's decision.
A thigh injection speeds absorption and dinner comes too late.

elimination.verdict: Check first and carry glucose tablets.

questions.stem: A patient with diabetic neuropathy has full leg strength. He stands steady with eyes open and sways badly with eyes closed. The findings are most consistent with which problem?

options.text: Weakness of the leg muscles
options.rationale: Strength was tested and is full.

options.text: A drop in blood pressure on standing
options.rationale: That would cause dizziness with eyes open as well.

options.text: Stiffness of the ankle joints
options.rationale: Stiff joints limit range. They do not change with eye closure.

options.text: Loss of position sense in the feet
options.rationale: Steady with vision and unsteady without it means his eyes were covering for missing proprioception.

questions.takeaway: Balance needs muscle, joint and nerve input. When closing the eyes unmasks sway, the missing piece is proprioception, so the plan is lighting and visual cues.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Find the detail that changes: only the eyes. Pick the cause that vision could compensate for.

steps.detail: Full strength rules out weakness.
Blood pressure and stiff ankles would not care whether he can see.

elimination.verdict: Loss of position sense.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old on bed rest for 3 weeks eats about a third of each meal and his thighs look thinner. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Weigh him weekly and continue the diet
options.rationale: Monitoring is useful, and it watches the loss without acting on it.

options.text: Add passive range of motion to both legs
options.rationale: Tempting because the muscle is wasting. Passive motion keeps joints flexible and does not build muscle or supply protein.

options.text: Offer small, frequent high-protein meals
options.rationale: Immobility breaks down protein while appetite falls. Small, frequent protein-rich meals fit both problems.

options.text: Encourage three larger meals each day
options.rationale: His appetite is low, so bigger portions mean more food left on the tray.

questions.takeaway: Immobility causes negative nitrogen balance, loss of lean muscle and poor appetite. Answer with protein in amounts the patient can finish.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides.
questions.strategy: Two cues are given: he eats little and he is losing muscle. Pick the option that answers both.

steps.detail: Muscle loss with low intake during immobility.

steps.action: Cut the option that only watches
steps.detail: Weekly weights change nothing.
Larger meals ignore the poor appetite. Small, frequent ones work with it.
Passive motion does not make a muscle work.

elimination.verdict: Small, frequent high-protein meals. Replace what immobility breaks down.

questions.stem: An unresponsive patient receives passive range of motion to both elbows three times a day. Which finding after 2 weeks shows the exercise is effective?

options.text: Upper arm muscles look fuller than before
options.rationale: Tempting as a sign of progress. Passive motion does not contract muscle, so it cannot build bulk.

options.text: Both elbows extend fully without resistance
options.rationale: Passive motion exists to keep joints mobile and prevent contracture. Full, easy range is the goal met.

options.text: Skin over both elbows is intact
options.rationale: Reflects turning and pressure relief, not joint exercise.

options.text: He withdraws his arms when they are moved
options.rationale: A change in responsiveness, and possibly a sign of pain. It does not measure joint mobility.

questions.takeaway: Passive range of motion maintains joints. It does not build strength. Evaluate it by range, not by muscle.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Ask what the intervention can do. A nurse moving the arm cannot make the muscle grow.

steps.detail: Flexible joints, no contracture.

steps.action: Cut what belongs to other interventions
steps.detail: Skin and responsiveness.
Only range is in passive motion's reach.

elimination.verdict: Full extension without resistance.

questions.stem: The nurse rechecks a patient whom assistive personnel just placed in Fowler's position. Which finding requires correction?

options.text: A small pillow supports the lower back
options.rationale: This keeps the normal lumbar curve.

options.text: Forearms rest on pillows at his sides
options.rationale: Supported arms prevent pull on the shoulders.

options.text: Knees are slightly flexed on a low support
options.rationale: Fowler's support allows flexion at the hips and knees.

options.text: A thick pillow pushes his chin to his chest
options.rationale: Neck flexion breaks cervical alignment and, held for hours, leads to a flexion contracture.

questions.takeaway: After repositioning, reassess alignment. Supports should keep the normal cervical, thoracic and lumbar curves.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: This asks for the one problem. Test each support against normal spinal alignment.

steps.detail: You are looking for the wrong finding.
Lumbar support, arm support and knee flexion all fit Fowler's.
Chin toward the chest is cervical flexion.

elimination.verdict: The thick pillow. Replace it with one that keeps the neck neutral.

questions.stem: During passive range of motion, the nurse feels the patient's shoulder resist at 90 degrees of abduction and the patient grimaces. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Stop at that point and return the arm to rest
options.rationale: Range of motion goes to resistance or pain and no farther. The limit is noted and compared with the other side.

options.text: Hold a gentle stretch just past the resistance
options.rationale: Tempting as a way to regain range. Moving past resistance with pain can injure the joint.

options.text: Skip the shoulder for the rest of the week
options.rationale: Leaving the joint unmoved lets it stiffen further.

options.text: Apply a warm pack, then continue to full range
options.rationale: Warmth does not change the rule. Full range is not forced through pain.

questions.takeaway: Range of motion goes to the point of resistance or pain and no farther. Note the limit and compare with the other side.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides.
questions.strategy: Two options push past the limit and one abandons the joint. Look for the option that respects the limit and keeps the joint moving.

steps.detail: Resistance and a grimace mark the limit.
Stretching beyond and continuing to full range.
Skipping the joint for a week invites stiffness.

elimination.verdict: Stop at the limit and return to rest.

questions.stem: A patient immobile after a stroke has a weak cough with coarse crackles, a heel that stays red when pressed and no bowel movement in 4 days. Which problem does the nurse address first?

options.text: The nonblanching heel
options.rationale: An actual injury and the strong runner-up. It is offloaded next, but it does not threaten oxygenation.

options.text: Constipation
options.rationale: Real and uncomfortable. It can wait behind lungs and skin.

options.text: Retained secretions
options.rationale: Secretions the patient cannot clear lead to atelectasis and pneumonia. Breathing outranks skin.

options.text: Risk for contracture
options.rationale: A potential problem, behind the actual ones.

questions.takeaway: When several immobility effects are present at once, rank them by airway and breathing first, then actual tissue injury, then the rest.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The heel and the lungs are both actual problems. Breathing breaks the tie.

steps.detail: Contracture has not happened.
Constipation.
Lungs before skin.

elimination.verdict: Retained secretions.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old on bed rest for 8 days will walk for the first time. Place the nurse's actions in order.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed, then sit her at the bedside to dangle
options.rationale: Second. A staged position change lets her circulation adjust.

options.text: Apply a gait belt and stand her at the bedside
options.rationale: Fourth. She stands only after sitting is tolerated, with the belt on.

options.text: Check her baseline blood pressure and pulse lying down
options.rationale: First. You need a baseline to judge what happens when she sits.

options.text: Walk a short distance with a chair close by
options.rationale: Last. Distance comes after she has passed sitting and standing.

options.text: Ask about dizziness and recheck blood pressure while she sits
options.rationale: Third. This is the checkpoint that decides whether she goes on.

questions.takeaway: First time up after bed rest is staged: baseline, sit and dangle, reassess, stand, then walk.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: After bed rest the pressure can drop on sitting up. Put a check before and after the first position change.

steps.detail: Lying vital signs come before any movement.
Sit, then stand, then walk.
Symptoms and pressure are rechecked while sitting, before standing.

elimination.verdict: Baseline, dangle, reassess, stand with belt, walk.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman whose bone density scan shows low bone mass is taught about exercise. Which statement shows she understood?

options.text: "I will swim laps every morning for my bones."
options.rationale: Good for the heart and joints. Water carries her weight, so bone is not loaded.

options.text: "I will walk briskly for 30 minutes most days."
options.rationale: Walking is weight bearing. Loading the skeleton is what maintains bone.

options.text: "I will do seated stretches each day for my bones."
options.rationale: Stretching helps flexibility. Seated, it puts no load on the long bones.

options.text: "I will ride my stationary bike in place of walking."
options.rationale: The seat carries her weight, so it does little for bone.

questions.takeaway: Bone is kept by loading it. For low bone mass the exercise has to be weight bearing.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy and Potter).
questions.strategy: All four are exercise. Ask in which one her skeleton carries her own weight.

steps.detail: Maintain bone density.
Is she holding up her own weight?
Water, a chair and a bike seat all carry the load for her.

elimination.verdict: Brisk walking. Weight bearing keeps bone.

questions.stem: On day 5 of bed rest a client breathes shallowly with a temperature of 37.9 C and oxygen saturation of 95%. Crackles at both bases clear after he coughs. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Request a sputum culture and antibiotics
options.rationale: Tempting with a temperature. Crackles that clear with coughing point to collapsed air sacs reopening, not infection yet.

options.text: Give acetaminophen and recheck the temperature
options.rationale: Treats the number and leaves the shallow breathing that caused it.

options.text: Apply oxygen by nasal cannula
options.rationale: His saturation is adequate. Oxygen does not reopen the bases.

options.text: Increase deep breathing, coughing and upright time
options.rationale: Shallow breathing in bed causes atelectasis. Lung expansion and position reverse it before pneumonia develops.

questions.takeaway: Immobility lowers lung expansion and leads to atelectasis. Early signs are answered with deep breathing, coughing, sitting upright and movement.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Use the one finding that separates the two explanations: the crackles clear when he coughs.

steps.detail: Crackles that clear with a cough mean the bases reopen.
Acetaminophen and oxygen do not expand the lungs.
Antibiotics fit an infection. These findings fit atelectasis, which nursing measures reverse.

elimination.verdict: Deep breathing, coughing and more time upright. Expand the lungs now.

questions.stem: A client on bed rest for 2 weeks has dark, strong-smelling urine and drank 900 mL yesterday. He has no fever, burning or flank pain. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Request a urine culture from the provider
options.rationale: Tempting because stasis raises infection risk. He has no fever or burning, and the low intake explains the urine.

options.text: Request a urinary catheter to keep the bladder empty
options.rationale: A catheter adds infection risk, and nothing in the stem shows a problem emptying the bladder.

options.text: Increase fluids through the day and recheck the urine
options.rationale: Concentrated urine with low intake calls for hydration, which also flushes the stasis that leads to infection and stones.

options.text: Record the urine as expected with bed rest
options.rationale: Stasis is a known effect of immobility. That makes it something to prevent, not accept.

questions.takeaway: Immobility causes urinary stasis, with infection and stone risk. Hydration keeps urine dilute and moving.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Check whether the stem gives signs of infection or only signs of low intake. Then match the action to what is there.

steps.detail: Dark urine and 900 mL intake. No fever, burning or pain.
A catheter creates the infection it is meant to prevent.
Nothing yet suggests infection. Low intake is the finding the nurse can act on.

elimination.verdict: Increase fluids and recheck the urine. Act on the cause that is present.

questions.stem: Ten minutes after being turned to a flat side-lying position, a client's respirations have gone from 18 to 26 and he says he cannot get comfortable. Alignment and skin look good. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Raise the head of the bed and recheck his breathing
options.rationale: After repositioning the nurse confirms the client can breathe comfortably. The rate change says this position is not tolerated.

options.text: Leave the position and recheck at the next turn
options.rationale: Waiting for the next turn leaves a client whose breathing has changed in the position that changed it.

options.text: Give the as-needed analgesic for discomfort
options.rationale: Tempting because he reports discomfort. The rising respiratory rate points to breathing, not pain.

options.text: Add a pillow between his knees for comfort
options.rationale: Good alignment support that does nothing for his work of breathing.

questions.takeaway: After every repositioning, reassess alignment, comfort, pressure areas, skin, tubes and the ability to breathe comfortably. Breathing outranks the rest.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two cues compete: discomfort and a faster respiratory rate. Let the breathing cue decide.

steps.detail: Respirations rose from 18 to 26 after the turn.
Rechecking at the next turn leaves him breathing hard.
An analgesic and a knee pillow answer comfort only.

elimination.verdict: Raise the head of the bed and recheck. A position that looks right still has to let him breathe.

questions.stem: A man with COPD walks 100 feet. Pulse rises from 84 to 108 and respirations from 18 to 28 per minute. Five minutes after sitting, pulse is 104 and respirations 28. What is the plan for the next walk?

options.text: Repeat the same 100 feet without changes
options.rationale: Reasonable if he had recovered. He did not return toward baseline in five minutes, so this distance is too much as designed.

options.text: Shorten the distance and add rest stops
options.rationale: He failed to recover after five minutes of rest. Keep him moving at a level he can recover from.

options.text: Increase to 150 feet to build endurance
options.rationale: Progressive activity is the goal. Progress follows tolerance, and he did not tolerate this.

options.text: Hold walking until the provider reassesses him
options.rationale: Protective, and immobility will lower his endurance further. Poor recovery calls for a smaller dose, not none.

questions.takeaway: Activity tolerance is judged by recovery. If pulse and breathing stay up after rest, reduce the workload and keep the client moving.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: A rise during activity is expected. Look at the numbers after rest to decide.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Read the response during the walk
steps.detail: Pulse and breathing rise, which is expected.
Still 104 and 28 after five minutes.
Less distance with rests, not more and not none.

elimination.verdict: Shorter distance with rest stops.

questions.stem: A client who walks steadily only with his walker left it at home. He asks to walk to the bathroom holding his IV pole. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Obtain a walker before he walks
options.rationale: His steady gait depends on the device he normally uses. Matching the baseline keeps him moving safely.

options.text: Let him steady himself on the IV pole
options.rationale: A rolling pole is not a support and can slide away from him.

options.text: Walk him with a gait belt and no device
options.rationale: Tempting because staff are beside him. It still removes the support his balance relies on.

options.text: Offer a urinal until his family brings the walker
options.rationale: Avoids the fall and costs him mobility when a walker can be supplied.

questions.takeaway: Start from the patient's baseline, including assistive devices. Keep him mobile with the support he normally uses.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Ask what made him steady before admission. The best option restores it without taking away the walk.

steps.detail: Steady only with a walker.
An IV pole rolls.
A urinal gives up mobility. A gait belt alone leaves out the device. A walker restores his baseline.

elimination.verdict: Get a walker first. Same support as at home, and he still walks.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old with hypertension controlled by medication wants to add strength exercises to her daily walks. Which instruction does the nurse include?

options.text: Choose wall sits and planks held as long as possible
options.rationale: Tempting because nothing moves and it feels gentle. A long isometric hold with a held breath raises blood pressure sharply while it lasts.

options.text: Use light weights and breathe out during each lift
options.rationale: Correct. Moving a light load through the range with steady breathing builds strength without the pressure surge of straining.

options.text: Lift the heaviest weight she can for a few repetitions
options.rationale: Heavy loads make her strain and hold her breath, which drives the pressure up.

options.text: Keep to walking until her medication is no longer needed
options.rationale: Hypertension modifies the activity plan. It does not rule out strengthening, and inactivity costs her muscle.

questions.takeaway: Hypertension modifies exercise and does not cancel it. Favor light isotonic work with steady breathing. Sustained isometric holds and straining raise blood pressure.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Ask what each option does to her blood pressure during the exercise itself. Straining and breath holding are the hazard.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Name the risk for this client
steps.detail: A pressure surge from straining or breath holding.

steps.action: Remove the options that cause it
steps.detail: Long holds and maximal weights.

steps.action: Compare the two that are left
steps.detail: Walking only gives up strengthening she can do safely.

elimination.verdict: Light weights with breathing out on the lift.

questions.stem: This morning a patient recovering from pneumonia pushed firmly against the nurse's hands with both arms. At noon his left arm lifts off the bed but gives way to light pressure. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Schedule active-assistive exercises for the left arm
options.rationale: Treats the weakness as deconditioning. Deconditioning is gradual and affects both sides.

options.text: Recheck the arm strength after he has rested
options.rationale: Tempting because fatigue is common in pneumonia. Fatigue does not weaken one arm within hours.

options.text: Report the new one-sided weakness right away
options.rationale: Correct. A sudden loss of movement on one side is a red flag for a neurological event.

options.text: Support the left arm on a pillow in alignment
options.rationale: Protects the joint and delays the report that matters.

questions.takeaway: Compare both sides and compare with the last assessment. Sudden or one-sided loss of strength is reported, not exercised.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two details decide it: one side only, and a change within hours.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: From full strength to moving against gravity only.
One arm, since morning.
Exercise, rest and positioning suit gradual weakness.

elimination.verdict: Report it now.

questions.stem: A patient with a spinal cord injury lies supine. Both legs roll outward so that the toes point away from the midline. Which support does the nurse add?

options.text: Trochanter rolls along both outer thighs
options.rationale: Correct. A roll from the hip to the knee stops external rotation and keeps the legs in neutral.

options.text: Small pillows placed beneath both of the knees
options.rationale: Flexes the knees and does nothing for rotation at the hip.

options.text: A footboard set against both soles
options.rationale: Tempting because it is a common alignment device. It prevents plantar flexion, not outward rolling.

options.text: A pillow placed between the two knees
options.rationale: Used in side-lying to keep the upper leg level.

questions.takeaway: Match the support to the misalignment. Outward rolling of the hips is corrected with trochanter rolls. Foot supports prevent foot drop.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides.
questions.strategy: Name the joint that is out of line. The feet look wrong, but the turn starts at the hip.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: External rotation at the hips.

steps.action: Match each device to what it corrects
steps.detail: Knee pillows flex, a footboard holds the ankle, a knee pillow is for side-lying.

elimination.verdict: Trochanter rolls.

questions.stem: A patient with left-sided weakness after a stroke can stand and pivot with one staff member. Where does the nurse place the chair for a transfer out of bed?

options.text: On his left side, so the weak leg leads
options.rationale: He would pivot onto a leg that cannot hold him.

options.text: Straight ahead, so he steps forward to it
options.rationale: Requires walking steps, which he has not shown he can do.

options.text: At the foot of the bed, facing the door
options.rationale: Lengthens the move and does not put the chair on his strong side.

options.text: On his right side, so the strong leg leads
options.rationale: Correct. He bears weight and pivots on the leg that works, a short distance from the bed.

questions.takeaway: Transfer toward the strong side. The strong leg carries the pivot and the weak side follows.
questions.coverage: Not in Lecture PPT. Covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Ask which leg takes his full weight during the turn, then put the chair where that leg can do the work.

steps.detail: The right.
Left placement loads the weak leg.
Straight ahead and the foot of the bed need steps.

elimination.verdict: Chair on the right.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man with coronary artery disease is cleared to begin a walking program. Which statement shows the teaching was effective?

options.text: "I will walk fast enough that I cannot talk."
options.rationale: Being unable to talk means the workload is too high for his heart.

options.text: "I will skip the warm-up to save my energy."
options.rationale: A warm-up raises the demand on the heart gradually.

options.text: "If my chest feels tight, I will stop and rest."
options.rationale: Correct. Chest discomfort means demand has passed supply, and he knows to stop.

options.text: "On tired days I will make it up the next day."
options.rationale: Tempting because it sounds committed. Doubling the next day's walk overloads him. Activity is advanced gradually.

questions.takeaway: Coronary artery disease modifies exercise and does not cancel it: gradual progression, a pace that allows talking, and stopping for chest discomfort.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Look for the statement that names a symptom and a safe response to it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Remove statements that raise workload abruptly
steps.detail: Too fast, no warm-up, doubling up.

steps.action: Keep the one that sets a limit
steps.detail: Stop and rest for chest tightness.

elimination.verdict: He stops and rests for chest tightness.

questions.stem: A 73-year-old with a weak right leg after knee surgery is taught to use a walker. Which observation shows the teaching was effective?

options.text: Pushes up from the chair arms, then grips the walker
options.rationale: Correct. A walker tips if it is pulled on. He rises from a stable surface and then takes hold.

options.text: Holds the walker grips and pulls himself up to stand
options.rationale: Tempting because the walker is right there. Pulling tips it toward him.

options.text: Moves the walker far ahead, then takes long steps
options.rationale: Puts his weight outside the frame.

options.text: Steps into the walker with his left leg first
options.rationale: The weak leg steps first, supported by his arms on the walker.

questions.takeaway: A walker supports a person who is already standing. Rise by pushing from the chair, move the walker a short distance, then step with the weak leg first.
questions.coverage: Not in Lecture PPT. Covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Picture where his weight goes in each option. In three of them it is on something that can tip or outside the frame.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pulling on a walker tips it.
Far ahead is unstable, and the strong leg does not lead.

elimination.verdict: He pushes up from the chair arms.

questions.stem: After 12 days of bed rest a 49-year-old stands. Blood pressure and pulse match his sitting values and he is not dizzy, but his knees shake and give. Which problem does the nurse plan for?

options.text: Orthostatic hypotension from venous pooling
options.rationale: Tempting because it is the expected first-stand problem. Unchanged vital signs and no dizziness rule it out.

options.text: Loss of position sense in both feet
options.rationale: Would show as swaying or misplaced feet, not knees that give way.

options.text: Contracture limiting knee extension
options.rationale: He was able to straighten enough to stand. A contracture limits range, not strength.

options.text: Muscle atrophy with loss of leg strength
options.rationale: Correct. Unused muscle loses mass and strength quickly, so the plan is assisted standing and gradual strengthening.

questions.takeaway: A first stand can fail for different reasons. Stable vital signs with buckling knees mean muscle weakness, and the plan is support and progressive strengthening.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy and Potter).
questions.strategy: The stem hands you normal vital signs for a reason. Use them to cross off the cardiovascular answer.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: No drop and no dizziness removes orthostatic hypotension.

steps.action: Use what the knees are doing
steps.detail: Shaking and giving way is strength, not range or sensation.

elimination.verdict: Muscle atrophy and weakness.

questions.stem: A patient deconditioned by a long illness has walked the hall with staff three times a day for a week. Which finding shows his endurance is improving?

options.text: Finishes the same walk and needs longer to recover
options.rationale: Slower recovery means the workload is costing him more.

options.text: Walks twice as far with the same rise in pulse
options.rationale: Correct. More work for the same cardiovascular cost, which is what improved endurance means.

options.text: Says he feels less tired since resting more
options.rationale: Tempting because fatigue matters. Feeling better from doing less does not show capacity.

options.text: Has a resting pulse higher than last week
options.rationale: A rising resting pulse suggests strain or illness.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate progressive activity by work done against the body's response: more distance for the same pulse and breathing, with prompt recovery.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Endurance is a ratio. Look for the option where the work went up and the cost did not.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: More activity for the same response.
Longer recovery and a higher resting pulse are worse. Less fatigue from rest measures nothing.

elimination.verdict: Twice the distance, same pulse rise.

questions.nursesNote: 0900: 69-year-old, second day of treatment for pneumonia, prescribed hallway walks three times daily. Before admission she walked her dog every day without a device. Says her right knee is stiff on waking and loosens by breakfast. Stopped twice on the way to the bathroom to catch her breath. Says the room spun when she sat up this morning. Rates right hip pain 7 of 10 when she stands. Sat unsupported at the bedside and straightened both knees. Receiving oxygen by nasal cannula from wall tubing that reaches only as far as the door.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that change how the nurse carries out this morning's walk.

segments.text: Before admission she walked her dog every day without a device
segments.rationale: Her baseline. It sets the goal and does not change this walk.

segments.text: Says her right knee is stiff on waking and loosens by breakfast
segments.rationale: Brief morning stiffness that resolves is expected at her age.

segments.text: Stopped twice on the way to the bathroom to catch her breath
segments.rationale: Limited activity tolerance. Plan a shorter distance with rest points.

segments.text: Says the room spun when she sat up this morning
segments.rationale: Dizziness on position change. She dangles and is rechecked before standing.

segments.text: Rates right hip pain 7 of 10 when she stands
segments.rationale: Pain limits movement and alters gait. Treat it before the walk.

segments.text: Sat unsupported at the bedside and straightened both knees
segments.rationale: She passed these mobility checks.

segments.text: Receiving oxygen by nasal cannula from wall tubing that reaches only as far as the door
segments.rationale: She needs portable oxygen to leave the room.

questions.takeaway: Before a walk, read tolerance, dizziness, pain and equipment. Each cue changes the plan in its own way, and none of them cancels the walk.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: For each line ask whether you would do anything differently because of it. Baseline and passed checks change nothing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Leave the baseline and the passed tests
steps.detail: Dog walks, sitting balance, knee extension.
Brief morning stiffness.
Breathlessness, dizziness, pain, short tubing.

elimination.verdict: Breathlessness, dizziness, hip pain and the oxygen tubing.

questions.scenario: A 52-year-old will be on bed rest in skeletal traction for a fractured left femur. The nurse plans care to prevent complications of immobility.
questions.stem: For each intervention, indicate the complication it is chosen to prevent.

rows.text: Incentive spirometer every hour while awake
rows.rationale: Deep breaths reopen small airways that collapse with shallow breathing.

rows.text: Ankle pumps with the right foot
rows.rationale: The calf muscle pump moves venous blood that would otherwise pool.

rows.text: Splint holding the right foot at a right angle
rows.rationale: Neutral alignment prevents the plantar flexion contracture called foot drop.

rows.text: Head of the bed raised for meals and care
rows.rationale: Sitting upright lets the lungs expand and helps the cough clear secretions.

rows.text: Sequential compression device on the right leg
rows.rationale: Intermittent squeezing replaces the muscle pump and reduces venous stasis.

rows.text: Range of motion to both arms and the right leg
rows.rationale: Moving each joint through its range keeps muscles and tendons from shortening.

questions.takeaway: Each immobility complication has its own prevention: lung expansion for atelectasis, leg movement and compression for thrombus, range of motion and neutral alignment for contracture.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Ask what each intervention moves: air, blood or a joint.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Spirometer and sitting upright.
Ankle pumps and compression.

steps.action: Find what moves or holds a joint
steps.detail: Range of motion and the foot splint.

elimination.verdict: Atelectasis, thrombus, contracture, atelectasis, thrombus, contracture.

questions.stem: A patient who uses a walker at home holds a stand, then marches in place and steps each foot forward and back steadily while gripping the walker. How does the nurse interpret this result?

options.text: He passed and walks with the walker and standby
options.rationale: An assistive device may be used for the test. He showed the balance and stepping needed to walk.

options.text: He did not pass because he relied on the walker
options.rationale: Using his usual device is allowed. The test asks whether he can step safely, not whether he can do it unaided.

options.text: He needs a sit-to-stand lift until he steps unaided
options.rationale: That equipment is for a patient who cannot hold a stand. He held it and stepped.

options.text: He needs the test repeated when therapy is present
options.rationale: The bedside assessment is a nursing tool. Waiting keeps a capable patient in bed.

questions.takeaway: An assistive device may be used during the bedside mobility assessment. A patient who steps safely with his usual device is at the fourth level and walks with it.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Ask what the test measures: safe standing balance and stepping. The walker is part of how he normally does that.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Held the stand, marched, stepped each foot steadily.

steps.action: Decide whether the device counts against him
steps.detail: It does not. It is his baseline.

steps.action: Drop the options that hold him back
steps.detail: A lift or a delay costs him strength.

elimination.verdict: He passed. Walk with the walker and standby help.

questions.stem: The wife of a patient with leg weakness was taught to help him from bed to chair at home. Which observation shows the teaching was effective?

options.text: She bends at the waist and pulls him up by the arms
options.rationale: Bending at the waist loads her back, and pulling the arms can injure his shoulders.

options.text: She keeps her feet together and twists her trunk toward the chair
options.rationale: A narrow base is unstable and twisting strains the spine.

options.text: She bends her knees, holds him close and pivots her feet
options.rationale: Bent knees let her leg muscles do the work, the load stays close to her body and her feet turn so her spine does not twist.

options.text: She stands at arm's length so he has room to move
options.rationale: A load held away from the body multiplies the strain on her back.

questions.takeaway: Body mechanics: wide base, bend the knees, keep the load close and pivot the feet in place of twisting.
questions.coverage: Not in Lecture PPT. Covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Check each option for the back: waist bending, twisting and reaching all fail.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Look at the base and the knees
steps.detail: Bent knees put the work in her legs. Feet together is a narrow base.
Close is safer than arm's length.
Feet pivot, spine does not twist.

elimination.verdict: Knees bent, close hold, pivot.

questions.stem: A patient with knee arthritis has full leg strength and a steady gait. He walks the hall willingly after his 0900 analgesic but declines the 0700 and 2000 walks, rubbing his knees. How does the nurse interpret this?

options.text: Pain is limiting his activity
options.rationale: He walks when the analgesic is working and refuses when it is not. The knee rubbing is the cue.

options.text: Fatigue late in the day is limiting his activity
options.rationale: Fatigue would not explain refusing the first walk of the morning.

options.text: Fear of falling is limiting his activity
options.rationale: His gait is steady and he walks willingly at 0900, so fear does not fit the pattern.

options.text: Leg weakness is limiting his activity
options.rationale: Strength is full, and weakness would not come and go with the dose.

questions.takeaway: Ask what is limiting the patient now. When activity follows the timing of the analgesic, pain is the limiter, so walks are planned around pain control.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Line up when he walks and when he refuses. The pattern follows the analgesic, not the clock or his strength.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Strength full, gait steady.
Walks after the dose, refuses before it and when it has worn off.
He refuses the first walk of the day too.

elimination.verdict: Pain is the limiter.

questions.stem: After a turn by assistive personnel, a patient lies straight on his side with his full weight on the hip. The skin over the hip bone is red and blanches. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Massage the reddened area to bring blood back
options.rationale: Massage over a bony prominence damages fragile tissue.

options.text: Tilt him back to 30 degrees on pillows
options.rationale: A 30 degree tilt moves weight off the trochanter onto the broader buttock.

options.text: Place a ring cushion under the hip
options.rationale: Ring cushions press on the surrounding tissue and cut off its blood flow.

options.text: Leave him and recheck at the next turn
options.rationale: Blanching redness is the early warning. Pressure should come off now.

questions.takeaway: Side-lying means a 30 degree tilt, not straight on the hip. Blanching redness is reversible if pressure is removed.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides.
questions.strategy: Two options touch the red skin and both harm it. Choose the one that moves the weight.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Red and blanching means early and reversible.
Massage and ring cushions.
A 30 degree tilt.

elimination.verdict: Tilt to 30 degrees with pillows.

questions.stem: Before a hip infection, an 82-year-old walked to her bathroom and kitchen with a wheeled walker. Which finding shows she has met her mobility goal for discharge?

options.text: She walks the hall holding the handrail
options.rationale: Without her walker she is less stable than her own baseline.

options.text: She sits in the chair for every meal
options.rationale: Sitting tolerance does not get her to her bathroom at home.

options.text: She walks to the bathroom with her walker
options.rationale: This is what she did before the illness. Baseline function is the goal.

options.text: She has full range of motion in both hips
options.rationale: Joint movement is needed and does not show she can get around.

questions.takeaway: Set the mobility goal from the patient's own baseline. Returning to that level, with the same device, is success.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: The stem gives her baseline. The answer is the option that matches it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Walker, bathroom and kitchen.
No device is beyond baseline and unsafe. Chair sitting is short of it.
Walker to the bathroom.

elimination.verdict: Walks to the bathroom with her walker.

questions.stem: Six weeks ago a sedentary 38-year-old began a walking plan aimed at moderate intensity. Which report shows the plan is working as intended?

options.text: "I walk slowly for an hour each Sunday."
options.rationale: Once a week at low intensity does not reach the weekly target.

options.text: "I jog until I cannot get a sentence out."
options.rationale: Unable to speak is vigorous, beyond the planned intensity for a beginner.

options.text: "I walk when I feel stressed, about twice a month."
options.rationale: Too infrequent to build fitness.

options.text: "I walk 25 minutes every day and can still talk."
options.rationale: Able to talk but working is moderate intensity, and daily walks add up to more than 150 minutes a week.

questions.takeaway: Moderate activity means you can talk but not sing, for about 150 minutes spread across the week.
questions.coverage: Not in Lecture PPT. Covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Check each report for both frequency and intensity.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Weekly and twice monthly fall short.
Unable to speak is too hard.

steps.action: Keep the one that meets both
steps.detail: Every day, able to talk.

elimination.verdict: Twenty-five minutes every day, able to talk.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man with a right ankle fracture was taught to climb stairs on crutches. Which observation shows the teaching was effective?

options.text: Steps up with the left leg, then brings the crutches up
options.rationale: The strong leg lifts the body. Crutches and the injured leg follow.

options.text: Places both crutches on the step, then hops up
options.rationale: Crutches leading upward leave him balanced on unstable support.

options.text: Steps up with the right leg while leaning hard on the rail
options.rationale: The injured leg cannot take his weight.

options.text: Turns and goes up the stairs backward on the crutches
options.rationale: Not a safe taught method and he cannot see the steps.

questions.takeaway: On stairs with crutches the strong leg goes up first. Going down, the crutches and injured leg lead.
questions.coverage: Not in Lecture PPT. Covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Find which leg is strong, then ask what has to lift his body up a step.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The left.
Only the strong leg can.
Crutches and the right leg follow.

elimination.verdict: Left leg up first.

questions.stem: A patient with right-sided weakness after a stroke will walk in the hall with a gait belt. Where does the nurse position herself?

options.text: At his left side, holding his left arm
options.rationale: His strong side does not need the support, and an arm hold gives no control.

options.text: At his right side, slightly behind, holding the belt
options.rationale: He will fall toward the weak side. The nurse stands where she can steady or lower him.

options.text: In front of him, walking backward
options.rationale: She cannot see hazards and cannot control a fall to the side.

options.text: Directly behind him with both hands on his shoulders
options.rationale: Shoulders give no hold on his center of gravity.
