questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: The word earliest asks for the body's first compensation. Remove the unreliable finding, then order the rest from first to last.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Thirst is weak in older adults.
Heart rate rises first; lying blood pressure and sunken eyes come late.
78 to 106 in a few hours is a change.

elimination.verdict: Heart rate up from 78 to 106.

questions.stem: A patient with a potassium of 6.1 mEq/L and peaked T waves received sodium polystyrene sulfonate six hours ago. Which finding best indicates the drug has been effective?

options.text: She has had three loose stools
options.rationale: Tempting because the binder leaves in the stool. Stools show the drug is moving, not that enough potassium left with it.

options.text: T waves on the monitor are normal height
options.rationale: The peaked T wave was the heart's response to the potassium. Its return to normal shows the level has fallen where it matters.

options.text: Urine output is 35 mL per hour
options.rationale: Adequate output, but the binder removes potassium through the gut, not the kidneys.

options.text: She reports less nausea than before
options.rationale: Nausea is not specific to potassium and does not show the level changed.

questions.takeaway: Judge hyperkalemia treatment by the heart. A drug's expected side effect is not proof that it worked.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Separate what shows the drug acted from what shows the patient improved. The outcome is the sign that made the potassium dangerous.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Find the danger sign in the stem
steps.detail: Peaked T waves.
The binder does not work through urine.
Stool is the mechanism. The T wave is the result.

elimination.verdict: Normal T waves.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old admitted with fluid volume deficit from fever and poor intake has had IV and oral fluids for 24 hours. Which findings indicate her fluid balance is improving? Select all that apply.

options.text: Pulse is 86, down from 110 on admission
options.rationale: The heart no longer has to race to hold blood pressure up.

options.text: She stands at the bedside without dizziness
options.rationale: No orthostatic symptoms means the vessels are filled well enough to tolerate standing.

options.text: Weight is up 0.7 kg since admission
options.rationale: In a patient who was dry, a modest gain over a day is replaced water.

options.text: Her tongue and mouth are moist
options.rationale: Mucous membranes are a reliable hydration sign in older adults.

options.text: Her eyelids and hands look puffy
options.rationale: New edema is fluid collecting in the tissues. It suggests too much fluid, not a return to balance.

options.text: She sleeps most of the day and is slow to wake
options.rationale: Tempting to read as rest. Lethargy is a neurologic finding that needs assessment, not a sign that fluid balance is returning.

questions.takeaway: Fluid replacement is working when the deficit signs reverse: pulse slows, standing is tolerated, weight returns and the mouth is moist. Edema or lethargy is a different problem.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: For each option ask whether it is an admission sign going away or a new finding. Only signs that are going away count as improvement.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pulse, standing, weight and mouth all move back toward normal.
Puffiness and lethargy are not deficit signs going away.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C and D.

questions.stem: A patient with hypovolemia from vomiting has a prescription for a 500 mL bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride. Place the nurse's actions in the order they are performed.

options.text: Listen to the lungs and measure blood pressure and pulse
options.rationale: A baseline comes first. Without it you cannot tell whether the bolus helped or overloaded the patient.

options.text: Start the bolus on the infusion pump
options.rationale: With a baseline recorded, give the prescribed volume at a controlled rate.

options.text: Repeat the lung sounds and vital signs during the bolus
options.rationale: Reassess while the fluid is running so new crackles are caught early.

options.text: Measure the urine output for the next hour
options.rationale: Urine output shows whether the added volume reached the kidneys. It takes time to change.

options.text: Report the response to the provider
options.rationale: Report last, when there is a complete before and after picture to give.

questions.takeaway: A fluid bolus runs through the nursing process: baseline, give, reassess during, measure the outcome, report.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Place the baseline first and the report last. The middle steps follow how fast each finding changes: lungs and pulse during, urine after.

steps.detail: Baseline before fluid; report after the outcome is known.
Lungs and vital signs change in minutes. Urine output needs an hour.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, E.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old on continuous tube feeding has a sodium of 153 mEq/L. She is newly agitated, with twitching in both hands. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Review the water flushes prescribed with her feeding
options.rationale: Formula without enough free water concentrates the blood. Agitation and twitching are the high sodium showing in nerve and muscle, so the fix starts with her water.

options.text: Apply mitts so she cannot pull out the feeding tube while agitated
options.rationale: Tempting for an agitated patient with a tube, but it restrains a symptom and skips less restrictive steps.

options.text: Request an as-needed sedative for the agitation
options.rationale: Sedation hides the neurologic sign you need to track and leaves the sodium untouched.

options.text: Slow the tube feeding to half the current rate
options.rationale: Cuts her calories and also cuts the water the formula itself supplies.

questions.takeaway: Agitation and twitching with a high sodium mean brain and muscle cells are losing water. Give back free water before you treat the behavior.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Do not treat the agitation as a behavior problem. Ask what the sodium is doing to her cells and what she is missing.

steps.action: Link the cue to the lab
steps.detail: Twitching and agitation are irritable nerve and muscle from high sodium.

steps.action: Cut the options that mask it
steps.detail: Mitts and a sedative manage behavior only.

steps.action: Pick the one that adds water
steps.detail: Flushes are how a tube fed patient gets free water.

elimination.verdict: Review the water flushes.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old with late-stage kidney failure is assessed at 0800. Which finding tells the nurse his fluid overload is getting worse?

options.text: Pitting edema of 2+ at both ankles and shins, the same as it was yesterday
options.rationale: Abnormal but unchanged, so it does not show a trend.

options.text: Neck veins newly distended with the head of bed at 45 degrees
options.rationale: Veins that stay full when he is upright mean the vascular space is overfilled now, and the lungs are next.

options.text: Urine output of 280 mL in 24 hours, his usual amount
options.rationale: Low, but expected for his kidneys and it is his baseline rather than a change.

options.text: Skin on the lower legs that is pale and cool
options.rationale: A finding of edema that goes along with the swelling he already has.

questions.takeaway: Edema tells you fluid is in the tissues. Distended neck veins and a bounding pulse tell you the vessels are overfilled, which is what leads to pulmonary edema.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: All four fit kidney failure. Look for the one that is new and that sits closest to the heart and lungs.

steps.detail: Edema and low output are his usual.
Neck veins reflect pressure in the central circulation.
Overfilled vessels push fluid into the lungs.

elimination.verdict: Distended neck veins at 45 degrees.

questions.stem: A patient with a potassium of 6.2 mEq/L and a wide QRS received IV calcium. Ten minutes later the QRS is narrower and the repeat potassium is 6.2 mEq/L. Which conclusion guides the nurse?

options.text: The calcium did not work, so a repeat dose is needed
options.rationale: The rhythm improved, which is exactly what calcium is for.

options.text: The calcium worked, and the potassium still has to be lowered
options.rationale: Calcium steadies the heart muscle and does not move potassium. Insulin with dextrose and a binder still have to bring the level down.

options.text: The repeat sample was probably hemolyzed and should be redrawn
options.rationale: Tempting when a lab does not move, but an unchanged value is the expected result here.

options.text: The remaining treatments can wait because the rhythm has improved
options.rationale: The protection is short lived. The potassium is still dangerous.

questions.takeaway: IV calcium protects the heart and does not lower potassium. An unchanged level after calcium is expected, and the lowering treatments still come next.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two results look like they disagree. Ask what each drug is supposed to change before calling it a failure.

steps.detail: It stabilizes the myocardium.
No shift or removal has happened yet.
A better rhythm on calcium is borrowed time.

elimination.verdict: It worked on the heart. Now lower the potassium.

questions.stem: A man with kidney failure who makes no urine has a magnesium of 4.2 mEq/L and is hard to arouse. IV calcium has been given. Which prescription does the nurse anticipate next?

options.text: IV furosemide with 0.9% sodium chloride
options.rationale: The usual way to flush magnesium, but it works only through kidneys that make urine. Here it adds volume he cannot remove.

options.text: Oral magnesium binder with meals
options.rationale: Not a treatment for a high magnesium level, and he is too drowsy to swallow safely.

options.text: Hemodialysis to remove the magnesium
options.rationale: With no urine output, dialysis is the only route left to remove the magnesium.

options.text: A repeat magnesium level in 12 hours
options.rationale: Monitoring alone leaves a patient who is hard to arouse with a rising risk of respiratory failure.

questions.takeaway: Fluids and a loop diuretic remove magnesium only if the kidneys work. In kidney failure, stop the source, give calcium and expect dialysis.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The usual answer is fluids and furosemide. Check the stem for the detail that takes that option away.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: He makes no urine.

steps.action: Test the standard treatment against it
steps.detail: A diuretic has nothing to act on.

steps.action: Pick the route that still works
steps.detail: Dialysis removes magnesium directly.

elimination.verdict: Hemodialysis.

questions.stem: A patient with hyperparathyroidism and a calcium of 13.1 mg/dL had a heart rate of 102 this morning. Which afternoon finding most concerns the nurse?

options.text: No bowel movement for three days
options.rationale: Expected with high calcium because the gut slows. It needs a plan, not an urgent response.

options.text: Knee reflexes weaker than this morning
options.rationale: Also expected. High calcium makes nerve and muscle harder to excite.

options.text: Reports feeling thirsty and urinating often
options.rationale: A common effect that calls for fluids.

options.text: Heart rate of 48 with cool, pale feet
options.rationale: Early high calcium speeds the heart. A slowing rate with poor perfusion means it is now depressing the heart.

questions.takeaway: In hypercalcemia the heart rate rises early and slows when the level is severe or prolonged. A falling rate with poor perfusion is the dangerous turn.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Three options are expected for this condition. Find the one that shows a change in the organ that can kill.

steps.detail: Constipation, weak reflexes and thirst all fit.
102 down to 48 is a change in direction.
Cool pale feet mean perfusion is falling.

elimination.verdict: Heart rate 48 with cool, pale feet.

questions.stem: Assistive personnel report that an 85-year-old's skin stays tented on the back of her hand and suggest she needs more fluids. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Check turgor over the sternum and look at her mouth
options.rationale: Hand skin tents in most older adults because it has lost elasticity. The sternum and the mucous membranes give a reading you can trust.

options.text: Start an hourly oral fluid schedule for the shift
options.rationale: Reasonable if she is dry, but you would be treating on a finding that is unreliable at her age.

options.text: Request a prescription for IV 0.9% sodium chloride
options.rationale: Jumps to treatment with no valid evidence of a deficit.

options.text: Ask the assistive personnel to recheck the other hand
options.rationale: Repeats the same unreliable site and hands an assessment to someone who cannot interpret it.

questions.takeaway: In older adults, assess skin turgor over the sternum and confirm with mucous membranes. Tenting on the hand proves nothing.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Before acting on a reported finding, ask whether that finding is reliable in this patient.

steps.detail: Hand turgor is unreliable after about age 65.
Oral or IV fluid needs a valid assessment first.
Assistive personnel collect, the nurse interprets.

elimination.verdict: Check the sternum and the mouth.

questions.stem: A man with kidney disease has a sodium of 151 mEq/L, a bounding pulse and edema to both knees. Which prescription does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Furosemide with a sodium-restricted diet
options.rationale: His sodium is high because the kidneys are holding sodium and water together. Remove both and stop adding sodium.

options.text: A fluid restriction of 1 L per day
options.rationale: Tempting because he is overloaded, but taking away water alone concentrates the sodium further.

options.text: A 300 mL bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride
options.rationale: Adds sodium and volume to a patient who has too much of both.

options.text: Oral water every hour while awake
options.rationale: Right for a dry patient with high sodium. He already has excess volume.

questions.takeaway: High sodium does not always mean a dry patient. Read the volume status: with a bounding pulse and edema, the plan is a diuretic and less sodium.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The sodium number points one way and the pulse points the other. Volume status decides the treatment.

steps.detail: Bounding pulse and edema mean excess.
Bolus and hourly water both do.
Restricting water raises sodium. A diuretic with less sodium fixes both.

elimination.verdict: Furosemide and sodium restriction.

questions.stem: A postoperative patient's pump has run at 250 mL per hour for four hours instead of the prescribed 75. His pulse is bounding, his lungs are clear and he breathes easily. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Request a prescription for IV furosemide
options.rationale: May well be needed, but the extra fluid is still running in while you make the call.

options.text: Reset the pump to the prescribed rate
options.rationale: Stops the cause at once. He is breathing easily, so removing the source comes before anything else.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed and apply oxygen
options.rationale: The right first move if he were short of breath. He is not.

options.text: Complete an event report for the rate error
options.rationale: Required, and it comes after the patient is safe.

questions.takeaway: When a treatment is causing the problem, correct the source first, then assess and report.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The stem already gives you the assessment. Ask which action stops more harm in the next minute.

steps.detail: Bounding pulse, clear lungs, easy breathing.
Each minute adds more fluid.
Reassess, report, then document.

elimination.verdict: Reset the pump to 75.

questions.nursesNote: 1400: 58-year-old with diabetes and kidney disease, takes lisinopril. Serum potassium 5.8 mEq/L. Reports tingling around the mouth and in both feet since noon. Legs now feel heavy when he walks. Three loose watery stools this shift, bowel sounds hyperactive. Apical pulse 52 and irregular. Fingerstick glucose within his usual range. Skin warm and dry. Reports a good appetite at lunch.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that require follow-up because of his potassium level.

segments.text: Reports tingling around the mouth and in both feet since noon
segments.rationale: Tingling and twitching are the early nerve signs of high potassium.

segments.text: Legs now feel heavy when he walks
segments.rationale: Weakness that starts in the legs and moves upward is the next stage.

segments.text: Three loose watery stools this shift, bowel sounds hyperactive
segments.rationale: High potassium speeds the gut. It is easy to blame food or a virus.

segments.text: Apical pulse 52 and irregular
segments.rationale: A slow irregular pulse means the heart's conduction is affected. This is what kills.

segments.text: Fingerstick glucose within his usual range
segments.rationale: Normal for him and not a potassium finding.

segments.text: Skin warm and dry
segments.rationale: Normal.

segments.text: Reports a good appetite at lunch
segments.rationale: Normal, and not related to the potassium.

questions.takeaway: High potassium: tingling first, then weakness that climbs, a fast gut, and a slow irregular heart. Check the pulse and rhythm before anything else.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The diarrhea looks like a separate stomach problem. With a high potassium it belongs to the same picture.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 5.8 with kidney disease and an ACE inhibitor.

steps.action: Collect nerve, muscle, gut and heart
steps.detail: Tingling, heavy legs, watery stools, slow irregular pulse.
Glucose, skin and appetite.

elimination.verdict: Tingling, heavy legs, watery stools and the pulse.

questions.stem: Six hours after burns to both legs, a client's face and hands are increasingly swollen. Her pulse is 122 and weak. Lactated Ringer's is infusing at the prescribed rate. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Keep the prescribed rate and monitor urine output
options.rationale: The swelling is fluid that left the plasma for the tissues. A weak rapid pulse shows the vessels are still underfilled, and urine output tells you whether the rate is enough.

options.text: Slow the infusion until the swelling stops getting any worse
options.rationale: Tempting because she looks overloaded. The swelling is outside the vessels, and her weak rapid pulse says the vessels are short of fluid, so slowing deepens the deficit.

options.text: Pause the infusion and elevate both arms
options.rationale: Pausing removes the only fluid going into vessels that are already underfilled.

options.text: Change to oral fluids to limit the swelling
options.rationale: Oral replacement fits a mild or moderate deficit. A weak pulse of 122 after burns is a severe one.

questions.takeaway: Swelling after burns is fluid shifted from plasma to tissue. Judge the vessels by the pulse and urine output, not by the swelling.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Ask where the fluid is. Swollen tissue does not mean full vessels. The weak rapid pulse answers the question.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 122 and weak means low volume in the vessels.

steps.action: Cut the options that reduce IV fluid
steps.detail: Slowing, pausing and switching to oral fluids all lower what reaches the vessels.

steps.action: Keep the option that measures the effect
steps.detail: Urine output shows whether the kidneys are being perfused.

elimination.verdict: Keep the prescribed rate and monitor urine output.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old with SIADH and a sodium of 126 mEq/L is on a fluid restriction and started tolvaptan yesterday. Which finding does the nurse report first?

options.text: Weight is 0.4 kg higher than yesterday
options.rationale: The closest runner up. It shows water is still being retained and needs follow up, but a change in the brain is the more urgent danger.

options.text: Thirst and a dry mouth all evening
options.rationale: Expected on a fluid restriction. It needs comfort measures, not a report.

options.text: Urine output has risen since yesterday
options.rationale: The intended effect. A vasopressin antagonist makes the kidneys let go of water.

options.text: Harder to wake than this morning
options.rationale: Low sodium moves water into brain cells, and the skull leaves no room for swelling. A falling level of alertness comes before seizures and coma.

questions.takeaway: In low sodium the brain is the organ at risk. A new drop in alertness is reported before weight, thirst or urine findings.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Sort the findings into expected, intended and new. Then ask which new one involves the brain.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Cut the expected and the intended
steps.detail: Thirst follows a fluid restriction. More urine is what tolvaptan is for.
A 0.4 kg gain is slow water retention. Harder to wake is the brain swelling now.

elimination.verdict: Harder to wake than this morning.

questions.stem: Four hours after a gastrointestinal bleed, a 54-year-old has made 12 mL of dark urine per hour. Blood pressure has fallen from 112/70 to 94/58. A new nurse suggests requesting a diuretic. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Request furosemide to raise the urine output
options.rationale: Low pressure and low volume trigger renin, angiotensin II and aldosterone, so the kidneys are holding water on purpose. A diuretic removes volume this client cannot spare.

options.text: Report the findings and anticipate IV fluid replacement
options.rationale: The scant urine is the kidneys saving volume, and the falling pressure shows that is no longer enough. The volume has to be replaced.

options.text: Document the low output as expected and recheck in four hours
options.rationale: Half right. Low output is the expected response to blood loss, but a pressure that keeps falling means compensation is failing.

options.text: Encourage oral fluids and remeasure the output next hour
options.rationale: Oral replacement fits a mild or moderate deficit. A falling pressure with scant urine is a severe one.

questions.takeaway: After blood loss the kidneys make little urine to save volume. Treat the cause by replacing volume, never with a diuretic.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Ask why the urine is low. Low pressure tells the kidneys to hold water, so the fix is more volume, not more urine.

steps.detail: Low pressure triggers the kidneys to keep sodium and water.
It removes the volume the body is trying to save.
A pressure falling to 94/58 rules out waiting and rules out oral fluids alone.

elimination.verdict: Report the findings and anticipate IV fluid replacement.

questions.stem: An 87-year-old with 2 days of diarrhea is dizzy when standing, with a standing blood pressure of 92/56. Which scheduled morning medications does the nurse hold and clarify with the provider? Select all that apply.

options.text: Furosemide
options.rationale: A diuretic removes more fluid from an older adult who is already losing it in stool.

options.text: Lisinopril
options.rationale: An antihypertensive lowers a standing pressure that is already 92/56. It also blocks the angiotensin response the body uses to hold pressure up.

options.text: Senna
options.rationale: A laxative adds to the stool losses that caused the deficit.

options.text: Loperamide
options.rationale: An antidiarrheal treats the cause of the fluid loss, so it is given.

options.text: Acetaminophen
options.rationale: It does not lower fluid volume or blood pressure, so there is no reason to hold it.

questions.takeaway: In a dehydrated older adult, question diuretics, laxatives and antihypertensives before giving them. Each one makes the deficit or the low pressure worse.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: For each drug ask one question: does it remove fluid or lower blood pressure? If yes, hold it and clarify.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Diarrhea with dizziness and a standing pressure of 92/56 means fluid deficit.
The diuretic and the laxative.
The antihypertensive.
The antidiarrheal slows the loss.

elimination.verdict: Hold furosemide, lisinopril and senna.

questions.stem: The nurse receives report on four clients with fluid imbalances at the start of the shift. Which client does the nurse see first?

options.text: Fluid overload from kidney failure, newly restless and sitting upright to breathe
options.rationale: A new change in breathing in a client with too much fluid points to pulmonary edema, the complication the overload plan exists to prevent.

options.text: Fluid deficit, blood pressure 96/58 after the first bolus, second bolus now infusing
options.rationale: A real circulation problem and the closest runner up. Treatment is already running, and a new breathing problem comes before it.

options.text: Fluid overload, weight up 1.6 kg, due for scheduled furosemide
options.rationale: Needs the dose on time. Nothing here says the breathing has changed.

options.text: Fluid deficit, dizzy when standing, resting in bed with the call light
options.rationale: A fall risk that is controlled while the client stays in bed.

questions.takeaway: In fluid overload, a new change in breathing means pulmonary edema until proven otherwise. Breathing comes before a circulation problem that is already being treated.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Look for the client whose condition is new and untreated, then rank by airway, breathing, circulation.

steps.detail: Only one client has a new change.

steps.action: Find what is already being treated
steps.detail: The low pressure has a bolus running. The dizzy client is in bed.
Restless and upright to breathe outranks the rest.

elimination.verdict: The client with fluid overload who is newly restless and sitting upright to breathe.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old with heart failure and a sodium of 113 mEq/L has received 3% sodium chloride for three hours. Which finding does the nurse report now?

options.text: Sodium is 117 mEq/L
options.rationale: A small rise is what the infusion is meant to produce.

options.text: She is drowsy but now answers questions
options.rationale: Still not back to normal, which makes it tempting. Answering questions shows the brain is recovering, so this is progress.

options.text: New crackles and shortness of breath
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline pulls water out of the cells into the vessels. With heart failure, that added volume is backing up into her lungs.

options.text: She says she is very thirsty
options.rationale: Thirst is the expected response to a concentrated solution. It needs comfort care, not a report.

questions.takeaway: Hypertonic saline pulls water into the vessels. Watch the brain for improvement and the lungs for fluid overload.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Sort each finding into expected or unexpected for 3% saline. Then ask which unexpected one threatens breathing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A slightly higher sodium and a more responsive client are the goal.
Thirst follows a concentrated solution.
New crackles with shortness of breath mean the vessels are overfilled.

elimination.verdict: New crackles and shortness of breath.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old starting long-term prednisone is taught how to watch for fluid retention at home. Which statement shows the teaching was effective?

options.text: "I'll weigh myself each morning and call about a sudden gain."
options.rationale: Rapid weight gain is the best indicator of fluid retention, and weighing at the same time each day makes the numbers comparable.

options.text: "I'll check my ankles at night because swelling shows up first."
options.rationale: Checking for edema is reasonable, which makes this tempting. Weight rises before swelling can be seen, so edema is a late warning.

options.text: "I'll drink extra water so my body lets go of the fluid."
options.rationale: Extra water adds to the fluid being retained.

options.text: "I'll call if my weight creeps up over several months."
options.rationale: A slow gain over months is body tissue. Fluid shows as a sudden gain over a day or two.

questions.takeaway: Long-term corticosteroids cause fluid retention. A sudden weight gain on a daily morning weight is the earliest and best sign.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two statements are about weight. Pick the one with the right time frame: daily and sudden.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Cut the statement that adds fluid
steps.detail: Extra water.
Sudden gain is fluid. A slow gain over months is not.
Weight changes first, swelling later.

elimination.verdict: Weigh each morning and call about a sudden gain.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old with a sodium of 162 mEq/L is receiving 0.45% sodium chloride with a goal of lowering the sodium gradually. Which reassessment requires the nurse to intervene?

options.text: After 8 hours: sodium 158 mEq/L, still confused at times
options.rationale: Tempting because the confusion has not cleared. A fall of 4 mEq/L in 8 hours is the gradual correction intended, and the brain recovers slowly with it.

options.text: After 6 hours: sodium 160 mEq/L, asking for water often
options.rationale: A small drop, and thirst is expected while the sodium is still high.

options.text: After 4 hours: sodium 161 mEq/L, drowsy but easy to wake
options.rationale: Slow, and moving in the right direction with no new neurologic change.

options.text: After 4 hours: sodium 150 mEq/L, new headache
options.rationale: A drop of 12 mEq/L in 4 hours is far too fast. Water moves into brain cells and causes cerebral edema, and the new headache is its first sign.

questions.takeaway: High sodium is lowered gradually. A rapid drop causes cerebral edema.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Compare how fast each sodium fell, then ask whether the neurologic finding is old or new.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Compare the size of each drop
steps.detail: 1 to 4 mEq/L over 4 to 8 hours versus 12 mEq/L in 4 hours.
Lingering confusion during a slow drop is expected. A new headache after a fast drop is not.

elimination.verdict: The sodium of 150 after 4 hours.

questions.stem: A 90-year-old has been NPO for 14 hours awaiting a delayed procedure. Maintenance IV fluid was prescribed but not started. She has voided 60 mL of dark urine in the past 8 hours. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Ask the provider to allow clear liquids until she is called
options.rationale: A reasonable request and the closest runner up. It waits on a new prescription while a fluid that is already prescribed has not been started.

options.text: Provide mouth care and reassess after the procedure
options.rationale: Mouth care adds comfort and no fluid. Scant dark urine shows the deficit has begun, and an older adult has less body water to lose.

options.text: Start the prescribed IV fluid now
options.rationale: Long NPO time is a cause of dehydration and older adults have little reserve. The fluid is already prescribed, so starting it replaces volume at once without breaking NPO status.

options.text: Call the procedure area to request an earlier time
options.rationale: Worth doing next. It may shorten the wait, but it replaces no fluid.

questions.takeaway: A long NPO period dehydrates an older adult quickly. Scant dark urine is the cue to replace fluid now by the route that is allowed.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Several options help. Only one replaces fluid now, keeps her NPO and needs no new prescription.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 60 mL of dark urine in 8 hours means the kidneys are conserving water.
Mouth care and a call about the schedule.

steps.action: Choose between the two that add fluid
steps.detail: Clear liquids need a new prescription. The IV fluid is prescribed and was never started.

elimination.verdict: Start the prescribed IV fluid now.

questions.stem: The RN on a medical unit is making assignments for the shift with one LPN. Which client is most appropriate for the RN to assign to the LPN?

options.text: Admitted an hour ago with dehydration, awaiting the first nursing assessment
options.rationale: The admission assessment and the first plan of care belong to the RN.

options.text: Chronic heart failure, weight stable for three days, on oral furosemide
options.rationale: Stable and predictable. Daily weight, oral drugs and intake and output are within LPN practice.

options.text: Sodium 115 mEq/L, receiving 3% sodium chloride on a pump
options.rationale: An unstable client on an emergency infusion needs frequent RN neurologic assessment.

options.text: Fluid overload with new crackles after an IV fluid bolus
options.rationale: A new change needs RN assessment and a decision about what to do next.

questions.takeaway: Assign the LPN the stable client with a predictable outcome. The RN keeps new admissions, new changes and high risk infusions.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Scan for the words that mean stable. New, awaiting first assessment and 3% saline all mean RN.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Admission assessment is RN work.
A sodium of 115 on hypertonic saline and new crackles both need RN judgment.
Weight unchanged for three days on an oral drug.

elimination.verdict: The client with chronic heart failure and a stable weight.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old with heart failure, leg edema and a sodium of 130 mEq/L asks for salty broth because his "sodium is low." Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "Broth is a good choice because it will raise your sodium."
options.rationale: Extra sodium fits a mild low sodium without fluid excess. With heart failure and edema, salt and broth hold more water.

options.text: "Your sodium reads low from extra water, so we limit fluids and salt."
options.rationale: Heart failure with edema means the sodium is diluted by retained water. Removing water corrects the number, and salt would add to the overload.

options.text: "A salt substitute will raise your sodium without adding any more fluid."
options.rationale: A salt substitute contains potassium, not sodium, and does nothing for the extra water.

options.text: "Drink extra water with meals to balance the salt you eat."
options.rationale: More water dilutes the sodium further.

questions.takeaway: Low sodium with edema is too much water, not too little salt. Restrict fluid and sodium.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The edema tells you which kind of low sodium this is. Find the response that removes water.

steps.detail: Heart failure with leg edema means fluid excess.

steps.action: Cut the responses that add salt or water
steps.detail: Broth and extra water.
A salt substitute is potassium.

elimination.verdict: Explain the dilution and limit fluids and salt.

questions.stem: A client with large draining wounds has generalized swelling, a blood pressure of 86/52 and scant urine. After IV albumin, which finding best indicates the albumin has been effective?

options.text: Weight is 0.8 kg higher than yesterday
options.rationale: Weight counts water in every compartment. It cannot show whether the water is now inside the vessels.

options.text: Hematocrit is higher than it was before the infusion started
options.rationale: A higher hematocrit means the blood is more concentrated. Albumin that works holds water in the plasma and dilutes it.

options.text: Pulse is bounding with distended neck veins
options.rationale: The vessels are now overfilled. That is a complication, not the goal.

options.text: Blood pressure is 108/64 and urine output has risen
options.rationale: Albumin raises oncotic pressure and holds water in the plasma. A better pressure and more urine show the vessels are filled and the kidneys are perfused.

questions.takeaway: A colloid works by holding water inside the vessels. Judge it by blood pressure and urine output.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The problem was low pressure and scant urine. The answer is the finding that shows those two have reversed without overshooting.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Low pressure and scant urine mean underfilled vessels.

steps.action: Cut the finding that cannot locate the water
steps.detail: Total weight.
Higher hematocrit is too dry. Bounding pulse with distended neck veins is too full.

elimination.verdict: Blood pressure of 108/64 with rising urine output.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old receiving IV 0.9% sodium chloride for dehydration has had seven watery stools in 12 hours, and her output still exceeds her intake. An as-needed antidiarrheal is prescribed. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Ask to increase the IV rate to match the losses
options.rationale: Reasonable as a later step. It replaces what is lost without slowing the loss, and a prescribed treatment for the cause has not been used yet.

options.text: Limit oral fluids to rest her bowel
options.rationale: Cutting intake widens the gap between intake and output.

options.text: Give the prescribed antidiarrheal
options.rationale: Treating the cause is part of dehydration care. The drug is already prescribed and it slows the loss that keeps her behind.

options.text: Continue the plan and total intake and output at 24 hours
options.rationale: The record already shows the plan is not keeping up.

questions.takeaway: Replacing fluid is half the treatment for dehydration. The other half is stopping the loss with the drug that treats the cause.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Ask what is still driving the deficit. Use what is already prescribed for it before asking for anything new.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Output still exceeds intake because the diarrhea continues.

steps.action: Cut the options that do not slow the loss
steps.detail: Limiting fluids and waiting 24 hours.
The antidiarrheal is prescribed now and treats the cause. A rate change needs a new prescription.

elimination.verdict: Give the prescribed antidiarrheal.

questions.stem: An 88-year-old who takes a diuretic and a daily laxative was oriented yesterday and is confused this morning. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Check her pulse, mouth and recent intake
options.rationale: In an older adult, acute confusion may be the first sign of a fluid or electrolyte imbalance. A diuretic and a laxative both raise that risk, so fluid status is checked first.

options.text: Reorient her often and keep the room well lit today
options.rationale: Good care for a confused client, which makes it tempting. It manages the confusion without looking for the cause.

options.text: Review her chart for a history of memory loss
options.rationale: Chronic memory loss does not appear overnight. She was oriented yesterday.

options.text: Set a bed alarm and recheck her orientation at lunch
options.rationale: The alarm is a sound safety measure. Waiting until lunch delays finding a cause that can be treated.

questions.takeaway: New confusion in an older adult is a fluid or electrolyte problem until shown otherwise, more so with diuretics or laxatives.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The confusion is new since yesterday. Look for a cause before managing the behavior, and let the drug list point to the cause.

steps.detail: Oriented yesterday, confused today. That rules out a chronic memory problem.
A diuretic and a laxative both remove fluid and electrolytes.

steps.action: Cut the options that manage without finding the cause
steps.detail: Reorienting and a bed alarm help with safety and leave the cause untouched.

elimination.verdict: Check her pulse, mouth and recent intake.

questions.stem: A client with nasogastric suction after bowel surgery had 2,000 mL of IV intake in 24 hours. Output was 750 mL of urine and 1,600 mL of suction drainage. Which conclusion guides the nurse?

options.text: Fluid balance is adequate because urine output is above 500 mL
options.rationale: Tempting because 750 mL of urine is above the level of concern. Urine is only part of the output.

options.text: Suction drainage is not counted, so intake exceeds output
options.rationale: Suction drainage is fluid lost from the body and is always counted.

options.text: Total output exceeds intake, so the deficit is growing
options.rationale: 750 plus 1,600 is 2,350 mL out against 2,000 mL in. The client is 350 mL behind for the day, and GI suction is a cause of dehydration.

options.text: Intake is adequate because it reached 2 L
options.rationale: An intake figure means nothing until it is compared with every loss.

questions.takeaway: Intake and output only tell the truth when every loss is counted. GI suction drainage is output.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Add every output before judging the intake. Then compare the two totals.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 2,000 mL in, 350 mL short.

steps.action: Cut the options that judge one number alone
steps.detail: Urine alone, intake alone, and the option that drops the suction drainage.

elimination.verdict: Total output exceeds intake, so the deficit is growing.

questions.stem: An alert 35-year-old who hiked all day without water reports thirst and scant dark urine. Blood pressure is 118/74 lying and standing, and he swallows without difficulty. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Request a prescription for an IV fluid bolus
options.rationale: IV fluid is for a severe deficit. His pressure holds when he stands, so the deficit is not severe.

options.text: Give oral fluids and reassess his urine
options.rationale: Thirst and dark scant urine are the body conserving water as it should. He is alert, swallows and has a steady pressure, so oral replacement is the right route.

options.text: Keep him lying flat and recheck his pressure in an hour
options.rationale: His pressure already holds when he stands. Rest alone replaces none of the water he lost.

options.text: Request electrolyte levels before he drinks anything
options.rationale: Assessing first is tempting. The findings needed to choose the route are already in hand, and waiting delays replacement.

questions.takeaway: Thirst and concentrated urine are normal water conservation. If the client is alert, swallows and has a stable pressure, replace by mouth.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The assessment is complete. A pressure that holds on standing in an alert client who can swallow means the oral route, now.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Alert, swallows, pressure 118/74 lying and standing.
Scant and dark means the kidneys are saving water.

steps.action: Match the route to the severity
steps.detail: Oral for mild to moderate, IV for severe.

elimination.verdict: Give oral fluids and reassess his urine.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old with presbycusis does not respond when the nurse gives discharge instructions from the doorway. His reading glasses are at home. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Sit facing him at eye level with the light on the nurse's face
options.rationale: Correct. He needs to see the speaker's face, and this fixes the distance and the lighting at once.

options.text: Hand him the printed discharge instructions to read
options.rationale: Tempting, because written information is a real strategy for hearing loss. Without his reading glasses he cannot use it.

options.text: Repeat the instructions from the doorway in a louder voice
options.rationale: Shouting distorts speech and raises the pitch he hears worst.

options.text: Give the instructions to his daughter by telephone
options.rationale: This goes around him. Hearing loss is a barrier to communication, not to learning, and the nurse has not yet communicated the right way.

questions.takeaway: Hearing loss: get close, face the client, put the light on your face, speak slowly in a lower pitch.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Written material is a good answer only when the client can see it. The missing glasses are the detail that decides.

steps.action: Cut the option that goes around him
steps.detail: The phone call to the daughter leaves him out.
Shouting distorts sound.
No reading glasses removes the printed sheet.

elimination.verdict: Sit facing him at eye level in good light.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old who works at a computer all day has burning eyes and blurred vision by midafternoon on workdays. Her eye exam last month was normal. Which instruction does the nurse give?

options.text: Raise the screen brightness and sit closer to it
options.rationale: More brightness and a shorter distance add to the strain.

options.text: Every 20 minutes, look 20 feet away for 20 seconds
options.rationale: The pattern fits digital eyestrain, and the 20-20-20 rule rests the focusing muscles through the day.

options.text: Schedule another eye exam to check for new glasses
options.rationale: Tempting because blur suggests a refractive change, but her exam a month ago was normal.

options.text: Wear tinted glasses indoors during the afternoon
options.rationale: Tinted lenses do not rest the eyes from close focus.

questions.takeaway: Eyestrain that follows the workday and clears with rest is managed with the 20-20-20 rule.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Use the timing. Symptoms that build over a day of screen work and a normal recent exam point to habit, not disease.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Workdays, midafternoon, screen job.
A repeat exam would find nothing new.

steps.action: Pick the measure that rests the eyes
steps.detail: Regular distance breaks.

elimination.verdict: The 20-20-20 rule.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old on bed rest for 8 days became confused about the date. The nurse added a large clock, family photos and scheduled visits. Which finding shows the plan is working?

options.text: He lies quietly and has stopped using the call light
options.rationale: Looks calm, but a quiet client who stops calling may be withdrawing further.

options.text: He watches television from breakfast until bedtime
options.rationale: More stimulation is not the same as meaningful stimulation, and it does not show orientation.

options.text: He names the day and the people in the photos
options.rationale: Orientation has returned and he is responding to stimuli that mean something to him.

options.text: He follows directions when the nurse repositions him
options.rationale: He could do that while still disoriented to time.

questions.takeaway: Sensory deprivation is treated with meaningful stimuli. You evaluate it by orientation and engagement.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Match the outcome to the problem. The problem was confusion about the date, so look for the option that shows orientation.

steps.detail: Disorientation from too little meaningful input.

steps.action: Cut calm that is not engagement
steps.detail: Lying quietly and following directions do not show orientation.
A television left on is quantity, not quality.

elimination.verdict: Names the day and the people in the photos.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old with new vision loss in both eyes has stopped going to her card group and has tripped twice this week on her back step. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Refer her to a low vision support group
options.rationale: Helpful for isolation, and it can follow once she is safe at home.

options.text: Explore how she feels about losing her sight
options.rationale: Therapeutic and important, but feelings rank below an injury that is already happening.

options.text: Arrange a ride so she can rejoin the card group
options.rationale: Addresses socialization, which is a real problem and not the most urgent one.

options.text: Mark the step edge and have a handrail secured
options.rationale: She has already tripped twice, so the fall hazard is an actual problem and safety comes first.

questions.takeaway: With sensory loss, risk for injury outranks socialization and coping. An actual hazard is fixed first.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: All four help her. Ask which problem has already caused harm this week.

steps.detail: Isolation, grief and falls.
Two trips on the same step.
Contrast on the edge and a secure rail.

elimination.verdict: Mark the step and secure a handrail.

questions.stem: An 85-year-old with a hearing aid has answered several questions incorrectly this morning. Which task does the nurse assign to the assistive personnel?

options.text: Clean the hearing aid, check the battery and reinsert it
options.rationale: Correct. Routine care of an assistive device is a standard task with a predictable result.

options.text: Find out why the client is answering incorrectly
options.rationale: Working out the cause is assessment, which stays with the nurse.

options.text: Teach the client how to tell when the battery is low
options.rationale: Teaching is the nurse's responsibility.

options.text: Decide whether a writing board would work better for this client
options.rationale: Choosing a communication method takes nursing judgment.

questions.takeaway: Assistive personnel care for the device. The nurse assesses, teaches and decides.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Look at the verbs. Find out, teach and decide belong to the nurse. Clean and check can be delegated.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find out, teach and decide are judgment.
Cleaning and checking a battery follows fixed steps.

elimination.verdict: Clean the aid, check the battery and reinsert it.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old with diabetic retinopathy lives alone and can no longer read the markings on her insulin syringe. She wants to keep managing her own insulin. Which plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Arrange for a neighbor to draw up and give each dose
options.rationale: This is safe, and it takes away the independence she asked to keep.

options.text: Teach her to use an insulin pen with audible dose clicks
options.rationale: Correct. It replaces the lost visual cue with sound, so she stays safe and stays independent.

options.text: Have her daughter prefill a week of syringes on each visit
options.rationale: Tempting and sometimes used. She still depends on someone else and cannot adjust a dose herself.

options.text: Advise her to use a brighter overhead kitchen light
options.rationale: More light can add glare and does not make fine markings readable with retinal damage.

questions.takeaway: Adapt the task to the senses that still work. Keep the client as independent as safety allows.
questions.coverage: Not in Lecture PPT. The Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Two options are safe. The stem says she lives alone and wants to do it herself, and that picks the one that keeps her in charge.

steps.action: Cut the option that does not fix the problem
steps.detail: Bright light does not restore fine vision.
A neighbor or daughter makes her dependent.
She wants to manage her own insulin.

elimination.verdict: The insulin pen with audible clicks.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old says she cannot tell where her feet are when she walks to the bathroom at night. Which statement shows the home safety teaching was effective?

options.text: "I keep the hall dark so I fall back asleep faster."
options.rationale: In the dark she loses the one sense that can stand in for position sense.

options.text: "I wear thick cushioned socks so my steps are softer."
options.rationale: Sounds protective, but padding dulls what her feet can still feel and socks slip.

options.text: "I walk there quickly so I am up for less time."
options.rationale: Tempting as less time at risk. Hurrying with poor position sense makes a misstep more likely.

options.text: "I leave a hall light on and hold the handrail."
options.rationale: Position sense declines after 60, so she replaces it with vision and a secure rail.

questions.takeaway: When a sense declines, safety depends on replacing it with another cue, such as light and a handrail, not on being careful with the sense that is fading.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Ask of each statement: does it give her another way to know where her feet are?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Position sense in the feet, an expected change after 60.
A dark hall and padded socks.
Speed does not replace a sense.
Light and a handrail.

elimination.verdict: The hall light and handrail statement.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old with chronic pain on a step-down unit is restless and cannot focus. Staff enter hourly at night for separate vital signs, laboratory draws and repositioning. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Request a prescription for a medication to help him sleep
options.rationale: Tempting, because he is not resting. A drug adds another factor that alters perception and leaves the cause in place.

options.text: Request transfer to a private room at the end of the hall
options.rationale: Tempting, because it lowers noise. The interruptions come from the care schedule and would follow him.

options.text: Combine the night tasks and schedule protected rest periods
options.rationale: Correct. The stem names the cause, hourly separate entries, and clustering care removes it.

options.text: Reorient him to place and time at every entry
options.rationale: Reorientation helps confusion. Doing it at every entry adds more stimulation.

questions.takeaway: Sensory overload: combine activities, schedule rest, set quiet time. Fix the environment before adding a drug.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Find the cause in the stem. It is the schedule, not the room and not the client.

steps.detail: Hourly separate entries at night.
Reorienting at every entry is more stimulation.

steps.action: Test the room and the drug
steps.detail: Neither one changes how often staff walk in.

elimination.verdict: Combine the tasks and protect rest periods.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old with macular degeneration says she manages her medications fine at home. Which assessment best tells the nurse whether that is safe?

options.text: Have her read a pill bottle label and set up a dose
options.rationale: Functional ability is judged by watching the task itself, here reading a label and preparing a dose.

options.text: Measure her visual acuity with a Snellen chart
options.rationale: Gives a number for distance vision, which does not show whether she can read a label.

options.text: Ask her daughter how she has been managing her pills at home
options.rationale: Useful background, but it is secondhand and the client is able to show the nurse directly.

options.text: Review the eye clinic's most recent examination

questions.stem: A 46-year-old carpenter has ringing in his ears after work, and testing shows mild high frequency hearing loss. He says the damage is already done. Which teaching is the priority?

questions.stem: A 77-year-old arrives on the unit at night, and the emergency department reports him as confused because he answers questions inappropriately. His daughter is at the bedside with his belongings. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Start a bed alarm and move him near the nurses' station
options.rationale: Tempting, because safety matters for a confused client. The cause is not known yet, and the answer may be in the bag of belongings.

options.text: Ask the daughter whether he uses hearing aids or glasses
options.rationale: Correct. Establishing the baseline comes first, and an uncorrected hearing deficit looks like confusion.

options.text: Request a prescription for a urinalysis and blood work
options.rationale: Reasonable if the confusion is real. A quick baseline check comes before testing.

options.text: Reorient him to place and time every hour
options.rationale: Reorientation does not help a client who cannot hear it.

questions.takeaway: In acute care, establish the baseline. Know whether the client already has a deficit before you label the behavior.

Asking about hearing aids and glasses.

questions.stem: A 73-year-old received his first hearing aid. Which statement shows he understood the teaching?

options.text: "At bedtime I will take it out, turn it off and open the battery door."
options.rationale: Correct. This saves the battery and lets moisture dry out.

options.text: "I will leave it in while I shower so I can hear the smoke alarm."
options.rationale: Water damages the aid. A flashing alert system covers alarm safety.

options.text: "I will put it in before I use hairspray so it stays in place."
options.rationale: Spray clogs the microphone. It goes in after hair products.

options.text: "If it whistles I will turn the volume up until it stops."
options.rationale: Whistling means poor fit or too much volume. Turning it up makes it worse.

questions.takeaway: Hearing aid care: keep it dry, off and open at night, in after hair products, reseat it if it whistles.

questions.stem: An 87-year-old with cataracts becomes agitated at dusk and tries to climb out of bed. The room is dim and her glasses are on the windowsill. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Turn on the bed alarm and raise all side rails
options.rationale: Tempting, because she is trying to get up. An alarm reports the attempt and does nothing about why she is frightened, and four rails act as a restraint.

options.text: Request a prescription for a sitter overnight
options.rationale: A sitter may be needed later. A simpler step has not been tried.

options.text: Turn on soft lighting and put her glasses on
options.rationale: Correct. Aging pupils and cataracts need more light, and the stem shows both the light and the glasses are missing.

options.text: Request a prescription for a low dose sedative
options.rationale: A sedative adds fall risk and clouds perception further.

questions.takeaway: Older eyes adapt poorly to the dark. Correct the light and the device before using alarms, sitters or drugs.

Light and glasses, then alarm, then sitter, then sedative.

questions.stem: An 81-year-old with muffled hearing and ear fullness had impacted cerumen removed by irrigation. Which finding best shows the treatment was effective?

options.text: He denies pain in the ear
options.rationale: Pain was not the problem being treated. This shows no harm, not benefit.

options.text: He reports no dizziness or nausea after the procedure
options.rationale: This means he tolerated the irrigation. It says nothing about his hearing.

options.text: The return fluid ran clear at the end
options.rationale: Clear return suggests the wax is out. It does not confirm that function returned.

options.text: He repeats words the nurse whispers from 2 feet away
options.rationale: Correct. The problem was conductive hearing loss, so restored hearing is the outcome that counts.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate by the problem you treated. Cerumen impaction is a correctable conductive loss, so check hearing.

questions.stem: An 89-year-old began an opioid and a sleeping pill 2 nights ago. She now misjudges the distance to her chair and reaches for objects that are not there. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Request an eye examination for new glasses
options.rationale: Tempting because the problem looks visual, but vision does not change in two nights without a cause.

options.text: Review the two new medications with the provider
options.rationale: The change is new and began with drugs known to alter perception, so the cause is addressed first.

options.text: Place a clock and calendar and reorient her
options.rationale: Right for deprivation. Her cues began with new medications, not with too little stimulation.

options.text: Explain to the family that perception declines with age
options.rationale: A new change is not assumed to be aging.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old with both eyes patched after a chemical splash is admitted. His hearing is normal. Which actions does the nurse include in his care? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: His hearing is intact. Speak in a normal voice.

options.rationale: Every change in layout erases the map he has learned.

questions.nursesNote: 0900: 82-year-old admitted 2 days ago with heart failure. Needs a brighter lamp to read the menu. Has trouble telling the blue cup from the green one. Misses high pitched voices in conversation. Says the left ear "went quiet" when she woke today. Started IV furosemide yesterday. Unsteady when standing this morning, steady yesterday.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that require follow-up and should not be attributed to aging.

segments.text: Needs a brighter lamp to read the menu
segments.rationale: Aging pupils dilate less, so more light is needed. Expected.

segments.text: Has trouble telling the blue cup from the green one
segments.rationale: Blue and green discrimination declines with age. Expected.

segments.text: Misses high pitched voices in conversation
segments.rationale: High frequencies are lost first in presbycusis. Expected and gradual.

segments.text: Says the left ear "went quiet" when she woke today
segments.rationale: Sudden hearing loss in one ear is new, not aging. It needs prompt evaluation.

segments.text: Started IV furosemide yesterday
segments.rationale: A loop diuretic is ototoxic, and the timing fits the new hearing loss. The provider needs to know.

segments.text: Unsteady when standing this morning, steady yesterday
segments.rationale: A new balance change with an ear change raises fall risk and points to the inner ear.

questions.takeaway: Gradual and both sides is aging. Sudden, one sided or new since yesterday is reported, and you look for an ototoxic drug.

questions.stem: A 53-year-old with expressive aphasia grimaces and holds his abdomen. An as-needed analgesic is prescribed for his knee pain. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Give the as-needed analgesic and reassess within the hour

options.rationale: Patience is part of aphasia care. On its own it delays assessment of a new pain.

options.text: Ask yes or no questions about the pain, using a communication board
options.rationale: The assessment is not done yet. Yes or no questions and a board let him tell the nurse where and what the pain is.

options.rationale: A sensible adaptation that accepts the change without finding out why it happened.

options.rationale: Cataract change is slow and painless over months.

questions.stem: A client with hearing loss nodded and said yes throughout insulin pen teaching. The nurse sat facing him in good light and spoke slowly. Which action does the nurse take next?

options.rationale: Defensible because written information supports hearing loss. It reinforces the teaching without showing whether he understood.

questions.stem: A client with Meniere disease follows a low-sodium diet and takes a diuretic. She reports fewer vertigo attacks this month, and says she twice dropped to the floor with no dizziness beforehand. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Reinforce the plan because the attacks have decreased
options.rationale: Fewer attacks is real progress. The two falls show a new and more dangerous problem.

options.rationale: Standard teaching for vertigo. These falls came with no warning, so there is nothing to act on.

options.text: Report the falls and add fall precautions
options.rationale: Sudden falls without warning are drop attacks. They mark a serious safety risk that the current plan does not cover.

options.rationale: Vestibular rehabilitation helps balance and tempts. It does not prevent a sudden drop with no warning.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old who lives alone says food has had no smell or taste since a viral illness. She cooks on a gas stove. Which plan is the priority?

options.text: Suggest stronger seasonings and varied textures
options.rationale: A sound plan for appetite, and it is the tempting choice. It does nothing about a leak or fire she cannot smell.

options.rationale: Reasonable follow-up for intake, but weight loss is a slower risk than gas or smoke.

options.rationale: Helps intake and isolation. It does not address the hazard in her kitchen.

options.rationale: Smell is her warning system for gas, smoke and spoiled food. Detectors and dated food replace it.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old with diabetic neuropathy says his feet are always cold in bed and asks for a heating pad. Which action does the nurse take?

questions.stem: A 90-year-old resident removes her hearing aids in the dining room, saying the clatter is unbearable, and now eats alone in her room. Which plan is best?

questions.stem: A withdrawn long-term care resident sits all day beside a television tuned to news she ignores. Her chart notes she taught piano for 40 years. Which plan is best?

options.rationale: Gets her attention first so she can use his face and lips from the first word.

options.text: He speaks loudly close to her better ear
options.rationale: Tempting because the better ear matters, but loud speech distorts and she loses his face.

options.text: He answers the nurse's questions on her behalf
options.rationale: Takes her out of the conversation.

questions.takeaway: With hearing loss, get attention and face the person before the first word. Rephrase what is missed.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Ask which behavior gives her the most cues. Volume and repetition add sound, not understanding.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Attention first, face to face, clear normal speech, rephrase.
Repeating and loud speech each break one rule.
She is left out.

elimination.verdict: Touches her arm and waits for eye contact.

questions.stem: A home health nurse visits a 93-year-old woman with reduced vision and poor balance. Which observations does the nurse identify as hazards to correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: A throw rug at the end of the hallway
options.rationale: A loose edge is a trip risk she may not see.

options.text: A raised threshold between the kitchen and hall
options.rationale: Thresholds should be level. She cannot judge the height change.

options.text: A bare bulb reflecting off a waxed floor
options.rationale: Glare washes out what she can see. Light should be bright and diffused.

options.text: Medications kept in the same kitchen drawer
options.rationale: Consistent locations help a person with low vision find things.

options.text: A dark handrail mounted on a pale wall
options.rationale: Sharp contrast makes the rail easy to find.

options.text: Newspapers stacked beside her chair
options.rationale: Clutter in a walking path is a fall hazard.

questions.takeaway: For low vision at home: clear the path, level the floor, cut glare, and keep contrast and consistent placement.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Judge each item alone. Ask whether it makes the space less predictable or harder to see.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Rug, threshold and stacked papers.
Bare bulb on a shiny floor is glare.
Same drawer and a contrasting rail are adaptations.

elimination.verdict: Rug, threshold, glare and clutter.

questions.scenario: A daughter is preparing her home for her mother, who has moderate hearing loss in both ears, wears hearing aids by day and is moving in next week. The daughter lists what she plans to do.
questions.stem: For each plan, indicate whether it supports or does not support the client's safety and communication.

rows.text: A doorbell and smoke alarm that flash a light
rows.rationale: A visual alert replaces a sound she may miss, most of all at night with her aids out.

rows.text: Keeping the television on in the background for company
rows.rationale: Background noise competes with voices and makes her aids less useful.

rows.text: An amplified telephone in her bedroom
rows.rationale: Lets her make and take calls on her own, including a call for help.

rows.text: Calling to her from the next room at mealtimes
rows.rationale: She needs the speaker's face. Go to her and get her attention first.

rows.text: Writing down appointment times and medication changes
rows.rationale: Written information backs up speech for details that must not be misheard.

rows.text: Answering the provider's questions for her at visits
rows.rationale: Saves time, but it removes her from her own care and hides what she did not hear.

questions.takeaway: For hearing loss at home: replace sound alerts with light, amplify the phone, write key details, cut background noise and keep her speaking for herself.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Test each plan with one question: does it give her another way to get the message, or does it add noise or take her place?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Keep what replaces or boosts sound
steps.detail: Flashing alerts, amplified phone, written notes.

steps.action: Cut what adds noise or distance
steps.detail: Background television and calling from another room.
She stays the one who answers.

elimination.verdict: Supports: flashing alerts, amplified phone, written notes. The other three do not.

questions.stem: A sedated 47-year-old on a ventilator does not respond to voice. The assistive personnel bathes him without speaking to him while discussing his prognosis with a coworker. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Have staff tell him each step before touching him
options.rationale: His ears may still receive sound even though no one can confirm what he perceives. Talking to him gives meaningful input and protects his dignity.

options.text: Turn on the television to give him background orientation
options.rationale: Unselected noise is not meaningful stimulation, and it does not fix the bedside conversation.

options.text: Ask staff to work quietly so he can rest
options.rationale: Tempting because rest matters. Silence during touch removes the only meaningful input he gets.

options.text: Document that he cannot perceive speech
options.rationale: Perception cannot be measured in a sedated client, so the nurse does not assume it is absent.

questions.takeaway: Reception can continue when response is absent. Speak to the unresponsive client as if he hears every word.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: No response tells you about reaction. It tells you nothing certain about reception. Choose the option that assumes he hears.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Reception, perception, reaction. Only reaction is visibly missing.
Documenting that he cannot perceive claims something nobody tested.
Quiet removes input. Explanation supplies meaningful input.

elimination.verdict: Explain each step to him before touching.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old stone mason was treated for a chip in his eye and taught eye protection. Which observation at his next visit shows the teaching was effective?

options.text: He wears dark sunglasses while cutting stone
options.rationale: Sunglasses cut glare and ultraviolet light. They leave the sides open and are not impact rated.

options.text: He wears wraparound safety glasses while cutting stone
options.rationale: Impact rated eyewear with side coverage worn during the hazard is the behavior the teaching aimed for.

options.text: He keeps saline in the truck to rinse his eyes
options.rationale: Useful after an exposure. It treats the injury and does not prevent it.

options.text: He looks away when the saw throws chips
options.rationale: Chips travel faster than he can turn.

questions.takeaway: Prevention of occupational eye injury means protective eyewear made for the hazard, worn every time the hazard is present.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Ask which option prevents the injury and which only responds to it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Saline is response.
Only one covers the sides and resists impact.
Turning away is not protection.

elimination.verdict: Wraparound safety glasses during the task.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old with worsening vision and diabetes has missed three eye appointments. He says, "I know I should go." Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Ask what has kept him from getting to the visits
options.rationale: He already knows the importance. The barrier, such as cost, transportation or time off work, has to be identified before any plan fits.

options.text: Explain again how diabetes damages the retina
options.rationale: He states he knows he should go, so more teaching answers a question he did not ask.

options.text: Book the next available appointment for him
options.rationale: Tempting because it is action. A fourth appointment fails for the same unknown reason.

options.text: Refer him to social services for assistance
options.rationale: May be the right step once the barrier is known.

questions.takeaway: Missed care is often an access problem, not a knowledge problem. Find the barrier before you teach or refer.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: His own words rule out one option. Then ask whether the nurse knows enough to act yet.

steps.detail: He knows he should go, so repeating the teaching adds nothing.
Nobody has asked why he misses visits.
Booking and referral come after the barrier is named.

elimination.verdict: Ask him what gets in the way.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old who plans to become pregnant next year does not know whether she had rubella vaccine as a child. Which plan best protects her baby's hearing and vision?

options.text: Give the rubella vaccine once pregnancy is confirmed
options.rationale: A live vaccine is not given during pregnancy.

options.text: Arrange hearing and vision screening for the newborn at birth
options.rationale: Screening detects a loss after it happens. The question asks for protection.

options.text: Check rubella immunity now and vaccinate before conception
options.rationale: Rubella in pregnancy damages the developing ear and eye. The vaccine is live, so immunity is settled before pregnancy.

options.text: Advise her to avoid sick contacts while pregnant
options.rationale: Helpful, and far less reliable than immunity.

questions.takeaway: Immunization prevents infectious causes of sensory loss. Rubella immunity is confirmed before pregnancy, not during it.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Two options act on the vaccine at opposite times. Timing decides.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Vaccinate before conception or after pregnancy is confirmed.
Not during pregnancy.
Newborn screening finds a loss. It does not prevent one.

elimination.verdict: Check immunity now and vaccinate before conception.

questions.stem: Staff were asked to keep the belongings of a 72-year-old with severe low vision in fixed places. Which finding best shows the plan is working?

options.text: She calls staff promptly whenever she needs her water
options.rationale: Shows she depends on staff, which is what the plan was meant to reduce.

options.text: A sign over the bed lists where each item belongs
options.rationale: A sign is a step in the plan. It does not show the result for the client.

options.text: She can describe where each of her belongings is usually kept
options.rationale: Tempting. Knowing the usual place does not show the items are actually there.

options.text: After cleaning she finds her call light and water unaided
options.rationale: Finding her own things after the room has been disturbed shows the placement stayed consistent and usable.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate an environmental plan by what the client can do on her own, not by whether staff completed a step.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Outcome questions ask what the client does. Cross out anything that is a staff action.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A sign is an intervention.
Calling for water is the problem continuing.
Finding the items beats describing them.

elimination.verdict: She finds her call light and water without help.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old with receptive aphasia after a stroke looks at the nurse blankly when told, "It is time to take your morning pills." Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Repeat the sentence more slowly and loudly
options.rationale: Receptive aphasia is a problem understanding language, not hearing it, so volume does not help.

options.text: Give him a written card that says pills
options.rationale: Reading uses the same language comprehension that is impaired.

options.text: Hand him the cup and mime swallowing
options.rationale: He cannot decode spoken or written words, so the message is sent by gesture and demonstration.

options.text: Ask him yes or no questions about the pills
