options.rationale: That is the approach for expressive aphasia, where he understands and cannot find words.

questions.takeaway: Receptive aphasia: he cannot understand words. Use gestures, demonstration and short simple cues. Yes or no questions are for expressive aphasia.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Decide which direction of language is broken. Three options still rely on words.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Understanding, not speaking.
Louder speech, a written card and questions all need comprehension.
Gesture and demonstration.

elimination.verdict: Show him. Hand him the cup and mime the action.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old has lost the left half of the visual field in both eyes after a stroke and is a fall risk. Where does the nurse place the call light and bedside table?

options.text: On his left, so that he must practice scanning to find them
options.rationale: Tempting as rehabilitation. A call light he cannot see fails him the first time he needs it.

options.text: On his right, while teaching him to turn his head left
options.rationale: Safety items go where he can see them now. Scanning toward the blind side is taught so he learns to compensate.

options.text: At the foot of the bed, centered in front of him
options.rationale: Out of reach, and half of it still falls in the lost field.

options.text: On whichever side the staff find most convenient
options.rationale: Placement follows his visual field, not staff workflow.

questions.takeaway: With a visual field loss, put safety items in the intact field and teach scanning toward the lost side.
questions.coverage: Not in Lecture PPT. The Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Safety before rehabilitation. The call light has to work today.

steps.detail: Right side or left side.
He must be able to see and reach the call light now.
The key still teaches head turning.

elimination.verdict: Intact side, plus scanning practice.

questions.scenario: The charge nurse reviews four clients whose behavior has changed.
questions.stem: For each client, indicate whether the plan should add meaningful stimulation or reduce stimulation.

rows.text: On bed rest for 11 days in a private room, bored, misjudges the time of day
rows.rationale: Restricted environment with poor time judgment is deprivation.

rows.text: In the emergency department hallway for 9 hours, restless, startles at each overhead page
rows.rationale: Constant noise and activity that the client cannot filter.

rows.text: Resident with no visitors this month, sits facing a blank wall and is tearful
rows.rationale: Loss of social contact and meaningful input.

rows.text: Chronic pain, hourly checks overnight, picks at the dressing and cannot focus
rows.rationale: Pain plus frequent monitoring is the overload setting.

rows.text: Both eyes patched after surgery, quiet room, reports seeing shapes that are not there
rows.rationale: Removing vision in a quiet room starves the brain of input, and perceptual changes follow.

questions.takeaway: Deprivation shows as boredom, withdrawal and distorted time or perception. Overload shows as restlessness and scattered attention. The plans are opposites.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Read the setting before the behavior. Isolation, bed rest and patches take input away. Hallways, alarms and hourly checks pile it on.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Private room, no visitors and patched eyes are low input.
Hallway and hourly checks are high input.
Bored or tearful against restless and startled.

elimination.verdict: Add, reduce, add, reduce, add.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old who became blind this year and hears well must learn to use an incentive spirometer after surgery. His wife will help him at home. Which approach does the nurse use?

options.text: Teach his wife the steps so she can coach him at home
options.rationale: Tempting because she will help at home. He is the one who must use the device every hour, so the teaching goes to him and includes her.

options.text: Speak slowly and loudly while demonstrating the device
options.rationale: He hears well, so the nurse speaks normally. A demonstration he cannot see teaches him nothing.

options.text: Describe each part in detail while he holds and explores the device
options.rationale: With vision loss the nurse speaks normally, describes objects in detail and allows touch. His hands and hearing replace what his eyes cannot give him.

options.text: Give him a large print instruction sheet to keep at the bedside
options.rationale: Large print helps low vision. The stem says he is blind.

questions.takeaway: Vision loss: speak normally, describe objects in detail and let the client touch them. Teach the client and include the family.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The stem gives two facts about his senses: blind, hears well. Pick the option that uses the senses he has and keeps him as the learner.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Blind and hears well.

steps.action: Cut what needs sight or louder speech
steps.detail: Large print and a watched demonstration need vision. Loud speech treats a hearing loss he does not have.
Teaching only his wife goes around him. Describing while he handles the device teaches him.

elimination.verdict: Describe it in detail and let him touch it.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old who depends on two hearing aids is leaving for a procedure where staff will give him instructions. The transporter says valuables stay on the unit. Which plan does the nurse use?

options.text: Hearing aids locked in the bedside drawer, with a note that he is hard of hearing
options.rationale: Tempting because it protects the aids from loss, which is the transporter's concern. It leaves him unable to hear the instructions.

options.text: Hearing aids in a tissue in his gown pocket, to put in if needed
options.rationale: Not in his ears when he needs them, and a tissue is how aids are thrown away.

options.text: One hearing aid in, the other kept on the unit as a spare
options.rationale: The stem says he depends on both, so one aid leaves him hearing less than his baseline.

options.text: Hearing aids in and working, and the devices listed on the transfer record
options.rationale: He needs to hear the instructions, so the aids go with him. Listing them on the transfer record answers the concern about loss.

questions.takeaway: Assistive devices go with the client to every test and procedure where he must communicate: in place, working and documented.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Two concerns compete: losing the aids and hearing the instructions. Ask which option answers both.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: He must hear instructions during the procedure.

steps.action: Cut the options with aids out
steps.detail: Drawer and pocket both leave him without hearing.
He depends on two, not one.
Documenting the devices tracks them without removing them.

elimination.verdict: Both aids in, working and documented.

questions.stem: A client with hearing loss faces the nurse in a quiet, well lit room. Twice the nurse says, "Take this with food," slowly and clearly, and he looks puzzled. Which action does the nurse take next?

options.text: Say the sentence a third time in a much louder voice
options.rationale: Shouting is avoided with hearing loss. It distorts the words he already missed twice.

options.text: Write the instruction down and show it to him
options.rationale: Face to face, slow, clear speech has been tried and has not worked. Written information is the next strategy for hearing loss.

options.text: Say the sentence a third time directly into his ear
options.rationale: He loses the face to face view of the nurse, and the same words are repeated.

options.text: Give the instruction to his wife when she visits tonight
options.rationale: Tempting because it gets the message home. It leaves the client out of his own care when another way to reach him is available now.

questions.takeaway: Hearing loss: face to face, slow clear speech, written information, no shouting. When speech has failed, write it down.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The stem shows the spoken strategies are already in place and failing. Look for the option that changes the channel.

steps.detail: Facing him, quiet, good light, slow clear speech.
Louder and into the ear both repeat the same spoken words.

steps.action: Keep the client as the receiver
steps.detail: Writing reaches him now. Waiting for his wife goes around him.

elimination.verdict: Write it down and show him.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews a discharge plan with an alert 84-year-old who has hearing loss. Her daughter is at the bedside. Which action by the nurse needs correction?

options.text: Gets the client's attention before starting to speak to her
options.rationale: Correct. She must be looking before the first word.

options.text: Explains the plan to the daughter while the client watches
options.rationale: The client is alert and is the one being discharged. The nurse speaks to her directly and includes the daughter.

options.text: Gives the client the instructions in writing as well
options.rationale: Correct. Written information backs up what was said.

options.text: Asks the client to explain the plan back
options.rationale: Correct. A nod does not show understanding.

questions.takeaway: With family present, speak to the client and include the family. Hearing loss does not make the family the audience.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Three actions involve the client. Find the one that goes around her.

steps.detail: You want the wrong action.
Three options are directed at the client.
One speaks only to the daughter.

elimination.verdict: Explaining it to the daughter instead of the client.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old on day 4 in intensive care is alert, picks at his IV dressing and needs reorienting every few minutes. The assistive personnel asks for mitt restraints. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Apply the mitts and check his skin every 2 hours
options.rationale: A restraint is the most restrictive choice and adds one more stimulus. The cause of the picking has not been treated yet.

options.text: Dim the lights, reduce noise and set a quiet time
options.rationale: Picking at dressings and needing constant reorientation are signs of sensory overload. Lowering the stimuli treats the cause and is the least restrictive step.

options.text: Reorient him each time he touches the dressing
options.rationale: Tempting because reorientation is good care. He already needs it every few minutes, which shows it is not holding while the stimulation continues.

options.text: Ask his family to stay and talk with him all day
options.rationale: Constant conversation adds stimulation to a brain that already cannot filter what it receives.

questions.takeaway: Picking at tubes or dressings with constant reorientation in intensive care points to sensory overload. Reduce the stimuli before you restrain.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two options manage the behavior and one manages the cause. Day 4 in intensive care tells you what the cause is.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Intensive care, picking at the dressing, reorienting every few minutes.
Mitts and all day conversation both add input.
Reorienting is already failing. Reducing stimuli removes the reason for it.

elimination.verdict: Reduce stimulation first. It is the least restrictive action that treats the cause.

questions.stem: The charge nurse reviews five clients. Which clients does the nurse identify as at risk for sensory deprivation? Select all that apply.

options.text: On bed rest in a private room, with no visitors this week
options.rationale: Bed rest is a restricted environment, and no visitors removes social interaction.

options.text: In isolation, where gowned and masked staff enter only briefly
options.rationale: Isolation limits both the amount and the quality of stimulation.

options.text: In intensive care with hourly checks and frequent monitor alarms
options.rationale: This is too much stimulation. Frequent monitoring is a setting for sensory overload.

options.text: An avid reader whose only glasses broke 5 days ago
options.rationale: A sensory deficit with no working device cuts off stimulation that was meaningful to this client.

options.text: On a stretcher in a busy emergency department hallway
options.rationale: A busy hallway gives excessive noise and activity, which is a setting for overload.

questions.takeaway: Deprivation risk: isolation, bed rest, restricted environments, no visitors, and a deficit without its assistive device. Intensive care and the emergency department are overload settings.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Ask of each client: is meaningful input missing, or is there more input than the brain can filter?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Hourly checks with alarms and a busy hallway are too much input.
Bed rest without visitors and isolation both limit stimulation.
Broken glasses take reading away from a client who relies on it.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D.

questions.stem: An 88-year-old in isolation for 5 days has been bored and withdrawn. This morning he is newly drowsy and does not know where he is. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Check vital signs, oxygen saturation and blood glucose
options.rationale: Drowsiness and disorientation that began this morning are a sudden change. A physical cause has to be looked for before the change is blamed on isolation or age.

options.text: Open the blinds and place a clock and calendar in view
options.rationale: Right for the boredom and withdrawal of deprivation, and it will be done. It does not explain a change that appeared overnight.

options.text: Ask his family to visit and bring familiar photos
options.rationale: Meaningful stimuli help deprivation over days. They do not address new drowsiness today.

options.text: Complete a full mental status examination
options.rationale: It describes the confusion in more detail without finding out why it started.

questions.takeaway: Deprivation explains slow changes such as boredom and withdrawal. A new or sudden change is assessed for a physical cause first and is never assumed to be age or the environment.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Split the stem in two: what has been true for days, and what is new this morning. The question is about the new part.

steps.detail: Drowsy and disoriented since this morning.
Blinds, clock, photos and visits fit the boredom of the past days.

steps.action: Pick the assessment that finds a cause
steps.detail: Vital signs, oxygen and glucose can be acted on. A longer mental status exam only describes the problem.

elimination.verdict: Check for a physical cause first, then add stimulation.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old in a busy emergency department is restless and cannot follow instructions. Lights are dimmed and care is combined. He rates his back pain 8 of 10, and an analgesic is prescribed. Which action does the nurse take next?

options.text: Reassess his pain rating in 30 minutes
options.rationale: The pain is already rated and it is severe. Waiting leaves the strongest stimulus in place.

options.text: Reorient him and repeat the instructions slowly
options.rationale: Tempting, but he cannot attend to words while severe pain is competing for his attention.

options.text: Bring a family member to the bedside for company
options.rationale: Company adds input and does nothing for the pain.

options.text: Give the prescribed analgesic
options.rationale: Pain is a stimulus. The environment has been quieted and the pain is assessed, so the remaining source of overload is treated.

questions.takeaway: Pain is one of the stimuli that causes sensory overload. When the room is already quiet and the pain is rated, treat the pain.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The stem tells you what has already been done and gives a pain rating. The assessment is complete, so look for the action.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Lights dimmed, care combined, pain rated 8 of 10.
A recheck in 30 minutes delays treatment of known severe pain.
Repeating instructions and adding a visitor both add stimulation.

elimination.verdict: Give the analgesic. Pain is the stimulus that is left.

questions.stem: The nurse receives morning report on four clients on a medical unit. Which client does the nurse see first?

options.text: Transferred from intensive care overnight, restless and tugging at his oxygen tubing
options.rationale: Restlessness and playing with tubes are behaviors of sensory overload, and losing his oxygen is an immediate risk to breathing.

options.text: On bed rest for a week, tearful and saying the days run together
options.rationale: Affective and time changes of sensory deprivation. They need a plan today, and they are not an immediate danger.

options.text: Hearing aid battery died, with discharge teaching due in an hour
options.rationale: A communication barrier that must be fixed before the teaching. It can wait an hour.

options.text: Blind since childhood, asking for help to set up his breakfast tray
options.rationale: A long-standing deficit and a routine request.

questions.takeaway: Among clients with sensory alterations, the one whose behavior threatens an airway, breathing or a line comes first.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: All four have a real sensory problem. Ask which one can be harmed in the next few minutes.

steps.detail: Blindness since childhood with a tray request is stable.

steps.action: Cut what has a time buffer
steps.detail: The battery has an hour. The tearful client needs a plan, not a rescue.
Tugging at oxygen tubing can remove his oxygen.

elimination.verdict: The restless client pulling at his oxygen tubing.

questions.stem: An 83-year-old began IV furosemide 3 days ago. Her daughter blames the drug for her hearing loss. The client has missed high-pitched voices for years and notices no change this week. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Hold the next dose and notify the prescriber of the hearing loss
options.rationale: Tempting because diuretics are ototoxic, and this is the right step for a new change. Her loss is years old and has not changed since the drug began.

options.text: Tell the daughter that this drug does not affect hearing
options.rationale: False reassurance. Diuretics are on the list of ototoxic drugs, so a later change would matter.

options.text: Ask for a hearing test before she receives another dose
options.rationale: Delays a needed drug for a loss that is long-standing and unchanged. A routine hearing exam can be arranged without holding treatment.

options.text: Record today's hearing as her baseline and have her report any change
options.rationale: High-pitched sounds lost over years with no change this week fit age related loss, not the drug. Because the drug is ototoxic, the nurse sets the baseline so that a new change can be recognized.

questions.takeaway: Ototoxic drugs (diuretics, aminoglycosides, NSAIDs, quinine drugs, chemotherapy) call for a hearing baseline. A new change is reported. An old, unchanged loss is documented and monitored.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Time the hearing loss against the drug. The loss is years old, the drug is 3 days old, and nothing has changed this week.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Years of high-pitched loss, no change since the drug started 3 days ago.
Diuretics can affect hearing, so the daughter cannot be told otherwise.

steps.action: Cut the options that stop the drug
steps.detail: Holding the dose or waiting for a test treats an old loss as a new one.
A recorded baseline is what lets a new change be caught.

elimination.verdict: Record the baseline and monitor. Nothing new has happened to report.

questions.stem: The family of a 70-year-old in intensive care with sensory overload was taught how to help during visits. Which statement shows the teaching was effective?

options.text: "One of us will sit quietly with him and let him nap."
options.rationale: Keeps a familiar person present while lowering stimulation and protecting rest.

options.text: "We will take turns so someone is always talking to him."
options.rationale: Constant conversation is more input for a brain that cannot filter it.

options.text: "We will keep the television on so he is not lonely."
options.rationale: Background television is noise without meaning, and it adds to the load.

options.text: "We will stay away until he leaves intensive care."
options.rationale: Tempting because it lowers stimulation. Absence of visitors brings isolation and loneliness, so one problem is traded for another.

questions.takeaway: In sensory overload, family help by being a calm, quiet presence and by protecting rest. They neither fill the silence nor stay away.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two statements add input and one removes the family completely. Look for the statement that lowers stimulation and keeps social contact.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Nonstop talking and a television both add stimulation.
Staying away and sitting quietly both reduce input.
Only sitting quietly keeps a familiar person with him.

elimination.verdict: One quiet visitor who lets him rest.

questions.stem: A stable client with long-standing low vision and hearing aids was admitted overnight, and the nurse has oriented him to the room. Which task does the nurse delegate to assistive personnel?

options.text: Determine how much his hearing loss limits his understanding of teaching
options.rationale: This is assessment, which stays with the nurse.

options.text: Keep his glasses, hearing aids and call bell in the same reachable places
options.rationale: A routine task with a predictable result for a stable client. Consistent placement and an accessible call bell are safety measures anyone on the team can maintain.

options.text: Teach his wife how to speak so that he understands her
options.rationale: Teaching stays with the nurse.

options.text: Decide which safety measures his fall risk calls for
options.rationale: Planning care requires nursing judgment.

questions.takeaway: Assistive personnel maintain the environment the nurse set up: devices in place, objects in consistent spots, call bell in reach. The nurse keeps assessment, teaching and planning.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Look at the first word of each option. Determine, teach and decide are nursing judgment. Keep is a task.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Determine, teach and decide all need judgment.
He is stable and already oriented by the nurse.
Keeping objects in place has a predictable result.

elimination.verdict: Delegate keeping his devices and call bell in consistent, reachable places.

questions.stem: A 92-year-old admitted from home scores in the impaired range on a mental status screening. His daughter then arrives with his hearing aids and glasses, which he was not wearing during the screening. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Document cognitive impairment and add fall precautions
options.rationale: The score was obtained while he could not hear or see well, so it may not reflect his thinking.

options.text: Request a referral for a dementia evaluation
options.rationale: A referral built on a score that may only measure a sensory deficit.

options.text: Repeat the screening with his hearing aids and glasses in place
options.rationale: Questions he could not hear or see cannot measure cognition. The baseline is set with his devices in and working.

options.text: Ask his daughter to answer the screening questions for him
options.rationale: Her answers would show her knowledge, not his mental status.

questions.takeaway: Establish the baseline with assistive devices in place. A sensory deficit can look like confusion, and a mental status score taken without hearing aids or glasses is not valid.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The stem adds one fact after the score: he was tested without his devices. Ask what that fact does to the score.

steps.detail: No hearing aids and no glasses during the screening.

steps.action: Cut actions built on the score
steps.detail: Documenting impairment and a dementia referral both trust a doubtful result.

steps.action: Keep the client as the source
steps.detail: The daughter cannot take the screening for him.

elimination.verdict: Put the devices in and repeat the screening.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man in protective isolation for 9 days is tearful, bored and slow to solve simple problems. The television runs all day, and masked staff enter briefly for tasks. Which change does the nurse make?

options.text: Add a radio so that the room is never silent
options.rationale: More sound is not more meaning. The television already runs all day and he is still deprived.

options.text: Request a prescription for an antidepressant
options.rationale: Tempting because he is tearful. The cues fit the affective and cognitive effects of deprivation, and the environment is changed first.

options.text: Have staff say their names and sit to talk during care
options.rationale: Deprivation is a lack of meaningful stimulation. Unhurried contact with a person he can identify supplies the social interaction he is missing.

options.text: Limit staff entries to protect him from infection
options.rationale: Fewer contacts would deepen the isolation that is causing the problem.

questions.takeaway: Sensory deprivation is about the quality of stimulation, not only the quantity. Meaningful stimuli and social interaction prevent it. Background noise does not.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The stem tells you he already has constant sound and is still tearful and bored. So sound is not what is missing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Constant television and brief task visits.
Meaningful contact with people.
A radio repeats the television. Fewer entries make it worse. A drug skips the cause.

elimination.verdict: Make each staff contact a real interaction.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old who is blind and walks independently is moved to a different room at 2100. He knew his first room well. Which action does the nurse take before leaving him?

options.text: Walk him through the room and bathroom, then hand him the call bell
options.rationale: A new room needs a complete orientation. Walking the route and placing the call bell lets him move safely and call for help.

options.text: Tell him this room is arranged much like his first one
options.rationale: A spoken summary is not an orientation. He has not touched or walked this room.

options.text: Turn on the bed alarm and ask him to stay in bed tonight
options.rationale: Tempting as a fall measure, but he walks independently. It restricts him when orientation would keep him safe.

options.text: Ask assistive personnel to look in on him every hour
options.rationale: Frequent monitoring helps, and it still leaves him alone in a space he does not know.

questions.takeaway: Every change of environment needs a complete orientation for a client with vision loss, with the call bell accessible before you leave.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The stem says he walks independently and knew the first room. What changed is the room, so the answer restores his knowledge of the room.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The room, not his ability.
A bed alarm and staying in bed limit a client who walks on his own.
Only walking him through it gives him a map of the room.

elimination.verdict: Orient him to the new room and give him the call bell.

questions.stem: An alert 44-year-old with mild dehydration from a stomach virus vomits each time he drinks a full cup of oral rehydration solution. An as-needed antiemetic is prescribed. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give the antiemetic, then offer small frequent sips
options.rationale: He is alert and can swallow, so the oral route still fits. Treating the vomiting and shrinking the volume lets him keep the fluid down.

options.text: Request a prescription for IV fluids
options.rationale: Tempting because he is not keeping fluids down. The dehydration is mild and the cause has a prescribed treatment that has not been tried.

options.text: Wait until the nausea passes, then offer another cup
options.rationale: The deficit grows while the nurse waits, and a full cup is what triggered the vomiting.

options.text: Switch from rehydration solution to plain water
options.rationale: Water replaces no electrolytes, and the volume is the trigger, not the type of fluid.

questions.takeaway: Dehydration care includes treating the cause. Use the prescribed antiemetic and small volumes before moving an alert patient to the IV route.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: IV fluids and the antiemetic both address the problem. Mild dehydration and an untried prescription tip it to the less invasive choice.

steps.detail: Alert and able to swallow. Only tolerance is missing.
An antiemetic and smaller volumes.
More invasive, and not yet needed for a mild deficit.

elimination.verdict: Give the antiemetic and offer small sips.

questions.stem: One hour after regular insulin with dextrose for a potassium of 6.4 mEq/L, a man is sweaty, shaky and anxious. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Request a repeat serum potassium level
options.rationale: Tempting because rebound hypokalemia is a watch item. Low potassium causes weakness and a slow gut, not sweating and shaking.

options.text: Give the prescribed IV calcium
options.rationale: Calcium protects the heart from high potassium. It does nothing for these new findings.

options.text: Check a fingerstick blood glucose
options.rationale: Sweaty, shaky and anxious after insulin points to hypoglycemia. A bedside glucose takes seconds and directs the treatment.

options.text: Give the next scheduled dose of patiromer
options.rationale: A binder removes potassium over hours. It does nothing for what is happening to him now.

questions.takeaway: Insulin shifts potassium into cells and can drop the glucose with it. Watch for hypoglycemia and rebound hypokalemia during treatment.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Match the new findings to the drug that was just given. Two complications are possible; the symptoms tell you which one.

steps.detail: The change came one hour after insulin.
Low glucose is sweaty and shaky. Low potassium is weak and limp.

steps.action: Pick the fastest check that directs care
steps.detail: A fingerstick glucose.

elimination.verdict: Check the glucose first.

questions.stem: A patient with breast cancer has a calcium of 11.9 mg/dL. Which scheduled item does the nurse hold and clarify with the provider?

options.text: IV 0.9% sodium chloride infusion
options.rationale: Fits. Saline helps the kidneys flush calcium out.

options.text: Oral hydrochlorothiazide
options.rationale: Thiazide diuretics make the kidneys keep calcium, so this one is stopped in hypercalcemia.

options.text: IV furosemide
options.rationale: Fits, and it is the tempting choice because it is also a diuretic. Loop diuretics help excrete calcium.

options.text: Subcutaneous calcitonin
options.rationale: Fits. It slows the release of calcium from bone.

questions.takeaway: In hypercalcemia, loop diuretics help and thiazides hurt. Stop every calcium source and anything that makes the kidneys hold calcium.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two options are diuretics. They do opposite things to calcium, so decide which one keeps it.

steps.detail: You want the item that does not belong.
Saline, furosemide and calcitonin all lower it.
Loop flushes calcium. Thiazide holds it.

elimination.verdict: Hold the hydrochlorothiazide.

questions.stem: A patient with a calcium of 12.6 mg/dL has received IV 0.9% sodium chloride and furosemide since yesterday. Which finding best indicates the calcium is coming down?

options.text: Urine output of 200 mL per hour
options.rationale: Tempting because the plan depends on flushing calcium out. It shows the drugs are producing urine, not that the calcium effect on the body has eased.

options.text: Heart rate has slowed from 96 to 54
options.rationale: A slowing heart is the severe, prolonged picture of high calcium. This is worsening.

options.text: Patient sleeps most of the day but wakes to voice
options.rationale: Lethargy is a high calcium finding. More sleep is not improvement.

options.text: Bowel sounds are active and the patient is alert
options.rationale: High calcium slows the gut and dulls the mind. Return of bowel sounds and alertness shows the excitability is recovering.

questions.takeaway: High calcium slows everything: heart, muscles, mind and gut. Improvement looks like those systems waking back up.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Separate proof that the drug is acting from proof that the patient is better. The outcome is in the patient.

steps.detail: Slow gut, weakness, lethargy, slowing heart.

steps.action: Remove findings that match high calcium
steps.detail: A heart rate of 54 and more sleeping are the problem itself.

steps.action: Compare output with the body response
steps.detail: Urine shows the mechanism. Bowel sounds and alertness show the result.

elimination.verdict: Active bowel sounds and a more alert patient.

questions.stem: An 88-year-old who takes furosemide and a daily laxative is seen during morning rounds. Which finding requires follow-up?

options.text: Skin on the back of the hand tents when pinched
options.rationale: Aging skin tents on the hand even when hydrated. Turgor is checked at the sternum.

options.text: She cannot state the day but could yesterday
options.rationale: Acute confusion may be the first sign of a fluid or electrolyte imbalance in an older adult. Both of her drugs waste fluid and electrolytes.

options.text: She says she is not thirsty this morning
options.rationale: Tempting because poor intake matters. A weak thirst reflex is an expected aging change, so the nurse offers fluids on a schedule rather than reporting it.

options.text: She voided 350 mL of yellow urine overnight
options.rationale: An adequate amount with a normal color. Concern starts below 500 mL in a full day.

questions.takeaway: In an older adult, new confusion is a change in condition. Check fluid status and labs before blaming age or dementia.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Sort each finding into expected with aging or new for this patient. Only the new one needs follow up.

steps.detail: Hand tenting and weak thirst.

steps.action: Check the urine against the threshold
steps.detail: 350 mL overnight is not low.
Oriented yesterday, not today.

elimination.verdict: The new disorientation.

questions.stem: The evening after a thyroidectomy, a woman who reported tingling lips now makes a high-pitched sound with each breath in. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Tap the cheek to check for facial twitching
options.rationale: More assessment, and tempting. The airway is already narrowing, so the time for bedside signs has passed.

options.text: Request a stat serum calcium level
options.rationale: Useful later. A lab draw does not open an airway.

options.text: Give the scheduled oral calcium dose early
options.rationale: Too slow, and swallowing is unsafe with stridor.

options.text: Call the rapid response team
options.rationale: Stridor after thyroid surgery means laryngospasm from low calcium. She needs airway help and IV calcium now.

questions.takeaway: Low calcium after neck surgery can close the airway. Tingling is the warning; stridor is the emergency.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Assess first is the reflex. Here the stem has already done the assessing, so act on the airway.

steps.detail: A high-pitched sound on breathing in is stridor.
Tingling plus stridor is enough to act.
Only the response team protects the airway now.

elimination.verdict: Call the rapid response team.

questions.stem: A patient with celiac disease and chronic diarrhea has a calcium of 8.1 mg/dL. Which findings does the nurse report as signs the low calcium is affecting nerves and muscles? Select all that apply.

options.text: Tingling around the lips
options.rationale: Nerves are firing too easily. This is the early sign.

options.text: One side of the face twitches when the cheek is tapped
options.rationale: A positive Chvostek sign.

options.text: Knee jerk reflexes are absent
options.rationale: Absent reflexes mean slowed nerves, as in high magnesium or high calcium.

options.text: Bowel sounds are hypoactive
options.rationale: Low calcium speeds the gut. A quiet gut fits high calcium or low potassium.

options.text: Painful calf cramps at night
options.rationale: Cramps come before tetany as muscles become overexcited.

questions.takeaway: Calcium is the brake on nerves and muscles. Low calcium means too much firing: tingling, twitching, cramps and spasm.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Ask of each finding: is this a nerve or muscle doing too much, or too little? Low calcium only explains too much.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Low calcium excites nerves and muscles.
Tingling, facial twitch and cramps.
Absent reflexes and a quiet gut point the other way.

elimination.verdict: A, B and E.

questions.stem: An 83-year-old with a sodium of 156 mEq/L from poor intake has received 0.45% sodium chloride for 8 hours. Which finding indicates the therapy is working as intended?

options.text: Sodium is 152 mEq/L and she is less agitated
options.rationale: A gradual fall with easing agitation is the goal. Sodium is lowered slowly.

options.text: Sodium is 139 mEq/L and she reports a new headache
options.rationale: Tempting because the number is normal. A drop this fast pulls water into brain cells, so the headache suggests cerebral edema.

options.text: Sodium is 156 mEq/L and urine output has increased
options.rationale: The sodium has not moved. More urine without a change in sodium is not the goal.

options.text: Sodium is 154 mEq/L and her twitching has become weakness
options.rationale: Twitching that progresses to weakness is the worsening pattern, even with a slightly lower number.

questions.takeaway: Replace free water and bring a high sodium down gradually. A fast fall to normal can swell the brain.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Read the number and the patient together. A normal value reached too fast with a new neuro symptom is a complication.

steps.detail: A slow fall plus a calmer brain.

steps.action: Remove the options where the patient is worse or unchanged
steps.detail: Weakness after twitching and a sodium that has not moved.
Four points with less agitation is safe. Seventeen points with a headache is not.

elimination.verdict: Sodium 152 and less agitated.

questions.stem: After three days of nasogastric suction, a patient has leg weakness, hypoactive bowel sounds and flat T waves on the monitor. Which prescription does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: IV 0.9% sodium chloride bolus
options.rationale: Tempting, since suction removes fluid. The findings are weak muscles, a quiet gut and flat T waves, which is potassium, not volume.

options.text: IV calcium gluconate
options.rationale: Low calcium excites nerves and the gut: tingling, cramps and diarrhea. This patient is slowed down.

options.text: IV potassium chloride diluted on a pump
options.rationale: GI suction removes potassium. Weakness, a quiet gut and flat T waves are the low potassium picture, replaced slowly on a pump.

options.text: Oral potassium chloride with food
options.rationale: The right electrolyte by the wrong route. A patient on nasogastric suction cannot take or keep oral doses.

questions.takeaway: GI losses drain potassium. Low potassium weakens skeletal muscle, quiets the gut and flattens the T wave.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two imbalances share weakness and a slow gut. Use the cause and the ECG to separate them.

steps.detail: Three days of suction is a potassium loss.
Low calcium twitches and cramps.
Flat T waves and a GI loss fit low potassium, not high calcium.

elimination.verdict: Diluted IV potassium on a pump.

questions.stem: A man with kidney failure who takes a magnesium antacid daily is drowsy with absent knee jerks and respirations of 9 per minute. Which prescription does the nurse anticipate first?

options.text: IV furosemide with 0.9% sodium chloride
options.rationale: A real treatment for high magnesium when the kidneys work. His do not.

options.text: A serum magnesium level in the morning
options.rationale: His breathing is already slowing. This cannot wait until morning.

options.text: Hemodialysis later today
options.rationale: Removes magnesium and he will likely need it. It takes hours to arrange, and his breathing needs protection now.

options.text: IV calcium gluconate
options.rationale: Calcium is the antidote. It opposes magnesium at the nerves and muscles while removal is arranged.

questions.takeaway: Magnesium toxicity runs from lost reflexes to slow breathing to the heart. Stop the source and give IV calcium first; removal comes after.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Dialysis and calcium are both right for him. Ask which one works in minutes.

steps.action: Cut the option his kidneys rule out
steps.detail: Fluids and a loop diuretic need working kidneys.
Respirations of 9 cannot wait.
Calcium acts now. Dialysis removes magnesium later.

elimination.verdict: IV calcium gluconate first.

questions.stem: A patient with a sodium of 118 mEq/L is drowsy and confused. Hypertonic saline is prescribed and is being prepared by pharmacy. Which action does the nurse take while waiting?

options.text: Perform a complete neurologic assessment
options.rationale: Tempting because neuro checks are part of the care. The stem already gives the neuro change, so repeating it leaves the patient unprotected.

options.text: Pad the side rails and place suction at the bedside
options.rationale: Confusion and drowsiness at this level are the steps before a seizure. Seizure precautions protect the patient now.

options.text: Start a fluid restriction of 1 liter per day
options.rationale: Restriction treats mild dilutional cases and needs a prescription. It does not protect a brain that may seize in the next hour.

options.text: Request a repeat sodium level to confirm the result
options.rationale: The patient's brain is already showing the effect. Confirming the number delays protection.

questions.takeaway: Low sodium swells brain cells inside a rigid skull. With confusion at a very low level, put seizure precautions in place before the seizure.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: When the assessment is already in the stem and the treatment is on its way, the open slot is safety.

steps.detail: The number, the neuro change and the prescription.

steps.action: Remove what makes it worse or only repeats data
steps.detail: A repeat lab, a repeat exam, an order the nurse cannot start.

steps.action: Ask what could happen in the next ten minutes
steps.detail: A seizure. Prepare for it.

elimination.verdict: Seizure precautions now.

questions.scenario: A 64-year-old with kidney failure has a potassium of 6.3 mEq/L and tall peaked T waves. Urine output has been 10 mL per hour. He uses a salt substitute at meals.
questions.stem: For each prescription, indicate whether the nurse anticipates it or questions it for this patient.

rows.text: Continuous cardiac telemetry
rows.rationale: The heart is the organ at risk. Peaked T waves need continuous watching.

rows.text: IV calcium
rows.rationale: Stabilizes the heart muscle while other drugs lower the potassium.

rows.text: Regular insulin with dextrose
rows.rationale: Shifts potassium into cells. Dextrose prevents hypoglycemia.

rows.text: IV furosemide to increase potassium excretion
rows.rationale: Diuretics remove potassium only when kidney function is adequate. He is making 10 mL per hour.

rows.text: Sodium polystyrene sulfonate
rows.rationale: A binder removes potassium through the gut, which does not depend on his kidneys.

rows.text: Continue the salt substitute on his meal trays
rows.rationale: Salt substitutes are a potassium source. All potassium sources stop.

questions.takeaway: High potassium: stop every source, protect the heart, shift potassium into cells, then remove it by a route that works for this patient.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two details in the scenario decide the questioned rows: almost no urine, plus a hidden potassium source on the tray.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Peaked T waves mean the heart. Telemetry and calcium fit.

steps.action: Check each removal route against his kidneys
steps.detail: A diuretic needs working kidneys. A binder does not.

steps.action: Hunt for potassium still going in
steps.detail: The salt substitute.

elimination.verdict: Anticipate telemetry, calcium, insulin with dextrose and the binder. Question furosemide and the salt substitute.

questions.stem: A patient with fluid overload needs a daily weight. Which instruction does the nurse give the assistive personnel?

options.text: Weigh him after breakfast, once he has voided
options.rationale: Voiding first is right. After breakfast adds the weight of the meal, and the time drifts from day to day.

options.text: Weigh him at the same time, on any free scale
options.rationale: Same time is right. Scales differ, so a change between scales is not a change in the patient.

options.text: Use the same scale before breakfast, in a similar gown
options.rationale: Same time, same scale, same clothing. Only then does a change mean fluid.

options.text: Weigh him at bedtime, after the day's fluids are counted
options.rationale: Evening weights include the day's food and drink and cannot be compared with morning ones.

questions.takeaway: A daily weight only means something if the time, the scale and the clothing stay the same.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Every option is a weighing instruction and each gets something right. Pick the one that controls all three variables.

steps.detail: Time, scale and clothing.
After breakfast, any scale and bedtime each change one variable.
Only one option fixes all three.

elimination.verdict: Same scale, before breakfast, similar gown.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old with dehydration had a hematocrit of 52% on admission. After 24 hours of IV fluid it is 43%. Her stools are brown and her lungs are clear. Which conclusion guides the nurse?

options.text: Expected as replaced fluid dilutes the blood
options.rationale: Dehydration concentrates the blood. As water returns, the same red cells sit in more plasma and the value falls to normal.

options.text: Possible hidden bleeding, so test her stool
options.rationale: Tempting, since a falling hematocrit can mean blood loss. Brown stools and the fluid she received explain it better.

options.text: Fluid overload, so stop the infusion
options.rationale: Tempting because overshoot is a real risk in older adults. Clear lungs and a value in the normal range argue against it.

options.text: A laboratory error, so repeat the sample
options.rationale: The change fits her treatment, so there is no reason to doubt it.

questions.takeaway: Dehydration makes hematocrit look high because the water is gone, not because cells were added. A fall toward normal during rehydration is the goal.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: A dropping hematocrit sounds like bleeding. Check what the stem gives you about bleeding and about her lungs before you choose.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 52% was concentrated blood.
Brown stools give no sign of blood loss.
Clear lungs and a normal value do not fit.

elimination.verdict: Expected dilution as fluid is replaced.

questions.stem: A patient on bed rest with bone cancer has a calcium of 12.9 mg/dL. The left calf is warm and larger than the right. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Measure both calves and recheck in four hours
options.rationale: More assessment is tempting. The difference is already found, and waiting four hours delays the report.

options.text: Apply the compression device to the left leg
options.rationale: Compression on a leg with a suspected clot can dislodge it.

options.text: Help the patient walk to keep blood moving
options.rationale: Walking helps prevent clots. Once a clot is suspected, activity can break it loose.

options.text: Keep the left leg still and notify the provider
options.rationale: High calcium raises clot risk in the legs and pelvis. A warm, larger calf is reported promptly while the leg is protected.

questions.takeaway: High calcium increases clotting. Compare calf size, temperature and color, then report a difference without squeezing or exercising the leg.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Three options do something to the leg or wait. With a possible clot, the finding is already made, so protect the leg and report.

steps.detail: One calf warm and larger.

steps.action: Remove anything that moves or squeezes the leg
steps.detail: Walking and compression.
A possible clot is not rechecked in four hours.

elimination.verdict: Keep the left leg still and notify the provider.

questions.stem: A patient with a head injury and rising intracranial pressure has a new prescription for 0.45% sodium chloride at 100 mL per hour. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Start the infusion and perform hourly neuro checks
options.rationale: Monitoring does not undo the harm. Hypotonic fluid moves water into brain cells.

options.text: Hold the fluid and clarify it with the provider
options.rationale: Hypotonic fluid pushes water into cells. In a swelling brain inside a rigid skull, that raises the pressure further.

options.text: Start the infusion at half the prescribed rate
options.rationale: Changing the rate is outside nursing scope and still delivers the wrong fluid.

options.text: Start the infusion and raise the head of the bed
options.rationale: Raising the head helps pressure, and it cannot offset fluid that swells brain cells.

questions.takeaway: Match the fluid to where the water needs to go. Hypotonic fluid swells cells, so question it when intracranial pressure is a concern.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Three options start the fluid with a safeguard added. Decide first whether the fluid itself fits this patient.

steps.detail: 0.45% sodium chloride is hypotonic.
Hypotonic fluid moves water into cells.
Brain cells inside a rigid skull have no room to swell.

elimination.verdict: Hold it and clarify the fluid.

questions.stem: A patient receiving IV fluids at 150 mL per hour develops new crackles and becomes short of breath lying flat. Place the nurse's actions in priority order.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed to a high sitting position
options.rationale: First. Positioning eases breathing immediately and needs no prescription.

options.text: Slow the IV fluid to a keep open rate
options.rationale: Next, reduce the fluid going in while keeping the access.

options.text: Notify the provider of the crackles and breathing change
options.rationale: With the patient positioned and the fluid slowed, report the findings to get treatment.

options.text: Give IV furosemide as prescribed
options.rationale: The loop diuretic removes the extra fluid once it is prescribed.

options.text: Recheck lung sounds and measure urine output
options.rationale: Last, evaluate whether the diuretic worked.

questions.takeaway: Fluid overload with new crackles: sit the patient up, cut the fluid going in, report, give the diuretic, then check the response.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Start with what the nurse can do alone in seconds, then what needs the provider, then the evaluation.

steps.detail: Upright positioning helps right away.
Slow the fluid but keep the line.
A diuretic needs a prescription and its effect needs checking.

elimination.verdict: Sit up, slow the IV, notify, furosemide, recheck.

questions.stem: A patient with Crohn disease has a calcium of 7.4 mg/dL and the hand spasms each time the blood pressure cuff inflates. Which intervention does the nurse add to the plan of care?

options.text: Walk the patient in the hall three times a day
options.rationale: Tempting because weight bearing protects bone. With nerves this excitable, the present need is calm and injury prevention.

options.text: Recheck for hand spasm with the cuff every hour
options.rationale: The sign is already positive. Repeating it provokes painful spasm and adds stimulation.

options.text: Keep the room quiet and limit visitors
options.rationale: Low calcium makes nerves fire too easily. Reducing stimulation lowers the chance of tetany while calcium is replaced.

options.text: Encourage 3 liters of fluid daily
options.rationale: Hydration to flush calcium is for a high level, the opposite problem.

questions.takeaway: Low calcium removes the brake on nerves. Keep the environment quiet, protect from falls and move the patient gently.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The hand spasm tells you the nerves are already irritable. Choose the option that lowers stimulation instead of adding it.

steps.detail: Spasm with the cuff means excitable nerves.
Hourly cuff testing and hall walks.
Flushing with fluid is for high calcium.

elimination.verdict: Quiet room, limited visitors.

questions.stem: A man with kidney failure had a magnesium of 3.4 mEq/L after using a magnesium laxative daily. Which statement shows the discharge teaching was understood?

options.text: "I will check antacid and laxative labels for magnesium."
options.rationale: Failing kidneys cannot clear magnesium, so the fix is to stop the sources. Antacids and laxatives are the common ones.

options.text: "I will drink extra water each day to flush the magnesium out."
options.rationale: Tempting because fluids and diuretics are used when kidneys work. His do not, so extra water will not clear it.

options.text: "I will use the magnesium laxative only once a week."
options.rationale: Still a magnesium source his kidneys cannot remove.

options.text: "I will stop taking my calcium supplement."
options.rationale: Calcium is not the cause. Calcium is the antidote for magnesium's effects.

questions.takeaway: High magnesium usually comes from kidney failure plus a magnesium product. Stopping every source is the first treatment.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The kidney failure in the stem rules out any plan that depends on the kidneys to remove magnesium.

steps.action: Find the cause in the stem
steps.detail: A magnesium laxative with kidneys that cannot excrete it.

steps.action: Remove plans that keep a source
steps.detail: Weekly use is still use.

steps.action: Test the flushing plan against his kidneys
steps.detail: It only works with adequate kidney function.

elimination.verdict: He will check labels and avoid magnesium products.

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure treated for fluid overload reviews his low sodium diet before discharge. Which statement requires further teaching?

options.text: "I season my food with lemon juice and dried herbs."
options.rationale: Correct. Flavor without sodium.

options.text: "I buy frozen vegetables without added sauce."
options.rationale: Correct. Plain frozen vegetables are low in sodium.

options.text: "I switched to deli turkey because it is lean."
options.rationale: Lean is not low sodium. Deli meats are processed and salty, and sodium pulls water back in.

options.text: "I check each label for sodium per serving."
options.rationale: Correct. Labels show the hidden sodium.

questions.takeaway: Sodium hides in processed, canned and deli foods. A food can be lean and healthy sounding and still load a heart failure patient with fluid.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: You are looking for the wrong statement. Do not judge by how healthy the food sounds; judge by how it was processed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the statement that shows a gap.
Herbs, plain frozen vegetables and label reading all limit sodium.
Deli meat is salty whatever its fat content.

elimination.verdict: Deli turkey needs more teaching.

questions.stem: The nurse receives report on four patients. Which patient does the nurse see first?

options.text: Potassium 5.9 mEq/L, kidney disease, weak legs, normal rhythm on monitor
options.rationale: A high value that needs treatment soon. The normal rhythm shows the heart is not yet affected.

options.text: Calcium 11.4 mg/dL, constipated, IV 0.9% sodium chloride infusing
options.rationale: Slow gut is expected with high calcium, and the treatment is already running.

options.text: Sodium 158 mEq/L, agitated this morning, now quiet and hard to wake
options.rationale: Quiet looks like improvement. Moving from agitation to hard to wake is a falling level of consciousness, which is the brain getting worse.

options.text: Fluid overload, weight up 0.8 kg, ankle edema unchanged, lungs clear
options.rationale: Needs attention today. The lungs are clear, so this patient is stable for now.

questions.takeaway: In sodium imbalance, a patient who goes from restless to quiet and hard to rouse is deteriorating, not settling.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Look for the patient whose condition changed since the last check, and ask whether the change is toward better or worse.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A slow gut in high calcium under treatment, and edema with clear lungs.
Normal rhythm, so not yet cardiac.

steps.action: Read the change in the sodium patient
steps.detail: Agitated to hard to wake is a step down.

elimination.verdict: The patient with sodium 158 who is now hard to wake.

questions.stem: A patient with a magnesium of 1.0 mEq/L has received IV magnesium sulfate for 3 hours. Her reflexes went from 4+ to 1+ and she is newly drowsy. Respirations are 14 per minute. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Pause the infusion and notify the provider
options.rationale: Reflexes below normal with new drowsiness mean the magnesium has passed the goal. Stop adding it before breathing slows.

options.text: Continue the infusion since the reflexes have calmed
options.rationale: Calmer reflexes look like success. The target is 2+, and 1+ with drowsiness is past it.

options.text: Recheck the reflexes and respirations in one hour
options.rationale: Tempting because respirations are still 14. Another hour of infusion moves her toward absent reflexes and slow breathing.

options.text: Request a magnesium level before changing anything
options.rationale: The level will be needed. The bedside signs already show the direction, so the infusion stops first.

questions.takeaway: Reflexes are the bedside gauge for magnesium. Normal is the goal. Below normal with drowsiness is early toxicity even when breathing is still fine.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The finding moved in the right direction and then went past the target. Ask where normal is.

steps.detail: Reflexes of 2+.
1+ and drowsy is below normal.
Respirations fall last. Waiting for them is waiting too long.

elimination.verdict: Pause the infusion and notify the provider.

questions.stem: A patient with bone metastases has new lethargy, constipation, thirst and a large urine output. Her morning glucose was 98 mg/dL. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give the prescribed stool softener and reassess later
options.rationale: Treats one symptom. The cluster points to a single cause that the stool softener will not touch.

options.text: Check a fingerstick blood glucose now
options.rationale: Thirst and a large urine output suggest high glucose. The stem already gives a normal glucose, so this repeats known data.

options.text: Let her rest and limit stimulation
options.rationale: Rest fits a tired patient with cancer. New lethargy is a change that needs a cause, not quiet.

options.text: Report the findings and request a calcium level
options.rationale: Bone metastases release calcium. Lethargy, constipation, thirst and a large urine output together are the picture of high calcium.

questions.takeaway: Bone cancer plus slowing of the brain and bowel with thirst and heavy urine output means high calcium until shown otherwise.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Do not treat the findings one at a time. Find the one cause that explains all four, then check what the stem has already ruled out.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Brain slow, bowel slow, thirsty, urinating a lot.
Glucose was 98.
Bone metastases raise calcium.

elimination.verdict: Report the findings and request a calcium level.

questions.stem: A patient with fluid overload has crackles, breathes comfortably at 18 per minute, and is due for IV furosemide. This morning's potassium is 3.1 mEq/L. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give the furosemide now and recheck potassium afterward
options.rationale: Tempting because crackles are a breathing finding. He is comfortable, and furosemide will push a low potassium lower.

options.text: Report the potassium before giving the furosemide
options.rationale: He is not in distress, so there is time. A loop diuretic on a potassium of 3.1 risks dysrhythmia, and the provider can add replacement.

options.text: Hold the furosemide until his breathing worsens
options.rationale: Waiting for distress is not a plan. The overload still needs treatment once potassium is addressed.

options.text: Give half the furosemide dose and report the potassium
options.rationale: Changing a dose is not a nursing decision, and even half a dose lowers a potassium that is already low.

questions.takeaway: When breathing is stable, check what the drug will do to the lab value before giving it. Furosemide wastes potassium.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Breathing versus a lab value looks like an ABC question. Read how the patient is breathing before letting ABCs decide.

steps.detail: Comfortable at 18 per minute. No urgency.
Potassium will fall below 3.1.

steps.action: Pick the option that treats both
steps.detail: The provider can order potassium with the diuretic.

elimination.verdict: Report the potassium first. The dose is delayed by minutes, and the heart is protected.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old with dehydration has received IV 0.9% sodium chloride for 10 hours. Which finding requires follow up first?

options.text: Heart rate is 108, down from 118
options.rationale: Still fast, and moving the right way. It shows the fluid is helping.

options.text: Skin on her forearm stays tented
options.rationale: Looks alarming. Forearm skin tents in most older adults, so it says little about her fluid status.

options.text: She asks for water several times
options.rationale: Thirst is expected with dehydration and is easy to address.

options.text: Urine output is 18 mL per hour
options.rationale: Below 30 mL per hour after 10 hours of fluid means the kidneys are still underperfused. This is the finding that shows replacement is not enough.

questions.takeaway: Urine output is the quiet measure of whether replaced fluid is reaching the organs. Under 30 mL per hour is not acceptable.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Sort each finding as improving, unreliable, expected or not responding. Only one is not responding.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Heart rate is coming down.
Forearm turgor in an 84-year-old.
Thirst is expected. Low output after 10 hours of fluid is failure to respond.

elimination.verdict: Urine output of 18 mL per hour.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman with a high-output ileostomy has a weak rapid pulse, a blood pressure of 94/56 and a sodium of 138 mEq/L. Which prescription does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: 0.9% sodium chloride
options.rationale: Her sodium is normal, so she lost water and salt together. An isotonic fluid stays in the vessels and restores blood pressure.

options.text: 0.45% sodium chloride
options.rationale: Tempting as a rehydrating fluid. It moves water into cells, which helps a high sodium, and leaves the vessels underfilled.

options.text: 5% dextrose in water
options.rationale: Becomes free water once the sugar is used and spreads into the cells instead of the vessels.

options.text: 3% sodium chloride
options.rationale: An emergency drug for severe low sodium with neurologic signs. Her sodium is normal.

questions.takeaway: Read the sodium to choose the fluid. Low volume with a normal sodium is an isotonic loss and gets an isotonic fluid.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Two fluids rehydrate. The sodium decides between them: normal sodium means fill the vessels, high sodium means give water back to the cells.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Low pressure with a sodium of 138: isotonic loss.
3% saline is for severe low sodium.
Hypotonic fluid moves into cells. Isotonic fluid stays in the vessels.

elimination.verdict: 0.9% sodium chloride.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old on bed rest for three weeks after a pelvic fracture is now cleared for weight bearing. Her calcium is 11.2 mg/dL and she feels weak. Which intervention does the nurse add?

options.text: Offer milk or yogurt with each meal
options.rationale: Adds calcium to a patient whose level is already high.

options.text: Limit oral fluids to 1 L per day
options.rationale: The kidneys need fluid to flush calcium out. Restricting fluid concentrates it.

options.text: Help her walk in the hall three times daily
options.rationale: Immobility pulls calcium out of bone. Weight bearing puts it back, and she is cleared to walk.

options.text: Keep her in bed until the weakness resolves
options.rationale: Tempting as fall prevention. More bed rest keeps the calcium rising, and the weakness with it.

questions.takeaway: Immobility causes high calcium. Weight bearing activity and fluids treat the cause; use assistance to manage the fall risk.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: When weakness comes from the imbalance, look for the option that treats the cause safely instead of the one that only avoids the risk.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Dairy adds it; fluid restriction concentrates it.
Walk with help or stay in bed.
She is cleared for weight bearing and bed rest caused the problem.

elimination.verdict: Help her walk in the hall.

questions.stem: A patient with SIADH and a sodium of 122 mEq/L started tolvaptan yesterday. Which finding best indicates the drug is working as intended?

options.text: Weight is up 0.5 kg since yesterday
options.rationale: A gain means water is still being held.

options.text: Urine output has doubled and sodium is 127 mEq/L
options.rationale: The drug blocks ADH so the kidneys release water. More urine with a sodium rising gradually is the goal.

options.text: Urine is darker and more concentrated
options.rationale: Concentrated urine means ADH is still holding water back.

options.text: He reports that he is much less thirsty than he was yesterday
options.rationale: Tempting as a sign of comfort. Losing water usually increases thirst, and thirst does not show the sodium is correcting.

questions.takeaway: A vasopressin antagonist makes the kidneys lose water: expect more dilute urine, a falling weight and a sodium that rises gradually.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: State what the drug does in one line, then find the option that shows exactly that. Tolvaptan removes water.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Water leaves; sodium concentrates.

steps.action: Cut the signs of held water
steps.detail: Weight gain and dark urine.
Thirst is subjective. Output and sodium show the effect.

elimination.verdict: More urine and a sodium of 127.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic hypocalcemia after parathyroid removal is going home on oral calcium and vitamin D. Which statement shows the teaching was effective?

options.text: "I'll take the calcium whenever my lips tingle."
options.rationale: Tempting because tingling is the warning sign. Tingling means the level is already low; the calcium is taken daily to prevent it.

options.text: "I can stop dairy now that I take the pills."
options.rationale: A calcium rich diet is part of the treatment along with the supplement.

options.text: "I'll double the dose if my muscles cramp."
options.rationale: Cramping is a reason to call. Extra doses without a level risk high calcium.

options.text: "I need the vitamin D so the calcium is absorbed."
options.rationale: Vitamin D is what lets the gut take up calcium. Without it the supplement does little.

questions.takeaway: Oral calcium is a daily preventive drug, and it needs vitamin D to be absorbed. Symptoms are a reason to call, not to self dose.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: In a teaching item, reject statements where the patient waits for symptoms or changes the dose alone.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Taking it for tingling and doubling it for cramps both wait for a low level.
Dairy stays.
Vitamin D makes the calcium usable.

elimination.verdict: The vitamin D statement.

questions.stem: A patient with a potassium of 2.7 mEq/L has a distended abdomen and no bowel sounds after five minutes of listening. His breakfast tray arrives. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Keep him from eating and report the abdomen
options.rationale: Absent sounds with distention suggest paralytic ileus, the severe gut effect of low potassium. Food into a bowel that is not moving causes vomiting and aspiration risk.

options.text: Serve the tray so he takes his oral potassium
options.rationale: Tempting because oral potassium goes with food. A bowel that is not moving cannot absorb it.

options.text: Give the as-needed laxative before he eats
options.rationale: Constipation is expected, but a laxative into an ileus worsens distention.

options.text: Recheck the bowel sounds after he has eaten
options.rationale: The assessment is complete. Feeding him first adds the risk before anyone has acted on it.

questions.takeaway: Severe low potassium can stop the bowel. Absent bowel sounds with distention mean nothing by mouth until the provider is told.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: The assessment is already done and it is abnormal. Choose the option that acts on it instead of feeding, treating a symptom or assessing again.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: No bowel sounds plus distention: possible ileus.

steps.action: Cut what puts things into the gut
steps.detail: Food, oral potassium and a laxative.
Five minutes of listening is enough.

elimination.verdict: Keep him from eating and report.

questions.stem: A patient with kidney failure has a potassium of 5.6 mEq/L with a regular rhythm, a weight gain of 1.8 kg and new dyspnea with crackles. Which problem does the nurse address first?

options.text: Risk for a dysrhythmia from the high potassium
options.rationale: Tempting because potassium threatens the heart. The rhythm is regular, so this is a potential problem that is monitored.

options.text: Fluid in the lungs impairing gas exchange
options.rationale: New dyspnea and crackles are an actual breathing problem happening now. Breathing comes before a risk.

options.text: Fatigue from the retained waste products
options.rationale: Real and chronic. It does not threaten life today.

options.text: Skin breakdown from the tissue edema
options.rationale: A risk that is managed over days.

questions.takeaway: An actual breathing problem outranks a potential cardiac one. Monitor the potassium while you treat the lungs.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Sort the options into actual and potential, then apply the ABCs to what is actual.

steps.detail: Dyspnea with crackles is happening. Dysrhythmia and skin breakdown are risks.
Fatigue waits.
Fluid in the lungs.

elimination.verdict: Fluid in the lungs comes first.

questions.stem: A patient taking losartan and spironolactone reports abdominal cramping, watery diarrhea since morning and tingling in both hands. Which assessment does the nurse perform first?

options.text: Check skin turgor over the sternum
options.rationale: Reasonable for fluid loss from diarrhea. It does not address why two potassium retaining drugs plus these symptoms matter.

options.text: Ask what she ate in the last day
options.rationale: Useful later to look for potassium sources or a food cause.

options.text: Count the apical pulse and check the rhythm
options.rationale: Both drugs hold potassium. Tingling with cramping and diarrhea are early high potassium signs, and the heart is where it becomes dangerous.

options.text: Listen to bowel sounds in all quadrants
options.rationale: Would confirm an active gut, which the diarrhea already shows.

questions.takeaway: Diarrhea with tingling in a patient on potassium retaining drugs suggests high potassium. Go to the heart first.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Link the drug list to the symptoms before choosing an assessment. All four are assessments, so pick the one aimed at the organ that can kill.

steps.detail: Two drugs that hold potassium, plus tingling and an overactive gut.

steps.action: Cut the assessment that adds nothing
steps.detail: Bowel sounds are already known to be active.
Turgor and diet matter. Rhythm matters first.

elimination.verdict: Apical pulse and rhythm.

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure still has edema and needs a diuretic. His potassium is 3.3 mEq/L despite supplements while taking furosemide. Which prescription change does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Furosemide dose increased
options.rationale: More loop diuretic removes more fluid and more potassium.

options.text: Hydrochlorothiazide added
options.rationale: A thiazide also wastes potassium, so the level would fall further.

options.text: Furosemide stopped with no replacement
options.rationale: Tempting because it removes the cause. He still has edema, so the fluid problem would go untreated.

options.text: Spironolactone in place of furosemide
options.rationale: A potassium sparing diuretic keeps removing fluid while holding on to potassium.

questions.takeaway: When a loop or thiazide diuretic keeps potassium low and the patient still needs diuresis, expect a switch to a potassium sparing diuretic.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The stem gives two needs: remove fluid and keep potassium. Only one option meets both.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: More furosemide and a thiazide share the same flaw.

steps.action: Check the remaining two against both needs
steps.detail: Stopping the diuretic ignores the edema.

steps.action: Keep the one that does both
steps.detail: Spironolactone.

elimination.verdict: Spironolactone in place of furosemide.

questions.scenario: The nurse reviews six patients to anticipate which acid base imbalance each is at risk for before blood gas results return.
questions.stem: For each patient, indicate whether the nurse anticipates acidosis or alkalosis.

rows.text: A 34-year-old found with an opioid overdose, breathing 6 times per minute
rows.rationale: Too little breathing keeps carbon dioxide, which is an acid.

rows.text: A patient who has vomited repeatedly for three days
rows.rationale: Stomach acid is lost, leaving the blood with too much base.

rows.text: A patient with five days of severe watery diarrhea
rows.rationale: Intestinal fluid is rich in bicarbonate. Losing it leaves acid behind.

rows.text: A patient in a panic attack breathing 36 times per minute
rows.rationale: Fast breathing blows off carbon dioxide.

rows.text: A patient with kidney failure who has missed dialysis
rows.rationale: Failing kidneys cannot excrete acid or make bicarbonate.

rows.text: A patient who takes sodium bicarbonate antacid many times a day
rows.rationale: Extra base is taken in.

questions.takeaway: Ask what was lost or kept. Kept carbon dioxide or lost bicarbonate gives acidosis; lost carbon dioxide or lost stomach acid gives alkalosis.
questions.coverage: Not in Lecture PPT. The Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Vomiting and diarrhea go opposite ways: the stomach loses acid, the bowel loses base. Slow breathing keeps acid, fast breathing loses it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Slow breathing: acidosis. Fast breathing: alkalosis.
Vomiting loses acid. Diarrhea loses bicarbonate.
Kidneys that fail keep acid. Bicarbonate antacid adds base.
