elimination.verdict: Acidosis, alkalosis, acidosis, alkalosis, acidosis, alkalosis.

questions.nursesNote: 1400: 91-year-old admitted from home after two days of fever. Heart rate 126 with a thready radial pulse. Blood pressure 132/78 lying and 104/60 standing. Hands warm with capillary refill of 2 seconds. Skin over the sternum tents. Urine 160 mL in 8 hours, dark amber. Lungs clear in all fields. Called her daughter by the wrong name twice; oriented yesterday. Ate half of her lunch.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that indicate fluid volume deficit and require follow-up.

segments.text: Heart rate 126 with a thready radial pulse
segments.rationale: A fast weak pulse is the heart compensating for low volume.

segments.text: Blood pressure 132/78 lying and 104/60 standing
segments.rationale: A large drop on standing is orthostatic hypotension. It also makes her a fall risk.

segments.text: Hands warm with capillary refill of 2 seconds
segments.rationale: A normal finding. It does not show the deficit and needs no follow-up.

segments.text: Skin over the sternum tents
segments.rationale: The sternum is the reliable site for turgor in an older adult.

segments.text: Urine 160 mL in 8 hours, dark amber
segments.rationale: Scant concentrated urine means the kidneys are holding on to water.

segments.text: Lungs clear in all fields
segments.rationale: Expected in fluid deficit. Nothing to follow up.

segments.text: Called her daughter by the wrong name twice; oriented yesterday
segments.rationale: New confusion can be the first sign of fluid imbalance in an older adult.

segments.text: Ate half of her lunch
segments.rationale: Worth noting for intake, but it is not a sign of the deficit itself.

questions.takeaway: In an older adult, trust pulse, orthostatic pressure, sternal turgor, urine and new confusion as signs of fluid deficit.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Read each line alone and ask whether low volume explains it. Normal findings and intake notes are not signs of the deficit.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Fast thready pulse and a drop on standing.
Tenting over the sternum is reliable at her age.
Scant dark urine and new confusion.
Normal capillary refill, clear lungs and a partial meal.

elimination.verdict: s1, s2, s4, s5 and s7.

questions.stem: A patient with a sodium of 155 mEq/L has a blood pressure of 84/52 and a weak rapid pulse. 0.9% sodium chloride is prescribed. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Hold the fluid and ask for 0.45% sodium chloride instead
options.rationale: Tempting because hypotonic fluid is the usual free water replacement, but it leaves the vessels quickly and will not restore her pressure.

options.text: Ask for dextrose 5% in water to lower the sodium faster
options.rationale: Fast lowering risks cerebral edema, and it does little for circulating volume.

options.text: Give oral water first and start the IV if she stays hypotensive
options.rationale: Too slow for a patient who is not perfusing.

options.text: Start the infusion as prescribed and recheck her pressure
options.rationale: Isotonic saline stays in the vessels and restores perfusion first. It is still more dilute than her blood, so the sodium drifts down slowly.

questions.takeaway: High sodium with low blood pressure: refill the vessels with isotonic saline first, then replace free water gradually.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Salt for a high sodium looks like an error. Read the blood pressure before you question it.

steps.detail: 84/52 with a weak rapid pulse is circulation.

steps.action: Match the fluid to that threat
steps.detail: Isotonic fluid stays in the vessels.
Slow lowering is what you want.

elimination.verdict: Start the 0.9% and reassess.

questions.stem: A patient taking lisinopril and a daily potassium supplement has a potassium of 5.7 mEq/L. His rhythm is regular with normal T waves and his kidney function is adequate. Which prescriptions does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Hold the supplement and give a potassium binder
options.rationale: No conduction change, so the plan is to stop the source and remove potassium through the gut.

options.text: Give IV calcium and continue the supplement
options.rationale: Calcium is for a heart that is showing changes, and continuing the supplement feeds the problem.

options.text: Give regular insulin with dextrose and hourly glucose checks
options.rationale: Used for moderate to severe levels. It carries a hypoglycemia risk he does not need to take.

options.text: Recheck the potassium in the morning with no changes
options.rationale: Leaves him taking potassium while the level is already high.

questions.takeaway: Match the hyperkalemia treatment to severity. No ECG change: stop the source and increase excretion. ECG change: calcium first, then shift.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The stem tells you what is absent. A regular rhythm with normal T waves removes the emergency options.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 5.7 with a normal ECG.
Calcium and insulin are for a threatened heart.
The supplement goes first.

elimination.verdict: Hold the supplement and give a binder.

questions.stem: Two hours after IV furosemide for fluid overload, a 74-year-old has voided 40 mL in total. Crackles have moved from the bases to the mid lungs and she is sitting upright. Which action does the nurse take next?

options.text: Encourage her to drink to help the diuretic work
options.rationale: Adds fluid to lungs that are filling.

options.text: Recheck her lungs and output in another two hours
options.rationale: She is getting worse now. Waiting lets pulmonary edema develop.

options.text: Insert a urinary catheter to measure output accurately
options.rationale: Tempting, but the low output is already measured and a catheter does not treat it.

options.text: Notify the provider of the low output and rising crackles
options.rationale: The treatment has failed and the overload is advancing. She is already upright, so the next step is a change in the plan.

questions.takeaway: Decreased urine output with rising crackles after a diuretic means the treatment is not working. Report it before pulmonary edema sets in.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The positioning is done and the assessment is in the stem. What is left is getting a different treatment.

steps.detail: Low output and higher crackles.
She is already upright.
A worsening trend needs a new prescription.

elimination.verdict: Notify the provider.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old with low blood pressure and edema is receiving IV albumin. Which finding during the infusion requires follow-up?

options.text: Blood pressure rising from 90/58 to 106/64
options.rationale: The intended effect.

options.text: Urine output increasing to 55 mL per hour
options.rationale: Shows the kidneys are being perfused again.

options.text: Respirations of 26 with a new bounding pulse
options.rationale: Albumin pulls fluid into the vessels. A bounding pulse with fast breathing means the vascular space is overfilling.

options.text: Ankle edema that is slightly less than before
options.rationale: Expected as fluid moves back into the vessels.

questions.takeaway: A colloid expands plasma volume by pulling water into the vessels. Watch for the swing into fluid overload, especially in older adults.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Three findings are the reason the drug was given. Look for the one that shows too much of a good thing.

steps.detail: Higher pressure, more urine, less edema.
Bounding pulse and fast respirations.
Overload goes to the lungs next.

elimination.verdict: Respirations 26 with a bounding pulse.

questions.stem: A man with fluid overload is going home on a 1.2 L daily fluid restriction. Which statement shows the teaching was effective?

options.text: "I only need to count the fluids that I drink from a cup or a glass."
options.rationale: Misses the fluid that hides in foods.

options.text: "I will count soup, gelatin and ice cream as part of my fluid."
options.rationale: Anything liquid at room temperature counts toward the limit.

options.text: "I will save most of my fluid for the evening."
options.rationale: Leaves him thirsty all day and likely to go over at night.

options.text: "I can drink more on days when I take my water pill."
options.rationale: The diuretic is removing excess. Drinking more undoes it.

questions.takeaway: On a fluid restriction, count every source of fluid, including foods that melt or pour, and spread the allowance across the day.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Look for the statement that makes his intake record accurate.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Soup, gelatin and ice cream.
Cups and glasses only.
Saving up or drinking more with the diuretic.

elimination.verdict: Count soup, gelatin and ice cream.

questions.stem: An 81-year-old with a sodium of 158 mEq/L is too drowsy to drink and starts IV 0.45% sodium chloride. Which interventions does the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Run the fluid on a pump at the prescribed rate
options.rationale: The sodium has to come down gradually. A pump keeps the rate from drifting.

options.text: Check level of consciousness every hour
options.rationale: The brain shows whether the sodium is improving, worsening or falling too fast.

options.text: Speed the rate if the next sodium is still high
options.rationale: A slow fall is the goal. Faster hypotonic fluid pushes water into brain cells.

options.text: Hold oral fluids until she is fully awake
options.rationale: A drowsy patient can aspirate. Oral water returns when she can swallow safely.

options.text: Report a new headache or worsening drowsiness
options.rationale: These suggest cerebral edema from a sodium that is dropping too quickly.

options.text: Offer broth when she wakes to replace losses
options.rationale: Broth is a sodium load for a patient whose sodium is already high.

questions.takeaway: Correcting high sodium by IV: steady prescribed rate on a pump, hourly neuro checks, nothing by mouth while drowsy, and report headache or deeper drowsiness.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: For each option ask one thing: does it keep the sodium falling slowly and the brain watched?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A pump at the prescribed rate.

steps.action: Keep what watches the brain and airway
steps.detail: Hourly neuro checks, no oral fluids while drowsy, report headache.

steps.action: Drop what speeds the fall or adds sodium
steps.detail: A faster rate and broth.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D, E.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A 62-year-old with breast cancer has a calcium of 12.8 mg/dL. She is lethargic, weak and has had no bowel movement for four days. She takes a daily calcium with vitamin D tablet, which has been stopped.

The nurse expects a prescription for [[1]].

Because of the calcium level, the nurse places her on [[2]].

To limit calcium leaving her bones, the nurse [[3]].

options.text: a fluid restriction with daily weights
options.rationale: Dehydration raises calcium. She needs volume to carry it out.

options.text: IV 0.9% sodium chloride with furosemide
options.rationale: Saline and a loop diuretic flush calcium out through the kidneys.

options.text: IV lactated Ringer's with a thiazide
options.rationale: That fluid contains calcium and a thiazide holds calcium in the body.

options.text: oral fluids with a chewable antacid
options.rationale: Too slow for a lethargic patient, and chewable antacids are often calcium carbonate.

options.text: seizure precautions
options.rationale: High calcium quiets nerve and muscle. Seizure risk belongs to low calcium and sodium problems.

options.text: a quiet room with few visitors
options.rationale: Reducing stimulation is for low calcium, when nerves are overexcitable.

options.text: a cardiac monitor
options.rationale: Dysrhythmias are the most serious effect of high calcium, so the rhythm is watched continuously.

options.text: a clear liquid diet
options.rationale: Does nothing for the calcium and she needs nutrition.

options.text: helps her walk in the hall several times a day
options.rationale: Weight bearing keeps calcium in bone. Immobility releases it.

options.text: keeps her in bed with the side rails up
options.rationale: Bed rest moves calcium out of bone and raises clot risk.

options.text: moves her joints through range of motion in bed
options.rationale: Tempting, but without weight on the bones it does not stop the calcium loss.

options.text: sits her in a chair for most of the day
options.rationale: Sitting is not weight bearing and adds to venous pooling.

questions.takeaway: High calcium: stop the sources, flush with 0.9% sodium chloride and a loop diuretic, watch the rhythm, and keep her walking with help.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: High calcium slows nerve and muscle. Any option meant for overexcitable nerves belongs to low calcium.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Pick the treatment that removes calcium
steps.detail: Saline with a loop diuretic. Reject anything with calcium or a thiazide.
Seizure precautions and low stimulation are for low calcium.
Weight bearing, with help because she is weak.

elimination.verdict: Saline with furosemide; cardiac monitor; assisted walking.

questions.stem: The nurse checks the cardiac monitors of four clients. Which finding requires the nurse to intervene?

options.text: Potassium 3.4 mEq/L, taking oral potassium: U wave unchanged since admission
options.rationale: A U wave fits low potassium, it is unchanged, and treatment is under way.

options.text: Receiving IV potassium chloride: new tall peaked T waves and a wider QRS
options.rationale: These are the signs of high potassium. The infusion is the source and has to stop.

options.text: Magnesium 1.5 mEq/L after replacement: QT interval now normal
options.rationale: The level is in range and the QT has corrected.

options.text: Given furosemide 2 hours ago: regular rhythm at a rate of 84
options.rationale: A normal rate and rhythm.

questions.takeaway: Low potassium: flat T wave and a U wave. High potassium: tall peaked T waves and a wide QRS. New peaked T waves during a potassium infusion mean stop it.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Look for the change that is new and that points the opposite way from the problem being treated.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Only one strip has a new change.
Peaked T and wide QRS mean the potassium is now too high.

elimination.verdict: The client on IV potassium with peaked T waves.

questions.stem: A malnourished 53-year-old taking a loop diuretic has ectopic beats and constipation. The nurse suspects an electrolyte deficit. Which additional finding points to low magnesium rather than low potassium?

options.text: Brisk 4+ knee reflexes with twitching hands
options.rationale: Low magnesium makes nerves and muscles more excitable, so reflexes are hyperactive and muscles twitch. Low potassium does the opposite.

options.text: Weak legs with diminished knee reflexes
options.rationale: Tempting because this client is at risk for both deficits. Weakness with reduced reflexes is the low potassium picture.

options.text: Hypoactive bowel sounds in all quadrants
options.rationale: Both deficits slow the gut, so this does not separate them.

options.text: Flat T waves with a U wave
options.rationale: These are the monitor changes of low potassium. Low magnesium prolongs the QT interval.

questions.takeaway: Low magnesium excites: hyperactive reflexes, twitching, cramps, tetany, seizures. Low potassium quiets: weakness and reduced reflexes. Both slow the gut and both disturb the rhythm.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two of the findings fit either deficit. Look for the option that only one of them can explain.

steps.detail: A slow gut happens in both, so bowel sounds cannot decide.
Reduced reflexes go with low potassium. Brisk reflexes go with low magnesium.
A U wave belongs to potassium.

elimination.verdict: Brisk reflexes with twitching.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old with chronic kidney disease has numb lips, painful calf spasms and a QT interval longer than this morning. Calcium is 6.9 mg/dL. Which prescription does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Oral calcium carbonate with each meal
options.rationale: The right electrolyte, and it suits mild or chronic low calcium. Spasms and a lengthening QT make this severe and symptomatic.

options.text: A vitamin D supplement with a calcium rich diet
options.rationale: Helps absorption over time. It cannot correct spasms and a rhythm change today.

options.text: A quiet room with fall precautions only
options.rationale: Good supportive care for low calcium, and it leaves the calcium uncorrected.

options.text: IV calcium with continuous cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Severe, symptomatic hypocalcemia is replaced by IV, and the lengthening QT means the heart has to be watched while it is corrected.

questions.takeaway: Low calcium prolongs the QT interval. Mild or chronic: oral calcium and vitamin D. Symptomatic with spasms or rhythm change: IV calcium on a monitor.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Three options are correct care for low calcium. The spasms and the changing QT tell you how fast it has to be fixed.

steps.detail: 6.9 mg/dL with painful spasms and a new QT change is severe and symptomatic.
Oral calcium, vitamin D and diet work slowly.
The QT change means cardiac monitoring.

elimination.verdict: IV calcium on the monitor.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old has a potassium of 6.8 mEq/L and a newly widened QRS. All four prescriptions have been written. Which does the nurse give first?

options.text: Regular insulin IV with dextrose
options.rationale: The strong runner up because it moves potassium into the cells. It does nothing for the heart while it takes effect, and the QRS is already wide.

options.text: IV calcium
options.rationale: Calcium stabilizes and protects the heart. It does not lower potassium, and with a widened QRS the heart is the immediate danger.

options.text: Patiromer by mouth
options.rationale: Binds potassium in the GI tract. Useful, and far too slow for a conduction change.

options.text: Furosemide IV
options.rationale: Increases potassium excretion if the kidneys work. It also comes after the heart is protected.

questions.takeaway: Hyperkalemia with ECG changes: protect the heart with IV calcium, shift potassium with insulin and dextrose, then remove it with binders or diuretics.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: All four are real treatments for high potassium. Ask which one deals with the thing that can kill the client in the next few minutes.

steps.detail: A widened QRS means conduction is already impaired.
Calcium protects, insulin shifts, the binder and the diuretic remove.
Lowering the level takes time the heart may not have.

elimination.verdict: IV calcium first.

questions.stem: A student nurse prepares to give potassium chloride to a 55-year-old with a potassium of 2.9 mEq/L. Which statement by the student needs correction?

options.text: "I will run it through the IV pump."
options.rationale: Correct. IV potassium is always on a pump.

options.text: "I will hang it diluted in the bag from pharmacy."
options.rationale: Correct. IV potassium must be diluted in IV fluid.

options.text: "I will push it slowly into the IV port over 5 minutes."
options.rationale: Right drug, wrong method. Potassium is never given IV push, however slowly, because it can stop the heart.

options.text: "I will keep him on the cardiac monitor."
options.rationale: Correct. Low potassium and its replacement both affect rhythm.

questions.takeaway: IV potassium is never given IV push. It is diluted and infused on a pump.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The word slowly makes a wrong method sound careful. Judge the method, not the adverb.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pump, diluted and monitored are all rules for IV potassium.

steps.action: Find the method that breaks the rule
steps.detail: A push is a push at any speed.

elimination.verdict: The IV push statement.

questions.stem: A client receiving IV magnesium sulfate for a magnesium of 0.9 mEq/L had 4+ knee reflexes and twitching. Now reflexes are 2+, twitching has stopped, she is awake and respirations are 16. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Stop the infusion and prepare IV calcium
options.rationale: The antidote is for toxicity. Reflexes are present and normal, she is awake and her breathing is adequate.

options.text: Pause the infusion and call the provider about the reflex change
options.rationale: Tempting because the reflexes fell. They fell to normal, which is the goal, not to reduced or absent.

options.text: Ask the provider to increase the rate
options.rationale: The findings show the current rate is working. Giving it faster only raises the risk of toxicity.

options.text: Continue the infusion and keep checking reflexes on schedule
options.rationale: Normal reflexes and no twitching show the excitability is settling. The infusion continues with the same frequent reflex checks.

questions.takeaway: During IV magnesium, reflexes moving from hyperactive to normal mean it is working. Reduced or absent reflexes, drowsiness or slow breathing mean toxicity.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: A falling reflex grade is not automatically bad. Ask where it started and where it landed.

steps.detail: 4+ to 2+ is hyperactive to normal.
She is awake and breathing 16 times a minute with reflexes present.
Nothing here calls for stopping, and monitoring goes on.

elimination.verdict: Continue and keep checking reflexes.

questions.stem: The morning after a total thyroidectomy, a client says her fingertips and the skin around her mouth feel like pins and needles. Her voice is clear and her breathing is quiet. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Call the rapid response team
options.rationale: Right if she had noisy breathing or a voice change. Her airway is clear, so there is time to assess and act early.

options.text: Tell her this is expected after anesthesia and recheck in 4 hours
options.rationale: Tingling of the lips and fingers after thyroid surgery is the first sign of low calcium from parathyroid injury, not an expected effect.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed and start oxygen
options.rationale: An airway and breathing action, and tempting after neck surgery. Her voice is clear and her breathing is quiet, and oxygen does nothing for the cause of the tingling.

options.text: Check for Chvostek and Trousseau signs and review her calcium level
options.rationale: Thyroid surgery can injure the parathyroid glands. Early tingling is the cue to confirm low calcium before it moves on to tetany and laryngospasm.

questions.takeaway: After thyroid surgery, tingling around the mouth and in the fingers means low calcium until shown otherwise. Catch it at tingling, before spasm and laryngospasm.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The stem tells you the airway is fine. That removes the emergency response and leaves the question of what this early cue means.

strategies: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings

steps.detail: A clear voice and quiet breathing mean no emergency yet, so the rapid response call and the oxygen are not needed.
This symptom after this surgery is not expected.

steps.action: Match the cue to the risk
steps.detail: Tingling points to calcium, so the nurse checks the bedside signs and the level.

elimination.verdict: Check the bedside signs and the calcium.

questions.stem: A client treated for a potassium of 6.7 mEq/L received regular insulin with dextrose, furosemide and a potassium binder. Which finding 6 hours later requires follow up?

options.text: New leg weakness with flat T waves
options.rationale: The treatment can overshoot. Weakness and flat T waves are signs of low potassium, which is as dangerous to the rhythm as the high level was.

options.text: Fingerstick glucose of 104 mg/dL
options.rationale: Normal. Low blood sugar is the insulin risk, and this is not low.

options.text: T waves no longer tall and peaked
options.rationale: This is the change you want to see as potassium falls.

options.text: Urine output of 90 mL per hour
options.rationale: Expected after furosemide, and it is how the potassium leaves.

questions.takeaway: While treating hyperkalemia, watch for two overshoots: low blood sugar from the insulin and low potassium from the combined treatment.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Three findings show the plan working. One shows it has gone past the target.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Normal glucose, normal T waves and brisk urine are all intended.

steps.action: Read the remaining pair of cues
steps.detail: Weakness plus flat T waves is the low potassium picture.

elimination.verdict: New weakness with flat T waves.

questions.stem: A drowsy 60-year-old who overused magnesium antacids has a magnesium of 3.2 mEq/L, respirations of 16, knee reflexes that are reduced but present and adequate kidney function. The antacids are stopped. Which prescription does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Hemodialysis later today
options.rationale: Dialysis is for severe cases or kidney failure. Kidney function is adequate here.

options.text: IV calcium to reverse the magnesium effects
options.rationale: The strong runner up. The antidote is for severe depression of the heart, muscles and breathing. Respirations of 16 with reflexes still present do not show that.

options.text: Oral fluids with a magnesium laxative
options.rationale: Adds another magnesium source when every source must stop.

options.text: IV fluids with a loop diuretic
options.rationale: With adequate kidneys, IV fluids and a loop diuretic flush the magnesium out.

questions.takeaway: High magnesium: stop all magnesium, then IV fluids with a loop diuretic if the kidneys work. IV calcium for severe heart or breathing depression. Dialysis if severe or in kidney failure.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two stem facts choose the treatment: the kidneys work, and breathing and reflexes are still holding.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Adequate kidneys can excrete magnesium, so dialysis is not needed.
A magnesium laxative adds to the problem.
Respirations of 16 and reflexes present mean the antidote is not yet called for.

elimination.verdict: IV fluids with a loop diuretic.

questions.stem: A client with a potassium of 2.4 mEq/L had weak legs, hypoactive bowel sounds, shallow breathing and an oxygen saturation of 89%. After 10 hours of IV potassium chloride, which finding best shows the priority problem is improving?

options.text: Bowel sounds are active in all four quadrants
options.rationale: A real improvement in the gut. The gut was not the problem that threatened life.

options.text: Repeat potassium is 3.0 mEq/L
options.rationale: The strong runner up because the level is rising. It is still below 3.5 mEq/L and says nothing about whether the breathing muscles have recovered.

options.text: Breathing is deep with an oxygen saturation of 96%
options.rationale: Weak breathing muscles were the most dangerous effect of the low potassium. Deep breaths and a normal saturation show that effect has reversed.

options.text: Able to stand at the bedside with help
options.rationale: Leg strength is returning, which lowers the fall risk. Breathing still ranks above it.

questions.takeaway: Severe low potassium can weaken the breathing muscles. Judge replacement first by breathing depth and oxygen saturation, then by strength, gut and the level.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Every option is a change for the better. Decide which of the four starting problems could have killed the client, then find that one reversed.

steps.detail: Shallow breathing with a saturation of 89% outranks weak legs and a slow gut.
3.0 mEq/L is higher and still below range, and it does not show how the client is breathing.
Deep breaths with a saturation of 96%.

elimination.verdict: Deep breathing with a saturation of 96%.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old with lung cancer has a calcium of 13.6 mg/dL and is weak and constipated. Which items does the nurse anticipate in the plan of care? Select all that apply.

options.text: IV 0.9% sodium chloride
options.rationale: Promotes calcium excretion by the kidneys.

options.text: IV furosemide
options.rationale: A loop diuretic increases calcium excretion.

options.text: Continuous cardiac telemetry
options.rationale: Dysrhythmias are the most serious effect of high calcium.

options.text: Calf measurements with checks of foot color and temperature
options.rationale: High calcium raises the risk of clots in the legs and pelvis.

options.text: Her scheduled calcium with vitamin D supplement
options.rationale: Calcium sources are held. Vitamin D increases calcium absorption.

options.text: Bed rest to save her energy
options.rationale: Immobility is a cause of high calcium.

options.text: Hydrochlorothiazide in place of furosemide
options.rationale: Thiazide diuretics raise calcium and are stopped.

questions.takeaway: Hypercalcemia: stop calcium and vitamin D, 0.9% sodium chloride with a loop diuretic, stop thiazides, telemetry, check the legs for clots.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Ask of each item: does it lower calcium or guard against its dangers, or does it add calcium?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 0.9% sodium chloride and furosemide.
Telemetry for dysrhythmias, leg checks for clots.
Supplements, a thiazide and immobility.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C and D.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old with heart failure, leg edema and adequate urine output has a potassium of 5.8 mEq/L. Which new prescription does the nurse question?

options.text: Furosemide IV twice daily
options.rationale: With adequate urine output a loop diuretic treats the edema and increases potassium excretion.

options.text: Spironolactone by mouth once daily
options.rationale: A potassium sparing diuretic is a cause of high potassium. It would treat the edema and push the potassium higher.

options.text: Patiromer by mouth once daily
options.rationale: A binder that removes potassium through the GI tract.

options.text: Continuous cardiac telemetry on the unit
options.rationale: High potassium can cause lethal dysrhythmias, so the monitor is expected.

questions.takeaway: Potassium sparing diuretics such as spironolactone raise potassium. In high potassium with working kidneys, the diuretic that helps is one that increases potassium excretion.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two options are diuretics and both would treat the edema. Ask what each one does to potassium.

steps.detail: You are looking for the prescription that does not fit.

steps.action: Clear the remover and the monitor
steps.detail: Patiromer binds potassium in the GI tract, and telemetry guards the heart.
Furosemide increases potassium excretion. Spironolactone holds potassium in.

elimination.verdict: The spironolactone.

questions.stem: A client with kidney failure and a magnesium of 4.6 mEq/L had respirations of 8 and absent knee reflexes. IV calcium was given. Which finding shows the calcium is working?

options.text: Respirations of 15 with knee reflexes present
options.rationale: Calcium counters the depressant effect of magnesium on muscles and the heart. Better breathing and returning reflexes are the proof.

options.text: A repeat magnesium level that is unchanged
options.rationale: Expected, because calcium does not remove magnesium. It is not evidence that the client is safer.

options.text: Heart rate down from 58 to 50
options.rationale: A slowing heart is the magnesium effect getting worse.

options.text: She is sleeping and hard to wake
options.rationale: Drowsiness moving toward coma is a sign of toxicity, not of rest.

questions.takeaway: IV calcium is the antidote for magnesium toxicity. It reverses the effects on breathing, reflexes and the heart and leaves the level where it was.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Ask what the antidote was given to fix, then look for that exact problem reversed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Respirations of 8 and absent reflexes.
Respirations of 15 and reflexes back.

steps.action: Do not rely on the level
steps.detail: Calcium does not lower magnesium, so the number cannot show the effect.

elimination.verdict: Breathing and reflexes have recovered.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old postmenopausal woman with low vitamin D intake has a calcium of 8.4 mg/dL. She has no tingling, a negative Trousseau sign and a normal QT interval. Which prescription does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: IV calcium with continuous cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: The right electrolyte, and the right choice for severe or symptomatic low calcium. She has no tingling, no spasm and a normal QT.

options.text: Calcitonin to protect her bones
options.rationale: Tempting for a postmenopausal woman. Calcitonin lowers blood calcium by moving it into bone, and her level is already low.

options.text: Oral calcium with vitamin D
options.rationale: Mild low calcium without symptoms is replaced by mouth, and vitamin D is what lets the gut absorb it.

options.text: IV 0.9% sodium chloride with furosemide
options.rationale: This promotes calcium excretion. It is treatment for a high calcium.

questions.takeaway: Mild or chronic low calcium without symptoms: oral calcium with vitamin D. IV calcium on a monitor is for severe or symptomatic low calcium.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The stem lists what is absent. No tingling, no spasm and a normal QT tell you how severe this is, and severity picks the route.

steps.detail: Calcitonin and saline with furosemide both bring calcium down.
8.4 mg/dL with no tingling, a negative Trousseau sign and a normal QT is mild.
Mild or chronic low calcium is replaced by mouth, with vitamin D for absorption.

elimination.verdict: Oral calcium with vitamin D.

questions.stem: A client with a potassium of 2.7 mEq/L and flat T waves has potassium chloride 40 mEq, diluted in 250 mL, prescribed to infuse over 1 hour through a forearm IV. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Start it on a pump as prescribed because of the T waves
options.rationale: Tempting because of the ECG changes. A dose of 40 mEq in one hour is far above the 5 to 10 mEq per hour limit and can itself stop the heart.

options.text: Hold the bag and clarify the rate with the provider
options.rationale: The dilution and the pump are right, but the rate is unsafe. The nurse does not give it until the prescription is corrected.

options.text: Run it over 4 hours and tell the provider at rounds
options.rationale: The slower rate is the safe one, but the nurse cannot rewrite a prescription alone and report it later.

options.text: Give half now by slow IV push and infuse the rest
options.rationale: Potassium is never given IV push at any speed.

questions.takeaway: IV potassium: diluted, on a pump, 5 to 10 mEq per hour, never pushed. A low level with ECG changes does not make a faster rate safe.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Check the prescription against each potassium rule in turn: diluted, pump, rate. One of them fails.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 40 mEq in 1 hour is four times the upper limit.
IV push potassium is out in every case.
Changing the rate alone is outside the nurse's role, so the prescription is clarified first.

elimination.verdict: Hold and clarify the rate.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old with a potassium of 2.8 mEq/L and weak legs is receiving IV potassium chloride on a pump. Which task does the nurse assign to assistive personnel?

options.text: Check the IV site each hour for burning
options.rationale: Site assessment during a high alert, vein irritating infusion is nursing assessment and stays with the nurse.

options.text: Explain which foods are high in potassium
options.rationale: Teaching belongs to the nurse.

options.text: Walk with her to the bathroom each time she gets up
options.rationale: Her weak legs make her a fall risk. Assisting with ambulation is a routine task with a predictable outcome.

options.text: Watch the monitor and decide if the rhythm has changed
options.rationale: Interpreting the rhythm is a nursing judgment, even though assistive personnel can report what they see.

questions.takeaway: Low potassium weakens muscles, so falls precautions apply. The nurse keeps assessment, teaching and judgment and hands off hands on safety help.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Sort each task: does it need assessing, teaching or deciding? Whatever needs none of those can be assigned.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The IV site check and the rhythm decision both need nursing judgment.
Diet teaching stays with the nurse.
Help with walking for a client with weak legs.

elimination.verdict: Assisted walks to the bathroom.

questions.stem: A client with kidney disease and a potassium of 5.9 mEq/L had tingling and twitching in both hands this morning. Which afternoon finding tells the nurse the high potassium is getting worse?

options.text: Weakness in both feet that is spreading up the legs
options.rationale: After the early tingling and twitching, high potassium moves on to weakness and flaccid paralysis that ascends from the hands and feet.

options.text: Hyperactive bowel sounds with two loose stools
options.rationale: Tempting because it is a high potassium finding. An active gut with loose stool is part of the early picture and does not mark progression.

options.text: Twitching still present in both hands
options.rationale: The same early sign as this morning. Unchanged is not worse.

options.text: Constipation with hypoactive bowel sounds
options.rationale: A slow gut is the low potassium picture. High potassium speeds the gut up.

questions.takeaway: High potassium: tingling and twitching come early. Weakness that climbs from the hands and feet toward flaccid paralysis means it is progressing.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Weakness makes you think of low potassium. In high potassium it is the late stage, so sort the options into early, unchanged and later.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Constipation with a quiet gut belongs to low potassium.

steps.action: Remove the early and unchanged findings
steps.detail: Loose stools with an active gut and continued twitching are the early picture.
Weakness that is moving upward is the next stage.

elimination.verdict: Weakness spreading up the legs.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old with diabetic ketoacidosis has received 2 liters of 0.9% sodium chloride. Blood pressure is now 118/72, and the provider changes the fluid to 0.45% sodium chloride. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Hang the 0.45% sodium chloride as prescribed
options.rationale: Once the pressure is stable, hypotonic fluid is the expected next step in diabetic ketoacidosis. It moves water back into dry cells.

options.text: Hold the fluid and question the order
options.rationale: Tempting because hypotonic fluid is wrong for low blood pressure or a brain problem. The pressure is now 118/72 and no brain problem is reported.

options.text: Keep the 0.9% sodium chloride running for now
options.rationale: Isotonic fluid refilled the vessels. Staying on it leaves the cells dry and adds volume the client no longer needs.

options.text: Ask for 5% dextrose in 0.9% sodium chloride
options.rationale: A hypertonic fluid pulls more water out of cells that are already dehydrated.

questions.takeaway: Hypotonic fluid is questioned with low blood pressure, head injury or increased intracranial pressure. In diabetic ketoacidosis with a stable pressure it is the expected order.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Do not question an order only because the fluid is hypotonic. Check the client for the contraindications first. Here the pressure is the detail that clears it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 0.45% sodium chloride is hypotonic and hydrates cells.
No brain problem is reported, and the pressure is no longer low.
More isotonic fluid stays in the vessels. Hypertonic fluid dries the cells further.

elimination.verdict: Hang it as prescribed. The order fits this client now.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old with a bone infection will go home on IV vancomycin for 6 weeks. Her forearm veins are scarred. Which device does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: A midline catheter in the upper arm
options.rationale: Tempting because a midline suits antibiotics and poor veins. Its dwell time is up to 4 weeks, and this therapy is 6.

options.text: A peripherally inserted central catheter
options.rationale: Weeks to months of therapy with an irritating drug fits a PICC, and it spares repeated sticks in scarred veins.

options.text: A short peripheral catheter restarted as needed
options.rationale: Six weeks of restarts in scarred veins means repeated failed sticks and phlebitis.

options.text: A nontunneled catheter in the subclavian vein
options.rationale: Short term acute care device with the highest infection risk. It is a poor choice for home.

questions.takeaway: Ask how long, how irritating and how good the veins are. Past 4 weeks a midline no longer fits, so the PICC is the answer.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Midline and PICC both go in at the upper arm and both carry antibiotics. The 6 weeks in the stem is what separates them.

steps.detail: A nontunneled line is for days in the hospital.
Scarred veins will not last 6 weeks.
A midline dwells up to 4 weeks. A PICC dwells weeks to months.

elimination.verdict: The PICC. Duration tips it.

questions.stem: The nurse started a unit of packed red blood cells 15 minutes ago on a stable 60-year-old. An AP is free to help. Which action is best?

options.text: Ask the AP to take the vital signs and report them
options.rationale: Tempting because vital signs on a stable patient are delegable. This set is a check for a transfusion reaction, which is assessment.

options.text: Increase the rate so the unit finishes within 4 hours
options.rationale: The rate is not raised until the 15 minute check shows no reaction.

options.text: Take the vital signs and assess the patient personally
options.rationale: The 15 minute reassessment looks for a reaction and needs the nurse's judgment, so the nurse does it.

options.text: Document the baseline vital signs and return in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Skips the 15 minute check, the point where most severe reactions appear.

questions.takeaway: The 15 minute transfusion check is an assessment for a reaction. The RN keeps it even when the patient looks stable.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides.
questions.strategy: The word stable invites delegation. Ask what the vital signs are for. Here they are the nurse's evaluation of a blood product.

steps.action: Cut the option that skips the check
steps.detail: Reassessment at 15 minutes is required.
You assess before you speed up.

steps.action: Decide who takes the vital signs
steps.detail: Looking for a reaction is interpretation, which stays with the RN.

elimination.verdict: The nurse takes the vital signs and assesses.

questions.stem: The nurse scrubs a forearm site with chlorhexidine and lets it dry. With the tourniquet on, the vein can no longer be seen. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Feel for the vein through a fresh pair of clean gloves
options.rationale: Tempting because the gloves are new. Clean gloves are not sterile, so touching the site undoes the prep.

options.text: Feel for the vein, then scrub again and let it dry
options.rationale: Touching the prepped skin contaminates it. If the vein must be felt again, the 30 second scrub and the full dry time are repeated.

options.text: Insert the catheter where the vein was seen earlier
options.rationale: A blind stick risks a missed vein or a nerve, and attempts are limited.

options.text: Feel for the vein, then wipe once with alcohol
options.rationale: A quick wipe is not a 30 second scrub with friction and a full dry time.

questions.takeaway: After the skin prep, the site is not touched. If you must palpate again, you prep again: scrub with friction for 30 seconds and let it air dry.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Three options try to save time. Ask whether the skin is still clean at the moment the catheter goes in.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: No touch after the prep.
Guessing at the vein is unsafe.
Only one restores the full prep afterward.

elimination.verdict: Palpate, then repeat the scrub and let it dry.

questions.stem: A confused 63-year-old with a serum sodium of 116 mEq/L has received 3% sodium chloride by pump for 6 hours. Which finding indicates the therapy is working as intended?

options.text: Sodium 136 mEq/L and the patient is now drowsy
options.rationale: Tempting because the number is normal. A rise of 20 mEq/L in 6 hours is far too fast, and the drowsiness is a new neurologic change.

options.text: Sodium 120 mEq/L and the patient states the correct date
options.rationale: A gradual rise with clearer thinking is the goal of hypertonic saline.

options.text: Sodium 117 mEq/L with new crackles in both lung bases
options.rationale: Almost no correction, plus a sign of circulatory overload from fluid pulled into the vessels.

options.text: Sodium 119 mEq/L with a new report of headache and nausea
options.rationale: The number is rising, but new neurologic symptoms need follow up before calling it a success.

questions.takeaway: With hypertonic saline, success is a slow rise in sodium with improving neurologic status and clear lungs.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides.
questions.strategy: The normal sodium looks like the win. Check how fast it got there and what the patient looks like.

steps.detail: Crackles are a listed risk of hypertonic fluid.
Headache and nausea are not improvement.
A slow rise with better orientation beats a fast rise with drowsiness.

elimination.verdict: Sodium 120 and oriented to the date.

questions.stem: The nurse hung 1,000 mL of lactated Ringer's to run over 8 hours by gravity with 15 drops per mL tubing. Ten minutes later it runs at 44 drops per minute. The client has no shortness of breath. Which action is best?

options.text: Stop the infusion and notify the provider
options.rationale: Tempting because the fluid is running too fast. Only 10 minutes have passed and the client has no shortness of breath, so the nurse corrects the rate and keeps monitoring.

options.text: Leave the rate and recount the drops in 1 hour
options.rationale: At 44 drops per minute the bag would empty hours early.

options.text: Adjust the clamp to 31 drops per minute
options.rationale: 1,000 mL over 8 hours is 125 mL per hour. 125 times 15, divided by 60, is 31 drops per minute.

options.text: Adjust the clamp to 21 drops per minute
options.rationale: This is the answer for 10 drops per mL tubing. The set in use delivers 15 drops per mL.

questions.takeaway: Drops per minute equals mL per hour times the drop factor, divided by 60. A gravity line drifts, so count it and correct it.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides.
questions.strategy: Work the number before reading the options. Then ask whether a fast rate with no symptoms needs more than a correction.

steps.detail: 1,000 divided by 8 is 125 mL per hour.
125 times 15, divided by 60, is about 31.
No shortness of breath, and only 10 minutes at the wrong rate. Correct it and reassess.

elimination.verdict: Set the clamp to 31 drops per minute.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old admitted with dehydration and a blood pressure of 92/58 has received 0.9% sodium chloride at 75 mL per hour for 12 hours. Which findings indicate the therapy is effective and tolerated? Select all that apply.

options.text: Blood pressure 114/70
options.rationale: Isotonic fluid stays in the vessels and restores volume, so the pressure rises toward normal.

options.text: Urine output rose from 20 to 45 mL per hour
options.rationale: Better kidney perfusion shows the volume is being restored.

options.text: Heart rate rose from 92 to 118
options.rationale: A rising heart rate means the volume is still low or the heart is straining. Neither is the goal.

options.text: New fine crackles in both lung bases
options.rationale: An early sign of fluid overload. Older adults have less cardiac and renal reserve.

options.text: Lungs clear with respirations of 16
options.rationale: Shows the client is tolerating the volume. Clear lungs are the tolerated half of the question.

options.text: New restlessness with neck vein distention
options.rationale: Signs of circulatory overload, which calls for slowing the fluid and notifying the provider.

questions.takeaway: Fluid replacement in an older adult is judged two ways: is the volume back, and are the lungs still clear.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The stem asks for effective and tolerated. Volume signs answer the first word. Lung and neck vein findings answer the second.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Is the volume back? Pressure and urine output say yes.
Is the client tolerating it? Clear lungs say yes.
A faster heart rate, crackles and neck vein distention all mean trouble.

elimination.verdict: Blood pressure up, urine output up, lungs clear. Three of six.

questions.stem: Halfway through an IV push given faster than prescribed, a 52-year-old becomes flushed and reports a pounding headache and chest tightness. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Take a full set of vital signs
options.rationale: Tempting as assessment first. The cues already identify the problem, and the drug is still going in.

options.text: Finish the dose slowly over the correct time
options.rationale: More drug worsens a reaction to rapid infusion.

options.text: Notify the provider of the reaction
options.rationale: Needed, after the cause is stopped.

options.text: Stop the injection
options.rationale: Flushing, headache and chest tightness during a rapid push are speed shock. Stopping the drug removes the cause.

questions.takeaway: Speed shock comes from a drug given too fast. Stop the drug first, then check vital signs and notify.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: When the stem already gives the assessment, the first step is the action that removes the cause.

steps.detail: A rapid push with flushing, headache and chest tightness.
It adds more of the cause.
Stop, then vital signs, then notify.

elimination.verdict: Stop the injection.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old with left arm paralysis from a stroke needs 2 days of isotonic fluid. She has a visible vein on the back of the right hand. Which site does the nurse choose?

options.text: The left forearm, to keep her working arm free
options.rationale: A paralyzed limb is a contraindicated site.

options.text: The right antecubital fossa
options.rationale: Avoided for short peripheral catheters because bending the elbow kinks and dislodges them.

options.text: The right forearm
options.rationale: A forearm vein in the unaffected arm fits the site rules and spares the fragile hand veins of an older adult.

options.text: The back of the right hand
options.rationale: Tempting because the rule is most distal site first. In older adults the dorsal hand is avoided: thin skin and fragile veins infiltrate easily.

questions.takeaway: Distal first applies among appropriate sites. For an older adult the appropriate range starts at the forearm, not the hand.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two rules compete here: start distal, and avoid the dorsal hand in older adults. Her age decides which rule wins.

steps.detail: Contraindicated regardless of convenience.

steps.action: Cut the bend of the elbow
steps.detail: Not for short peripheral catheters.
At 82, skip the hand.

elimination.verdict: The right forearm.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old with a hemoglobin of 6.9 g/dL, dizziness and a heart rate of 112 received 2 units of packed red blood cells. Which finding indicates the transfusion was effective?

options.text: Hemoglobin 7.2 g/dL and heart rate 108
options.rationale: Two units should raise the hemoglobin about 2 g/dL. This is almost no change.

options.text: Hemoglobin 9.0 g/dL with new crackles
options.rationale: Tempting because the number is right. New crackles mean the volume overloaded the circulation, which is a complication.

options.text: Heart rate 94 with chills and a new fever
options.rationale: The slower heart rate looks good, but chills and fever point to a transfusion reaction.

options.text: Hemoglobin 8.8 g/dL and heart rate 88
options.rationale: About 1 g/dL per unit, and the heart no longer has to race to deliver oxygen.

questions.takeaway: Expect roughly 1 g/dL per unit of red cells, with the symptoms of anemia easing and no new problem from the transfusion.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Effective means the goal was met without harm. Check each option for the expected rise and for a new finding that spoils it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 6.9 plus about 2 is near 9.
7.2 is too small a rise.
Crackles and fever are complications, whatever the hemoglobin.

elimination.verdict: 8.8 g/dL with a heart rate of 88. Goal met, nothing new.

questions.stem: A nurse has taught an orientee about infection prevention with IV lines. Which action by the orientee shows the teaching was effective?

options.text: Wipes the needleless connector for 5 seconds before a flush
options.rationale: Too short. The scrub is at least 15 seconds.

options.text: Scrubs the needleless connector for 15 seconds before each access
options.rationale: Scrub the hub for at least 15 seconds every time the line is entered.

options.text: Fans the chlorhexidine dry before inserting the catheter
options.rationale: The antiseptic must air dry on its own. Fanning or blotting cuts its effect.

options.text: Changes an intact, dry transparent dressing every 2 days
options.rationale: Two days is the gauze interval. An intact transparent dressing stays 7 days, and extra changes expose the site.

questions.takeaway: Hub scrub at least 15 seconds every access. Antiseptic air dries. Transparent dressing every 7 days, gauze every 2.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Each option holds one number or one technique detail. Check each against the slide value.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Only 15 meets the minimum.
Air dry only.
Every 2 days belongs to gauze.

elimination.verdict: The 15 second scrub before each access.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old has had a femoral nontunneled central line for 9 days. Which finding does the nurse follow up first?

options.text: The tubing label is a week old
options.rationale: Overdue for a change and needs correcting. It is a risk, not yet a problem in the patient.

options.text: The dressing is damp and lifted at one corner
options.rationale: Tempting because a damp dressing must be changed. It can be changed right after the patient is assessed.

options.text: New confusion with a temperature of 38.9 C
options.rationale: Fever and new confusion with a high risk line suggest a bloodstream infection. An actual systemic problem comes before the risks.

options.text: The insertion site is pink and slightly tender
options.rationale: A local finding that is watched and reported. The systemic signs are more urgent.

questions.takeaway: Femoral site plus many line days is the highest risk combination. Fever and new confusion with no other source point to CRBSI.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: All four need attention. Rank actual before potential and systemic before local.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Old tubing and a damp dressing raise risk.
A pink site is local. Fever and confusion are systemic.
A possible bloodstream infection cannot wait.

elimination.verdict: New confusion with fever. Think sepsis from the line.

questions.scenario: A 79-year-old has 0.9% sodium chloride running through a left hand catheter. The pump has alarmed twice. The hand is cool, pale and puffy, and no blood return is obtained.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the patient is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Stop the infusion and remove the catheter
options.rationale: The slide action for infiltration: stop immediately and remove.

options.text: Elevate the left arm
options.rationale: Elevation helps the leaked fluid reabsorb.

options.text: Slow the rate and recheck in 1 hour
options.rationale: Fluid keeps entering the tissue at any rate.

options.text: Flush the catheter with saline to clear it
options.rationale: Pushes more fluid into tissue that is already full.

options.text: Infiltration
options.rationale: Cool, pale, puffy skin, a pump that keeps alarming and no blood return.

options.text: Phlebitis
options.rationale: Phlebitis is warm and red with a streak or cord along the vein.

options.text: Venous thrombosis
options.rationale: Thrombosis swells and pains the limb. It does not make the skin at the site cool and pale.

options.text: Catheter related bloodstream infection
options.rationale: That is systemic: fever, chills, hypotension.

options.text: Size of the edema and the infiltration grade
options.rationale: Shows whether the swelling is resolving, and the grade is documented.

options.text: Sensation and capillary refill in the fingers
options.rationale: Swelling in thin older skin can press on nerves and vessels.

options.text: Length of the red streak along the vein
options.rationale: A phlebitis measure. This hand is cool and pale, not warm and red.

options.text: Blood culture results
options.rationale: Nothing here suggests bloodstream infection.

questions.takeaway: Cool, pale and puffy with no blood return is infiltration. Stop, remove, elevate, then grade it and keep reassessing the hand.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Decide the condition from skin temperature first. Then pick the actions and the monitoring that belong to that condition only.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Cool and pale is infiltration. Warm and red is phlebitis.

steps.action: Cut actions that keep fluid running
steps.detail: Slowing or flushing adds to the leak.
Edema, grade and circulation in the fingers follow from infiltration.

elimination.verdict: Stop and remove, elevate; infiltration; edema and grade, sensation and capillary refill.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old with thin skin and small forearm veins is prescribed 1 unit of packed red blood cells. Which catheter does the nurse select?

options.text: An 18 gauge catheter
options.rationale: Tempting because 18 is the preferred blood gauge. In fragile veins the larger catheter raises the risk of vein trauma and hematoma.

options.text: A 16 gauge catheter
options.rationale: Large bore is for trauma and rapid resuscitation, and rapid infusion is poorly tolerated at 84.

options.text: A 24 gauge catheter
options.rationale: Kind to the vein but below the 18 to 20 gauge required for blood products.

options.text: A 20 gauge catheter
options.rationale: Meets the 18 to 20 gauge requirement for blood while following the older adult rule of the smallest effective gauge.

questions.takeaway: Blood needs an 18 to 20 gauge. Older adults get the smallest gauge that does the job. The overlap is a 20.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two rules apply at once. Find the size that satisfies both instead of choosing one rule and ignoring the other.

steps.detail: One unit at 84 does not call for rapid infusion.
Outside the range for blood.
Fragile veins tip it to the smaller acceptable size.

elimination.verdict: The 20 gauge.

questions.stem: An 88-year-old receiving subcutaneous fluid in the abdomen for mild dehydration is now hard to rouse with a blood pressure of 78/44. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Request an order for IV access and fluids
options.rationale: Subcutaneous fluid absorbs slowly and is not used in severe dehydration or shock. The client needs a route that reaches the vessels directly.

options.text: Raise the subcutaneous rate to the maximum
options.rationale: The route tops out at about 1 mL per minute, far too slow for shock.

options.text: Add a second subcutaneous site in the thigh
options.rationale: Tempting because it doubles the volume. Two slow sites are still too slow, and absorption is poor when perfusion is low.

options.text: Give oral fluids and recheck in 20 minutes
options.rationale: The client is hard to rouse, so oral fluid is an aspiration risk and a delay.

questions.takeaway: Hypodermoclysis is for mild to moderate dehydration. Once the patient is in shock, the route has to change.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The assessment is done and the client is unstable. Ask whether the current route can ever deliver enough, then change it.

steps.detail: Mild dehydration has become hypotension with a falling level of consciousness.
Subcutaneous fluid is slow by design.

steps.action: Cut what keeps the slow route
steps.detail: More rate and a second site stay subcutaneous. Oral fluid is unsafe.

elimination.verdict: Call for IV access. The route no longer fits the patient.

questions.stem: While a client sits up in bed, the cap falls off his subclavian central line. He gasps, grabs his chest and reports sudden shortness of breath. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Clamp the catheter
options.rationale: Air is entering through the open line. Closing it stops more air before anything else is done.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed higher
options.rationale: Tempting for any dyspnea. For air embolism he goes on the left side with the head down to trap air in the right atrium.

options.text: Apply oxygen at 100%
options.rationale: Needed, and it follows clamping and positioning. Oxygen does not stop air from entering.

options.text: Call the rapid response team
options.rationale: Needed, and it comes after the source of air is closed.

questions.takeaway: Air embolism: clamp, left side with head down, 100% oxygen, call rapid response. Stop the air first.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Every option except one belongs in the response. Ask which action stops the cause, because the cause is still active.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Open central line plus sudden dyspnea and chest pain.
Upright lets air travel toward the lungs.
Clamp, position, oxygen, call.

elimination.verdict: Clamp the catheter. Then left side, head down, oxygen and help.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old with a hemoglobin of 6.5 g/dL is prescribed 1 unit of packed red blood cells. The type and crossmatch is complete. Place the nurse's actions in order.

options.text: Confirm written informed consent is on file
options.rationale: Consent must be on file before the blood leaves the blood bank.

options.text: Record baseline vital signs
options.rationale: Taken before the unit is picked up so the 4 hour clock is not used on preparation, and so later changes can be judged.

options.text: Obtain the unit from the blood bank
options.rationale: The clock starts at issue, so everything else is ready first.

options.text: Verify the unit with a second nurse at the bedside
options.rationale: Two licensed nurses independently match the label to the identification band, then both sign.

options.text: Start the transfusion and reassess at 15 minutes
options.rationale: The infusion begins only after verification, with the first reassessment at 15 minutes.

questions.takeaway: Consent and baseline vital signs come before the blood is picked up. The 4 hour limit starts when the unit is issued.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Students fetch the blood first because it feels like the start. Anything that can be done without the unit in hand is done before the clock starts.

steps.action: Find what must exist before retrieval
steps.detail: Consent on file.

steps.action: Do the assessment before the unit arrives
steps.detail: Baseline vital signs.
Pick up, verify with a second nurse, start, reassess at 15 minutes.

elimination.verdict: Consent, baseline vital signs, obtain unit, two nurse check, start and reassess.

questions.stem: A patient going home with a PICC in the right arm has completed teaching. Which statement shows the teaching was understood?

options.text: "I can swim as long as I wear the waterproof cover."
options.rationale: Tempting because the cover is correct for showers. The arm is never submerged, so swimming and baths are out.

options.text: "Flushing should take a firm push if the line is sluggish."
options.rationale: Resistance means stop and call. Forcing a flush is unsafe.

options.text: "If I get a fever or chills, I will call right away."
options.rationale: Fever over 38 C or chills are warning signs of a line infection that need care immediately.

options.text: "My blood pressure can be taken on either arm."
options.rationale: No blood pressure cuffs or needle sticks on the PICC arm.

questions.takeaway: PICC at home: keep it dry, shower with a cover, never submerge, no cuff on that arm, stop if a flush resists, report fever or chills at once.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The swimming option is half right. The cover is real, and it is for showering only.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Resistance means do not use the line.
The PICC arm is off limits for a cuff.
A cover does not make submerging safe.

elimination.verdict: Calling right away for fever or chills.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old trauma patient has a tibial intraosseous line placed 20 hours ago during resuscitation. Two forearm peripheral IVs now run well. Which plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Keep the intraosseous line as backup until discharge from the unit
options.rationale: Tempting because extra access feels safer in a trauma patient. The device is limited to 24 hours and working IV access now exists.

options.text: Ask the provider about removing the intraosseous line now
options.rationale: Intraosseous access is a bridge when IV access fails. With IVs working and the 24 hour limit close, it should come out.

options.text: Move the maintenance fluid to the intraosseous line to rest the veins
options.rationale: Adds use of an emergency device that is due for removal.

options.text: Change the intraosseous dressing and reassess next shift
options.rationale: That would pass the 24 hour limit.

questions.takeaway: Intraosseous access is emergency access, limited to 24 hours. Once IV access is established, plan its removal.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Count the hours in the stem. Twenty hours in with two good IVs means the reason for the device is gone.

steps.detail: 24 hours.

steps.action: Notice three options keep the device
steps.detail: Backup, more use and a later recheck all extend the dwell.

steps.action: Pick the one that removes it
steps.detail: The need has ended.

elimination.verdict: Ask about removing it now.

questions.stem: During a morning peritoneal dialysis exchange, a 55-year-old's outflow is cloudy. She has no fever and says she feels fine. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Continue exchanges and check her temperature each shift
options.rationale: Tempting because she looks well. Cloudy outflow is often the first sign, before fever or pain.

options.text: Warm the next bag of dialysate a little longer
options.rationale: Warming is for comfort and has nothing to do with cloudiness.

options.text: Record it and compare with the next exchange
options.rationale: Waiting for a second cloudy bag delays treatment of a peritoneal infection.

options.text: Report the cloudy outflow to the provider now
options.rationale: Cloudy effluent means peritonitis until proven otherwise, and it is reported when first seen.

questions.takeaway: With peritoneal dialysis, look at the outflow every exchange. Cloudy means peritonitis until proven otherwise, even in a patient who feels well.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Do not let a normal temperature cancel an abnormal finding. Ask whether cloudy outflow is ever expected.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Outflow should be clear.
No fever and feeling fine do not rule out early infection.
Monitoring and comparing later both delay the report.

elimination.verdict: Report it now. Cloudy outflow is the early sign.

questions.stem: Ten minutes into a unit of packed red blood cells, a patient reports itching and has hives on the chest. Vital signs match the baseline. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Stop the transfusion and keep the vein open
options.rationale: Hives are a listed reaction sign. Every reaction starts the same way: stop the blood so no more enters, then keep the vein open with saline through new tubing.

options.text: Slow the rate and give prescribed diphenhydramine
options.rationale: Tempting because the reaction looks mild and vitals are stable. Blood keeps entering while a reaction is under way.

options.text: Take a full set of vital signs
options.rationale: Vitals are needed and come after the blood is stopped. The stem already gives stable vitals.

options.text: Notify the provider and the blood bank
options.rationale: Required, and it follows stopping the transfusion.

questions.takeaway: Any sign of a transfusion reaction, mild or severe, gets the same first action: stop the blood.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides.
questions.strategy: All four are real steps in a reaction. Put them in order and pick the one that stops the exposure.

steps.detail: Itching and hives during blood is a reaction.
Vitals are given and stable.
Stop, saline with new tubing, vitals, notify.

elimination.verdict: Stop the transfusion.

questions.stem: After removing a peripheral IV catheter from the forearm, the nurse sees the tip is jagged and shorter than expected. The patient has no symptoms. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Take vital signs and watch for chest pain
options.rationale: Assessment is tempting because the patient feels fine. The fragment can still travel, so it is contained first.

options.text: Notify the provider and save the catheter
options.rationale: Both are required and follow securing the limb. They do not keep the fragment in the arm.

options.text: Apply a tourniquet high on that arm
options.rationale: A missing tip means a piece is in the vein. A tourniquet high on the limb keeps it from reaching the heart and lungs.

options.text: Apply pressure to the site and elevate the arm
options.rationale: Routine after removal. It does nothing for a fragment already in the vein.

questions.takeaway: A catheter that comes out short is a catheter embolism. Trap the fragment in the limb first, then notify and keep the piece.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: No symptoms does not mean no problem. Infer what the jagged tip means, then choose the action that prevents the harm.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A piece broke off inside the vein.
Travel to the heart or lungs.
Only the tourniquet stops travel.

elimination.verdict: Apply a tourniquet high on the arm.

questions.stem: A patient who had a right mastectomy with lymph node removal 6 years ago has a dialysis fistula in the left forearm. She needs IV antibiotics. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Use the left hand, below the fistula
options.rationale: The right arm is excluded, which makes the left look like the answer. The whole fistula arm is off limits.

options.text: Use the right forearm, since the surgery was years ago
options.rationale: Time does not restore the lymph drainage. That arm stays protected.

options.text: Use a vein on the top of the foot
options.rationale: Tempting because both arms are out. Legs are on the avoid list for adults, so the foot fails the same check the arms do.

options.text: Ask the provider about another access option
options.rationale: Every site offered is on the avoid list, and a restricted limb is not used without a provider's order. The provider decides on other access.

questions.takeaway: Never use the mastectomy side, the fistula arm or an adult's leg. When every site is excluded, the answer is to escalate, not to pick the least bad site.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Check each site against the avoid list before comparing them. If every site fails, the answer is the option that is not a site.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Mastectomy with node removal.
Fistula, including the hand below it.
Legs are on the avoid list for adults.

elimination.verdict: Ask the provider about another access option.

questions.stem: The RN is busy with a patient who has new chest tightness. Which task does the RN assign to the LPN?

options.text: Start the second unit of packed red blood cells
options.rationale: It sounds routine because it is a second unit. Starting any unit of blood stays with the RN.

options.text: Hang the next liter of saline on a stable patient
options.rationale: A routine fluid on an established line in a stable patient is within the LPN role.

options.text: Choose the IV site for a patient after mastectomy
options.rationale: Initial access assessment and site selection are RN judgment.

options.text: Flush the PICC that met resistance this morning
options.rationale: LPNs flush established lines, which makes this tempting. Resistance is a problem that needs RN assessment, and a line is not flushed against it.

questions.takeaway: Delegate the routine task on the stable patient. Blood, site selection and any line with a problem stay with the RN.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: For each task ask two things: is it routine, and is the patient or the line stable? One detail in each wrong option answers no.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Any unit is an RN start.
Site selection is assessment.
Resistance makes it unstable.

elimination.verdict: The next liter of saline on a stable patient.

questions.stem: A 77-year-old with heart failure has 0.9% sodium chloride running at 100 mL per hour. She is newly short of breath with crackles in both bases. The forearm site is soft and painless. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Slow the infusion and sit her upright
options.rationale: Isotonic fluid is overloading her circulation. Slowing it to the lowest rate and raising the head of the bed act on the cause at once and keep the access she will need.

options.text: Stop the infusion and remove the catheter
options.rationale: Tempting because stopping is the first action for a bad site. Her site is fine. The problem is volume, and the line is needed for a diuretic.

options.text: Call the provider to request a diuretic
options.rationale: Needed, and it follows the actions the nurse can take right away.

options.text: Take full vital signs and total the intake and output
options.rationale: Tempting as assessment first. Dyspnea and crackles on IV fluid already identify the problem, and fluid keeps running while you count.

questions.takeaway: Circulatory overload: slow the IV, sit the client upright, give oxygen, take vital signs, notify. Stop and remove is the response to a failing site, not to too much volume.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Decide whether the problem is the site or the volume. The stem tells you the site is soft and painless, so the catheter stays and the rate changes.

steps.detail: New dyspnea and crackles in a weak heart on isotonic fluid.
Soft and painless, so there is no reason to remove the catheter.
Slow and sit upright, then vital signs, then call for a diuretic.

elimination.verdict: Slow the infusion and sit her upright.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old with cellulitis needs 10 days of a nonirritating IV antibiotic. Two short forearm catheters have failed in 3 days. Which device does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Another short peripheral catheter
options.rationale: Familiar and quick. The forearm veins have already failed twice and therapy runs well past 6 days.

options.text: A midline catheter in the upper arm
options.rationale: Fits therapy of up to 4 weeks with a nonvesicant drug and poor forearm veins, without the risks of a central line.

options.text: A peripherally inserted central catheter
options.rationale: Tempting because it also suits longer therapy. Nothing here needs a central tip: the drug is nonirritating and the course is 10 days.

options.text: A nontunneled subclavian catheter
options.rationale: For emergencies and critical care. It carries the highest infection risk of the central lines.

questions.takeaway: Choose the least invasive device that fits the length of therapy and the drug. Days to 4 weeks of a nonvesicant with poor veins is a midline.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
