questions.strategy: Ask how long, how irritating, how are the veins. Two options handle the duration; the drug decides between them.

steps.detail: 10 days is too long for short catheters in these veins.
Nonirritating, so a peripheral tip is acceptable.
Midline before a central line.

elimination.verdict: A midline catheter.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old's right arm with a PICC is 3 cm larger around than yesterday and aches, and the infusion has slowed. Skin color and temperature are normal. Which complication does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Infiltration
options.rationale: A slowed rate fits. Infiltration belongs to a peripheral catheter and gives cool, pale swelling at the site, not a whole arm that aches.

options.text: Phlebitis
options.rationale: Phlebitis is warm, red and tender along the vein, often with a cord. The skin color and temperature are normal.

options.text: Catheter-related thrombosis
options.rationale: A swollen, painful limb with a slowed rate is a clot around the catheter. The arm is never massaged.

options.text: Catheter-related bloodstream infection
options.rationale: That shows as fever, chills or low blood pressure with no other source. None is described.

questions.takeaway: A limb that swells and aches around a central catheter while the rate slows is thrombosis until proven otherwise. Do not massage it.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Use the skin findings to cut options. Normal temperature and color remove the warm complication and the cool one.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Not warm and red, not cool and pale.
Larger and aching, not just the site.
None, so infection drops out.

elimination.verdict: Thrombosis.

questions.stem: On day 3 of IV vancomycin, a 43-year-old's forearm site is red and warm with a tender cord along the vein. The nurse has removed the catheter. Which action comes next?

options.text: Apply a warm moist compress to the site
options.rationale: Red, warm and corded is phlebitis. After the catheter is out, warm moist heat eases the inflamed vein.

options.text: Apply a cold pack to the site
options.rationale: Tempting, because cold is the usual answer for swelling. For an inflamed vein the treatment is warm moist heat.

options.text: Restart the infusion lower in the same vein
options.rationale: Tempting because the vein is already located. Sites below a phlebitis are avoided, so a new catheter goes in the other arm.

options.text: Cover the site with a pressure dressing
options.rationale: Pressure is for a hematoma, where blood is leaking. This site is inflamed, not bleeding.

questions.takeaway: Phlebitis is warm, red and corded. Take the catheter out, apply a warm moist compress, grade it, and restart away from that vein.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Name the complication from the skin first. Warm and red is the vein wall, cool and pale is fluid in the tissue, and each has its own compress.

steps.detail: Warm, red, tender cord is phlebitis.
The catheter is already out.
An inflamed vein gets warm moist heat.

elimination.verdict: The warm moist compress.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old has had a left tibial intraosseous line for 6 hours after a crash. Which finding does the nurse follow up first?

options.text: He rates pain at the needle site 4 on a 0 to 10 scale
options.rationale: Discomfort at the site is common and deserves treatment. It does not by itself show a limb at risk.

options.text: Fluid runs only when a pressure bag is used
options.rationale: Expected. Marrow resists flow, so intraosseous lines often need pressure.

options.text: A forearm IV attempt has just failed
options.rationale: Matters because the line has a 24 hour limit. Eighteen hours remain to gain access.

options.text: The left calf is tense, cool and mottled
options.rationale: Signs of pressure building in the muscle compartment, the rare and serious complication of this route. Blood flow to the leg is at risk now.

questions.takeaway: With an intraosseous line, check the limb below it. A tense, cool, mottled calf is compartment syndrome until proven otherwise.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Three options are problems with the line. One is a problem with the leg, and the leg is what cannot be replaced.

steps.detail: Pain and a pressure bag are expected with this route.
Needing other access is a problem for later today.
Tense, cool and mottled is happening now.

elimination.verdict: The calf.

questions.stem: A phlebotomist prepares to draw morning labs just above a right forearm catheter infusing 0.9% sodium chloride in a 73-year-old. Her left arm has no IV or restrictions. Which direction does the nurse give?

options.text: Draw the sample from the left arm
options.rationale: Blood is drawn from the arm opposite an infusion so the sample is not diluted by the fluid.

options.text: Stop the fluid, then draw above the site
options.rationale: Tempting, because stopping seems to remove the dilution. The rule is the opposite arm, never above an infusing catheter, and her left arm is available.

options.text: Draw the sample from the catheter
options.rationale: Short peripheral catheters are not used for routine blood draws.

options.text: Draw below the site with the fluid running
options.rationale: Below is better than above, and it still uses the infusing arm when a free arm is available.

questions.takeaway: Draw blood from the arm opposite an infusion. Never draw above an infusing IV.
questions.coverage: Not in Lecture PPT. Covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Before you fix the infusing arm, ask whether you need that arm at all.

steps.action: Count the arms in the options
steps.detail: Three use the right arm. One leaves it alone.
Interrupting her fluid is unnecessary when the left arm is free.
Opposite arm.

elimination.verdict: The left arm.

questions.stem: A unit of packed red blood cells has 3 hours left to run through a patient's only IV catheter. An IV antibiotic for sepsis is due now. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give the antibiotic through the Y port of the blood tubing
options.rationale: Nothing except 0.9% sodium chloride goes through a blood line. Drugs are never added to blood.

options.text: Give the antibiotic after the unit finishes
options.rationale: Protects the blood, and delays a sepsis antibiotic by 3 hours.

options.text: Pause the blood, flush and give the antibiotic
options.rationale: Tempting because it uses the line already in place. It still puts a drug through the blood tubing and uses up the unit's 4 hour limit.

options.text: Start a second IV site for the antibiotic
options.rationale: Both therapies are due now and cannot share a line, so the answer is another access.

questions.takeaway: Blood runs alone with 0.9% sodium chloride. When a drug is due during a transfusion, give it through a separate site.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two needs, one line. When neither therapy can wait and they cannot mix, look for the option that adds access.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The Y port and the pause both send drug through the blood line.
Sepsis antibiotics are time sensitive.
A second site.

elimination.verdict: Start a second IV site.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old with burns over 30% of the body has received lactated Ringer's for 8 hours. Which finding best indicates the fluid replacement is effective?

options.text: Weight is up 2 kg since admission
options.rationale: Shows fluid was given and kept. Much of it may be sitting in burned tissue and not in the vessels.

options.text: Urine output averages 50 mL per hour
options.rationale: Urine output shows the kidneys are being perfused, which is the sign that the vessels are full enough.

options.text: He reports that his thirst is gone
options.rationale: Thirst is subjective and unreliable as a measure of volume.

options.text: Swelling increases around the burns
options.rationale: Expected early in burns as fluid shifts into tissue. It does not show that circulation is adequate.

questions.takeaway: In burn fluid replacement, watch urine output. It is the bedside sign that the fluid is reaching the organs.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides.
questions.strategy: Ask which finding proves the fluid stayed in the vessels and reached an organ. Weight only proves it went in.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Perfusion, not just volume given.
Thirst.
Weight counts fluid in tissue too. Urine shows perfusion.

elimination.verdict: Urine output of 50 mL per hour.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old with a new implanted port will have chemotherapy every 3 weeks. Which statement shows she understood the teaching about the port between treatments?

options.text: "I can't swim or take baths while I have it."
options.rationale: That is PICC teaching. A port has nothing outside the skin, so she can swim and bathe between treatments.

options.text: "The dressing gets changed once a week."
options.rationale: A PICC or an accessed port has a dressing. Between treatments the port is under intact skin with no dressing.

options.text: "It gets flushed monthly when it isn't in use."
options.rationale: A port not in use is flushed monthly to keep it open. Her treatments at 3 week intervals cover that.

options.text: "I can't lift over 10 pounds on that side."
options.rationale: A lifting limit for the PICC arm. It is not part of port teaching between treatments.

questions.takeaway: An implanted port is under the skin: no dressing and no water limits between uses, and a monthly flush when it is not in use.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Three statements are correct for a different device. Ask which rule depends on having a catheter outside the skin.

steps.detail: Nothing exits the skin.
Water limits, dressing changes and lifting limits belong to the PICC.

steps.action: Keep what a buried device needs
steps.detail: Flushing.

elimination.verdict: The monthly flush.

questions.scenario: The charge nurse reviews new IV prescriptions for five patients before the fluids are hung.
questions.stem: For each prescription, indicate whether it is appropriate or should be questioned.

rows.text: 0.45% sodium chloride for a patient with a head injury and rising intracranial pressure
rows.rationale: Hypotonic fluid moves water into brain cells and worsens the swelling.

rows.text: 0.9% sodium chloride for a patient vomiting blood with a blood pressure of 86/52
rows.rationale: Isotonic fluid stays in the vessels and restores volume.

rows.text: 5% dextrose in water as the volume expander for a hypotensive patient
rows.rationale: Once the dextrose is used it acts as free water and leaves the vessels.

rows.text: 3% sodium chloride by pump for a patient with a sodium of 114 mEq/L and a seizure
rows.rationale: Hypertonic saline is for severe symptomatic hyponatremia, given slowly on a pump.

rows.text: Parenteral nutrition through a midline catheter
rows.rationale: A midline tip is peripheral. Parenteral nutrition needs a central line.

questions.takeaway: Look for the mismatch: hypotonic with a brain problem or low pressure, dextrose in water as a volume expander, concentrated solutions through a peripheral tip.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: For each row ask where the water will go, then ask whether this patient can afford that.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Hypotonic into cells, isotonic stays in vessels, hypertonic pulls water out.
Swollen brain, empty vessels, low sodium.
A midline is not central.

elimination.verdict: Question, appropriate, question, appropriate, question.

questions.nursesNote: The nurse observes an orientee start a peripheral IV on a 61-year-old. The orientee performs hand hygiene and puts on gloves. She selects a vein in the antecubital fossa. She shaves the hair over the site. She scrubs with chlorhexidine back and forth for 30 seconds. She fans the site to dry it faster. After insertion she tapes the tubing connection to secure it. She labels the dressing with the date.
questions.stem: Highlight the actions that show the orientee needs more teaching.

segments.text: The orientee performs hand hygiene and puts on gloves
segments.rationale: Correct. Hand hygiene is the single most effective measure.

segments.text: She selects a vein in the antecubital fossa
segments.rationale: The antecubital fossa is avoided for short catheters. The forearm is preferred.

segments.text: She shaves the hair over the site
segments.rationale: Shaving nicks the skin. Hair is clipped.

segments.text: She scrubs with chlorhexidine back and forth for 30 seconds
segments.rationale: Correct technique and time.

segments.text: She fans the site to dry it faster
segments.rationale: The antiseptic works as it air dries. Fanning, blotting or wiping undoes that.

segments.text: she tapes the tubing connection to secure it
segments.rationale: Connections are secured with Luer locks and are not taped.

segments.text: She labels the dressing with the date
segments.rationale: Correct. The site and dressing are dated.

questions.takeaway: Forearm before the antecubital fossa, clip instead of shave, let chlorhexidine air dry, lock connections instead of taping them.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Read each action as true or false on its own. Actions that look like extra care, such as fanning and taping, are the ones to check.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Hand hygiene, 30 second scrub, dated dressing.
Antecubital and shaved.
Fanned dry and taped.

elimination.verdict: Site choice, shaving, fanning and taping.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old who takes warfarin has an INR of 4.6 and oozing from his gums. Fresh frozen plasma was given before urgent surgery. Which finding shows the plasma worked?

options.text: INR 1.5 and the oozing has stopped
options.rationale: Plasma replaces clotting factors. A corrected INR and no bleeding show it did.

options.text: Hemoglobin rose from 9.4 to 10.6 g/dL
options.rationale: Red cells raise hemoglobin. Plasma carries clotting factors and no red cells.

options.text: Platelet count rose to 210,000/mm3
options.rationale: Plasma does not supply platelets. His bleeding came from a high INR.

options.text: Blood pressure rose from 104/62 to 122/70
options.rationale: Plasma adds some volume, and volume was not why it was ordered.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate each blood product by what it replaces: plasma by clotting times and bleeding, red cells by hemoglobin, platelets by the count.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Each option is a real transfusion outcome. Match the outcome to the product that was hung.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Clotting factors.

steps.action: Cut the red cell and platelet outcomes
steps.detail: Hemoglobin and platelet count belong to other products.
Pressure is a side effect, not the goal.

elimination.verdict: INR 1.5 with no more oozing.

questions.stem: A unit of platelets arrives for a client with leukemia and nosebleeds. The nurse needs about 20 minutes to finish another client's care. What does the nurse do with the unit?

options.text: Place it in the unit's medication refrigerator
options.rationale: Cold damages platelets. They are stored at room temperature.

options.text: Send it back to the blood bank until the nurse is free
options.rationale: Possible, and it delays a product the client needs now. Twenty minutes at room temperature does no harm.

options.text: Keep it at room temperature and hang it when the nurse is free
options.rationale: Platelets are stored at 20 to 24 C. The unit stays good on the counter for 20 minutes, and the bleeding client gets it without a trip back to the blood bank.

options.text: Warm it under running water before hanging it
options.rationale: Platelets are never warmed.

questions.takeaway: Platelets are kept at room temperature, 20 to 24 C. Red cells are the product stored cold.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The habit from red cells is to keep blood cold. Ask which product this is before reaching for the refrigerator.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Platelets, not red cells.
Room temperature.

steps.action: Cut the cold, the warm and the delay
steps.detail: None of them helps this unit or this client.

elimination.verdict: Leave it at room temperature and hang it as soon as the nurse is free.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old in septic shock needs a vasopressor and three other continuous infusions started now. He has one forearm catheter. Which device does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: A PICC placed in the basilic vein
options.rationale: A PICC is central and could carry these drugs. It is chosen for weeks of therapy, not for an emergency with several drips.

options.text: A nontunneled central catheter
options.rationale: Placed quickly at the bedside into a large vein for emergency and intensive care use, with lumens for several infusions.

options.text: A midline catheter in the upper arm
options.rationale: Its tip is still peripheral. It is not for continuous vasopressors.

options.text: A second short forearm catheter
options.rationale: A vasopressor can destroy tissue if it leaks from a peripheral vein.

questions.takeaway: Nontunneled central catheters are for emergencies and intensive care: days to weeks, placed fast. They carry the highest infection risk of the central lines.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Ask three things: how long, how irritating, how urgent. A vesicant rules out peripheral tips, and urgency picks between the central lines.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A vasopressor needs a central vein, so the midline and short catheter are out.
Both reach a central vein.
The nontunneled line is the emergency device.

elimination.verdict: A nontunneled central catheter.

questions.stem: A 37-year-old with paraplegia needs 8 weeks of IV antibiotics. He moves himself with his arms and a wheelchair. Which device fits him best?

options.text: A midline catheter
options.rationale: A midline lasts up to 4 weeks. His therapy runs twice that long.

options.text: A PICC in the upper arm
options.rationale: The usual choice for weeks of antibiotics, and tempting. His arms do all his lifting and wheeling, which strains an arm line.

options.text: A nontunneled subclavian catheter
options.rationale: Meant for days to weeks in acute care, with the highest infection risk.

options.text: A tunneled central catheter
options.rationale: It sits on the chest, lasts months, and its cuff anchors it and blocks germs. His arms stay free.

questions.takeaway: Device choice weighs duration, the solution, the veins and the patient. A tunneled chest catheter suits long therapy when the arms must stay free.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Duration alone points to a PICC. Read the detail about how he moves before settling on it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 8 weeks rules out the midline and the short term central line.

steps.action: Compare the two long term lines
steps.detail: A PICC and a tunneled catheter both last.
He depends on his arms.

elimination.verdict: A tunneled central catheter.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old with a midline catheter in the right upper arm has a new prescription for total parenteral nutrition. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Start it through the midline at half the rate
options.rationale: A slower rate does not change the concentration that reaches a peripheral vein.

options.text: Dilute the solution with 0.9% sodium chloride
options.rationale: Nurses do not alter a pharmacy admixture.

options.text: Check the midline for a blood return, then start it
options.rationale: A working midline is still a peripheral line.

options.text: Ask the provider about central access
options.rationale: A midline tip stops below the axilla. Parenteral nutrition is too concentrated for a peripheral vein and needs a central line.

questions.takeaway: The tip decides peripheral or central. A midline is peripheral: no vesicants, no parenteral nutrition, no continuous vasopressors.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: A long catheter is not a central catheter. Find where the tip ends, then ask whether this solution may go there.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Below the axilla, so peripheral.
Parenteral nutrition is highly concentrated.

steps.action: Cut every option that uses the midline
steps.detail: Rate, dilution and blood return do not move the tip.

elimination.verdict: Ask the provider about central access.

questions.stem: A PICC was placed in a 62-year-old 30 minutes ago and flushes easily with a blood return. The first antibiotic dose is due through it. What does the nurse do next?

options.text: Look for the chest x-ray report of the tip position
options.rationale: A PICC is a central line. The tip must be confirmed by x-ray before anything is given through it.

options.text: Give the dose, since the line flushes with a blood return
options.rationale: A blood return shows the catheter is in a vein. It does not show the tip reached the superior vena cava.

options.text: Measure the arm above the insertion site
options.rationale: Useful as a baseline for later swelling. It does not clear the line for use.

options.text: Check the blood pressure in that arm
options.rationale: No blood pressure is taken in an arm with a PICC.

questions.takeaway: Treat a PICC as the central line it is: tip position confirmed by x-ray before the first use.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The flush and blood return are there to make the line look ready. Ask what a central line needs that a peripheral one does not.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Central, despite the arm insertion.

steps.action: Recall the rule before first use
steps.detail: Tip confirmed by x-ray.
Blood return proves a vein, not the tip position.

elimination.verdict: Find the x-ray report first.

questions.stem: After a missed IV attempt in the left forearm, a 71-year-old has a raised, bruised, tender lump at the puncture site. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Apply a tourniquet above the lump and try again
options.rationale: A tourniquet raises pressure in the vein and pushes more blood into the tissue.

options.text: Apply gentle pressure, then use another site
options.rationale: This is a hematoma. Gentle pressure limits the bleeding, and the next attempt goes somewhere else.

options.text: Massage the lump to spread the blood
options.rationale: Rubbing restarts bleeding and adds to the bruise.

options.text: Insert the next catheter just below the lump
options.rationale: The same vein is damaged. Fluid given below it can leak out at the puncture.

questions.takeaway: Hematoma: bruising, swelling, tenderness. Apply gentle pressure, do not restart in the same site, and watch that it does not expand.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Name the problem first: blood in the tissue. Then reject anything that adds pressure, friction or a second hole to that vein.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A bruised, tender lump after a miss is a hematoma.

steps.action: Cut what makes it bleed more
steps.detail: Tourniquet and massage.
Below the lump still drains through the damaged spot.

elimination.verdict: Gentle pressure and a different site.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old with heart failure will receive IV furosemide twice a day. No IV fluids are prescribed. How does the nurse plan to keep her forearm catheter usable?

options.text: Run 0.9% sodium chloride at 30 mL per hour
options.rationale: A slow drip keeps a vein open, and it adds over 700 mL a day to a heart that cannot handle extra volume.

options.text: Remove it and restart one before each dose
options.rationale: Two new punctures a day in an older adult with fragile veins is harm without a reason.

options.text: Cap it as a saline lock and flush around each dose
options.rationale: A lock gives access for the drug with no fluid running, which fits a patient who must not get extra volume.

options.text: Run 5% dextrose in water at a keep open rate
options.rationale: Still unprescribed fluid, and it needs an order with a rate.

questions.takeaway: A saline lock is a capped, flushed catheter with no fluid running. Use it when the patient needs IV drugs and no extra fluid.
questions.coverage: Not in Lecture PPT. Covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options keep the vein open with fluid. Her diagnosis is the reason those are the wrong pair.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Heart failure, on a diuretic.
Neither is prescribed and both add volume.
Older veins are fragile.

elimination.verdict: Saline lock, flushed before and after each dose.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old has an epidural opioid infusion after abdominal surgery. Which set of findings shows the infusion is effective and safe?

options.text: Pain 0 of 10, respirations 8, hard to wake
options.rationale: The pain is gone because the client is oversedated. Respiratory depression is the main risk of spinal opioids.

options.text: Pain 2 of 10, respirations 14, moves both legs
options.rationale: Pain is controlled, breathing is adequate and leg movement shows the nerves are not affected.

options.text: Pain 3 of 10, respirations 16, new numb, heavy legs
options.rationale: Pain and breathing look fine. New numbness and weakness suggest the catheter has moved.

options.text: Pain 7 of 10, respirations 18, walks in the hall
options.rationale: Safe, and not effective. The pain is not controlled.

questions.takeaway: Intraspinal infusions: watch for respiratory depression, infection and catheter migration. Good pain relief counts only with safe breathing and intact legs.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The lowest pain score is the trap. Read all three findings in each option before choosing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A rate of 8 with sedation fails.
New numbness fails.
7 of 10 fails. One option passes all three.

elimination.verdict: Pain 2, respirations 14, legs moving.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old with obesity needs a peripheral IV for a scheduled antibiotic. Two attempts in the forearm have failed, and no veins can be seen or felt. Which plan is best?

options.text: Request ultrasound guided insertion
options.rationale: Ultrasound shows deep veins in real time and cuts failed attempts. It is the standard of care for difficult access.

options.text: Try a vein on the back of the hand
options.rationale: A third blind attempt adds pain and uses up veins.

options.text: Tighten the tourniquet and lower the arm
options.rationale: Helps fill veins that are there to find. After two misses with nothing to feel, it is more of the same.

options.text: Ask the provider for an intraosseous line
options.rationale: That route is for emergencies when IV access fails, such as cardiac arrest. Nothing here is an emergency.

questions.takeaway: For difficult access, bring in ultrasound guidance and the vascular access specialist. Repeated blind attempts are not the answer.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options repeat what already failed and one jumps to an emergency route. Look for the step in between.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Two, with no vein seen or felt.
Hand vein and a tighter tourniquet are still blind sticks.
Intraosseous access is for emergencies.

elimination.verdict: Ultrasound guided insertion.

questions.stem: On day 6, a client with a nontunneled subclavian catheter is eating, takes all medications by mouth and has had no IV therapy for 2 days. The site is clean. What does the nurse do on rounds?

options.text: Change the dressing to gauze so the site can be seen daily
options.rationale: Gauze hides the site and needs changing every 2 days. It does nothing about a line with no use.

options.text: Flush each lumen and leave the line for possible later use
options.rationale: Keeping a line just in case is the habit the bundle is meant to end. Every extra day adds infection risk.

options.text: Draw blood cultures from the line as a precaution
options.rationale: Cultures are drawn for signs of infection, not as a routine on a clean site.

options.text: Ask whether the catheter can come out today
options.rationale: Daily review of need and prompt removal are part of the bundle. The client no longer uses the line.

questions.takeaway: Ask every day whether the line is still needed. A central line that is not being used should come out.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: A clean site makes the line look harmless. The question to ask is whether it has a job, not whether it looks good.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: List what the line is used for
steps.detail: Nothing for 2 days.
Daily review and prompt removal.

steps.action: Cut the options that keep or test it
steps.detail: None of them lowers the infection risk.

elimination.verdict: Ask about removing the catheter today.

questions.stem: A nurse watches an orientee start a peripheral IV for maintenance fluid on an 87-year-old with thin skin and veins that roll. Which observations show the orientee's technique was correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Chose a 22 gauge catheter
options.rationale: Small, fragile veins take a 22 to 24 gauge, which is enough for maintenance fluid.

options.text: Tied the tourniquet tightly to make the veins stand out
options.rationale: A tight tourniquet bruises thin skin and can burst a fragile vein.

options.text: Held the skin with gentle traction below the site
options.rationale: Gentle traction steadies a rolling vein without tearing the skin.

options.text: Placed the catheter in a vein on the back of the hand
options.rationale: The back of the hand is avoided in older adults. The skin is thin and the veins are fragile there.

options.text: Recorded the skin condition before and after the attempt
options.rationale: Thin skin tears and bruises easily, so its condition is documented around every attempt.

options.text: Listened to the lungs after the fluid had run for a while
options.rationale: Older adults overload easily. Dyspnea, crackles and new confusion are the checks.

questions.takeaway: Older adult IV: 22 to 24 gauge, loose tourniquet, gentle traction, forearm over hand, lower rates, document the skin, watch the lungs and mental status.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Picture thin skin and fragile veins. Anything forceful or on the back of the hand is wrong for this client.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A tight tourniquet.
The back of the hand.

steps.action: Keep the gentle and the watchful
steps.detail: Small gauge, light traction, skin notes, lung checks.

elimination.verdict: A, C, E, F.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A 68-year-old is to receive maintenance fluid at 25 mL per hour by gravity. To count the slow rate accurately the nurse chooses [[1]].

At 0800 the nurse finds his bag was spiked at 0600 the previous day and is one third full. The nurse [[2]].

His catheter site is covered with a dry, intact gauze dressing dated 2 days ago. The nurse [[3]].

options.text: a microdrip set, 60 drops per mL
options.rationale: At 60 drops per mL, 25 mL per hour is 25 drops per minute, which is easy to count and adjust.

options.text: a macrodrip set, 10 drops per mL
options.rationale: That gives about 4 drops per minute, too few to set accurately.

options.text: a blood administration set
options.rationale: Its filter and large drops are for blood products.

options.text: a secondary piggyback set
options.rationale: A short set for intermittent drugs that attaches to a primary line.

options.text: lets the bag finish, since it is not empty
options.rationale: The limit is time, not volume.

options.text: hangs a new bag now
options.rationale: A container hangs no longer than 24 hours once spiked. This one has hung 26.

options.text: adds a label with today's date
options.rationale: Relabeling hides how long it has hung.

options.text: speeds the rate to empty the bag
options.rationale: That changes the prescribed rate and risks overload.

options.text: leaves it until day 7
options.rationale: Seven days is the interval for a transparent dressing.

options.text: reinforces it with tape
options.rationale: Tape does not replace a dressing that is due.

options.text: changes it today
options.rationale: Gauze is changed every 2 days because the site cannot be seen through it.

options.text: removes it and leaves the site open
options.rationale: An insertion site stays covered.

questions.takeaway: Microdrip, 60 drops per mL, for slow rates. A bag hangs 24 hours at most. Gauze dressings change every 2 days, transparent every 7.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Each blank has a time or a number behind it. A dressing or bag that looks fine can still be past its limit.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Pick the set by the rate
steps.detail: Slow rates need small drops.

steps.action: Count the hours on the bag
steps.detail: 0600 yesterday to 0800 today is 26 hours.

steps.action: Match the interval to the dressing
steps.detail: Gauze 2 days, transparent 7.

elimination.verdict: Microdrip; new bag now; change it today.

questions.stem: A client's PICC has a transparent dressing that was changed 2 days ago. Today moisture is visible under one corner, and the site is not red. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Reinforce the damp corner with sterile tape
options.rationale: Tempting, because it keeps the dressing on. Taping seals the moisture against the insertion site.

options.text: Change the dressing now using sterile technique
options.rationale: A PICC dressing is changed on schedule or as soon as it is wet or soiled. Moisture under the dressing lets organisms reach the site.

options.text: Leave it until the 7 day change, since the site is not red
options.rationale: The 7 day interval applies only while the dressing stays clean, dry and intact. A clean looking site today does not make a wet dressing safe.

options.text: Dry the corner and press it back onto the skin
options.rationale: The dressing is no longer intact or sterile underneath once moisture has entered.

questions.takeaway: A central line dressing is changed at its interval or at once if it is wet, soiled or loose. Clean, dry and intact is the standard.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options wait and two act. Ask what moisture under a central line dressing means for the schedule.

steps.detail: Moisture under the dressing. It is no longer clean, dry and intact.
Tape and pressing it back down keep a wet dressing over the site.
The schedule gives way when the dressing is wet.

elimination.verdict: Change the dressing now with sterile technique.

questions.stem: An assistive personnel cares for a client who has a PICC in the left arm. Which action by the assistive personnel needs correction?

options.text: Covers the PICC with a waterproof cover before the shower
options.rationale: Correct. The dressing is kept dry, and a shower with a waterproof cover is allowed.

options.text: Tells the nurse the dressing edge looks damp
options.rationale: Correct. The assistive personnel reports and the nurse assesses and changes a wet dressing.

options.text: Wraps the blood pressure cuff on the left upper arm
options.rationale: No blood pressure cuff goes on the arm with a PICC. Cuff pressure irritates the vein and can lead to phlebitis.

options.text: Takes the temperature and reports 38.2 C to the nurse
options.rationale: Correct. Fever above 38 C is reported because it can mean a line infection.

questions.takeaway: PICC arm: no blood pressure cuffs and no blood draws on that arm. Keep the dressing clean, dry and intact.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: You are looking for the wrong action. Three options protect the line or report a finding.

steps.detail: Needs correction means find the unsafe action.
Reporting a damp dressing and a fever are both right.

steps.action: Find the action on the PICC arm
steps.detail: The cuff on the left arm.

elimination.verdict: The cuff on the PICC arm.

questions.stem: A client's central line was found open and has now been clamped. He is short of breath with chest pain. Which position does the nurse use?

options.text: Left side with the head lowered
options.rationale: Left side with the head down traps the air in the right atrium, away from the lungs.

options.text: Right side with the head lowered
options.rationale: The side is off. On the right side the air can move on toward the lungs.

options.text: Left side with the head raised 45 degrees
options.rationale: The head position is off. With the head up, air rises out of the right atrium.

options.text: Flat on the back with the head lowered
options.rationale: The side is off. Without the left side turn the air is not held in the right atrium.

questions.takeaway: Air embolism: clamp, then left side with the head down, 100% oxygen and rapid response.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: There are two parts to the position: which side, and head up or down.

steps.detail: Left.
Down.
Only one has left side and head lowered.

elimination.verdict: Left side, head lowered.

questions.stem: A student cares for a client with a hemodialysis catheter in the chest and a forearm catheter. An IV antibiotic is due. Which action by the student needs correction?

options.text: Scrubs the forearm catheter's connector for 15 seconds
options.rationale: Correct. The hub is scrubbed for at least 15 seconds before each access.

options.text: Prepares to give the dose through the dialysis catheter
options.rationale: A hemodialysis catheter is for dialysis only and is managed by dialysis staff. It is not used for routine IV drugs or blood draws.

options.text: Checks the forearm site for redness and swelling first
options.rationale: Correct. The site is assessed before it is used.

options.text: Flushes the forearm catheter before and after the dose
options.rationale: Correct. The line is flushed before and after medications.

questions.takeaway: A hemodialysis catheter is for dialysis only: no routine IV access and no blood draws.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Three actions involve the forearm catheter and one involves the dialysis catheter.

steps.detail: Find the wrong action.
Three use the forearm catheter correctly.
The dialysis catheter is not for medications.

elimination.verdict: Giving the dose through the dialysis catheter.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old with hypertonic dehydration has received 0.45% sodium chloride for 8 hours. Which finding does the nurse report now?

options.text: Oral mucous membranes are moist
options.rationale: Expected. The cells are taking water back in, which is the goal of a hypotonic fluid.

options.text: Urine output averages 45 mL per hour
options.rationale: Adequate output. It shows the kidneys are being perfused.

options.text: New headache and increasing drowsiness
options.rationale: Hypotonic fluid moves water into cells. A new headache with drowsiness means brain cells may be swelling, which is the risk named for this fluid.

options.text: Serum sodium fell from 158 to 154 mEq/L
options.rationale: The sodium is still high and is coming down slowly, which is the intended result. It draws the eye only because it is a lab value.

questions.takeaway: A hypotonic fluid sends water into cells. Watch the brain: a new headache or a drop in alertness is reported at once.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Three findings show the fluid is doing its job. One shows the water has gone too far into the cells.

steps.detail: 0.45% sodium chloride moves water into cells.
Moist membranes, adequate urine and a slowly falling sodium are the goals.
Headache with drowsiness is new and points to cell swelling in the brain.

elimination.verdict: The new headache and drowsiness.

questions.stem: The provider prescribes 0.45% sodium chloride for four clients. Which prescription does the nurse question?

options.text: Client with diabetic ketoacidosis whose blood pressure is 118/74 after isotonic fluid
options.rationale: Appropriate. Hypotonic fluid is used in ketoacidosis after the first fluid resuscitation.

options.text: Client with 3 days of fever, dry mucous membranes and a blood pressure of 124/76
options.rationale: Appropriate. The cells are dry and the pressure is adequate, so water can safely move into the cells.

options.text: Client with a serum sodium of 153 mEq/L who is alert and oriented
options.rationale: Appropriate. A high sodium means hypertonic dehydration, which is an indication. No contraindication is listed for this client.

options.text: Client with pancreatitis, third spacing and a blood pressure of 82/48
options.rationale: Hypotonic fluid leaves the vessels. In a client who is hypotensive with third spacing it lowers the pressure further.

questions.takeaway: Hypotonic fluid is unsafe with increased intracranial pressure, head trauma, hypotension or third spacing, because the water does not stay in the vessels.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: All four are dehydrated in some way. Ask which one needs the fluid to stay inside the vessels.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: You are looking for the unsafe match.

steps.action: Clear the dry cells with good pressure
steps.detail: Ketoacidosis after resuscitation, fever with a normal pressure and a high sodium all fit.
82/48 with third spacing needs isotonic volume.

elimination.verdict: The client with third spacing and a blood pressure of 82/48.

questions.stem: The nurse receives four reports at the same time. Which client does the nurse see first?

options.text: Has chills and a temperature of 38.3 C during a red blood cell transfusion
options.rationale: Fever with chills during a transfusion points to a transfusion reaction, which can worsen quickly while the blood keeps running.

options.text: Forearm site is red and warm with a tender cord while an antibiotic infuses
options.rationale: Phlebitis. The catheter must come out soon, and the harm is local and slow.

options.text: Hand is cool, pale and puffy while 0.9% sodium chloride infuses
options.rationale: Infiltration of a nonvesicant fluid. It needs attention next, and the tissue harm is local.

options.text: PICC dressing is lifting at one edge and is due to be changed today
options.rationale: A loose dressing raises infection risk over time. It is the least urgent of the four.

questions.takeaway: Fever or chills during a transfusion is a possible reaction. It outranks any local site problem.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides.
questions.strategy: Three clients have a problem at the site. One has a problem that affects the whole body and is still receiving the cause.

steps.detail: Phlebitis, infiltration and a loose dressing are local.

steps.action: Ask which is still getting worse
steps.detail: The blood is still infusing into the client with the fever.
Systemic and worsening comes before local.

elimination.verdict: The client with chills and fever during the transfusion.

questions.stem: At the bedside, two nurses find the blood type and client name match, and the unit number on the bag differs from the transfusion record by one digit. Which action is correct?

options.text: Hang the unit, since the name and blood type match
options.rationale: Tempting because two checks pass. Every item must match, and a wrong unit number can mean a unit crossmatched for someone else.

options.text: Correct the number on the record and have both nurses sign
options.rationale: Changing the record hides the mismatch and does not show which unit is right.

options.text: Start the unit slowly and watch closely for 15 minutes
options.rationale: Watching for a reaction does not make an unverified unit safe to start.

options.text: Do not hang the unit and contact the blood bank
options.rationale: The label must match the record on every point. A mismatch stops the process until the blood bank resolves it.

questions.takeaway: The two nurse check is all or nothing: identification band, ABO and Rh type, unit number and expiration date must all match before blood is hung.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Three options start the blood in some way. One does not.

steps.detail: Three options end with this unit going into the client.
A unit that fails any part of the check is not hung.
Do not hang it, and take the mismatch to the blood bank.

elimination.verdict: Do not hang it. Contact the blood bank.

questions.stem: A client going home with a PICC in the left arm has completed teaching. Which statement needs follow-up by the nurse?

options.text: "If the line is hard to flush, I will push a little harder."
options.rationale: Resistance means the line is not used. Forcing a flush can rupture the catheter or push a clot into the circulation.

options.text: "I will cover the arm with a waterproof sleeve to shower."
options.rationale: Correct. Showers are allowed with a waterproof cover, and baths and swimming are not.

options.text: "I will not carry my 9 kg grandson with my left arm."
options.rationale: Correct. Heavy lifting with the PICC arm is avoided, and 9 kg is well over the limit.

options.text: "I will come in right away if that arm swells or aches."
options.rationale: Correct. Arm swelling or pain can mean a clot or infection and is reported at once.

questions.takeaway: PICC teaching: never flush against resistance. Keep the dressing dry, avoid heavy lifting with that arm and report swelling, pain, fever or shortness of breath.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: You are looking for the unsafe statement. Three statements protect the line and one forces it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Needs follow-up means find the wrong statement.
Covering for the shower, avoiding lifting and reporting swelling are all taught.
Pushing harder against resistance damages the line.

elimination.verdict: The plan to push harder when the line is hard to flush.

questions.stem: Lactated Ringer's is infusing through a client's only IV catheter, which flushes easily. A unit of packed red blood cells has been verified at the bedside. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Piggyback the blood into the lactated Ringer's line
options.rationale: Tempting, because the line is already running. Blood runs with 0.9% sodium chloride only and through its own access.

options.text: Run 5% dextrose in water with the blood to keep the vein open
options.rationale: Dextrose in water is not used with blood. Only 0.9% sodium chloride is.

options.text: Return the unit until the lactated Ringer's has finished
options.rationale: The unit has a limited time once issued, and the line can be made ready now.

options.text: Flush with 0.9% sodium chloride, then run the blood alone
options.rationale: Blood products are given with 0.9% sodium chloride only. The other fluid is stopped and cleared from the line first.

questions.takeaway: Blood runs with 0.9% sodium chloride only, through access used for nothing else while the unit infuses.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The catheter works and the unit is verified. The only open question is what may share the line with blood.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Blood is given with 0.9% sodium chloride and nothing else.

steps.action: Cut the two that mix fluids
steps.detail: Lactated Ringer's and dextrose in water both break the rule.
Sending the unit back wastes its time limit when a saline flush solves the problem.

elimination.verdict: Flush with 0.9% sodium chloride and run the blood alone.

questions.stem: A client has a right femoral intra-arterial catheter infusing chemotherapy to a pelvic tumor. Which finding does the nurse report now?

options.text: A 2 cm bruise at the site, unchanged since the last check
options.rationale: Tempting, because bleeding is watched for with an arterial catheter. A small bruise that is not growing is not active bleeding.

options.text: The right foot, warm an hour ago, is cool and pale
options.rationale: A foot that turns cool and pale below an arterial catheter means blood flow to the limb is cut off by spasm or a blocked artery.

options.text: Soreness at the groin site rated 2 on a 0 to 10 pain scale
options.rationale: Mild soreness at an insertion site is expected.

options.text: Mild nausea since the chemotherapy began
options.rationale: Nausea is an expected effect of chemotherapy and is treated with an antiemetic. It does not threaten the limb.

questions.takeaway: With an intra-arterial infusion, watch for bleeding, arterial spasm and limb ischemia. A change in color, warmth or pulse below the site is reported at once.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Look for the finding that has changed, and ask what an arterial catheter can do to the limb below it.

steps.detail: The bruise is unchanged, the soreness is mild and nausea is expected with chemotherapy.
The foot was warm and is now cool and pale.
Loss of arterial flow to the leg is limb ischemia.

elimination.verdict: The right foot that has turned cool and pale.

questions.stem: A client with a PICC for 12 days has chills, a temperature of 38.6 C and a blood pressure of 94/56. Blood cultures and an IV antibiotic are prescribed, and the antibiotic has arrived. Which action comes first?

options.text: Draw the blood cultures
options.rationale: Cultures are drawn before the first antibiotic dose so the organism can still be grown and identified.

options.text: Hang the antibiotic, then draw the cultures
options.rationale: Tempting, because infection with a low pressure needs the antibiotic fast. Giving it first can make the cultures falsely negative.

options.text: Remove the PICC and send the tip to the laboratory
options.rationale: Removal follows only if the catheter proves to be the source and the provider prescribes it. It is not the first step.

options.text: Change the PICC dressing and the administration set
options.rationale: Part of later care. It does not treat or identify a bloodstream infection.

questions.takeaway: Suspected catheter related bloodstream infection: two sets of blood cultures first, then the IV antibiotic without delay.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Giving the antibiotic first and drawing cultures first are the two real choices. Ask which one cannot be done later.

steps.detail: Cultures then antibiotic, or antibiotic then cultures.
Cultures drawn after the antibiotic may not grow the organism.
Removal is not prescribed and a dressing change treats nothing.

elimination.verdict: Draw the cultures, then start the antibiotic.

questions.stem: A left forearm catheter infiltrated and was removed. The client is right handed and needs 2 more days of IV fluid. Which site does the nurse choose?

options.text: A vein on the back of the left hand
options.rationale: Tempting, because it is the nondominant arm and the most distal site. It lies below the infiltration, and sites distal to an infiltration are avoided.

options.text: A vein in the right forearm
options.rationale: The forearm is the preferred site. The dominant arm is a preference, and it gives way to avoiding the injured vein.

options.text: The left antecubital fossa
options.rationale: It is above the infiltration, and the antecubital fossa is avoided for short peripheral catheters.

options.text: A vein on the top of the left foot
options.rationale: Lower extremity sites are avoided in adults.

questions.takeaway: After an infiltration, do not place the next catheter distal to it. Hand dominance is a preference and comes second to a safe vein.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Hand dominance pulls you toward the left arm. Check each left arm option against the sites that are avoided.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Lower extremities are avoided in adults.
The hand is distal to the infiltration and the antecubital fossa is avoided.
Using the dominant arm is less convenient and still safe.

elimination.verdict: The right forearm.

questions.stem: A confused 83-year-old keeps picking at her forearm catheter. She needs IV antibiotics for 2 more days. Which action is best?

options.text: Apply soft wrist restraints to both arms
options.rationale: Restraints are the most restrictive choice and a last resort. A less restrictive way to protect the catheter is available.

options.text: Wrap the forearm from wrist to elbow in rolled gauze
options.rationale: Protects the catheter and hides the site, so infiltration or phlebitis would be missed.

options.text: Cover the site with a protective device that leaves it visible
options.rationale: Protects the catheter, keeps the tubing out of reach and still lets the nurse see the site.

options.text: Move the catheter to a vein on the back of the hand
options.rationale: Hand veins are avoided in older adults, and a new site does not stop the picking.

questions.takeaway: With a confused client, protect the catheter in the least restrictive way and keep the insertion site visible for assessment.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options protect the catheter without restraints. Ask which one still lets you assess the site.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Restraints come last.
The back of the hand is avoided in older adults.
Gauze hides the site. A clear protective device does not.

elimination.verdict: A protective cover that leaves the site visible.

questions.stem: A client with cerebral edema is receiving 3% sodium chloride by pump through a central line. Which findings does the nurse report? Select all that apply.

options.text: Serum sodium rose from 141 to 157 mEq/L
options.rationale: Hypernatremia is a named risk of hypertonic saline. The serum sodium is monitored for this reason.

options.text: New crackles with shortness of breath
options.rationale: Hypertonic fluid pulls water into the vessels, so circulatory overload is a risk.

options.text: Urine output of 60 mL per hour
options.rationale: Adequate output. It shows the kidneys are handling the fluid.

options.text: New disorientation to place
options.rationale: Neurologic status is watched closely. A new change can mean the brain is worse or the sodium is too high.

options.text: Headache is easing
options.rationale: The intended effect. Water is leaving swollen brain cells and the pressure is falling.

options.text: Pupils equal and reactive to light
options.rationale: A normal neurologic finding.

questions.takeaway: Hypertonic saline: monitor serum sodium, neurologic status and fluid balance. Report hypernatremia, signs of overload and any new neurologic change.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Judge each finding alone. Hypertonic saline has three things to watch: the sodium, the brain and the volume in the vessels.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Hypernatremia, circulatory overload and neurologic change.
A sodium of 157, new crackles and new disorientation each match one risk.
Good urine output, an easing headache and normal pupils are wanted results.

elimination.verdict: The sodium of 157, the new crackles and the new disorientation.

questions.stem: The nurse completes the checklist during a subclavian central line insertion. The provider's sterile sleeve brushes the bed rail, and the provider continues. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Tell the provider to stop the procedure now
options.rationale: Any break in sterile technique during insertion is stopped at once. The checklist gives the observer that role.

options.text: Record the break on the checklist and report it afterward
options.rationale: Tempting, because it avoids interrupting. By then the contaminated sleeve has been over the sterile field.

options.text: Apply extra chlorhexidine to the site before the dressing goes on
options.rationale: Skin cleaning afterward does not undo contamination carried in during the insertion.

options.text: Check the client's temperature every 4 hours for 2 days
options.rationale: Monitoring finds an infection after it starts. The goal is to prevent it.

questions.takeaway: The catheter related bloodstream infection bundle includes maximal sterile barriers and a checklist. Anyone who sees a break stops the procedure.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Three options deal with the contamination after the line is in. One deals with it now.

steps.detail: The sterile sleeve touched a surface that is not sterile.
Reporting later, cleaning later and monitoring later all let the insertion go on.
Stopping now is the only choice that prevents the infection.

elimination.verdict: Tell the provider to stop now.

questions.stem: The nurse removed an infiltrated hand catheter and placed a new one in the opposite forearm. Which entry best documents the event?

options.text: "Hand catheter infiltrated because the client kept bending the wrist. Removed. New catheter placed, client tolerated well."
options.rationale: It assigns a cause and leaves out the site findings, the grade and where the new catheter is.

options.text: "Left hand cool, pale, edema 3 cm, grade 2. Infusion stopped, catheter removed intact, arm elevated. 22 gauge placed right forearm, 1 attempt."
options.rationale: It records what was seen, the grade, each action, and the new site, gauge and number of attempts.

options.text: "Left hand site checked hourly per policy with no problems noted until infiltration found. Provider aware. Infusion restarted in other arm."
options.rationale: It defends the monitoring and omits the findings, the grade, the actions and the new catheter details.

options.text: "Left hand swollen. Infusion appears to have leaked into tissue. Catheter removed and warm compress applied. Will continue to monitor site."
options.rationale: Closer, with one finding and two actions. It lacks the grade, the measurement and any record of the new catheter.

questions.takeaway: Document a complication with objective findings, the grade, each action taken, and the new site, gauge and number of attempts.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Look for the entry made of things the nurse saw and did, with numbers, and no opinion about cause.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Blaming the wrist and citing policy are not findings.
One gives a single finding. The other gives findings, grade and actions.
Only one entry records the new site, gauge and attempts.

elimination.verdict: The entry with findings, grade, actions and the new catheter details.

questions.stem: The RN is planning the shift with an LPN and an assistive personnel. Which task does the RN keep?

options.text: Flushing an established saline lock on a stable client
options.rationale: Flushing an established line is within the LPN role.

options.text: Taking routine vital signs on a stable client receiving maintenance fluid
options.rationale: Routine vital signs on a stable client can go to assistive personnel.

options.text: Starting a second unit of red blood cells after the first went well
options.rationale: Starting any blood product is an RN task. Tolerating the first unit does not make the second unit routine.

options.text: Making routine checks of peripheral IV sites on stable clients
options.rationale: Routine site monitoring is within the LPN role. The RN follows up on what is found.

questions.takeaway: The RN starts every blood product and every high alert IV drug. An LPN monitors sites, flushes established lines and hangs routine fluids.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Ask which task is always the RN's, however stable the client is.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Flushing, vital signs and routine site checks are delegated.
The client did well with the first unit, which makes the second sound routine.
Initiating blood is never delegated.

elimination.verdict: Starting the second unit of red blood cells.

questions.stem: While the nurse advances a catheter near the wrist, blood appears in the chamber and the client reports electric tingling shooting into the thumb. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Finish advancing the catheter, since it is in the vein
options.rationale: Tempting because of the blood return. Tingling means the needle is at a nerve, and advancing can cut it.

options.text: Secure the catheter and recheck the tingling in 15 minutes
options.rationale: Leaving the catheter in keeps pressure on the nerve.

options.text: Pull back slightly and redirect toward the vein
options.rationale: Redirecting moves a sharp needle around the nerve again.

options.text: Stop, remove the catheter and choose another site
options.rationale: Tingling or pins and needles during insertion signals nerve contact. The insertion is stopped and the catheter removed.

questions.takeaway: Tingling, numbness or shooting pain during an IV insertion means nerve contact: stop, remove the catheter and use a different site.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The blood return says the catheter is in the vein. The tingling says something else is being touched too.

steps.detail: Blood return is good. Shooting tingling is a nerve sign and outranks it.
Three options leave the catheter in the arm.

steps.action: Keep the one that removes it
steps.detail: A nerve sign ends this attempt.

elimination.verdict: Stop and remove the catheter, then use another site.

questions.stem: A carpenter arrives with a nail fragment protruding from his right eye. He is in pain and asks the nurse to pull it out. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Shield the eye without touching the object
options.rationale: A protruding object is never removed by the nurse. Protecting it from movement prevents more damage until the eye care provider arrives.

options.text: Irrigate the eye with saline to clear debris
options.rationale: Right for a surface foreign body and tempting here. Irrigation can move a penetrating object.

options.text: Apply a pressure patch over the eye
options.rationale: Pressure on a penetrated eye can push out its contents.

options.text: Remove it gently and cover the eye with gauze
options.rationale: Only the eye care provider assesses and removes it.

questions.takeaway: A penetrating eye injury is left alone and protected. Only the eye care provider removes the object.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Three options put force or fluid on the eye. One protects it.

steps.detail: Protruding means penetrating, not surface.
Removal, irrigation and pressure.
A shield with no contact.

elimination.verdict: Shield the eye and leave the object in place.

questions.stem: A client with open-angle glaucoma has used latanoprost nightly for 6 months. Which statement indicates the treatment goal is being met?

options.text: "My eyes feel comfortable and never ache."
options.rationale: Tempting, but open-angle glaucoma is silent, so comfort tells you nothing about the optic nerve.

options.text: "My side vision is starting to come back."
options.rationale: Lost vision does not return. This statement shows a wrong expectation.

options.text: "My field test is unchanged from last time."
options.rationale: The goal is to prevent further damage. A stable visual field is exactly that.

options.text: "My pressure is normal, so I use drops as needed."
options.rationale: Treatment is lifelong and daily. Stopping lets the pressure climb again.

questions.takeaway: Glaucoma treatment succeeds when nothing more is lost. It does not restore vision and it does not depend on how the eye feels.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Comfort sounds like success. In a painless disease, the only evidence is a measurement that has not worsened.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Prevent further damage, not restore vision.
Vision returning and drops as needed.

steps.action: Compare comfort with a stable test
steps.detail: This disease never hurt, so comfort proves nothing.

elimination.verdict: The unchanged field test.

questions.stem: A very nearsighted client awaiting scleral buckling for a retinal detachment wants to walk to the lounge to read. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Walk with him to the lounge and offer an arm for guidance
options.rationale: Tempting because it prevents a fall, but walking and reading both move the eye and head and can extend the detachment.

options.text: Keep him resting with head still and the affected eye patched
options.rationale: Before surgery, head movement and activity are restricted and a patch reduces eye movement.

options.text: Bring a large print book to his bedside chair
options.rationale: Keeps him in the room, but reading moves the eye back and forth.

options.text: Raise the lighting so he can read in bed
options.rationale: Good for low vision in general. Here the problem is eye movement, not light.

questions.takeaway: Before retinal detachment repair, the priority is to stop the detachment from spreading: limit activity and head movement and patch the eye.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Three options help him read safely. Ask whether he should be reading or walking at all.

steps.detail: More retina can detach before surgery.

steps.action: Notice three options keep him reading
steps.detail: Reading means eye movement.
Safe walking is still activity he should not have.

elimination.verdict: Rest, head still, eye patched.

questions.stem: An 83-year-old's daughter sorts his morning and evening pills into a blue box and a green box. He took the evening pills this morning. Which plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Have the daughter give every dose herself
options.rationale: Solves the error by removing his independence when a simpler fix exists.

options.text: Add a bright fluorescent light over the pill boxes
options.rationale: More light helps aging eyes, but fluorescent glare makes it worse and blue still looks like green.

options.text: Switch the boxes to violet and blue
options.rationale: Blues, greens and violets are the colors aging eyes separate least well.

options.text: Label the boxes in large high contrast print
options.rationale: Aging eyes lose blue and green discrimination, so the cue must be print and contrast, not color.

questions.takeaway: Never teach an older adult medications by color, especially blue, green or violet. Use large print, contrast and shape.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: More light is a real need in older eyes, so that option pulls. The error here came from two colors he cannot tell apart.

steps.action: Find the cause of the error
steps.detail: Blue and green look alike to him.

steps.action: Cut the option that repeats the cause
steps.detail: Violet and blue.
Labels keep him independent; the daughter taking over does not.

elimination.verdict: Large high contrast labels.

questions.stem: The clinic nurse has four clients waiting. Which client does the nurse see first?

options.text: A client with open-angle glaucoma whose eye pressure today is 26 mmHg
options.rationale: Elevated and needs attention, but this is a chronic, slow problem that will not change in the next hour.

options.text: A contact lens wearer with a painful red eye and a hazy cornea
options.rationale: The cornea has no blood supply of its own, so a possible corneal infection is an emergency.

options.text: A client with cataracts who reports worse glare when driving
options.rationale: Gradual and expected. Safety teaching can wait.

options.text: A client 1 month after LASIK who sees halos at night
options.rationale: A known complication that is not an emergency.

questions.takeaway: Sudden and painful with a hazy cornea outranks any slowly progressive eye problem, even one with an abnormal number.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The pressure of 26 is the only number on the page, which makes it look like the priority. Acute beats chronic.

steps.detail: Three are gradual or expected.
26 is open-angle range and chronic.
Painful red eye with a hazy cornea.

elimination.verdict: The contact lens wearer.

questions.stem: Two days after cataract surgery a client calls the clinic. Which report indicates recovery is not progressing as expected?

options.text: "The eye feels a little scratchy."
options.rationale: Mild scratchiness is expected early.

options.text: "I still can't see sharply out of that eye."
options.rationale: Best vision takes 4 to 6 weeks, so blurry vision on day 2 is expected.

options.text: "I could see better yesterday than I can today."
options.rationale: Vision should improve steadily. A drop from one day to the next is a vision loss to report now.

options.text: "I bent to pick up a shoe before I remembered."
options.rationale: Bending raises eye pressure and needs reteaching, but one slip with no symptoms is not a failing recovery.

questions.takeaway: After cataract surgery, vision that is imperfect is expected. Vision that is getting worse is not.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two options mention poor vision. One is slow improvement and the other is a decline.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Scratchiness.
Not sharp yet versus worse than yesterday.
A teaching need without any symptom.

elimination.verdict: Vision worse today than yesterday.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old who is legally blind, lives alone and prepares her own meals receives her lunch tray. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Describe where each item sits and let her touch it
options.rationale: Describing in detail and allowing touch lets her eat on her own, as she does at home.

options.text: Stay and feed her to prevent spills and burns
options.rationale: Tempting as the safest choice, but she manages meals alone at home and feeding her removes independence she has.

options.text: Ask assistive personnel to cut and feed the meal
options.rationale: Delegation is allowed, but it is still more help than she needs.

options.text: Cut the food and butter the bread for her
options.rationale: Kindly meant and less than feeding her, but she prepares her own meals at home and can do this once she knows where things are.

questions.takeaway: For vision loss: speak normally, describe in detail, allow touch. Give the least help that keeps the patient safe.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Feeding her looks like the safety answer. The detail that she lives alone and prepares her own meals tells you she already feeds herself.

steps.detail: She lives alone and prepares her own meals, so she eats without help.
Both do the task for her.
Preparing her food is still doing it for her.

elimination.verdict: Describe the tray and let her touch it.

questions.stem: A machinist felt something strike his eye while grinding steel. No object is visible, and an MRI of the orbits is prescribed. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Irrigate the eye with saline before the scan
options.rationale: Right for a surface foreign body, but a high speed metal fragment may have penetrated, and irrigation is not for that.

options.text: Send him and tell the technologist about the grinding
options.rationale: Tempting because the information is passed on. He should not reach the scanner at all.

options.text: Check his acuity and proceed if it is normal
options.rationale: Normal acuity does not rule out a small metal fragment inside the eye.

options.text: Hold the scan and report the metal exposure
options.rationale: MRI is contraindicated when a metal fragment is suspected. X-ray or CT is used instead.

questions.takeaway: Suspected metal in the eye means no MRI. The magnet can move the fragment and cause more injury.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Three options end with him in the scanner. The stem already told you why that is unsafe.

steps.detail: Grinding steel means metal.

steps.action: Cut what sends him to the scanner
steps.detail: Irrigating first, telling the technologist and checking acuity all end in MRI.
Hold and report so X-ray or CT is ordered.

elimination.verdict: Hold the scan and report the metal.

questions.stem: A client had a laser peripheral iridotomy for angle-closure glaucoma this morning. Which finding best indicates the procedure was effective?

options.text: Eye pressure 16 mmHg with the pain gone
options.rationale: The iridotomy reopens drainage, so pressure falls into the normal range and the pain goes with it.

options.text: No nausea since the antiemetic was given
options.rationale: Tempting, but the drug explains this. It says nothing about the pressure.

options.text: Client resting quietly in a darkened room
options.rationale: Quiet may be relief or may be sedation. It does not measure anything.

options.text: Eye redness slightly less than on arrival
options.rationale: A good sign that lags behind and is too soft to judge the procedure.

questions.takeaway: Judge a treatment by the thing it was meant to change. For angle closure that is the pressure, measured.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Several findings look like improvement. Ask which one could only come from the iridotomy working.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Blocked drainage and high pressure.
The antiemetic and the dark room.
16 mmHg is inside the normal range.

elimination.verdict: Pressure 16 mmHg with pain relieved.

questions.stem: A client with open-angle glaucoma starts timolol eye drops. Which statements show the teaching was understood? Select all that apply.

options.text: "I will press the inner corner of my eye after each drop."
options.rationale: Punctal occlusion keeps the drug in the eye and limits absorption into the body.

options.text: "I can stop the drops once my pressure reading is normal."
options.rationale: The pressure is normal because of the drops. Treatment is lifelong.

options.text: "I will use them every day even when my eyes feel fine."
options.rationale: Open-angle glaucoma has no symptoms to guide dosing, so strict adherence is what protects the nerve.

options.text: "New glasses will sharpen what the glaucoma took away."
options.rationale: Vision lost to glaucoma is nerve damage and is not corrected by lenses.

options.text: "If I skip a few days I will feel it and restart."
options.rationale: Rising pressure in open-angle glaucoma is silent, so there is nothing to feel.

questions.takeaway: Glaucoma drops are lifelong and daily. Punctal occlusion limits systemic effects, and lost vision does not return.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Judge each statement alone. Any statement that treats glaucoma as something the client can feel or reverse is wrong.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pressing the inner corner after each drop.
Daily use without symptoms.
Stopping, feeling it and regaining vision all assume the disease is reversible or noticeable.

elimination.verdict: A and C.

questions.stem: The nurse assesses an 88-year-old who has had poor intake for 3 days. Which finding most needs follow up?

options.text: Eyes that look sunken and dull in the orbits
options.rationale: Expected with age related loss of orbital fat, so not a reliable hydration sign in an older adult.

options.text: Sclera with a dull yellow tint
options.rationale: Common in older adults. Eye appearance is not used to judge jaundice at this age.

options.text: Dry furrowed tongue with scant dark urine
options.rationale: These are reliable signs of fluid deficit and fit 3 days of poor intake.

options.text: Eyes that feel gritty and dry
options.rationale: Reduced tear production is an expected aging change.

questions.takeaway: Do not use the sclera or eye appearance to judge hydration or jaundice in older adults. Look at the mouth and the urine.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The eye findings look alarming. In an 88-year-old they are the least trustworthy data.

steps.detail: Three options rest on eye appearance.
Eye appearance misleads in older adults.

steps.action: Take the finding outside the eye
steps.detail: Tongue and urine.

elimination.verdict: Dry furrowed tongue with scant dark urine.

questions.stem: A client with a corneal infection from contact lens wear completes discharge teaching. Which statement indicates the teaching was effective?

options.text: "I'll use the drops until the pain is gone."
options.rationale: The full antibiotic course is finished even after symptoms stop.

options.text: "I'll wear glasses until I'm told it has healed."
options.rationale: No contact lenses until the cornea is fully healed, and healing is confirmed by the provider.

options.text: "I'll put my lenses back in once the redness clears."
options.rationale: Tempting because it waits for improvement, but a clear looking eye is not a healed cornea.

options.text: "I'll save the leftover drops for next time."
options.rationale: Leftover drops mean the course was not finished.

questions.takeaway: Corneal infection teaching: finish the antibiotics and keep contacts out until the cornea is fully healed, not just until it looks better.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two options delay the contacts. One uses the client's own judgment and one uses the provider's exam.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Stopping when pain ends and saving leftovers.
Redness clearing versus confirmed healing.
Symptoms fade before the cornea is whole.
