elimination.verdict: Glasses until told it has healed.

questions.stem: A client going home with a corneal ulcer is prescribed antibiotic drops every hour for the first 24 hours. He asks to skip the night doses so he can sleep. Which response is best?

options.text: "Use two drops at bedtime and two when you wake."
options.rationale: Doubling a dose does not replace the steady level that hourly dosing gives.

options.text: "I will ask whether an ointment can cover the night."
options.rationale: Tempting because it respects his need for sleep. The first 24 hours call for hourly dosing as prescribed.

options.text: "Restart the hourly schedule in the morning."
options.rationale: Leaves the infection untreated for hours when vision is at risk.

options.text: "Set an alarm, because the hourly drops continue overnight."
options.rationale: The cornea has no blood supply of its own, so the drops are its only defense and the first day is the critical one.

questions.takeaway: A corneal infection is an emergency. Antibiotic drops are often hourly for the first 24 hours, day and night.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Sleep is a comfort need. Weigh it against what a gap in dosing can cost.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Corneal infection can take vision quickly.

steps.action: Cut the options that leave a gap
steps.detail: Double doses and restarting in the morning.
An ointment request delays a schedule that matters tonight.

elimination.verdict: The hourly drops continue overnight.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old with cataracts has stopped driving at night and can no longer read her pill labels. She asks if she should wait until they are worse. Which response is most appropriate?

options.text: "Surgery is timed by how it limits daily life."
options.rationale: Surgery is the only treatment and is done when ADLs are affected. Night driving and reading labels are ADLs.

options.text: "Stronger glasses and brighter light may be enough for now."
options.rationale: Reasonable early on and tempting as the conservative choice. Her daily function is already limited, so it is past that point.

options.text: "Surgery is done once the pupil turns bluish white."
options.rationale: A mature cataract is not the trigger. Function is.

options.text: "Eye drops can slow the clouding while you wait."
options.rationale: No drop treats a cataract. That belongs to glaucoma.

questions.takeaway: Cataract surgery is timed by function, not by how the lens looks. When ADLs are affected, it is time.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The conservative option would be right for a client who is still functioning. Two details in the stem say she is not.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: No night driving, cannot read labels.
Drops and waiting for a white pupil.
Fine before ADLs are affected, not after.

elimination.verdict: Surgery is considered now because ADLs are affected.

questions.scenario: A telephone triage nurse takes six calls from adult clients about their eyes.
questions.stem: For each report, indicate whether the nurse arranges an immediate evaluation or provides routine teaching.

rows.text: A 47-year-old now holds the menu at arm's length to read it
rows.rationale: Presbyopia is expected from the 40s on.

rows.text: A 57-year-old has had a painless gray shadow over one eye since waking
rows.rationale: Sudden and painless with a curtain suggests retinal detachment. Painless does not mean minor.

rows.text: An 80-year-old cannot see for a minute after walking into a dark room
rows.rationale: Poor dark adaptation is an aging change. Teach night lights and pausing in doorways.

rows.text: A client 5 days after scleral buckling woke with sudden sharp pain in that eye
rows.rationale: Sudden pain after retinal surgery is reported immediately.

rows.text: A client 3 weeks after LASIK has dry eyes and halos at night
rows.rationale: Known complications of LASIK that are not emergencies.

rows.text: A 62-year-old has sudden severe pain in a red eye with blurred vision
rows.rationale: Sudden pain, redness and vision loss fit angle-closure glaucoma, a medical emergency.

questions.takeaway: Sudden is never aging. Gradual changes get teaching; sudden changes get seen, with or without pain.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Ask one question of each row: did this come on suddenly? Do not let the absence of pain lower the urgency.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Three are gradual or expected after a procedure.
A sudden shadow is still an emergency.
Sudden pain is on the report list.

elimination.verdict: Routine, immediate, routine, immediate, routine, immediate.

questions.stem: At 0800 a client's pupils were 3 mm, equal and brisk. At 1200 the right is 3 mm and the left is 6 mm and sluggish. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Recheck the pupils in 30 minutes for a trend
options.rationale: Tempting, but the nurse already has a baseline and a change. Waiting adds delay, not information.

options.text: Notify the provider of the change now
options.rationale: A new unequal, sluggish pupil is a change from a documented baseline and is reported right away.

options.text: Document the sizes and continue routine checks
options.rationale: Recording size in mm is right. Stopping there treats a new finding as stable.

options.text: Ask if his pupils have always been unequal
options.rationale: Some people do have a small lifelong difference. The 0800 exam already shows these were equal.

questions.takeaway: Record pupil size in mm every time so that a change is obvious. A new unequal or sluggish pupil is reported now.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Two options gather more data. The 0800 baseline in the stem already answers both of them.

steps.detail: Equal at 0800, unequal at 1200.
History and recheck are answered by the baseline.
A new change needs action.

elimination.verdict: Notify the provider now.

questions.stem: A landscaper has tearing and light sensitivity after debris blew into his eye. The fluorescein exam shows a speck on the surface with no penetration. Which action does the nurse take next?

options.text: Lift the speck off with a dry cotton swab
options.rationale: A dry swab can scratch the cornea.

options.text: Shield the eye and wait for the eye surgeon
options.rationale: The right move for a penetrating object and tempting as the cautious choice. The exam showed the speck is on the surface.

options.text: Start IV antibiotics and a tetanus booster
options.rationale: These are the steps before surgery for a penetrating injury.

options.text: Irrigate the eye with sterile saline
options.rationale: A surface foreign body is treated with a fluorescein exam and then saline irrigation.

questions.takeaway: Surface foreign body: fluorescein exam, then saline irrigation. Penetrating object: leave it, protect it, get the eye care provider.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Leaving it alone is the rule for a penetrating injury. One phrase in the stem tells you this is not one.

steps.detail: On the surface, no penetration.
Shielding and IV antibiotics belong to a different injury.
Saline does not scratch.

elimination.verdict: Irrigate with sterile saline.

questions.nursesNote: Health fair screening. 64-year-old Black man with type 2 diabetes. Mother used daily eye drops for "pressure". Says he has clipped door frames with his shoulder lately. Sees halos around streetlights. Denies eye pain. Reads the 20/20 line with each eye. Uses reading glasses for small print. Tonometry 27 mmHg in both eyes.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that support referring this client for glaucoma evaluation.

segments.text: 64-year-old Black man with type 2 diabetes
segments.rationale: African American over 40 is a risk group, and diabetes raises risk.

segments.text: Mother used daily eye drops for "pressure"
segments.rationale: A family history of glaucoma.

segments.text: Says he has clipped door frames with his shoulder lately
segments.rationale: Peripheral vision is lost first, and he may not notice it as a vision problem.

segments.text: Sees halos around streetlights
segments.rationale: Halos around lights are listed with open-angle glaucoma.

segments.text: Denies eye pain
segments.rationale: Open-angle glaucoma is painless, so this neither supports nor rules it out.

segments.text: Reads the 20/20 line with each eye
segments.rationale: Central acuity stays normal until late. A normal result here is falsely reassuring, not a reason to refer.

segments.text: Uses reading glasses for small print
segments.rationale: Presbyopia, expected at his age.

segments.text: Tonometry 27 mmHg in both eyes
segments.rationale: Above normal and inside the 22 to 32 open-angle range.

questions.takeaway: Open-angle glaucoma hides behind a normal Snellen result and no pain. Risk group, family history, side vision loss and pressure are what find it.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The 20/20 acuity and absent pain make him sound healthy. Neither one tests the part of vision glaucoma takes first.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Age and race, diabetes, family history.
Bumping door frames, halos, pressure of 27.

steps.action: Leave the normal and the expected
steps.detail: No pain, 20/20, reading glasses.

elimination.verdict: Risk profile, family history, door frames, halos and tonometry.

questions.stem: A client with open-angle glaucoma and COPD started timolol drops 2 weeks ago. Intraocular pressure fell from 28 to 17 mm Hg. He mentions new wheezing on the stairs. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Document that the treatment goal is being met
options.rationale: Tempting because the pressure is now normal. The new wheeze is an unexpected finding that the pressure reading does not cancel.

options.text: Reteach punctal occlusion and recheck him next month
options.rationale: Tempting because punctal occlusion does cut systemic absorption. It is teaching for an actual breathing problem that the prescriber needs to hear about today.

options.text: Report the wheezing to the prescriber before the next dose
options.rationale: The deciding detail is new wheezing in a client with COPD on a beta blocker drop. The drug is reaching his lungs, and breathing outranks a good pressure reading.

options.text: Advise using his rescue inhaler before each eye drop
options.rationale: Treats the symptom and keeps giving the cause. Changing how he uses another drug is not the nurse's call.

questions.takeaway: A beta blocker eye drop can act on the lungs and heart. A good eye pressure does not make the plan effective if the drop causes wheezing.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Two results are in the stem. One is expected and good. Ask which one is new and belongs to breathing.

steps.detail: Pressure 17 is the goal. Wheezing is new.

steps.action: Link the wheeze to the drug
steps.detail: Timolol is a beta blocker and he has COPD.
Reteaching is slower than reporting an actual airway effect.

elimination.verdict: Report the wheezing before the next dose.

questions.stem: The clinic nurse has four clients waiting. Each problem began or was noticed this morning. Which client does the nurse see first?

options.text: Very nearsighted client with a painless shadow at one edge of vision
options.rationale: The quiet one is the urgent one. A new painless shadow in a nearsighted client suggests the retina is detaching, and it spreads while the client waits.

options.text: Client 1 day after cataract surgery with a scratchy eye and vision not yet sharp
options.rationale: Sounds like a surgical problem and is expected on day 1. Mild scratchiness and vision that is not yet sharp are normal, with no pain or sudden loss.

options.text: Client with a corneal abrasion who has tearing and marked light sensitivity
options.rationale: The most uncomfortable client. Tearing and photophobia are expected with an abrasion that is already diagnosed.

options.text: Client with open-angle glaucoma whose side vision has narrowed since the last visit
options.rationale: Tempting because vision is being lost. This is slow, chronic loss that a short wait will not change.

questions.takeaway: Painless does not mean minor. A new shadow or curtain is acute and can progress, so it outranks expected discomfort and chronic loss.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Three clients have findings that fit what they already have. Find the one whose finding is new and unexplained.

steps.detail: Day 1 cataract scratchiness and blur, abrasion tearing and photophobia.
Open-angle glaucoma loss is gradual.
New shadow in a nearsighted eye.

elimination.verdict: The nearsighted client with the new shadow.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old on a dim medical unit received a first dose of an anticholinergic 2 hours ago. She now reports brow pain, halos around the night light and nausea. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Give the prescribed as-needed antiemetic and reassess
options.rationale: Tempting because nausea is the complaint she wants fixed. Here nausea is a sign of rising eye pressure, so treating it alone delays the real problem.

options.text: Check visual acuity in each eye with a chart
options.rationale: Tempting as assess first. The stem already gives the cue cluster, and a chart reading in a dim room will not change what must happen next.

options.text: Offer a cool cloth and darken the room further
options.rationale: A comfort measure for headache. Dim light dilates the pupil more and can worsen a blocked drainage angle.

options.text: Notify the provider now and hold the next dose
options.rationale: The deciding detail is a pupil dilating drug plus dim light followed by eye pain, halos and nausea. That cluster means a suddenly blocked drain, which is an emergency.

questions.takeaway: Eye pain with halos and nausea after a dilating drug or dim light is angle closure until proven otherwise. Recognize it and escalate.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: First decide what the three symptoms add up to and what happened 2 hours ago. Then pick the action that matches that problem, not the loudest symptom.

steps.detail: Brow pain, halos, nausea, dim room, anticholinergic.
Sudden rise in eye pressure.
Antiemetic and cool cloth do not lower pressure.
Enough is known to call.

elimination.verdict: Notify the provider now and hold the next dose.

questions.stem: Three days after cataract surgery, a client says vision is sharper each day and the eye itches a little. He adds that a few new floaters and one flash appeared last night. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Document steady improvement and confirm the next visit
options.rationale: Tempting because acuity is improving and itching is expected. New floaters and a flash are not part of normal recovery.

options.text: Arrange for him to be examined today
options.rationale: The deciding detail is new floaters with a flash of light. They warn of a retinal tear even while central vision is getting better.

options.text: Reinforce no bending, lifting or straining
options.rationale: Correct teaching after cataract surgery and worth repeating. It does not address a finding that needs an eye examination.

options.text: Ask him to call if a curtain appears
options.rationale: Tempting because a curtain is the classic sign. Waiting for it means waiting for the detachment to progress.

questions.takeaway: Improving sharpness can hide a new problem. New floaters or flashes after eye surgery need a same day examination.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The stem gives good news first and the important detail last. Judge the recovery by the worst new finding, not the average.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sharper vision and mild itching.
Floaters and a flash.
A curtain is a late sign.

elimination.verdict: Arrange an examination today.

questions.stem: A client who is legally blind and walks steadily was shown the route to the bathroom once on admission. At 0200 she wants to walk there alone and refuses the bedpan. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Turn on the bed alarm and ask her to call each time
options.rationale: Tempting as a fall precaution. It restricts a client who can walk and does nothing to build safe independence.

options.text: Place a commode at the bedside for the night
options.rationale: Tempting because it shortens the distance. It changes her environment without orienting her to it and avoids the route she must learn.

options.text: Walk with her offering an elbow and describe the route again
options.rationale: The deciding detail is one orientation only. She is able to walk, so the least restrictive safe action is to guide and reorient until she can do it alone.

options.text: Clear the path and let her go while watching from the door
options.rationale: Respects her wish and tempts for that reason. One walk through is not enough for her to know the route in the dark.

questions.takeaway: For vision loss, give the least help that keeps the client safe: orient, describe, guide by the elbow, then step back as she learns the room.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Safety and independence both matter here. Look for the option that serves both instead of trading one for the other.

steps.detail: Fall safety and least restrictive care.
Alarm and commode limit her.
She has had only one orientation.

elimination.verdict: Guide her by the elbow and describe the route again.

questions.stem: Four days after cataract surgery, a client says he has not had a bowel movement since the operation and now feels the urge. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Advise him to bear down gently with the urge
options.rationale: Any bearing down raises pressure inside the healing eye.

options.text: Tell him this is expected and will resolve
options.rationale: Constipation may be common, but waiting leads to straining.

options.text: Request a stool softener and warn against straining
options.rationale: Treats the constipation now and protects the eye from a pressure rise.

options.text: Advise extra fiber and more fluids over the next week
options.rationale: Good long-term advice and tempting, but he has the urge now and will strain today.

questions.takeaway: After eye surgery, anything that makes the client strain raises eye pressure. Prevent the strain.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Connect the bowel complaint to the eye. The best option deals with today's risk, not next week's.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Link the cue to the surgery
steps.detail: Straining raises eye pressure.
Bearing down and waiting.
Fiber works in days. He needs relief now.

elimination.verdict: Stool softener and no straining.

questions.stem: A client with a bacterial infection in both eyes was taught to use the prescribed antibiotic drops. Which statement shows the teaching was effective?

options.text: "I use the bottle marked left only in my left eye."
options.rationale: Separate bottles keep organisms from one eye out of the other.

options.text: "I stop the drops once both eyes look clear."
options.rationale: The full course is completed even when the eyes look better.

options.text: "I wipe the dropper tip with a tissue between eyes."
options.rationale: Tempting because it sounds clean, but wiping contaminates the tip.

options.text: "I do the better eye first with the same bottle."
options.rationale: Order does not protect a shared bottle from contamination.

questions.takeaway: Both eyes infected means one bottle per eye and the full course.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Look for the statement that keeps the two eyes completely separate.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Separate bottles, finish the course.
Clear eyes are not the end point.
Wiping or ordering still shares one tip.

elimination.verdict: A labeled bottle for each eye.

questions.stem: One week after LASIK, a 29-year-old reports dry, gritty eyes and halos around headlights. She has no pain and reads without glasses. How does the nurse evaluate this?

options.text: Possible angle-closure glaucoma needing emergency care
options.rationale: Halos make this tempting, but angle closure brings sudden pain and vision loss, and she has neither.

options.text: Known effects of the surgery to review at follow-up
options.rationale: Dry eyes and halos are recognized after LASIK, and her vision is good.

options.text: A failed correction that will need repeating
options.rationale: She reads without glasses, so the correction is working.

options.text: A corneal infection that needs antibiotic drops
options.rationale: Infection brings pain and a hazy cornea.

questions.takeaway: Halos mean different things in different clients. After LASIK with no pain and clear vision, they are a known effect.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Use what is absent. No pain and good acuity rule out the emergencies.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Dry eyes, halos, no pain, clear vision.
Angle closure and infection both hurt.
She sees without glasses.

elimination.verdict: Known effects; review at follow-up.

questions.stem: After a dilated eye examination, a 52-year-old says he will drive straight back to work, where he reads blueprints. Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "Wait 15 minutes here, then you can drive."
options.rationale: Dilation lasts hours, not minutes.

options.text: "You may drive if you wear your regular glasses."
options.rationale: Glasses do not correct the blur and light sensitivity from dilated pupils.

options.text: "Rinse your eyes with saline to clear the drops."
options.rationale: The drug has already been absorbed. Rinsing does not reverse it.

options.text: "Arrange a ride and wear sunglasses until it wears off."
options.rationale: Dilated pupils cannot limit light or focus up close for several hours.

questions.takeaway: Dilating drops leave the client light sensitive and blurred for hours. Plan the ride and the sunglasses before he leaves.
questions.coverage: Not in Lecture PPT. The Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Ask what a dilated pupil cannot do. The answer covers both driving and his close work.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Glare and blurred near vision for hours.
Fifteen minutes, glasses and rinsing do not shorten it.

steps.action: Pick the option that covers safety
steps.detail: A ride and sunglasses until it wears off.

elimination.verdict: Ride home and sunglasses.

questions.stem: At an annual visit, a 60-year-old woman whose sister has glaucoma has an eye pressure of 25 mmHg. She has no pain and says her vision is fine. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Refer her for a prompt glaucoma evaluation
options.rationale: The reading is in the open-angle range and she has a family history. Damage is silent, so she needs an eye care visit soon.

options.text: Send her to the emergency department now
options.rationale: An emergency would be sudden pain, redness and vision loss with a higher pressure.

options.text: Recheck the pressure at next year's visit
options.rationale: Tempting because she feels fine, but open-angle glaucoma takes side vision without symptoms.

options.text: Teach her to report halos or eye pain
options.rationale: By the time symptoms appear the nerve damage is permanent.

questions.takeaway: A raised pressure with no symptoms is the usual picture of open-angle glaucoma. It needs referral, not an emergency response and not a wait.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two options overreact or underreact. Match the urgency to a silent, slowly damaging problem.

steps.detail: Above normal, below the emergency picture.
No pain, no vision loss.
No symptoms does not mean no damage.

elimination.verdict: Prompt referral.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old with type 2 diabetes and hypertension has clear vision and asks how to protect his eyesight. Which teaching is the priority?

options.text: Wear sunglasses that block ultraviolet light outdoors
options.rationale: True for cataract prevention and tempting, but his largest risks are his two diseases.

options.text: Control glucose and blood pressure, with yearly exams
options.rationale: These are his major modifiable risks, and yearly exams find damage before he notices it.

options.text: Rest your eyes every 20 minutes at the computer
options.rationale: Eases eyestrain. It does not protect the retina.

options.text: Return for an eye exam if vision blurs
options.rationale: Waiting for symptoms misses early, treatable damage.

questions.takeaway: For a client with diabetes and hypertension, disease control plus scheduled exams protects vision more than any eye-specific habit.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Several options are true. Ask which one targets the risk factors named in the stem.

steps.detail: Diabetes and hypertension.
Damage comes before blur.
Sunglasses and rest help less than controlling the diseases.

elimination.verdict: Control both diseases and get yearly exams.

questions.stem: After retinal detachment repair with a gas bubble, a client prescribed face-down positioning is found asleep on his back at 0300. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Let him sleep and reposition him at breakfast
options.rationale: Tempting because sleep matters, but the bubble only presses on the repair in the prescribed position.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed to 45 degrees
options.rationale: Not the position the surgeon prescribed.

options.text: Wake him and help him back to face-down
options.rationale: The bubble holds the retina in place only when he is positioned as prescribed.

options.text: Call the surgeon to report the position change
options.rationale: The nurse can correct this now. A call adds delay without changing the fix.

questions.takeaway: After retinal repair, the surgeon's positioning is the treatment. Restore it as soon as you find it lost.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The nurse already knows the prescribed position, so the next step is to act, not to wait or report.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Position keeps the bubble against the repair.
Breakfast is hours away.
The correction is within the nurse's role.

elimination.verdict: Wake him and reposition.

questions.stem: A client with open-angle glaucoma says she never misses her nightly drops. Which finding suggests the adherence teaching was not effective?

options.text: Eye pressure is 18 mmHg at this visit
options.rationale: Within the normal range.

options.text: She keeps the bottle beside her toothbrush
options.rationale: Tying the drop to a nightly habit supports adherence.

options.text: She presses the inner corner after each drop
options.rationale: Correct technique that limits systemic absorption.

options.text: Her one month bottle was last refilled 9 weeks ago
options.rationale: The supply has lasted more than twice as long as it should, so doses are being missed.

questions.takeaway: Check adherence with objective data such as refill dates, not only with what the client reports.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: The stem asks for the finding that does not fit. Three options show good habits or a good result.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Looking for evidence of a problem.
Routine placement and inner corner pressure.
A one month bottle should not last 9 weeks.

elimination.verdict: The late refill.

questions.stem: A client with glaucoma is learning to instill one drop each of two prescribed eye medications. Place the steps in the correct order.

options.text: Release one drop into the pocket without touching the eye
options.rationale: The tip stays off the eye and lashes so the bottle stays clean.

options.text: Wait several minutes, then instill the second medication
options.rationale: Spacing keeps the second drop from washing out the first.

options.text: Wash the hands
options.rationale: Clean hands come before touching the eye area or the bottle.

options.text: Close the eye gently and press the inner corner
options.rationale: Keeps the drug on the eye and out of the bloodstream.

options.text: Tilt the head back and pull the lower lid down
options.rationale: Forms the pocket that will hold the drop.

questions.takeaway: Clean hands, make a pocket, drop without touching, press the inner corner, then wait before the next drug.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Anchor the first and last steps, then order the middle by what must exist before the drop can go in.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Hand washing first, second drug last.
Pocket, drop, then inner corner pressure.

elimination.verdict: Wash, pocket, drop, press, wait.

questions.scenario: A retired teacher reports that over the past year vision in both eyes has grown blurry, colors look faded and oncoming headlights make night driving hard. She has no eye pain and her side vision is full. She has stopped reading and recently missed a curb.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the client is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Refer her for an eye examination
options.rationale: The diagnosis is confirmed with an ophthalmoscope, slit lamp and acuity testing.

options.text: Review home lighting and trip hazards with her
options.rationale: She has already missed a curb. Safety is addressed while she waits for care.

options.text: Keep her on bed rest with the eye patched
options.rationale: That is care before retinal detachment repair.

options.text: Advise that stronger glasses will correct it
options.rationale: Clients often blame their glasses, but a clouded lens is treated with surgery.

options.text: Cataracts
options.rationale: Painless, gradual blur with faded colors and trouble driving at night.

options.text: Open-angle glaucoma
options.rationale: That takes side vision first, and hers is full.

options.text: Retinal detachment
options.rationale: That is sudden, with flashes, floaters or a curtain.

options.text: Angle-closure glaucoma
options.rationale: That is sudden and painful.

options.text: Ability to read and manage daily activities
options.rationale: Surgery is timed by the effect on daily life.

options.text: Visual acuity at each visit
options.rationale: Tracks how far the clouding has progressed.

options.text: Eye pain rating every shift
options.rationale: Cataracts are painless.

options.text: Pupil size every hour
options.rationale: Not relevant to a slowly clouding lens.

questions.takeaway: Gradual, painless blur with faded color and night driving trouble points to cataracts. Refer, keep her safe, and track function.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Use two cues to sort the conditions: speed of onset and pain. Then use side vision to separate cataract from glaucoma.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Gradual and painless removes detachment and angle closure.
Full fields argue against open-angle glaucoma.
Referral and home safety.

elimination.verdict: Cataracts; refer and make home safe; monitor function and acuity.

questions.stem: After 4 months of latanoprost in the right eye, a client's pressure in that eye is 15 mmHg. The right iris is browner with longer lashes. She has no pain, redness or vision change. How does the nurse evaluate this?

options.text: A reaction that requires stopping the drops
options.rationale: Stopping lets the pressure rise and nerve damage resume. The change is cosmetic.

options.text: An expected drug effect, with the goal met
options.rationale: Prostaglandin drops can darken the iris and lengthen lashes in the treated eye. The pressure is within normal range.

options.text: A sign that the drops are being overused
options.rationale: The effect occurs at the normal dose.

options.text: Inflammation that needs an urgent eye exam
options.rationale: Tempting because the eye looks different. She has no pain, redness or vision change.

questions.takeaway: Prostaglandin eye drops lower pressure and can permanently darken the iris and lengthen lashes. Expected, so the drops continue.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Ask two things: is the treatment goal met, and is the new finding harmful or only different?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 15 mmHg is within the normal range.
No pain, redness or vision change.
Known effect of this drug class.

elimination.verdict: Expected effect. Goal met, drops continue.

questions.stem: A 37-year-old with a wood splinter penetrating the eye is being prepared for surgery. The eye is shielded and IV antibiotics are running. Which information does the nurse obtain next?

options.text: The fluorescein staining pattern of his cornea
options.rationale: Staining means instilling dye and handling an eye already known to be penetrated. It adds nothing before surgery.

options.text: The date of his last tetanus immunization
options.rationale: A penetrating wound from wood carries tetanus risk, and a booster is given before surgery if he is due.

options.text: Whether he wears contact lenses
options.rationale: Does not change what is done before surgery for a penetrating injury.

options.text: His intraocular pressure by tonometry
options.rationale: Tonometry presses on the eye and is not done on a penetrating injury.

questions.takeaway: Before surgery for a penetrating eye injury: shield, imaging by X-ray or CT, IV antibiotics and tetanus status.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two things are already done. Ask what remains on the preoperative list that does not touch the eye.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Shield and antibiotics.

steps.action: Cut anything that touches the eye
steps.detail: Fluorescein staining and tonometry.
Tetanus booster status.

elimination.verdict: Ask about his last tetanus booster.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old fishing guide whose mother had cataract surgery at 60 asks what he can do now to protect his eyes. Which teaching is the priority?

options.text: Have his eye pressure measured every 6 months
options.rationale: Pressure screening looks for glaucoma and does nothing to slow lens changes.

options.text: Use lubricating drops before and after work
options.rationale: Comfort for dry eyes. It does not protect the lens.

options.text: Begin yearly eye exams now rather than waiting until age 40
options.rationale: Tempting because exams matter. An exam finds a cataract, and sunglasses reduce the exposure that causes one.

options.text: Wear ultraviolet blocking sunglasses whenever outdoors
options.rationale: Chronic sun exposure is a modifiable cause of cataract, and his work exposes him daily.

questions.takeaway: Ultraviolet protection lowers the risk of cataract and ocular melanoma. Prevention acts on the exposure. Screening only finds the result.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: He asked what he can do to protect his eyes. Separate the options that prevent from the ones that detect.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Daily sun on the water.
Pressure checks and exams detect.
Ultraviolet light and the lens.

elimination.verdict: Ultraviolet blocking sunglasses outdoors.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old reports burning, gritty eyes that are worse by evening. Her corneas are clear, there is no discharge and her vision sharpens when she blinks. Which plan does the nurse suggest?

options.text: Lubricating eye drops through the day
options.rationale: Tear production falls with age. Clear corneas and vision that clears with blinking fit dry eye.

options.text: Same day evaluation for a corneal infection
options.rationale: An infected cornea is hazy and painful, usually with discharge. Hers is clear.

options.text: Warm compresses and antibiotic ointment
options.rationale: There is no sign of infection to treat.

options.text: Resting the eyes with both lids patched
options.rationale: Patching removes her vision, raises fall risk and does not replace tears.

questions.takeaway: Reduced tears are a normal aging change. Burning and grittiness with a clear cornea and no discharge are treated with lubrication.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Check the cornea first. Clear and no discharge takes infection off the table.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Clear cornea, no discharge.
Vision clears when tears spread.
Patching both eyes of an older adult.

elimination.verdict: Artificial tears.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old had laser photocoagulation last week to seal a small retinal tear. Which finding best shows the treatment was effective?

options.text: She has had no eye pain since the procedure
options.rationale: Retinal tears and detachment are painless, so the absence of pain says nothing.

options.text: Her reading vision is sharper than before
options.rationale: Sealing a tear protects vision. It is not expected to improve focus.

options.text: No new floaters or flashes, and full side vision
options.rationale: The laser was meant to stop the tear from becoming a detachment, so the absence of detachment signs is the outcome.

options.text: Her eye pressure measures 19 mmHg
options.rationale: A normal pressure relates to glaucoma, not to the retina staying attached.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate retinal tear treatment by the absence of detachment signs: no flashes, no new floaters, no curtain. Pain is not part of this condition.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Recall what a detachment feels like. An outcome can only be judged by a symptom the condition actually produces.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sudden, painless flashes, floaters, curtain.
It was never painful.
No progression to detachment.

elimination.verdict: No flashes, no new floaters, full visual field.

questions.stem: A client is going home after cataract removal by phacoemulsification. Which instructions does the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Wear dark glasses outdoors
options.rationale: The eye is light sensitive after surgery.

options.text: Sleep on the side of the operated eye
options.rationale: Lying on that side puts pressure on the eye.

options.text: Lift nothing heavier than 10 lb
options.rationale: Heavy lifting raises eye pressure.

options.text: Expect your final vision by the end of the first week
options.rationale: Best vision arrives at about 4 to 6 weeks.

options.text: Report sudden pain or loss of vision at once
options.rationale: Signals bleeding, infection or raised pressure.

questions.takeaway: After cataract surgery: dark glasses, avoid anything that raises eye pressure, report sudden pain or vision loss, and expect best vision at 4 to 6 weeks.

steps.detail: No heavy lifting.
Sudden pain or vision loss.
Lying on the operated side and a one week timeline.

questions.scenario: A client is going home after scleral buckling with a gas bubble for a retinal detachment. The nurse listens to what the client and her husband plan to do.
questions.stem: For each statement, indicate whether the discharge teaching was effective or needs more teaching.

rows.text: "My husband will read the mail to me this week."
rows.rationale: Reading and close work are avoided for the first week because of the rapid eye movements.

rows.text: "I will keep my head in the position the surgeon showed me."
rows.rationale: Position keeps the bubble against the repair.

rows.text: "I will fly to my sister's on Friday while I rest."
rows.rationale: Gas expands at altitude and raises eye pressure. No air travel until the surgeon clears it.

rows.text: "I will ask my son to carry the laundry baskets."
rows.rationale: Avoids lifting and straining that raise eye pressure.

rows.text: "If my vision dims suddenly I will mention it at my checkup."
rows.rationale: A sudden vision change is reported immediately.

questions.takeaway: After retinal repair: hold the prescribed position, no reading for a week, nothing that raises eye pressure, no flying with a gas bubble, and report sudden changes at once.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Test each statement against two rules: protect the repair from pressure and movement, and report sudden change now.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Reading, lifting and flying.
As the surgeon prescribed.
Sudden change cannot wait for a checkup.

elimination.verdict: Effective, effective, more teaching, effective, more teaching.

questions.stem: A client treated for open-angle glaucoma for years calls. An hour ago her right eye became very painful and red with blurred vision. She plans to use an extra drop and keep tomorrow's appointment. Which response is best?

options.text: "Use the extra drop and call back in an hour if it still hurts."
options.rationale: Tempting because her drops do lower pressure. Sudden pain with redness is a blocked drain, and an extra dose of her usual drop only delays emergency treatment.

options.text: "Rest in a dark room with the eye closed until the pain eases."
options.rationale: A comfort measure that delays care while the pressure keeps damaging the nerve.

options.text: "This needs emergency eye care now. Do not wait for tomorrow."
options.rationale: Sudden pain, redness and blurred vision are the angle closure pattern, a medical emergency. It is new and different from her silent chronic disease.

options.text: "Keep the appointment. Pressure changes are part of your condition."
options.rationale: Open-angle glaucoma is gradual and close to painless. A sudden painful red eye is not part of it.

questions.takeaway: A chronic diagnosis does not explain a sudden symptom. Sudden pain, redness and vision loss mean angle closure until proven otherwise.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Compare what she has now with what her known disease looks like. Open-angle is slow and quiet, so sudden and painful is something new.

steps.detail: Sudden, painful, red, blurred. That is not the quiet open-angle picture.
The extra drop, the dark room and tomorrow's visit all delay care.

steps.action: Keep the one that moves her
steps.detail: Only one option gets her treated now.

elimination.verdict: Emergency eye care now.

questions.stem: A client with a corneal laceration has the eye shielded and is awaiting surgical repair. An antiemetic is prescribed as needed. He reports nausea and starts to retch. Which action is the priority?

options.text: Give the as needed antiemetic now
options.rationale: Retching is straining, which raises the pressure inside an open eye and can push its contents out through the laceration. Stopping it protects the eye.

options.text: Recheck visual acuity in the injured eye
options.rationale: Useful data, and it does nothing to stop the retching that threatens the eye right now.

options.text: Have him lean forward over an emesis basin
options.rationale: Tempting as basic care for vomiting. Bending forward adds to the pressure in the eye and lets the retching continue.

options.text: Remove the shield to inspect the laceration
options.rationale: The shield protects the eye. Handling the eye adds risk and tells the nurse nothing that changes the action.

questions.takeaway: With an open eye injury, anything that raises eye pressure (retching, coughing, straining, bending) can force eye contents out. Stop the cause first.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: The assessment is already given: a lacerated cornea and active retching. Ask which option removes the threat to the eye.

steps.detail: The injury, the shield and the prescription are all stated. Nothing more is needed to act.
Straining raises eye pressure, and a lacerated cornea can let contents prolapse.
Acuity, a basin and inspection do not stop the retching.

elimination.verdict: Give the antiemetic now.

questions.stem: Before the 0900 timolol eye drop, a 67-year-old with open-angle glaucoma says she nearly fainted when she stood up this morning. What does the nurse check first?

options.text: Her most recent eye pressure reading
options.rationale: Shows whether the drop is working. It does not explain a near faint.

options.text: Whether she presses the inner corner after each drop
options.rationale: Tempting, because skipping this step lets more drug reach the blood. It finds a cause, and her safety right now comes first.

options.text: Her side vision by confrontation
options.rationale: Tracks the glaucoma, which does not cause faintness on standing.

options.text: Her apical pulse and blood pressure
options.rationale: A beta blocker drop can be absorbed and slow the heart. These are the findings that decide whether the drop is given or held.

questions.takeaway: Eye drops are still drugs. A beta blocker drop can reach the bloodstream, so near fainting calls for a pulse and blood pressure before the next dose.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Ask what a beta blocker does to the body, then pick the check that tells you whether giving it is safe.

steps.detail: Timolol is a beta blocker.
Near fainting on standing fits a slow pulse or low blood pressure.
Technique explains how it happened. Pulse and blood pressure tell you if she is safe now.

elimination.verdict: Apical pulse and blood pressure first.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old who has taken prednisone daily for 3 years for rheumatoid arthritis reports slowly worsening blur and glare from headlights. She has no eye pain. How does the nurse interpret this?

options.text: Loss of near focus that reading glasses will correct
options.rationale: Presbyopia affects close work. Glare from headlights and overall blur point to the lens clouding.

options.text: Dry eyes that lubricating drops will relieve
options.rationale: Tempting, because dry eye blurs vision too. It does not explain glare, and it ignores the steroid.

options.text: A likely steroid related lens change that needs an eye examination
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are a cause of cataracts and of secondary glaucoma. Gradual painless blur with night glare fits a cataract and needs an examination.

options.text: An emergency that needs evaluation within the hour
options.rationale: Emergencies are sudden. This has built slowly and without pain.

questions.takeaway: Cataracts are not only from aging. Long term corticosteroids cause them, so gradual painless blur and glare in a steroid user needs an eye examination.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Sort by the three questions: sudden or gradual, painful or painless, and what the client takes.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Gradual and painless rules out the emergency option.
Three years of prednisone is a known cause of lens opacity.
Reading glasses and lubricant do not explain headlight glare.

elimination.verdict: A steroid related change. Arrange an eye examination.

questions.stem: At a wellness visit, a 77-year-old describes changes in her vision over the past few years. Which report needs follow up rather than routine teaching?

options.text: She needs a much brighter lamp to sew
options.rationale: The aging pupil dilates less, so more light is needed. Expected.

options.text: She mixes up navy and dark green clothing
options.rationale: Blue and green discrimination drops with age. Expected.

options.text: Her eyes feel dry by evening
options.rationale: Tear production falls with age. Expected, and managed with lubricating drops.

options.text: She is startled by people who approach from the side
options.rationale: Loss of side vision is not an aging change. It is how open-angle glaucoma starts, and it is permanent if missed.

questions.takeaway: Aging changes the lens, pupil, color sense and tears. It does not take away side vision. Peripheral loss needs a glaucoma evaluation.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Match each report to a known aging change. The one with no match is the one to follow up.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: More light, blue and green confusion and dry eyes are all on the list.

steps.action: Find the one that is not
steps.detail: Missing things at the side is a visual field loss.
Peripheral loss comes first in glaucoma and does not return.

elimination.verdict: Startled from the side. Refer for evaluation.

questions.stem: The nurse cannot see a red reflex in the left eye of an 86-year-old whose vision has blurred slowly for years. The left pupil looks bluish white and she has no pain. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Record the finding as an expected aging change
options.rationale: Tempting, because cataracts are common with age. An absent red reflex is an abnormal finding that is acted on.

options.text: Refer for cataract evaluation and ask how vision limits daily tasks
options.rationale: An absent red reflex with a bluish white pupil is a mature cataract. Surgery is the only treatment and is timed by its effect on daily activities.

options.text: Send her for an emergency eye examination within the hour
options.rationale: Emergencies are sudden. This is slow, painless and long standing.

options.text: Teach that daily eye drops will clear the lens
options.rationale: Drops treat glaucoma. Nothing but surgery removes a cataract.

questions.takeaway: A clouded lens blocks light on its way to the retina, so the red reflex disappears. That is a mature cataract: not an emergency, and not something to chart as normal.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two options sit at the extremes (do nothing, do everything now). The stated cues, slow and painless, place this in between.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Slow, painless, no red reflex, bluish white pupil.
It is not normal, and it is not an emergency.
Only surgery treats a cataract, and function decides the timing.

elimination.verdict: Refer for cataract evaluation and review daily function.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old with extreme myopia plays competitive racquetball and asks how to protect her vision. Which teaching is the priority?

options.text: Wear protective sports eyewear every time she plays
options.rationale: Extreme myopia already raises her risk of retinal detachment, and eye trauma is another risk factor. The trauma is the one she can remove.

options.text: Take a 20 second break every 20 minutes of screen time
options.rationale: Relieves digital eyestrain. It does not protect the retina.

options.text: Wear sunglasses that block ultraviolet light outdoors
options.rationale: Good advice that lowers cataract risk over decades. Her sport is the nearer threat.

options.text: Use lubricating drops before each game
options.rationale: Treats dryness, which the stem does not report.

questions.takeaway: Extreme myopia and eye trauma are both risk factors for retinal detachment. Match prevention teaching to the client's own exposure.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: All four are real eye health advice. Ask which one fits the two facts in the stem: very nearsighted, and a sport with a fast ball.

steps.detail: Extreme myopia and racquetball.
Both point to the retina: one is a standing risk, the other is trauma.
Sunglasses, screen breaks and lubricant are general advice.

elimination.verdict: Protective sports eyewear.

questions.stem: Two days after scleral buckling, a client's wife calls. He has a deep ache in the operated eye with nausea and wants to take an antiemetic and sleep. Which instruction does the nurse give?

options.text: Give the antiemetic and call back if he vomits
options.rationale: Tempting, because vomiting would raise eye pressure. Pain with nausea after this surgery is itself a finding to report immediately, and the drug would only hide it.

options.text: Have him rest in his prescribed position and recheck in an hour
options.rationale: Positioning matters, and waiting an hour delays an examination he needs now.

options.text: Bring him in to be examined now
options.rationale: Pain with nausea after retinal surgery is reported immediately. Together they suggest rising pressure in the eye.

options.text: Apply a cool compress and give the prescribed pain medicine
options.rationale: Treats the ache without finding its cause.

questions.takeaway: After retinal surgery, sudden pain, pain with nausea or a sudden vision change is reported immediately, never managed at home.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Nausea alone could be treated at home. Ask what changes when it arrives together with eye pain.

steps.detail: Eye pain plus nausea is on the report immediately list.
The antiemetic, the compress and the analgesic treat symptoms and mask the cause.
Rechecking in an hour is still waiting.

elimination.verdict: He is examined now.

questions.stem: A client is on activity restriction with an eye patch while awaiting retinal detachment repair. Which task does the nurse delegate to assistive personnel?

options.text: Explaining why he must limit head movement
options.rationale: Teaching stays with the nurse.

options.text: Asking whether the shadow in his vision has grown
options.rationale: This is assessment of his vision, which the nurse keeps.

options.text: Finding out what he understands about the surgery
options.rationale: Evaluating understanding is the nurse's role.

options.text: Helping him wash and eat while he stays in bed
options.rationale: Routine care with a clear instruction. It also supports the restriction on activity and head movement.

questions.takeaway: Assistive personnel take routine care with clear limits. The nurse keeps teaching, assessment and evaluation.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Label each option as teach, assess, evaluate or do. Only the doing task can be delegated.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Explain is teaching. Asking about the shadow is assessment. Checking understanding is evaluation.
Bathing and feeding help is standard care.
Help in bed keeps his head and body still.

elimination.verdict: Help with washing and eating in bed.

questions.stem: At a community health fair, six adults with no eye symptoms ask whether they need a glaucoma evaluation. Which clients does the nurse refer as higher risk? Select all that apply.

options.text: 46-year-old African American man
options.rationale: Risk rises from age 40 in African American adults.

options.text: 64-year-old Hispanic woman
options.rationale: Risk rises from age 60 in Hispanic or Latino adults.

options.text: 50-year-old woman who has taken a daily oral corticosteroid for 5 years
options.rationale: Steroids are a cause of secondary glaucoma, whatever her age.

options.text: 48-year-old white woman who just started using reading glasses
options.rationale: Presbyopia is an expected change and is not a glaucoma risk factor.

options.text: 30-year-old man who wears contact lenses for mild nearsightedness
options.rationale: Contact lens wear raises corneal infection risk. It is not a glaucoma risk factor.

options.text: 66-year-old white man with no family history
options.rationale: Age 60 and older is a risk factor on its own.

questions.takeaway: Open-angle glaucoma is silent, so risk decides who is referred: age 60 and older, African American from 40, Hispanic or Latino from 60, family history, and causes of secondary glaucoma such as steroids.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: No one has symptoms, and that is the point. Judge each client against the risk list and ignore how well they say they see.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 66 qualifies on age alone.
African American from 40 and Hispanic from 60 both qualify.
Long term steroid use can raise eye pressure at any age.
Reading glasses and contact lenses are eye issues with no link to glaucoma risk.

elimination.verdict: Refer the 46, 64, 50 and 66-year-olds.

questions.stem: A client with open-angle glaucoma instills her prescribed drops correctly and refills them on time. Her eye pressure is 26 mmHg and her side vision has narrowed since the last visit. Which does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Repeating the teaching on drop technique and adherence
options.rationale: The usual first thought when pressure stays high. The stem states her technique and refills are correct, so teaching is not the gap.

options.text: A discussion of laser trabeculoplasty
options.rationale: Pressure above normal with new field loss despite correct use means the drops have failed. Laser trabeculoplasty is the next step.

options.text: An emergency laser peripheral iridotomy
options.rationale: This is the first line treatment for angle closure, which is sudden and painful.

options.text: New glasses to widen her side vision
options.rationale: Vision lost to glaucoma is nerve damage that lenses cannot correct.

questions.takeaway: Glaucoma treatment is judged by pressure and by whether the visual field holds. When correctly used drops fail, the next step is laser trabeculoplasty.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Ask why the treatment is failing. The stem rules out adherence, so the plan itself has to change.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 26 mmHg and a narrower field mean the goal is not met.
Correct technique and on time refills are stated.
Trabeculoplasty is for open-angle. Iridotomy is for angle closure.

elimination.verdict: Laser trabeculoplasty is discussed.

questions.stem: Six weeks after right cataract surgery, a client sees sharply with the right eye. He says the left eye has grown slowly blurrier with more glare and no pain. How does the nurse evaluate this?

options.text: The left cataract is progressing; arrange a routine evaluation
options.rationale: Both eyes may develop cataracts and they progress at different rates. Slow painless blur with glare in the other eye fits that.

options.text: A surgical complication; arrange an examination today
options.rationale: A complication would show in the operated eye, and it would be sudden pain or vision loss.

options.text: A retinal detachment; keep him still and call the surgeon
options.rationale: Detachment is sudden, with flashes, floaters or a curtain. None is reported.

options.text: A normal aging change; no follow up is needed
options.rationale: Tempting, because it is slow and painless. It still limits vision and is treatable.

questions.takeaway: Cataracts often affect both eyes at different rates. After a good result in one eye, slow painless blur in the other is the second cataract, not a complication.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Notice which eye has the problem and how fast it came on. The operated eye is doing well.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sharp vision at 6 weeks is the expected result.
Slow and painless excludes the urgent options.
It is not ignored, because it is treatable.

elimination.verdict: The other cataract is progressing. Routine evaluation.

questions.stem: The charge nurse makes assignments on a unit that includes four clients with eye problems. Which client is most appropriate to assign to the LPN?

options.text: A client who reported new flashes and floaters this morning
options.rationale: A new, unexplained change that may be a retinal detachment needs RN assessment.

options.text: A client with long standing open-angle glaucoma due for scheduled drops
options.rationale: A stable chronic condition with a routine medication is within the LPN role.

options.text: A client going home today after cataract surgery who needs discharge teaching
options.rationale: Initial discharge teaching belongs to the RN.

options.text: A client admitted an hour ago with a penetrating eye injury
options.rationale: A new emergency admission with an unpredictable course needs the RN.

questions.takeaway: Assign the stable client with predictable care to the LPN. The RN keeps new symptoms, new admissions and initial teaching.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Sort the four by stable versus unstable and by the kind of work needed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: New flashes and a new penetrating injury stay with the RN.
Discharge teaching stays with the RN.
Scheduled drops for a chronic condition.

elimination.verdict: The client with stable glaucoma due for drops.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old admitted with abdominal pain has sclerae that look slightly yellow. Which approach does the nurse use to judge whether he is jaundiced?

options.text: Chart jaundice based on the color of the sclerae
options.rationale: In older adults the appearance of the sclera is not a reliable sign of jaundice.

options.text: Look at the sclerae again under brighter light
options.rationale: Better light does not make an unreliable sign reliable.

options.text: Use other indicators, such as urine color and the bilirubin result
options.rationale: The sclera can look yellow with age alone, so the judgment rests on findings outside the eye.

options.text: Ask his family whether his eyes have always looked this way
options.rationale: Tempting as a baseline check. It still depends on eye appearance, which is the unreliable sign.

questions.takeaway: Do not use the sclera or eye appearance to judge jaundice or hydration in an older adult. Use other findings.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Three options keep relying on how the eye looks. One moves the judgment somewhere else.

steps.detail: Eye appearance misleads in older adults.
Charting it, relighting it and asking about it all still use the sclera.
Urine color and bilirubin do not depend on the eye.

elimination.verdict: Use indicators other than the sclera.

questions.stem: On day 4 of antibiotic drops for a corneal ulcer, a client says the pain and redness are gone. He wears his glasses, has 3 days of drops left and asks to stop them. Which response is best?

options.text: "Stop them now and restart if the pain comes back."
options.rationale: Tempting because he feels well. Feeling better is not the same as a cleared infection, and a corneal infection that returns is an emergency because the cornea has no blood supply of its own.

options.text: "Use every dose that is left. Feeling better does not mean the infection is cleared."
options.rationale: The full antibiotic course is completed for a corneal infection. Relief of pain and redness on day 4 shows the drops are working, not that treatment is finished.

options.text: "Cut back to one drop a day for the last 3 days."
options.rationale: Tempting as a compromise. A reduced dose is still an incomplete course.

options.text: "Stop the drops, and keep wearing glasses until the eye is checked."
options.rationale: Staying out of contact lenses is right. Stopping the antibiotic early is not.

questions.takeaway: Corneal infection: complete the full antibiotic course and stay out of contact lenses until fully healed, even when the eye feels normal.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Three options shorten the course in some way. Ask what an early end to symptoms tells you about the infection.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pain and redness gone on day 4, with 3 days of drops left.
Stopping, cutting back and stopping while keeping glasses all end the full course early.
Only one response has him use every remaining dose.

elimination.verdict: Finish the full course.

questions.stem: Two weeks after cataract surgery with a lens implant, a client says his vision is clearer each day but still not sharp. He has no pain and asks whether the surgery failed. Which response is best?

options.text: "Vision should be sharp by now. I will arrange an examination today."
options.rationale: Tempting, because vision complaints after eye surgery deserve attention. His vision is improving daily without pain, which is the expected course, not a complication.

options.text: "The implant may need to be replaced with a different strength."
options.rationale: Nothing in his report points to an implant problem, and this is not the nurse's conclusion to offer.

options.text: "Keep the eye patched and rested until the vision sharpens."
options.rationale: Patching does not speed recovery and takes away the vision he has, which raises his fall risk.

options.text: "Steady improvement is expected. Best vision comes at 4 to 6 weeks."
options.rationale: Vision that improves daily with no pain is the expected course, and best vision is reached about 4 to 6 weeks after surgery.

questions.takeaway: After cataract surgery, best vision arrives at 4 to 6 weeks. Improving and painless is expected; worsening vision or sudden pain is reported.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Sort the report into expected or unexpected. The direction of change and the absence of pain decide it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Clearer each day with no pain is recovery moving the right way.
Nothing suggests an implant problem, and patching is not a postoperative instruction and adds a fall risk.
It would be right if vision were worsening or pain had started. Neither is in the stem.

elimination.verdict: D matches the cues: improving, painless, and still inside the 4 to 6 week window.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old on day 6 of contact isolation now believes it is 1990. Vital signs and glucose are normal. Her hearing aids are in a drawer and the blinds are closed. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Request a prescription for a sitter at the bedside
options.rationale: A sitter adds supervision but does not treat the cause the stem already shows.

options.text: Complete a full cognitive screening tool
options.rationale: Tempting because assessment usually comes first. The stem already gives the cause, and a screen done without her hearing aids would only measure what she cannot hear.

options.text: Insert her hearing aids and open the blinds
options.rationale: Physical causes are already checked and the cues point to sensory deprivation. Restoring meaningful input is the least restrictive fix.

options.text: Ask the provider about a dementia evaluation
options.rationale: New confusion after days of isolation is not labeled dementia before a reversible cause is corrected.

questions.takeaway: New confusion in isolation with normal vital signs and hearing aids in a drawer is sensory deprivation until proven otherwise. Give the input back first.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The stem hands you the assessment. When the cause is already visible, the next step is to fix it.

steps.detail: Normal vital signs and glucose, aids in a drawer, blinds closed, six days alone.

steps.action: Notice the assess option is late
steps.detail: A cognitive screen without hearing aids gives a false result.
Hearing aids and daylight cost nothing and treat the cause.

elimination.verdict: Insert the hearing aids and open the blinds.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old with poorly controlled diabetes has used antibiotic ear drops for external otitis for 7 days. Which finding requires immediate follow-up?

options.text: Deeper, worsening ear pain with new drainage
options.rationale: Worsening pain and drainage in a client with diabetes suggests necrotizing otitis spreading into bone, which can be fatal.

options.text: Pain when the tragus is pressed
options.rationale: This is the expected sign of external otitis and does not show spread.

options.text: A plugged feeling with muffled hearing in the treated ear
options.rationale: Canal swelling causes temporary hearing loss. It is expected while the canal heals.

options.text: A request to resume wearing earbuds
options.rationale: This needs teaching to keep earbuds out for 7 to 10 days. It is not a sign of a complication.

questions.takeaway: External otitis should improve on drops. Worsening pain in a diabetic or immunocompromised client means possible necrotizing otitis.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Three findings are expected for swimmer's ear. Look for the one moving in the wrong direction in a high risk client.

steps.detail: Tragus pain and a plugged ear belong to the diagnosis.
Diabetes is why the stem mentions it.
Worse after 7 days of treatment is the red flag.

elimination.verdict: Deeper, worsening pain with new drainage.

questions.stem: A client is going home after a tympanoplasty. Which statement indicates a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I will keep my mouth open if I have to sneeze."
options.rationale: Correct. It keeps pressure off the repair.

options.text: "My husband will carry the laundry baskets."
options.rationale: Correct. Lifting is straining.

options.text: "I will dab my nose and not blow it."
options.rationale: Correct. Nose blowing pushes pressure into the middle ear.

options.text: "I fly out to see my daughter this weekend."
options.rationale: Air travel changes middle ear pressure and can disrupt the graft, so it is avoided until the surgeon clears it.

questions.takeaway: After ear surgery, avoid anything that changes middle ear pressure: straining, nose blowing and air travel.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: You are looking for the wrong statement. Ask which plan puts pressure on the repair.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Needs more teaching means find the error.
Open mouth sneeze, no lifting, no nose blowing.
A flight.

elimination.verdict: The flight this weekend.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old roofer newly diagnosed with Meniere disease has had three vertigo attacks this month. He plans to return to work tomorrow. Which plan is most important?

options.text: Start a low sodium diet and limit caffeine
options.rationale: Tempting because it is the core long term teaching. It reduces attacks over time but does not protect him on a roof tomorrow.

options.text: Arrange work off ladders until attacks are controlled
options.rationale: An attack on a roof or ladder could kill him, and attacks are not yet controlled, so the safety risk is addressed first.

options.text: Begin vestibular rehabilitation exercises with a therapist
options.rationale: Balance exercises help over weeks and do not prevent an attack.

options.text: Discuss surgical options with the provider
options.rationale: Surgery is a last resort after lifestyle and drug therapy fail.

questions.takeaway: In Meniere disease, safety comes before education. No ladders or driving while attacks are uncontrolled.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: All four are real parts of Meniere care. His job and his plan for tomorrow decide which one cannot wait.

steps.action: Find the detail that tips it
steps.detail: He is a roofer and goes back tomorrow.
Diet lowers attack frequency slowly.
Surgery is not first line.

elimination.verdict: Keep him off ladders and roofs.

questions.stem: An 86-year-old resident has seemed to ignore staff for a week. He reports itching and fullness in the right ear and turns his left ear toward people who are speaking. Which problem does the nurse suspect first?

options.text: Cerumen impaction
options.rationale: One sided fullness, itching and hearing loss over a short time fit a blocked canal, the most common and most correctable cause in older adults.

options.text: Worsening presbycusis
options.rationale: Tempting because of his age. Presbycusis is gradual and affects both ears, and it does not cause itching or fullness.

options.text: Early dementia
options.rationale: Unheard words can look like inattention. The ear symptoms point to hearing, not cognition.

options.text: Sensory overload
options.rationale: Overload causes restlessness and scattered attention from too much stimulation, which the stem does not describe.

questions.takeaway: Before blaming age or cognition, look in the ear. One sided fullness and itching in an older adult suggests impacted cerumen.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Age makes presbycusis the reflex answer. One sided and itchy does not fit it.

steps.detail: One ear, a week, fullness, itching.
Gradual and bilateral does not match.
Wax explains every cue.

elimination.verdict: Cerumen impaction.

questions.stem: A parent reports that a 4-year-old pushed a dried bean into the ear an hour ago. A standing order allows ear irrigation for foreign bodies. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Irrigate gently with body temperature water
options.rationale: Tempting because the technique is correct and an order exists. Water makes a bean swell and wedge tighter.

options.text: Instill mineral oil and wait before removal
options.rationale: Oil is used to suffocate a live insect. It does not help with a bean.

options.text: Soften it with ear drops, then irrigate
options.rationale: That is the plan for cerumen. Drops and water both add fluid to a bean.

options.text: Leave it and arrange removal by the provider
options.rationale: Vegetable matter expands with water, so irrigation is withheld and the provider removes it.

questions.takeaway: Never irrigate vegetable matter. It swells with water and locks itself in the canal.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: An order and perfect technique do not make an action safe. Ask what the object is made of.

steps.detail: A dried bean is vegetable matter.
Good technique cannot fix the wrong procedure.

steps.action: Send it to the right person
steps.detail: Manual removal by the provider.

elimination.verdict: No irrigation. The provider removes it.

questions.stem: The nurse receives four call lights at once. Which client does the nurse see first?

options.text: Client with otitis media whose severe pain stopped suddenly an hour ago
options.rationale: Tempting because it is unexpected and means the eardrum likely perforated. It must be reported, but the pressure is released and the client is not in immediate danger.

options.text: Client one day after tympanoplasty asking for a pain medication
options.rationale: Postoperative pain is expected and can wait a few minutes.

options.text: Client with Meniere disease standing at the sink who says the room began spinning
options.rationale: The client is upright during an attack and can drop without warning. An actual, immediate fall risk comes first.

options.text: Client on gentamicin asking when the trough level will be drawn
options.rationale: A question about a scheduled lab is stable and can wait.

questions.takeaway: Ear disorders are balance disorders. A client who is standing as vertigo starts is the one about to be injured.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two clients have unexpected changes. Ask which one can be hurt in the next minute.

steps.detail: Expected pain and a lab question.
Perforation has already happened. The fall has not.
Get the client seated or into bed now.

elimination.verdict: The standing client with Meniere disease.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old at a blood pressure check mentions he woke yesterday unable to hear from his left ear. His wife says his hearing has been fading for years. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Schedule a routine audiology screening
options.rationale: Tempting because audiometry is the most reliable hearing test. A routine appointment treats a sudden change as if it were gradual.

options.text: Report the change to the provider today
options.rationale: Sudden one sided loss is never assumed to be aging and needs same day evaluation.

options.text: Teach him about hearing aid styles
options.rationale: Devices are for established loss after the cause is known.

options.text: Reassure the couple that presbycusis progresses with age
options.rationale: Presbycusis is gradual and bilateral. This explanation dismisses a new finding.

questions.takeaway: New or sudden changes are not assumed to be age related. Sudden loss in one ear is reported the same day.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The wife's comment pulls you toward aging. The words woke yesterday and left ear pull you back.

strategies: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings

steps.detail: Years of fading is old. Overnight in one ear is new.

steps.action: Check the timing of each option
steps.detail: Routine screening is too slow.
It explains away the cue.

elimination.verdict: Report it to the provider today.

questions.stem: A competitive swimmer was treated for external otitis and returns for follow-up. Which statement shows the prevention teaching was effective?

options.text: "I went back to the pool once the pain eased on day 3."
options.rationale: Water is avoided for 7 to 10 days, not until the pain eases.

options.text: "I wear my earbuds at practice to keep the water out."
options.rationale: Sounds protective, but earbuds are one of the causes and are avoided during healing.

options.text: "I use the leftover drops after every swim."
options.rationale: Leftover antibiotic drops are not a prevention plan.

options.text: "I stopped cleaning my ears with cotton swabs."
options.rationale: Swabs injure the canal skin, which is a listed cause of external otitis.

questions.takeaway: External otitis is prevented by protecting the canal skin: no swabs or hairpins, and no water or earbuds for 7 to 10 days during treatment.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Ask which statement removes a cause of the problem.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Trauma from swabs, earphones, water.
Pain easing is not healing.
