questions.stem: In a cold emergency room, a patient with a sprained right ankle has a right foot that feels cool. The pedal pulse is palpable and capillary refill is 2 seconds. Which action does the nurse take next?

options.text: Notify the provider of impaired circulation
options.rationale: Tempting because a cool extremity is a red flag, but pulse and refill are normal and the comparison is not done yet.

options.text: Feel the temperature of the left foot
options.rationale: Neurovascular findings are judged against the other side. Two equally cool feet in a cold room is not a circulation problem.

options.text: Wrap the foot in a warmed blanket
options.rationale: Warming before comparing can hide a real difference between the feet.

options.text: Lower the leg below heart level
options.rationale: Dependent positioning increases swelling in a fresh sprain.

questions.takeaway: Start with the injured side, then compare with the other. One finding alone is not a red flag until the comparison is done.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Here the assess first reflex is right. The stem gives half an assessment: one foot.

steps.detail: Pulse and refill are normal. The other foot has not been checked.
The provider will ask how the left foot feels.
Compare sides.

elimination.verdict: B. Compare sides before deciding it is abnormal.

questions.stem: An 81-year-old with kyphosis walks with a widened gait and says she feels unsteady getting up from her low sofa. Which interventions does the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Sit in a firm chair with armrests
options.rationale: A higher seat with arms lets her push up while her balance catches up.

options.text: Practice walking with the feet closer together
options.rationale: The widened gait is how she compensates for a shifted center of gravity. Narrowing it takes away her base of support.

options.text: Ask about a referral to assess the need for a cane or walker
options.rationale: A device widens the base of support, and therapy judges which one fits.

options.text: Wear supportive shoes that fit well
options.rationale: Stable footwear improves contact with the floor.

options.text: Replace daily walks with seated exercises
options.rationale: Sounds safer, but weight-bearing activity is what maintains bone and leg strength. Walking is made safe, not removed.

questions.takeaway: Kyphosis and a widened gait shift the center of gravity. Support balance with chairs with arms, a device if needed and good shoes, and keep her walking.
questions.coverage: Not in Lecture PPT. Covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Judge each option alone: does it steady her while keeping her active? Options that take away her base of support or her walking fail.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Armrests, a device evaluation and shoes.
A wide stance is her compensation, so narrowing it is unsafe.
Giving up weight bearing speeds bone and muscle loss.

elimination.verdict: Armrests, device referral, supportive shoes. Three of five.

questions.stem: A patient on bed rest after hip surgery wears sequential compression devices and does ankle pumps hourly. Which finding on day 4 indicates the plan is effective?

options.text: Both calves are equal in size, soft and nontender
options.rationale: Equal, soft, nontender calves show no sign of thrombus, which is what the plan targets.

options.text: The patient sleeps through the night with the sleeves on
options.rationale: Shows the device is tolerated, which does not measure clot prevention.

options.text: Pedal pulses are strong in both feet
options.rationale: Arterial pulses do not show whether venous stasis was prevented.

options.text: The patient reports less incisional pain
options.rationale: A good outcome for analgesia, unrelated to this plan.

questions.takeaway: Judge an intervention by the complication it targets. Compression and leg exercises target venous stasis and thrombus.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Strong pulses look like a circulation win. They are arterial. The plan is about veins.

steps.detail: Prevent venous stasis and thrombus.
Sleep, arterial pulses and incision pain.
Equal, soft, nontender.

elimination.verdict: A. Calves without signs of thrombus.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old has left groin pain and cannot bear weight after a fall. The hip x-ray shows no fracture and a bone scan is scheduled. She asks to walk to the bathroom. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Walk her with a gait belt and a walker
options.rationale: Tempting because the x-ray shows no fracture and the equipment looks safe. A walker still puts weight through a hip that may be broken.

options.text: Pivot her to a commode placed beside the bed
options.rationale: A pivot is still weight bearing on the painful leg.

options.text: Keep her off the leg and offer a bedpan
options.rationale: Pain with inability to bear weight after a fall is a hidden fracture until the bone scan says otherwise.

options.text: Give the analgesic, then reassess her ability to stand
options.rationale: Pain relief does not make the bone safe to load.

questions.takeaway: A normal test does not beat a clearly abnormal patient. Protect the limb while the next test finds the answer.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Ask why a bone scan was ordered after an x-ray that showed no fracture. The provider still suspects a fracture, so the nurse acts as if there is one.

steps.detail: Groin pain, cannot bear weight, another test pending.
Three options put weight on the leg in some form.
No weight bearing and toileting in bed.

elimination.verdict: Off the leg, bedpan. An occult fracture is assumed until ruled out.

questions.stem: The nurse checks a client the day after a needle biopsy of the tibia. Which finding requires follow up?

options.text: Site pain of 3 of 10 when walking
options.rationale: Mild pain the day after a bone biopsy is expected.

options.text: A dry stain no larger than yesterday's outline
options.rationale: Old drainage that has not spread means the bleeding stopped.

options.text: A small bruise around the puncture site
options.rationale: Tempting because it is visible. A small bruise is expected after a needle through tissue.

options.text: Skin around the site that is warm and tender
options.rationale: Warmth, tenderness or redness at a biopsy site suggests infection and is reported.

questions.takeaway: After a bone or muscle biopsy, watch for active bleeding and for tenderness, redness or warmth that suggests infection.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Sort each finding as expected or unexpected for day 1. Bruising and mild pain are expected. Warmth is not.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The stain is dry and unchanged.
Small and local, an expected result of the needle.
Warm and tender is an infection cue.

elimination.verdict: Warm, tender skin. Report possible infection.

questions.stem: A client about to leave for a CT of the spine with contrast mentions breaking out in hives after a dye test years ago. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Hold transport and call the provider
options.rationale: A prior reaction to iodine contrast must reach the team before any contrast is given. They decide whether to premedicate, change the test or proceed.

options.text: Add the reaction to the chart, then send her
options.rationale: Charting is needed, but the chart alone does not stop the contrast.

options.text: Send her and alert radiology staff to watch closely
options.rationale: Tempting because radiology manages reactions. Watching for a reaction is not the same as preventing one.

options.text: Ask about shellfish allergy before sending her
options.rationale: Shellfish allergy is no longer treated as a contrast risk. The prior contrast reaction is the cue.

questions.takeaway: Before a CT with contrast, ask about any earlier contrast reaction. A yes answer pauses the test until the team decides.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Three options send her to the scanner. Ask whether the new information should change the plan before she goes.

steps.detail: Hives after dye is a prior contrast reaction.
Three options let the contrast go ahead.
The provider and radiology decide what happens next.

elimination.verdict: Hold transport and call. The decision belongs to the team before contrast is given.

questions.stem: A woman treated for a muscle disease could not climb stairs or comb her hair last month. Which finding best indicates the treatment is effective?

options.text: Creatine kinase unchanged, grip strength stronger
options.rationale: Tempting because strength improved. Her deficit was near the trunk, not in the hands, and the enzyme shows muscle is still leaking.

options.text: Less morning joint stiffness, stairs still difficult
options.rationale: Stiffness was not her problem, and the lost function has not returned.

options.text: Aldolase falling, climbs one flight unaided
options.rationale: A falling muscle enzyme means less muscle damage, and the function she lost has come back.

options.text: AST falling, still cannot rise from a chair alone
options.rationale: AST also comes from the liver, and her hip weakness is unchanged.

questions.takeaway: Damaged muscle leaks enzymes: CK-MM, LDH, AST, aldolase. Improvement shows as falling levels plus return of the lost function.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Go back to what she could not do: stairs and hair, both proximal. The best evidence is a better lab and that same function returning.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Weak hips and shoulders.
Grip and joint stiffness were never the problem.
Only one pairs a falling enzyme with returned function.

elimination.verdict: Aldolase down and one flight climbed. Lab and function agree.

questions.scenario: A 76-year-old has been on bed rest for 8 days with a plan of turning every 2 hours, range of motion, incentive spirometry, fluids and compression devices.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it shows the plan is effective or not effective.

rows.text: Breath sounds clear to both bases
rows.rationale: Lung expansion is maintained, so no atelectasis.

rows.text: Left ankle cannot be brought up to neutral
rows.rationale: A plantar flexion contracture is forming despite range of motion.

rows.text: Sacral skin intact and blanches
rows.rationale: Turning is relieving pressure.

rows.text: No bowel movement for 5 days
rows.rationale: Reduced motility has become constipation.

rows.text: Urine pale yellow and clear
rows.rationale: Good flow with no sign of stasis or infection.

rows.text: Feels lightheaded each time the head of the bed is raised
rows.rationale: Orthostatic intolerance is developing. The client needs gradual position changes and leg exercises before standing.

questions.takeaway: Immobility touches every system, so evaluate the plan one system at a time: lungs, joints, skin, bowel, urine, circulation.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: For each row ask which complication the finding belongs to and whether it happened.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Pair each finding with a system
steps.detail: Lungs, joint, skin, bowel, urine, circulation.
Contracture, constipation and lightheadedness did.

elimination.verdict: Effective, not, effective, not, effective, not.

questions.stem: A patient on bed rest keeps two pillows under the knees all day because it eases his back. Which intervention does the nurse include in the plan?

options.text: Add a third pillow under the calves
options.rationale: More flexion and more pressure behind the knees.

options.text: Schedule periods with the legs extended and range of motion
options.rationale: Knees and hips held flexed all day shorten, so the joints need time in extension and movement.

options.text: Remove the pillows and keep him flat
options.rationale: Ignores his comfort when a schedule solves both.

options.text: Raise the knee section of the bed instead
options.rationale: The same constant flexion by another method.

questions.takeaway: A joint held in one position shortens. Prevent contractures with position changes, alignment and range of motion.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Two options keep the knees bent and one takes away all comfort. The plan that alternates is the workable one.

steps.action: Remove the options that keep constant flexion
steps.detail: Extra pillow and knee gatch.
Alternating respects comfort and protects the joints.

elimination.verdict: B. Alternate extension with range of motion.

questions.stem: On day 2 after abdominal surgery, a client has diminished breath sounds at both bases, rates incisional pain 8 of 10 and refuses the incentive spirometer. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Explain how the spirometer prevents pneumonia
options.rationale: He is not refusing from lack of knowledge. He is refusing because it hurts.

options.text: Give the prescribed analgesic
options.rationale: Pain at 8 of 10 is the barrier. Once it is controlled he can sit up, splint and breathe deeply.

options.text: Coach him through ten spirometer breaths now
options.rationale: He cannot take a deep breath through this pain, so coaching fails.

options.text: Sit him upright and splint the incision
options.rationale: Tempting because both help lung expansion. They come second: at this pain level he still will not breathe deeply.

questions.takeaway: Pain blocks deep breathing and movement. Control it first so lung expansion can happen.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: The assessment is already done: pain is 8 and he refuses. Ask what is stopping him and remove that first.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pain of 8 of 10, not lack of understanding.
Neither changes the pain.
Analgesic first, then upright with splinting.

elimination.verdict: Analgesic first. Then position, splint and use the spirometer.

questions.stem: On day 9 of bed rest a 47-year-old says, "Every day is the same. I can't do anything for myself." Which intervention does the nurse include?

options.text: Have him plan the day and share in his care
options.rationale: He named loss of independence. Giving him choices and tasks he can do answers what he said.

options.text: Remind him the bed rest is temporary and he is healing
options.rationale: Brushes past the feeling he just described.

options.text: Ask the provider about an antidepressant
options.rationale: Tempting because immobility can lead to depression. One statement of frustration calls for nursing measures and continued assessment first.

options.text: Keep the television on and arrange more visitors
options.rationale: Tempting because it treats boredom. His second sentence is about control, which this leaves untouched.

questions.takeaway: Immobility has psychosocial effects: boredom, isolation, loss of independence, depression. Give back control wherever the client can take it.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Listen to both sentences. The first is boredom. The second is loss of independence, and the best option answers that one.

strategies: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings

steps.detail: "I can't do anything for myself."
It dismisses what he said.
Only one option hands him decisions and tasks.

elimination.verdict: Let him plan the day and share his care. Independence is the problem he named.

questions.stem: The nurse receives report on four patients who are on bed rest. Which patient does the nurse see first?

options.text: One with a heel that is red and blanches
options.rationale: Early pressure and needs offloading soon, but the skin is intact.

options.text: One whose casted foot is cool with new tingling
options.rationale: A true red flag and the strongest runner up. A limb is at risk, while another patient's breathing is failing.

options.text: One with sudden shortness of breath and chest pain
options.rationale: After bed rest this suggests a clot that has moved to the lung. Breathing comes before limb.

options.text: One with no bowel movement for 3 days
options.rationale: Uncomfortable and not urgent.

questions.takeaway: Two urgent patients: rank by ABCs. Sudden dyspnea in an immobile patient outranks a threatened limb, which is seen next.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides.
questions.strategy: Do not stop at the first red flag you recognize. Read all four, then rank airway and breathing above circulation to a limb.

steps.detail: Blanching heel and constipation.
Breathing before limb circulation.

elimination.verdict: C. Sudden shortness of breath.

questions.stem: After a hallway walk, a patient's heart rate rose from 76 to 98 beats per minute and returned to 78 within 3 minutes. He reports mild tiredness and no dyspnea or dizziness. Which decision about tomorrow's walk is most appropriate?

options.text: Cancel the walk and reassess in two days
options.rationale: Nothing shows intolerance, and rest costs strength.

options.text: Have him walk only to the doorway
options.rationale: Reduces activity after a good response.

options.text: Repeat the same distance each day for a week
options.rationale: Tempting as the cautious choice, but a quick recovery with no symptoms supports progressing.

options.text: Increase the distance a little and reassess
options.rationale: A modest rise with fast recovery means he tolerated it, so activity advances gradually.

questions.takeaway: Tolerance is judged by the response and the recovery. A quick return to baseline without symptoms supports progressive activity.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: The recovery time is the detail that tips it. Three minutes back to baseline is a pass.

steps.detail: Mild rise, mild tiredness, no warning symptoms.
Baseline in 3 minutes.
Small increase with reassessment.

elimination.verdict: D. Progress gradually.

questions.nursesNote: 1400: day 10 of bed rest after pelvic fracture. Turned to left side with pillows. Urinary catheter tubing lies under the right thigh. Heels rest on the mattress. Respirations 18 and unlabored. Right foot warm with palpable pulse. Reports pain at 2 of 10. Left ear folded under the head.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that require follow-up after this repositioning.

segments.text: Urinary catheter tubing lies under the right thigh
segments.rationale: Tubing under the body presses on skin and can block drainage.

segments.text: Heels rest on the mattress
segments.rationale: Heels are a pressure point and should be floated.

segments.text: Respirations 18 and unlabored
segments.rationale: The client is breathing comfortably in the new position.

segments.text: Right foot warm with palpable pulse
segments.rationale: Normal circulation.

segments.text: Reports pain at 2 of 10
segments.rationale: Mild pain, expected after a turn.

segments.text: Left ear folded under the head
segments.rationale: A folded ear on the down side is a pressure area.

questions.takeaway: After every reposition, recheck alignment, comfort, pressure areas, skin, tubes and lines, and breathing.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Walk the reassessment list. Three findings are pressure or tubing problems the turn created.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Respirations unlabored and pain mild.
Tubing, heels and ear need correcting.

questions.stem: During a mobility assessment, a patient sits at the bedside for 4 minutes but tips sideways when asked to reach across to shake the nurse's hand. Which conclusion guides the transfer plan?

options.text: He needs total assist equipment for transfers
options.rationale: He cannot reach across midline, so seated balance fails and he stays at mobility level 1, the lowest level, despite sitting upright.

options.text: He can try straightening each knee next
options.rationale: Tempting because he sat for 4 minutes, but every part of the first test must be passed before moving on.

options.text: He can stand with a walker and one staff helper
options.rationale: Standing is two levels beyond what he has shown.

options.text: He can transfer with standing equipment
options.rationale: Standing equipment is for a client who straightens both knees but cannot stand. He has not passed the first test.

questions.takeaway: Sit and shake has three parts: sit unassisted over 2 minutes, reach across midline, shake the hand. Miss one and the patient is mobility level 1, the lowest level, and needs total assist.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Sitting time alone looks like a pass. The tipping on the reach is the cue that decides it.

steps.detail: Sitting time only.
Reaching across midline.
Fail any part, stay at that level.

elimination.verdict: A. Mobility level 1, total assist.

questions.stem: A client is being admitted for same-day knee arthroscopy. Which finding does the nurse report to the surgeon before the procedure?

options.text: He asks how long to use ice afterward
options.rationale: A teaching need the nurse can meet.

options.text: The knee is warmer and redder than the other knee
options.rationale: Warmth and redness on one side suggest infection, and an infected joint rules out arthroscopy.

options.text: The knee is swollen and painful when bent to 90 degrees
options.rationale: Tempting because it sounds abnormal. Swelling and pain are why he is having the procedure, and the joint still moves.

options.text: The knee has clicked and given way since the injury
options.rationale: The complaint that led to the arthroscopy.

questions.takeaway: Arthroscopy needs a joint that can move and is not infected. Signs of infection are reported before the procedure.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Separate the findings that explain why he needs the scope from the one finding that would cancel it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Swelling, pain, clicking and giving way belong to the injury.
One knee warmer and redder than the other is new information.
Infection is a contraindication.

elimination.verdict: Warm, red knee. Report possible infection before the scope.

questions.stem: Four hours after a forearm cast, a client's fingers are pink and warm with brisk capillary refill. He now reports tingling and cannot feel light touch on the fingertips. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Elevate the arm, apply ice and recheck in 45 minutes
options.rationale: Tempting because elevation and ice are right for swelling. New loss of sensation is a change in the nerve check and should not wait 45 minutes.

options.text: Document intact circulation and continue hourly checks
options.rationale: Tempting because color, warmth and refill are normal. Circulation is only half of the check, and sensation has changed.

options.text: Give the as-needed analgesic and reassess comfort
options.rationale: Treats discomfort. It can mask a finding that is getting worse.

options.text: Notify the provider of the change in sensation now
options.rationale: The deciding detail is new tingling and lost light touch. Nerve findings change before color and pulses do, so a normal looking hand does not clear him.

questions.takeaway: A neurovascular check has two halves. Normal color, warmth and refill do not cancel a new change in sensation or movement.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The stem leads with reassuring findings. Check every part of the neurovascular check before deciding the limb is fine.

steps.detail: Color, temperature, refill, sensation, movement, pain.
Sensation.
Elevation helps swelling. A new deficit is reported.

elimination.verdict: Notify the provider now.

questions.stem: After 5 days of bed rest a client dangles at the bedside. Blood pressure falls from 126/78 to 108/66 and he feels slightly lightheaded. He is alert and eager to walk. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Keep him sitting, have him pump his ankles, then recheck
options.rationale: The deciding details are that he is alert, sitting and only slightly lightheaded. Gradual progression continues at the step he has not yet tolerated.

options.text: Return him to supine and defer walking until tomorrow
options.rationale: Tempting as the safest choice. More bed rest worsens the orthostatic problem, and his symptoms do not require lying flat.

options.text: Stand him with a gait belt and two staff members
options.rationale: Tempting because help is present and he is eager. Dizziness while sitting means he is not ready for the next step.

options.text: Offer fluids and try standing after he drinks
options.rationale: Fluids help prevent orthostatic drops. Drinking does not replace rechecking his pressure and symptoms first.

questions.takeaway: Sit, dangle, then stand. If a step is not tolerated, stay at that step and recheck. Do not push on and do not give up the day.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Safety says stop. Mobility says keep going. Look for the option that holds him where he is until the numbers say move.

steps.detail: Orthostatic drop after bed rest.
Dizzy while sitting means no standing yet.
Bed rest is the cause.

elimination.verdict: Keep him sitting, pump the ankles and recheck.

questions.stem: An unconscious client has had passive range of motion to the hips, knees and arms for 2 weeks. Those joints move fully. Both feet rest pointed down and cannot be brought to neutral. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Continue the current plan because joint motion is maintained
options.rationale: Tempting because most joints look good. The ankles show the plan left a joint out.

options.text: Increase passive range of motion to build leg strength
options.rationale: Tempting to do more of what works. Passive movement keeps joints flexible and does not build strength, and it misses the ankle.

options.text: Add ankle range of motion and neutral alignment supports
options.rationale: The deciding detail is feet fixed in plantar flexion. Foot drop is developing, so the ankle needs range of motion, neutral positioning and a supportive device.

options.text: Request physical therapy for isometric leg exercises
options.rationale: Therapy input is reasonable. Isometric exercise needs a client who can contract muscles on request.

questions.takeaway: Judge a mobility plan by every joint. Feet that rest pointed down are an early plantar flexion contracture and need neutral alignment, range of motion and support.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Most of the stem is good news. The evaluation turns on the one joint that was not listed in the plan.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Hips, knees and arms treated. Ankles not.
Foot drop.

steps.action: Check each fix against the client
steps.detail: The client is unconscious, so only passive care and positioning apply.

elimination.verdict: Add ankle range of motion and neutral supports.

questions.stem: A nurse and an assistive personnel are planning morning care. Which activity does the nurse keep rather than delegate?

options.text: Walking a client who walked steadily in the hall twice yesterday
options.rationale: Routine and stable. The client's response is already known, so it can be delegated.

options.text: Passive range of motion for a stable unconscious client
options.rationale: Tempting to keep because the client cannot report pain. It is a routine task in an established plan with a predictable outcome.

options.text: Turning a client whose reddened sacrum was assessed earlier
options.rationale: Tempting because skin is a concern. The nurse has already assessed, and turning on schedule is a task.

options.text: First dangle and stand after a week of bed rest
options.rationale: The deciding detail is first time up. The response is unknown, so the nurse assesses tolerance and blood pressure before anyone else takes over.

questions.takeaway: Delegate routine tasks with predictable outcomes. The first time out of bed after bed rest is an assessment, and assessment stays with the nurse.
questions.coverage: Not in Lecture PPT. Covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: For each option ask one thing: is the client's response already known? Tasks delegate. Unknown responses do not.

steps.detail: Three repeat a known routine.
No one has seen this client upright yet.
Unconscious and reddened skin sound risky, but both are stable and assessed.

elimination.verdict: The first dangle and stand after bed rest.

questions.stem: On day 6 of bed rest a client's left calf is painless, warm and 2 cm larger than the right. Compression sleeves are off for a bath and a hallway walk is due. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Leave the sleeves off, cancel the walk, notify the provider
options.rationale: The deciding detail is one calf warmer and larger than the other. Prevention steps stop once a clot is suspected, because squeezing or walking could dislodge it.

options.text: Reapply the sleeves and walk him to improve blood flow
options.rationale: Tempting because both are the right way to prevent clots. This is now a possible actual clot, not a risk.

options.text: Elevate the leg, apply warmth and recheck in an hour
options.rationale: Sounds like comfort care for swelling. It delays reporting, and no treatment is started without the provider.

options.text: Measure both calves again at the end of the shift
options.rationale: Tempting because he has no pain. A painless clot is still a clot, and the difference is already measured.

questions.takeaway: Compression and walking prevent clots. A warm, swollen calf on bed rest is treated as an actual clot: stop, keep him resting and report.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides.
questions.strategy: Decide first whether this is a risk or an actual problem. Prevention rules apply only to the risk.

steps.detail: One warm, larger calf after bed rest.
Actual problem beats prevention routine.
No pain does not rule it out.

elimination.verdict: Leave the sleeves off, cancel the walk and notify the provider.

questions.stem: An 86-year-old resident walked to every meal yesterday. This morning she cannot get herself out of bed. She denies pain and has not fallen. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Check vital signs and mental status
options.rationale: A sudden loss of mobility in an older adult is often the first sign of a new illness. Find out what changed before deciding how to move her.

options.text: Request a physical therapy evaluation
options.rationale: Reasonable for a gradual decline. This change happened overnight, which points to illness, and a referral delays finding it.

options.text: Use a lift to bring her to breakfast
options.rationale: Solves the transfer and skips the question of why she suddenly needs one.

options.text: Start range of motion in bed
options.rationale: Protects her joints if she stays in bed. It treats the result of the change and not its cause.

questions.takeaway: Mobility works like a vital sign in older adults. A sudden loss means look for a new illness first.
questions.coverage: Not in Lecture PPT or Reading.
questions.strategy: The cue is the speed of the change. Yesterday to today is acute, and acute changes get assessed before they get managed.

steps.detail: Independent yesterday, unable today.
Three manage immobility. One asks why it happened.
Cause comes before management.

elimination.verdict: Assess her. The lost mobility is the symptom.

questions.stem: A 53-year-old struggles to rise from a chair and to lift her arms to a shelf. Hand grip, foot strength and sensation are normal. Which problem do these findings most suggest?

options.text: A nerve problem in the hands and feet
options.rationale: Nerve problems show up far from the trunk, in the hands and feet, and bring numbness. Her hands, feet and sensation are normal.

options.text: Loss of position sense
options.rationale: That causes unsteadiness and falls with normal strength. Her problem is weakness, and only near the trunk.

options.text: A muscle problem near the trunk
options.rationale: Weakness at the hips and shoulders with normal hands, feet and sensation is the muscle pattern. Expect muscle enzymes such as CK and aldolase to be checked.

options.text: Stiff joints from aging
options.rationale: Aging stiffens joints gradually and limits range. It does not pick out hip and shoulder strength while sparing grip.

questions.takeaway: Weakness near the trunk points to muscle. Weakness in the hands and feet with numbness points to nerve.
questions.coverage: Not in Lecture PPT. Covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Map where the weakness is. Hips and shoulders weak, hands and feet fine, feeling intact: the pattern answers the question.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Chair and shelf are hip and shoulder tasks.
Normal sensation and grip rule out the nerve options.
Aging limits range; it does not cause selective weakness.

elimination.verdict: Muscle problem near the trunk.

questions.stem: A woman lay on her kitchen floor for two days before she was found. Her thigh muscles are swollen and tender, and x-rays show no fracture. Which laboratory result best fits her muscle injury?

options.text: Alkaline phosphatase above the normal range
options.rationale: Tempting when a bone injury is suspected. Alkaline phosphatase rises with bone activity, and her x-rays show no fracture.

options.text: Serum calcium below the normal range
options.rationale: Low calcium points toward bone loss or poor intake. It does not show that muscle was crushed.

options.text: AST elevated with a normal CK MM
options.rationale: AST leaks from muscle, but it is also a liver enzyme. With a normal CK MM it does not point to muscle.

options.text: CK MM far above the normal range
options.rationale: CK MM is the skeletal muscle enzyme. Two days of pressure on the thighs crushes muscle and the enzyme leaks into the blood.

questions.takeaway: Muscle enzymes leak from damaged muscle. After a long lie on the floor, expect a very high CK MM, and read AST only alongside it.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Name the tissue that was hurt before reading the labs. The x-ray took bone out of the picture, so look for the muscle enzyme.

steps.detail: Swollen, tender thighs with no fracture means muscle.
Alkaline phosphatase and calcium both answer a bone question.
AST is shared with the liver. CK MM belongs to skeletal muscle.

elimination.verdict: The very high CK MM.

questions.stem: Six hours after knee arthroscopy, a client has kept the leg iced and elevated. Which finding best shows that recovery is on track?

options.text: Foot warm, pulse equal to the other foot, toes move
options.rationale: Neurovascular status is the priority after arthroscopy. A warm foot with an equal pulse and moving toes shows blood flow and nerves are intact.

options.text: Pain rated 2 of 10 an hour after the analgesic
options.rationale: Good comfort, and it mostly shows the drug worked. It says nothing about circulation below the knee.

options.text: Dressing dry with no visible drainage
options.rationale: A good sign for bleeding. It does not show what is happening to the foot.

options.text: Client says the knee feels less tight
options.rationale: Encouraging, and subjective. The priority check is objective and done on the limb below the joint.

questions.takeaway: After arthroscopy, the outcome that matters most is an intact neurovascular check, compared with the other leg.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: All four are good news. Ask which one answers the priority question for a procedure on a limb: is the limb below it getting blood and nerve supply?

steps.action: Name the priority after this procedure
steps.detail: Neurovascular checks.
Pain, dressing and tightness are comfort and wound findings.
Warmth, pulse and movement, compared with the other side.

elimination.verdict: The warm foot with an equal pulse and moving toes.

questions.stem: Last week a patient could only slide her weak leg sideways on the bed. Today she lifts it off the bed, and it drops when the nurse pushes lightly. How does the nurse interpret this?

options.text: Strength is unchanged; revise the plan
options.rationale: Sliding without lifting is movement with gravity removed. Lifting off the bed is a step higher, so there is a change.

options.text: Strength is worse; notify the provider
options.rationale: The leg dropping with a push sounds like failure. Last week she could not lift it at all.

options.text: Strength is full; stop the exercises
options.rationale: Full strength holds against the nurse's full push. Hers gives way to a light one.

options.text: Strength is better; continue the plan
options.rationale: She moved from movement without gravity to movement against gravity. The plan is working and is not finished.

questions.takeaway: Grade strength by what the limb can overcome: nothing, gravity removed, gravity, some resistance, full resistance. Moving up a step is improvement.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Do not let "it drops" decide the item. Compare today with last week, not today with normal.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Slides only: movement without gravity.
Lifts but cannot resist: movement against gravity.
One step up, two steps short of full.

elimination.verdict: Improved, so continue the plan.

questions.stem: After 6 days of bed rest with extra fluids and leg exercises, a 51-year-old sits at the bedside for the first time. Which finding shows the plan prevented orthostatic hypotension?

options.text: He says he feels strong and ready to walk
options.rationale: Motivation is welcome and it is not a measurement. Patients often feel fine until they stand.

options.text: Blood pressure 122/74 lying, 116/72 sitting, no dizziness
options.rationale: Pressure held within a few points with the position change and he has no symptoms. That is the outcome the plan was aimed at.

options.text: Heart rate rises from 70 to 106 on sitting
options.rationale: A jump that large means the heart is working hard to hold the pressure up. The plan has not fully worked.

options.text: Both calves are soft, equal and nontender
options.rationale: Shows that the leg exercises helped prevent a clot. It does not test the response to sitting up.

questions.takeaway: Judge orthostatic prevention by the pressure and symptoms during the position change, not by how the patient feels beforehand.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Match the finding to the complication named in the stem. A good calf exam is a real outcome for a different complication.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Stable pressure and no dizziness on rising.
Feeling ready is not evidence.
Calves answer the clot question.
A 36 beat rise is compensation.

elimination.verdict: The stable sitting pressure with no dizziness.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old with a history of breast cancer and new rib pain received the isotope for a bone scan at 0900. The scan is at 1400. Which actions does the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Confirm no contrast or isotope test is scheduled before 1400
options.rationale: No other contrast or isotope study is done during the 4 to 6 hour wait.

options.text: Tell her she will lie still for 30 to 60 minutes
options.rationale: Preparing her for the position helps her tolerate the scan.

options.text: Treat her pain before she goes to the scan
options.rationale: She cannot hold still for up to an hour if the rib pain is not treated.

options.text: Have her empty her bladder just before the scan
options.rationale: The tracer leaves through the urine. A full bladder hides the pelvic bones and makes an hour of lying still harder.

options.text: Collect her urine in a shielded container
options.rationale: No special precautions are needed for urine or stool after the tracer.

options.text: Keep her without food or fluids until the scan
options.rationale: The scan needs no fasting, and fluids help clear the tracer afterward.

questions.takeaway: The bone scan wait is 4 to 6 hours with no competing contrast or isotope test. Prepare the patient to lie still, control pain, and have her void before the scan.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Judge each option alone. The two wrong ones are precautions borrowed from other tests, which is why they sound safe.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The wait, the stillness.
Pain control and an empty bladder so she can lie still.
Shielded urine and fasting are not part of this test.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C and D.

questions.stem: The nurse uses the bedside mobility assessment to decide how to move a 75-year-old on day 2 after a stroke. Place the nurse's actions in order.

options.text: Have him sit unsupported and reach across to shake the nurse's hand
options.rationale: First. Trunk control and balance come before anything is asked of the legs.

options.text: Have him straighten each knee and point the toes while seated
options.rationale: Second. Shows whether the legs are strong enough to consider standing.

options.text: Confirm he is not confused and can follow directions
options.rationale: Third. Cognition is checked before anyone is asked to stand.

options.text: Have him lift his buttocks off the bed for a count of 5
options.rationale: Fourth. The stand test, done only after the first two steps and the cognition check.

options.text: Have him march in place and step one foot forward and back
options.rationale: Last. Stepping is tested only after he can stand.

questions.takeaway: Sit and shake, stretch and point, check cognition, stand, then step. The first step he fails sets the level of help.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Build from the trunk outward and from sitting to moving. The step most often dropped is the cognition check just before standing.

steps.action: Start with the least demanding test
steps.detail: Sitting balance.

steps.action: Test the legs while still seated
steps.detail: Knee extension.
Before the first test that could drop him.
Stand, then step.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, E.

questions.scenario: Five clients are seen in an urgent care clinic. The nurse anticipates the imaging each will have next.
questions.stem: For each client, select the test the nurse anticipates.

rows.text: A 71-year-old fell on an outstretched hand an hour ago and the wrist looks bent
rows.rationale: A suspected break starts with a plain film to show the fracture and its alignment.

rows.text: A 36-year-old whose x-ray shows the heel bone in several pieces, with surgery planned
rows.rationale: The x-ray already found the break. CT gives the detailed bone images a complex fracture needs before repair.

rows.text: A 48-year-old with a soft, swollen lump behind the knee that may hold fluid
rows.rationale: Ultrasound shows fluid collections, with no radiation and no preparation.

rows.text: A 67-year-old woman who avoids dairy and is 4 cm shorter than five years ago, with no pain
rows.rationale: Height loss with low calcium intake after menopause points to low bone density, which DEXA measures.

rows.text: A 23-year-old whose shoulder looks squared off and out of place after a tackle
rows.rationale: A dislocation is a bone and alignment question, so the first test is a plain film.

questions.takeaway: Ask what needs to be seen. Break or alignment: x-ray. Complex break: CT. Fluid: ultrasound. Bone density: DEXA.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Most injuries start with a plain x-ray. Move past it only when the x-ray is already done or the question is not about a break.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A bent wrist and a displaced shoulder have had no imaging yet.
The heel fracture is known and needs more bone detail.
A fluid lump goes to ultrasound and silent height loss goes to DEXA.

elimination.verdict: X-ray, CT, ultrasound, DEXA, x-ray.

questions.stem: A client with severe ARDS was placed prone 2 hours ago. Which finding best shows the position is working?

options.text: He rests without pulling at his lines
options.rationale: Comfort matters after any reposition. It does not show that the lungs are exchanging gas better.

options.text: Skin over the forehead and chest is intact
options.rationale: A needed check in the prone position, and it shows safety, not benefit.

options.text: Oxygen saturation rose from 86% to 93%
options.rationale: Prone positioning is used in severe ARDS to improve oxygenation, so a rising saturation is the outcome that counts.

options.text: Respirations slowed from 30 to 26
options.rationale: A small drop in rate is encouraging but can also mean tiring. The saturation measures the goal directly.

questions.takeaway: Prone positioning is first line for critically ill patients with severe ARDS. Judge it by oxygenation.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two options are safety checks and two are breathing outcomes. Pick the one that measures the reason the position was chosen.

steps.detail: To improve oxygenation in severe ARDS.
Skin and comfort are monitored. They are not the goal.
Saturation measures oxygenation. Rate is indirect.

elimination.verdict: Saturation up from 86% to 93%.

questions.stem: A steady 69-year-old on day 3 after pneumonia passed every step of the bedside mobility test. She refuses to walk, saying, "I fell last year and I'm scared." Which plan is best?

options.text: Walk a short way with a gait belt, the nurse beside her
options.rationale: Her test supports walking with standby help. A belt, a short distance and a nurse at her side answer the fear and keep her moving.

options.text: Let her rest today and offer the walk tomorrow
options.rationale: Respects her wish, and it is tempting. Each day in bed costs strength and makes the next walk more frightening.

options.text: Request a physical therapy evaluation before walking
options.rationale: Therapy helps with gait problems. She already passed the walking step, so waiting only delays her.

options.text: Explain that staying in bed leads to blood clots
options.rationale: True, and facts alone do not make her feel safe on her feet.

questions.takeaway: Fear of falling is a behavior that limits activity. Answer it with support and a small first step, not with more bed rest.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Her body is ready and her confidence is not. Pick the option that gets her up and deals with the fear at once.

strategies: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings

steps.detail: She passed the walking step, so walking is safe with standby help.
Resting and waiting for therapy both keep her in bed.
Warning her about clots ignores what she said.

elimination.verdict: Short walk, gait belt, nurse beside her.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman who walks daily, smokes and has three glasses of wine most nights was taught how to protect her bones. Which statement shows the teaching was effective?

options.text: "I'll take extra calcium so I can skip the vitamin D."
options.rationale: Vitamin D is what lets the gut absorb the calcium. One does not replace the other.

options.text: "I'll swap my walks for swimming to spare my joints."
options.rationale: Swimming is good exercise, and the water carries her weight, so it does not load the bones. She would give up the one habit that protects them.

options.text: "I'll rest more until my bones have gotten stronger."
options.rationale: Bone gets stronger with use. Less activity speeds bone loss.

options.text: "I'll cut back on the wine and work on quitting smoking."
options.rationale: Tobacco and heavy alcohol both harm bone. She kept her walking and changed the two risks in her own history.

questions.takeaway: Bone health: weight-bearing exercise, calcium with vitamin D, good nutrition, no tobacco, limited alcohol.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Match the answers to her history. Her walking already protects her bones; the smoking and the wine do not.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Tobacco and nightly alcohol. Her daily walks are a strength.
Skipping vitamin D, giving up the walks and resting all make her bones worse off.

steps.action: Pick the one that changes both risks
steps.detail: Less wine and no tobacco.

elimination.verdict: Cut back on the wine and work on quitting smoking.

questions.stem: A deconditioned 60-year-old has walked the hall and lifted light hand weights daily for 3 weeks. Which finding best shows this exercise plan met its purpose?

options.text: He dresses and walks to the dining room unaided
options.rationale: Exercise that moves the joints builds strength for real tasks. Doing those tasks alone is the outcome.

options.text: He tightens each thigh firmly and holds it
options.rationale: That shows he can do an exercise with no joint movement. It was not his plan, and it does not show function.

options.text: His joints move fully when the nurse moves them
options.rationale: Full passive range shows flexible joints. It says nothing about his strength.

options.text: His resting pulse is the same as 3 weeks ago
options.rationale: A resting pulse that has not changed does not show gain or loss of function.

questions.takeaway: Walking and lifting move the joints and build functional strength. Evaluate them by what the patient can now do.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Ask what moving exercise is for: everyday tasks. Then find the option that describes an everyday task.

steps.detail: Strength for walking and self care.

steps.action: Cut the findings about other exercise types
steps.detail: Holding a thigh contraction and passive range measure different things.
An unchanged pulse proves nothing.

elimination.verdict: Dresses and walks to meals without help.

questions.stem: The nurse takes a history from an 84-year-old woman admitted after a fall. Which findings raise her risk for a musculoskeletal problem and need follow-up? Select all that apply.

options.text: She broke her wrist 40 years ago
options.rationale: Ask about every past injury, however old. An old fracture can leave weakness or deformity and hints at fragile bone.

options.text: She has avoided milk products all her life because they upset her stomach
options.rationale: Lactose intolerance often means a low calcium intake over many years.

options.text: She is 84 years old
options.rationale: Bone density, muscle mass and joint flexibility all fall with age.

options.text: She walks to the mailbox and back every day
options.rationale: Regular weight-bearing activity protects bone and muscle.

options.text: She was told years ago that she has osteoporosis
options.rationale: Porous bone breaks easily, and she has just fallen.

options.text: She takes vitamin D with her breakfast
options.rationale: Vitamin D helps her absorb calcium. It lowers the risk.

questions.takeaway: In the history, old injuries, low calcium intake, advanced age and known osteoporosis all raise musculoskeletal risk.
questions.coverage: Not in Lecture PPT. Covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Judge each line alone: does it weaken bone or muscle, or protect them? An injury counts no matter how long ago it happened.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Daily walking and vitamin D.
Time does not remove it from the history.

steps.action: Keep the calcium and bone clues
steps.detail: No dairy, age 84 and osteoporosis.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, E.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old's wrist was mildly swollen and bruised at 1400 after a fall. At 1500, which change does the nurse report first?

options.text: The bruise has darkened from red to purple
options.rationale: Bruises darken as the blood under the skin changes. This is expected.

options.text: She rates the ache 4 of 10, the same as before
options.rationale: Unchanged moderate pain is treated. It is not a new warning.

options.text: Her fingers feel stiff, though she can move them all
options.rationale: Stiffness with full movement is common beside a swollen joint.

options.text: Swelling now extends from the hand to mid forearm
options.rationale: Rapid swelling is a red flag. It can mean bleeding or a fracture and can press on vessels and nerves.

questions.takeaway: Red flags after a limb injury: rapid swelling, new deformity, severe pain, new numbness, weak pulses, a cool or pale limb, loss of movement.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Compare each finding with the hour before. Only one has changed quickly and in a way that threatens the limb.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Look for change over the hour
steps.detail: Pain is the same and movement is kept.
Bruise color shifts on its own.
Swelling that spreads in one hour.

elimination.verdict: Report the rapidly spreading swelling.

questions.stem: On day 10 of bed rest a 70-year-old has a temperature of 38.4 C and new flank pain. Urine is cloudy and foul. Lungs are clear and both calves are soft. Which complication do these findings suggest?

options.text: Atelectasis from shallow breathing
options.rationale: A fever fits. Clear lungs and urine findings point elsewhere.

options.text: A clot in a deep leg vein
options.rationale: That shows as a warm, swollen calf. Both calves are soft.

options.text: Low fluid intake with concentrated urine
options.rationale: Concentrated urine is dark and strong. It is not cloudy and does not bring fever or flank pain.

options.text: Urinary infection from urine that pools
options.rationale: Lying flat lets urine sit in the kidneys and bladder. Cloudy foul urine, fever and flank pain fit infection or a stone.

questions.takeaway: Immobility causes urinary stasis, then infection and stones: cloudy, foul urine and flank pain. A new finding on bed rest is a complication until proven otherwise.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Use the normal findings to rule systems out. Clear lungs and soft calves leave the urinary tract.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Breath sounds are clear.
Calves are soft.
Fever and flank pain mean infection, not just concentration.

elimination.verdict: Urinary infection from stasis.

questions.stem: The nurse receives report on four clients on an orthopedic unit. Which client does the nurse see first?

options.text: One in an ankle splint who can no longer move her toes
options.rationale: Sudden loss of movement below an injury is a red flag. Nerve or blood supply may be failing, and this change is new.

options.text: One reporting knee pain of 4 of 10 four hours after arthroscopy
options.rationale: Mild to moderate pain is expected after arthroscopy and is managed with the prescribed analgesic.

options.text: One with an aching biopsy site and a small dry stain on the dressing
options.rationale: A dry stain and an ache are expected after a bone biopsy. Bleeding that spreads or warmth and redness would change this.

options.text: One aged 88 with stiff knees who needs extra time to stand
options.rationale: Stiff joints and slowed movement are long-standing changes of aging. This client needs patience and can wait.

questions.takeaway: Sudden loss of movement below an injury is a red flag. New and unexpected comes before expected and chronic.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Sort each client as expected or unexpected for the situation. Only one finding is a new loss of function.

steps.detail: Moderate pain after arthroscopy and a dry stain after biopsy are expected.
Stiff knees at 88 are not new.
Toes that can no longer move.

elimination.verdict: The client who can no longer move her toes.

questions.stem: After a long leg cast is applied, the nurse cannot feel the pedal pulse on that foot. The toes are pink and warm. Which step does the nurse take next?

options.text: Record the pulse as absent and recheck in 1 hour
options.rationale: The timing is off. A pulse that cannot be felt is checked by Doppler now, and waiting an hour delays finding a real loss of flow.

options.text: Palpate the femoral pulse in place of the pedal pulse
options.rationale: The site is off. Pulses are checked below the level of the injury.

options.text: Use a Doppler over the pedal pulse of that foot
options.rationale: When a pulse is not palpable, the nurse uses a Doppler to find it below the injury.

options.text: Accept the pink, warm toes as proof the pulse is present
options.rationale: Color and temperature are separate parts of the check and do not replace the pulse.

questions.takeaway: If a pulse below an injury or cast cannot be felt, use a Doppler to find it. Then compare with the other limb.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The stem says one part of the check is missing. Choose the option that finds that part, at that site, now.

steps.detail: The pedal pulse.
Below the cast, so the femoral pulse is out.
Doppler.

elimination.verdict: Doppler over the pedal pulse.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman with low bone density walks daily and avoids dairy because of lactose intolerance. Which statement shows that teaching about her bones was effective?

options.text: "I'll take calcium with vitamin D since I skip milk."
options.rationale: Lactose intolerance commonly leaves calcium intake too low. Calcium with vitamin D, which helps absorb it, slows bone loss.

options.text: "My daily walks are enough, so what I eat matters less."
options.rationale: Walking is weight bearing and worth keeping. Bone also needs the calcium she is not getting from food.

options.text: "I'll stop the walks so I don't risk a fracture."
options.rationale: Weight-bearing exercise slows bone loss. Stopping it speeds the loss.

options.text: "If my blood calcium is normal, I don't need more."
options.rationale: Blood calcium is kept steady by drawing calcium out of bone, so a normal level does not show that intake is adequate.

questions.takeaway: Bone health needs both weight-bearing activity and enough calcium and vitamin D. Lactose intolerance is a cue that calcium intake may be low.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two cues are in the stem: she already walks, and she avoids dairy. The right statement fixes the gap that is left.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Activity is covered. Calcium is not.

steps.action: Drop the statements that give something up
steps.detail: Stopping walks or ignoring diet loses one of the two.
Blood calcium is held steady at the expense of bone.

elimination.verdict: Calcium with vitamin D.

questions.stem: A client's bone scan shows one area of increased activity in the femur. He asks, "So it's cancer?" Which response does the nurse give?

options.text: "A bone scan cannot show cancer, so that is unlikely."
options.rationale: False reassurance. A bone scan can detect tumors.

options.text: "Increased activity on the scan usually means a tumor."
options.rationale: This goes past what the scan shows. A tumor is only one cause of increased bone activity.

options.text: "Active bone can mean a hidden break, an infection or a tumor."
options.rationale: A bone scan shows areas of increased bone activity. Hidden fractures, infection and tumors all cause it, so the result alone does not name the cause.

options.text: "Try not to worry until your provider reviews it."
options.rationale: Tempting because the provider gives the diagnosis. It brushes off his question, which the nurse can answer truthfully.

questions.takeaway: A bone scan shows where bone is more active. Occult fracture, infection and tumor can all look that way, so the finding needs more workup before it has a name.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options answer yes or no for certain. Look for the response that says what the test can and cannot tell him.

strategies: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings

steps.detail: Telling him not to worry leaves the question unanswered.
Cannot show cancer and usually a tumor are both wrong.
Increased activity has several causes.

elimination.verdict: Active bone can mean a hidden break, an infection or a tumor.

questions.stem: Assistive personnel report on a client whose left forearm was splinted 2 hours ago. Which report does the nurse act on first?

options.text: He rates the arm pain 3 of 10 when he moves it
options.rationale: Mild pain with movement is expected after a new injury. Severe pain would be a red flag.

options.text: His left hand is as puffy as at the last check
options.rationale: Tempting because swelling matters under a splint. It is unchanged, and the red flag is swelling that increases rapidly.

options.text: His left fingers look paler than the right and feel cool
options.rationale: A pale, cool extremity that differs from the other side is a red flag for poor blood flow. The nurse goes to assess the hand now.

options.text: He asks for another pillow under the arm
options.rationale: A comfort request that can be met after the hand is checked.

questions.takeaway: A cool, pale extremity compared with the other side is a red flag. When assistive personnel report one, the nurse does the neurovascular check right away.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Sort each report as expected, unchanged or new. Then look for the red flag.

steps.detail: Mild pain with movement.
Swelling that is the same as before.
Fingers paler and cooler than the other hand.

elimination.verdict: The pale, cool fingers.

questions.stem: The nurse assesses an 83-year-old admitted for elective eye surgery. She reports no injury. Which finding needs follow up instead of being accepted as aging?

options.text: Both knees and both hips bend a little less than the full range
options.rationale: Range of motion decreases with age, and here it is the same on both sides.

options.text: Calf muscles look smaller on both legs
options.rationale: Muscle tissue atrophies with age. Equal on both sides fits aging.

options.text: Right leg resists a firm push; left drops with a light push
options.rationale: Aging weakens both sides about equally. One leg at full strength and the other only able to move against gravity is a one-sided loss that needs a cause.

options.text: She takes extra time to rise and to walk
options.rationale: Movement slows with age. The nurse does not rush her.

questions.takeaway: Aging changes are gradual and about equal on both sides. A clear difference in strength between two limbs is not aging until proven otherwise.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Compare sides. Three findings are symmetric or general. One describes two legs that do not match.

steps.detail: Less range of motion, muscle atrophy, slowed movement.

steps.action: Match three options to the list
steps.detail: Knees, calves and slow movement all fit, on both sides.
Full strength on the right, movement against gravity only on the left.

elimination.verdict: The leg strength that differs between sides.

questions.stem: After knee arthroscopy, a new nurse reports the client's foot is pink and warm with a strong pulse and brisk refill, the same as the other foot. Which direction does the charge nurse give?

options.text: Chart the check as normal and repeat it in an hour
options.rationale: Tempting because every finding so far is normal. The check is not finished, so it cannot be charted as normal.

options.text: Confirm the pulse with a Doppler
options.rationale: A Doppler is for a pulse that cannot be felt. This one is strong.

options.text: Raise the leg higher and look at the color again
options.rationale: Color is already normal and equal to the other foot. This repeats what is known.

options.text: Ask if he can feel touch and move his toes
options.rationale: Color, temperature, refill and pulse are done and compared. Sensation, movement and pain are still missing from the check.

questions.takeaway: A neurovascular check covers color, temperature, capillary refill, pulses, sensation, movement and pain, compared with the other side. Good circulation does not finish it.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: List what the report covers, then what it leaves out. The right direction fills the gap.

steps.detail: Color, temperature, pulse, refill, compared with the other foot.
Doppler and another look at color recheck circulation.
Sensation and movement.

elimination.verdict: Ask if he can feel touch and move his toes.

questions.stem: Two hours after an open bone biopsy of the femur, the bright red stain on a client's dressing has doubled in 15 minutes. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Apply firm pressure over the dressing
options.rationale: Bleeding is the complication to watch for after a bone biopsy. A bright red stain that doubles in 15 minutes is active bleeding, and pressure controls it while help is called.

options.text: Outline the stain and recheck it in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Right for a small stain that is not changing. This one has already shown its rate, so waiting only lets the client lose more blood.

options.text: Give the prescribed mild analgesic
options.rationale: Analgesics treat the expected ache. They do nothing for bleeding.

options.text: Remove the dressing to inspect the incision
options.rationale: Lifting the dressing releases what pressure there is on a site that is bleeding.

questions.takeaway: After a bone or muscle biopsy, watch for bleeding and for signs of infection. Active bleeding is treated with direct pressure first.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The stem gives the trend, so the assessment is done. Choose the action that stops the bleeding over the one that keeps watching it.

steps.detail: Bright red and doubled in 15 minutes means active bleeding.
Outlining and rechecking fits a stable stain.
Pressure controls bleeding. Analgesia and inspection do not.

elimination.verdict: Firm pressure over the dressing.

questions.stem: A 73-year-old woman with osteoporosis has walked daily and taken calcium and vitamin D for a year. Which finding best shows the plan is working?

options.text: Her serum calcium is 9.4 mg/dL
options.rationale: Within range, but the blood level is held steady by hormones and does not measure how much mineral is in the bone.

options.text: Her bone density scan matches last year's
options.rationale: A DEXA scan measures bone mineral density. No further loss over a year is the direct evidence that bone is being protected.

options.text: She reports no back pain this year
options.rationale: Good news, but bone loss is silent until a fracture, so comfort does not show density.

options.text: She walks farther than she did one year ago
options.rationale: This shows better endurance. It does not show what is happening in the bone.

questions.takeaway: DEXA measures bone mineral density, so it is the test that shows whether osteoporosis treatment is holding bone loss.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Ask what each finding measures. Only one measures the bone itself.

steps.detail: Stop further loss of bone density.
Blood calcium, comfort and endurance do not measure density.
The bone density scan.

elimination.verdict: The unchanged bone density scan.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old with stiff, arthritic hands lives alone and goes home tomorrow. Which assessment best shows the nurse whether she can manage her own care?

options.text: Grade her grip strength in both hands
options.rationale: Tempting because strength matters. A grade does not show whether the tasks she must do alone get done.

options.text: Note how far each finger joint bends
options.rationale: Joint movement describes the hand. It does not show what she can do with it.

options.text: Inspect both hands for swelling and deformity
options.rationale: Inspection describes how the hands look, not how they work.

options.text: Watch her button a shirt and open a pill bottle
options.rationale: A functional assessment shows directly whether she can carry out the tasks of daily care with her hands.

questions.takeaway: Musculoskeletal assessment focuses on function. To learn whether a client can manage, watch her do the task.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The question asks about managing care, not about the hands. Choose the assessment that watches her do it.

steps.detail: Can she care for herself alone?
Strength, joint movement and appearance describe the hands.

steps.action: Find the one that tests function
steps.detail: Buttoning and opening a bottle.

elimination.verdict: Watch her button a shirt and open a pill bottle.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old is going home after arthroscopic repair of a knee ligament. Which statement shows the client needs more teaching?

options.text: "I'll wait for the surgeon's word before I start the bending exercises."
options.rationale: Correct. Range of motion exercises may not be allowed right after arthroscopic surgery.

options.text: "If my calf gets sore and swollen, I'll mention it next week."
options.rationale: A sore, swollen calf suggests thrombophlebitis, one of the complications the client reports to the provider at once.

options.text: "I'll keep ice on the knee until this time tomorrow."
options.rationale: Correct. Ice is used for about 24 hours.

options.text: "I'll keep the leg up on pillows tonight."
options.rationale: Correct. The limb is elevated for 12 to 24 hours.

questions.takeaway: After arthroscopy, swelling, severe joint or limb pain, signs of a clot and signs of infection are reported right away. They do not wait for the 1 week visit.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: You are looking for the unsafe statement. Three describe routine home care. One delays reporting a complication.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the statement that is wrong.
Ice for a day, elevation overnight and waiting for permission to exercise are all correct.
A swollen, sore calf held for a week.

elimination.verdict: Waiting a week to report the swollen calf.

questions.stem: An 85-year-old resident walks steadily to the dining room but takes twice as long as she did two years ago. Assistive personnel suggest a wheelchair to save time. Which plan does the nurse make?

options.text: Use the wheelchair for meals and walk her at other times
options.rationale: Tempting as a compromise. It removes the walks she already does safely every day, and regular activity is what keeps her able to walk.

options.text: Request a physical therapy evaluation of her slow gait
options.rationale: Tempting because a change in gait can need a referral. Her gait is steady and the slowing came over years, which fits aging, so there is nothing new to evaluate.

options.text: Have her meals brought to her room
options.rationale: This ends the walk and the activity with it.

options.text: Start her walk earlier so she is not rushed
options.rationale: Movement slows with age. She is steady, so the nurse gives her time and keeps the regular activity that maintains function.

questions.takeaway: Slowed movement is an expected change of aging. Give the time, keep the activity, and save referrals for a change that is new or unsteady.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two cues decide it: steady, and slower over years. Pick the plan that keeps her walking.

steps.detail: Slow but steady, over two years: expected with aging.

steps.action: Drop the plans that cut walking
steps.detail: The wheelchair and the room tray both reduce her activity.

steps.action: Compare the referral with more time
steps.detail: Nothing is new or unsafe, so time is the answer.

elimination.verdict: Start her walk earlier so she is not rushed.

questions.scenario: A 58-year-old man has had weakness in both thighs and shoulders that has worsened over 3 months. The nurse reviews his laboratory results.
questions.stem: For each result, indicate whether it is within range or should be reported.

rows.text: Creatine kinase 2,900 units/L
rows.rationale: Total creatine kinase in men is 55 to 170 units/L. A value this high means muscle damage.

rows.text: Lactate dehydrogenase 160 units/L
rows.rationale: The range is 100 to 190 units/L.

rows.text: Aldolase 21 units/dL
rows.rationale: The range is 3.0 to 8.2 units/dL. High aldolase goes with muscle disease.

rows.text: Aspartate aminotransferase 24 units/L
rows.rationale: The range is 0 to 35 units/L.

rows.text: Phosphorus 1.5 mg/dL
rows.rationale: The range is 3.0 to 4.5 mg/dL.

rows.text: Alkaline phosphatase 90 units/L
rows.rationale: The range is 30 to 120 units/L.

questions.takeaway: Muscle enzymes rise with muscle damage: creatine kinase (men 55 to 170 units/L), lactate dehydrogenase 100 to 190, aspartate aminotransferase 0 to 35, aldolase 3.0 to 8.2 units/dL.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Judge each row against its own range. Do not let the diagnosis make every muscle enzyme look abnormal.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Creatine kinase 55 to 170, lactate dehydrogenase 100 to 190, aldolase 3.0 to 8.2, aspartate aminotransferase 0 to 35, phosphorus 3.0 to 4.5, alkaline phosphatase 30 to 120.
160, 24 and 90 sit inside.

elimination.verdict: Report, within range, report, within range, report, within range.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old admitted with pneumonia walks to the bathroom limping on his left leg. He did not limp yesterday and says nothing happened. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Request a physical therapy gait evaluation today
options.rationale: A sound step once the nurse knows what is wrong. The therapist evaluates gait in depth after the nurse has looked at the leg.

options.text: Inspect and palpate both legs, comparing sides
options.rationale: A new limp is a new finding with no cause yet. The nurse collects the data first: deformity, swelling, tenderness and movement, with the other leg as the standard.

options.text: Give him a walker to use until discharge
options.rationale: A device treats the limp without finding out why it appeared.

options.text: Walk him in the hall to observe the gait further
options.rationale: This is also assessment, but more walking loads a leg with a new, unexplained limp. The leg is examined first.

questions.takeaway: Any limp or asymmetric leg movement is noted and assessed. Compare the affected limb with the other before deciding who else is needed.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The stem gives a new finding and no cause. When data are missing, the nurse assesses before referring or treating.

steps.detail: New since yesterday, unexplained.
Examining the leg comes before walking farther on it.
Assessment comes before the referral and the device.

elimination.verdict: Inspect and palpate both legs, comparing sides.

questions.stem: A therapist grades a client's left leg strength as 2 on the 0 to 5 scale. The client wants to exercise the leg himself between sessions. Which exercise does the nurse suggest?

options.text: Raise the straight leg off the bed ten times
options.rationale: Lifting off the bed is movement against gravity, grade 3. He cannot do it yet.

options.text: Push the foot against the nurse's hand
options.rationale: Working against resistance is grade 4, two steps above his strength.

options.text: Let the nurse move the leg through its range
options.rationale: Tempting because the leg is weak. He can move it himself when gravity is removed, and he asked to do the work.

options.text: Slide the leg out and back across the sheet
options.rationale: Grade 2 is movement without gravity. With the bed holding the weight of the leg, he can move it himself.

questions.takeaway: Grade 2 strength means the limb moves only when gravity is removed. Match the exercise to the grade: supported sliding at 2, lifting at 3, resistance at 4.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Turn the grade into what the leg can overcome. Then test each exercise against it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 2 is movement without gravity.
Lifting needs 3 and resistance needs 4.
He can move the leg himself if the bed carries it, so he does not need the nurse to move it.

elimination.verdict: Slide the leg out and back across the sheet.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old has a splint on a fractured left lower leg. The left foot is cooler than the right, and its pulse is weaker than an hour ago. Which finding would concern the nurse most at the next check?

options.text: The left toes now feel numb to light touch
options.rationale: Loss of sensation added to a cool foot and a fading pulse shows that nerve and blood supply are getting worse. This is the change that cannot wait.

options.text: He rates leg pain 5 of 10 before the next analgesic
options.rationale: Moderate pain as a dose wears off is expected with a fracture. Severe pain would be a red flag.

options.text: The left foot has a bruise across the top
options.rationale: Bruising is expected near a fracture and does not show flow or nerve function.

options.text: Capillary refill in the left toes is 2 seconds
options.rationale: Brisk refill is reassuring. It is weighed with the pulse and temperature, and it does not signal a new problem.
