questions.takeaway: In a neurovascular check, new numbness, a weaker pulse, a cool or pale limb, severe pain and loss of movement are red flags. A trend that worsens is reported at once.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two red flags are already present. Look for the finding that adds a third instead of an expected effect of the fracture.

steps.detail: Cooler foot, weaker pulse.
Moderate pain and bruising go with a fracture.
Refill of 2 seconds is normal.
Numb toes.

elimination.verdict: New numbness in the left toes.

questions.stem: An assistive worker reports that a patient admitted after a fall this morning "seems sleepier than before lunch." Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Call the provider with the assistive worker's report
options.rationale: Tempting because a change after a fall is urgent. The nurse has no findings of her own yet, so there is nothing specific to report.

options.text: Go to the bedside to check alertness and command following
options.rationale: A reported change is a cue that the nurse must assess herself right away and compare with baseline.

options.text: Ask the assistive worker to recheck in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Waiting delays the assessment. Judging level of consciousness is not the assistive worker's role.

options.text: Review the chart for sedating medications given today
options.rationale: A reasonable cause to consider after the patient has been seen.

questions.takeaway: A secondhand report of a change is a cue. The nurse assesses the patient herself before she calls.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Calling and assessing both sound urgent. The stem gives a report from someone else and no nursing assessment, so assessment is still due.

steps.action: Ask what the nurse knows firsthand
steps.detail: Nothing yet. "Sleepier" is another person's impression.
A 30 minute recheck and a chart review both leave the patient unseen.
A call needs findings and a baseline comparison.

elimination.verdict: Go to the bedside and assess level of consciousness now.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old admitted with cellulitis had equal hand grips at 0730. Which finding at 1130 is most concerning?

options.text: Fine tremor in both hands, unchanged since admission
options.rationale: Abnormal, yet it matches the admission baseline.

options.text: Needs both arms to push up from the chair
options.rationale: Tempting because it is weakness. It is the same on both sides and common with age, so it does not point to the brain.

options.text: Takes longer to answer, with correct answers
options.rationale: Slower processing with accurate answers is an expected change with aging.

options.text: Right grip weaker than the left
options.rationale: A new one sided difference from this morning's baseline points to a new neurologic problem.

questions.takeaway: Compare right with left and now with baseline. New asymmetry is the finding you act on.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two options describe weakness. Ask which one is new and which one is on one side only.

steps.detail: The tremor is documented as unchanged.
Pushing up with both arms and slower answers affect both sides equally.
Grips were equal at 0730 and are not equal now.

elimination.verdict: The weaker right grip. New asymmetry needs immediate follow up.

questions.stem: During an admission assessment, a 79-year-old gives answers unrelated to the questions. His daughter is present. His hearing aids are in a bag at the bedside. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Insert the hearing aids and then repeat the questions
options.rationale: A patient who cannot hear the question is not confused. Set him up first, then judge his thinking.

options.text: Document disorientation as his admission baseline
options.rationale: A baseline recorded without his hearing aids may be false, and every later check would be compared with it.

options.text: Ask his daughter whether this is his usual thinking
options.rationale: Useful for a baseline and tempting. It comes after the nurse removes the barrier she can see.

options.text: Report new confusion to the provider right away
options.rationale: Reporting is right for true confusion. The hearing aids in the bag mean the finding is not yet reliable.

questions.takeaway: Set the patient up before you test cognition: hearing aids in, glasses on, interpreter if needed.
questions.coverage: Not in Lecture PPT. The Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Before you label the answers as confusion, look for a stem detail that explains them another way.

steps.detail: The hearing aids are in a bag, so he may not hear the questions.
Documenting or reporting confusion assumes the finding is real.
The daughter can describe his baseline later. The nurse can fix the hearing now.

elimination.verdict: Hearing aids in, then ask again.

questions.stem: A patient develops a new left facial droop and slurred speech. The stroke team is on the way. The patient asks for water to take the morning blood pressure pill. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give the pill with a small sip while sitting upright
options.rationale: Tempting because blood pressure matters in stroke and upright positioning helps. Swallowing has not been screened, so any sip risks aspiration.

options.text: Crush the pill in applesauce
options.rationale: Still an oral intake in a patient whose swallow is unknown.

options.text: Keep the patient NPO until a swallow screen is done
options.rationale: New droop and slurred speech signal aspiration risk, so nothing goes by mouth, including medications.

options.text: Offer ice chips to check swallowing
options.rationale: Testing with ice chips is an unscreened swallow trial.

questions.takeaway: New facial droop or slurred speech means NPO, including medications, until swallowing is screened. Airway comes before the medication schedule.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Three options put something in the mouth. The cue is the new droop, which makes every one of them unsafe.

steps.detail: New droop and slurred speech point to cranial nerve weakness.
A sip, applesauce and ice chips are all oral intake.
The pill can wait or go by another route once ordered.

elimination.verdict: Keep the patient NPO until the swallow screen.

questions.stem: A patient's left pupil has been irregular since cataract surgery. On admission yesterday both pupils reacted briskly. Which finding this evening requires follow up?

options.text: Left pupil remains irregular in shape
options.rationale: Abnormal shape, yet it is this patient's documented baseline.

options.text: Right pupil now reacts sluggishly to light
options.rationale: A change from brisk to sluggish is new. Change from baseline is what matters most.

options.text: Both pupils measure 4 mm
options.rationale: Within the normal range of 2 to 6 mm and equal.

options.text: Pupils constrict when focusing on a near object
options.rationale: Normal accommodation.

questions.takeaway: A pupil finding matters when it differs from the patient's own baseline. Sluggish after brisk is an early warning.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The irregular pupil looks like the abnormal one. The stem tells you it was already there, so look for what changed.

steps.detail: 4 mm and accommodation are normal.
The irregular shape dates from the surgery.
Brisk on admission, sluggish this evening.

elimination.verdict: The newly sluggish right pupil.

questions.stem: A patient with a head injury pulled his hand away from nail bed pressure at 0400. At 0600, right nail bed pressure makes both arms flex to the chest, wrists curled. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Document withdrawal from pain and continue hourly checks
options.rationale: Withdrawal pulls only the touched hand away. Both arms flexing to the chest is a different and worse response.

options.text: Request a sedative for the new agitated arm movements
options.rationale: Posturing is a reflex, not agitation. Sedation would hide the neuro status.

options.text: Report to the provider that he now localizes pain
options.rationale: Tempting because it also reports a change. Localizing means reaching toward the pain, which would be an improvement. This is not that.

options.text: Report the new abnormal flexion posturing to the provider now
options.rationale: Both arms flexing to the core with curled wrists is decorticate posturing, a decline from withdrawal that is reported now.

questions.takeaway: Withdrawal pulls the touched limb away. Both arms flexing to the core is posturing. New posturing is reported now.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two options report to the provider. Name the response correctly before you choose between them.

steps.detail: Both arms flex to the chest though only the right hand was pressed. That is abnormal flexion.
He withdrew before, so this is a step down the motor scale.
Localizing would be better than withdrawal. Abnormal flexion is worse.

elimination.verdict: Report new abnormal flexion posturing.

questions.stem: After a stroke, a patient follows commands correctly but struggles to find words and becomes frustrated. Which intervention should the nurse include in the plan?

options.text: Offer a picture board and extra time to answer
options.rationale: Understanding is intact and word production is the problem, so give another way to express and do not rush.

options.text: Speak loudly and repeat each instruction twice, slowly
options.rationale: The patient follows commands correctly, so the message already gets through. Volume and repetition add nothing.

options.text: Ask the family to answer the questions for the patient
options.rationale: Takes away the patient's voice and adds to the frustration.

options.text: Demonstrate each instruction with gestures
options.rationale: Helps a patient who cannot understand words, which is not this patient's problem.

questions.takeaway: Match the aid to the deficit. A patient who understands but cannot find words needs time and another way to express.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Gestures and a picture board both sound like communication aids. One helps the patient understand and the other helps the patient express.

steps.detail: Follows commands, so understanding works. Word finding does not.
Loud speech, repetition and gestures.

steps.action: Keep the patient in the conversation
steps.detail: Family answering removes the patient.

elimination.verdict: Picture board plus extra time.

questions.stem: A patient is scheduled for an MRI of the brain to evaluate new weakness. Which statement by the patient indicates the teaching was understood?

options.text: "I will wash my hair and skip hair gel that morning."
options.rationale: This is preparation for an EEG.

options.text: "I will lie on my side with my knees pulled up."
options.rationale: This is the position for a lumbar puncture.

options.text: "I will tell the staff about my aneurysm clip."
options.rationale: MRI uses a strong magnet, so implanted metal must be reported before the scan.

options.text: "I can shift around in the scanner if my back gets sore."
options.rationale: The patient must lie still for clear images.

questions.takeaway: MRI gives detailed soft tissue images with a magnet. The safety check is metal. The patient must lie still.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Each wrong statement is correct teaching for a different test or the opposite of MRI teaching. Match the statement to this test.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A magnet, so metal is the hazard.
Clean hair is EEG. Side lying with knees up is lumbar puncture.
Movement blurs the images.

elimination.verdict: Reporting the aneurysm clip shows understanding.

questions.stem: A patient admitted after a fall does not open his eyes when the nurse says his name in a normal voice. Which action is next?

options.text: Press firmly on a nail bed with a pen
options.rationale: A painful stimulus is used only after voice and touch have failed.

options.text: Call his name loudly, then shake his shoulder
options.rationale: Stimulation goes from least to most noxious: normal voice, loud voice, gentle shake, then pain.

options.text: Record eye opening as none on the Glasgow Coma Scale
options.rationale: He has not been given the stronger stimuli yet, so the best response is still unknown.

options.text: Squeeze the trapezius muscle for up to 10 seconds
options.rationale: A correct way to apply pain, and tempting. It skips the two gentler steps.

questions.takeaway: Raise the stimulus in order: normal voice, loud voice, gentle shake, then pain. Score the best response.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Two options use pain. Ask what the nurse has not tried yet.

steps.detail: Nail bed pressure and the trapezius squeeze are both painful stimuli.
None is recorded only after every level of stimulus fails.
Only a normal voice has been tried.

elimination.verdict: Loud voice, then a gentle shake.

questions.stem: A patient with dementia is disoriented to time and place at baseline. Which finding at noon requires immediate follow up?

options.text: States the year is 1985
options.rationale: Disorientation to time is this patient's baseline.

options.text: Asks when her late husband will visit
options.rationale: Fits her baseline memory and orientation problems.

options.text: Opens her eyes only after repeated shaking
options.rationale: She now needs strong stimulation to wake, which is a drop in level of consciousness.

options.text: Pushes the lunch tray away and refuses to eat anything
options.rationale: Worth following. It is not a neurologic change.

questions.takeaway: Orientation and level of consciousness are separate. A patient who is always disoriented can still have a new drop in alertness.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two options are disorientation, which she already has. Look for the option that is about how awake she is.

steps.detail: The wrong year and the question about her husband are baseline.
Refusing lunch is not an acute neurologic sign.
Hard to arouse is new.

elimination.verdict: Difficulty arousing her. That is a change in level of consciousness.

questions.stem: The nurse teaches an 80-year-old with decreased sensation in both feet about safety at home. Which statement indicates the teaching was effective?

options.text: "I will dip my toes in the bath first to test it."
options.rationale: The feet cannot judge temperature, so this risks a burn.

options.text: "I will use a heating pad on my feet when they feel cold."
options.rationale: Heat on skin that cannot feel it causes burns.

options.text: "I will go barefoot indoors so I can feel the floor."
options.rationale: Unprotected feet can be injured without the patient knowing.

options.text: "I will check the bath water with a thermometer."
options.rationale: Uses a tool in place of the lost sensation.

questions.takeaway: When sensation is reduced, safety has to come from something other than the patient's own feeling.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Three statements rely on the feet to sense heat or injury. One replaces the missing sensation with a measurement.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The feet do not feel temperature or pain well.
Toes, heating pad and bare feet all depend on feeling.
A thermometer does not depend on sensation.

elimination.verdict: Checking bath water with a thermometer.

questions.stem: An 83-year-old recovering from a hip fracture was oriented at breakfast. At 1530 she is suddenly confused and picking at the blanket. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Measure the oxygen saturation
options.rationale: Hypoxia is the cause that harms fastest and is the quickest to check. It sits at the top of the ABCs.

options.text: Take an oral temperature
options.rationale: Infection is a common cause and is checked next, after oxygenation.

options.text: Review the medications given today
options.rationale: A real cause of sudden confusion. A chart review takes the nurse away from the patient and comes after the bedside checks.

options.text: Request a serum electrolyte panel
options.rationale: Electrolytes can cause confusion, but the result takes time and needs a prescription.

questions.takeaway: Sudden confusion in an older adult is never aging. Check oxygen saturation first, then glucose, temperature and medications.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: All four look for a cause of confusion. Rank them by how fast the cause harms and how fast you can check it.

steps.action: Accept that all four are valid
steps.detail: Hypoxia, infection, drugs and electrolytes all cause sudden confusion.
Oxygenation is the breathing check and takes seconds.
Temperature next, then the chart, then the lab.

elimination.verdict: Oxygen saturation first.

questions.stem: A patient with a frontal lobe injury keeps getting up alone, so a bed alarm was started. Which finding best indicates the plan is effective?

options.text: The patient says, "I will call before I get up."
options.rationale: Tempting as a teaching outcome. Frontal injury impairs judgment and impulse control, so a promise does not predict behavior.

options.text: The patient repeats the fall precautions correctly
options.rationale: Recall is intact. Acting on it is what the injury prevents.

options.text: Staff reach him before he stands at each alarm
options.rationale: The goal is no unassisted rising. This shows the alarm is doing the job the patient cannot.

options.text: The patient stays in bed when all four side rails are raised
options.rationale: Four rails act as a restraint and raise the risk of injury.

questions.takeaway: With frontal lobe injury, measure safety by what happens, since the patient's own judgment cannot be relied on.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: A correct statement by the patient usually proves teaching worked. In this patient the deficit is the gap between knowing and doing.

steps.detail: Judgment and impulse control.

steps.action: Cut outcomes that rely on it
steps.detail: Promising and repeating instructions.
Four side rails are a restraint.

elimination.verdict: Staff arriving before he stands shows the alarm is working.

questions.stem: A patient with Parkinson disease says, "For weeks nothing has interested me. I see no point in therapy." Which intervention should the nurse include first?

options.text: Explain that therapy keeps him moving and encourage attendance
options.rationale: Tempting because therapy matters. It answers the refusal and skips the mood change behind it.

options.text: Screen for depression using a standard tool
options.rationale: Weeks of lost interest in a chronic neurologic condition is a cue to screen for depression.

options.text: Arrange a chaplain visit to discuss meaning
options.rationale: Reasonable support once the nurse knows what the problem is.

options.text: Tell him that many patients feel this way at first
options.rationale: Dismisses what he said and closes the conversation.

questions.takeaway: Psychosocial status is part of the neurologic assessment. Lost interest for weeks calls for depression screening before solutions.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Encouragement and a chaplain are both kind actions. The stem gives a cue that has not been assessed yet.

strategies: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings

steps.detail: "For weeks" and "nothing interests me."
"Many patients feel this way" denies his feelings.
Screening comes before encouragement or referral.

elimination.verdict: Screen for depression first.

questions.stem: An 81-year-old, normally oriented to person, place, time and situation (x4), was admitted with new confusion from a urinary infection. Which finding on day 3 best indicates the neurologic problem has resolved?

options.text: Repeat urine culture shows no bacterial growth
options.rationale: Shows the infection is treated. It does not show that her thinking is back to baseline.

options.text: Sleeps through the night without calling out for her family
options.rationale: Quiet sleep can also mean a lower level of alertness.

options.text: Tells the nurse her full name and her date of birth correctly
options.rationale: Orientation to person only. Her baseline is oriented x4.

options.text: States the date, the hospital and why she is here
options.rationale: Oriented to time, place and situation again, which matches her baseline.

questions.takeaway: Neurologic recovery is measured against the patient's own baseline, not against the lab result.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: A clean urine culture and full orientation are both good news. The question asks about the neurologic problem. Her baseline was oriented x4.

steps.detail: Return to oriented x4.
The culture tracks the infection, not her thinking.
Name alone is one of four.

elimination.verdict: Full orientation to time, place and situation.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for four patients on a neurology unit with one assistive worker. Which task is appropriate to assign to the assistive worker?

options.text: Walking a patient who has a chronic unsteady gait
options.rationale: A stable, chronic problem and a routine task with a predictable outcome.

options.text: Taking vital signs on a patient who just became confused
options.rationale: Tempting because vital signs are routine. A sudden change makes the patient unstable, so the nurse goes herself.

options.text: Checking whether a patient with a new facial droop can swallow water
options.rationale: A swallow screen is an assessment with aspiration risk.

options.text: Asking orientation questions of a patient admitted an hour ago
options.rationale: Establishing the baseline is a nursing assessment.

questions.takeaway: Delegate routine tasks for stable patients. New changes, baselines and swallow screens stay with the nurse.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Vital signs are usually delegated. The words "just became confused" make that patient unstable.

steps.detail: Only the chronic gait problem is stable.
Swallow screening and orientation are assessments.
Routine task, unstable patient.

elimination.verdict: Walking the patient whose unsteady gait is chronic.

questions.stem: A patient admitted 2 days ago with a stroke has stable left arm weakness. At the start of the shift, which assessment plan is most appropriate?

options.text: A comprehensive neurologic examination as on admission
options.rationale: Tempting as the thorough choice. It suits a new admission. This patient already has a documented baseline.

options.text: Vital signs only, unless the patient reports a change
options.rationale: Misses changes the patient may not notice or report.

options.text: A focused neurologic check compared with the last findings
options.rationale: A known condition is monitored with a targeted exam. Comparison is how change is caught.

options.text: A Glasgow Coma Scale score alone
options.rationale: Does not capture arm strength, speech or pupils.

questions.takeaway: Comprehensive exams set the baseline. Focused exams, compared with that baseline, monitor a known problem.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two options are real neurologic assessments. "Admitted 2 days ago" and "stable" tell you the baseline exists.

steps.detail: Vital signs alone or one score alone miss too much.
Day 2 with stable findings.
Targeted and compared with the prior shift.

elimination.verdict: A focused check compared with the last findings.

questions.scenario:
A 76-year-old, alert and oriented after hip surgery, received IV hydromorphone 30 minutes ago. He now opens his eyes only when shaken.
Respirations are 8 per minute and SpO2 is 88%.
Pupils are small and equal. He moves all four limbs equally and his face is symmetric.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the patient is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Stimulate him, open the airway and apply oxygen
options.rationale: Breathing comes first. He is under breathing and his oxygen level is low.

options.text: Give naloxone as prescribed
options.rationale: Reverses the opioid that is depressing his breathing and alertness.

options.text: Give the next scheduled opioid dose
options.rationale: More opioid deepens the sedation.

options.text: Let him sleep and recheck in one hour
options.rationale: Hard to arouse with respirations of 8 is not sleep.

options.text: Acute stroke
options.rationale: Equal movement and a symmetric face show no one sided deficit.

options.text: Opioid induced sedation with slowed breathing
options.rationale: A recent opioid dose, a global drop in alertness, small equal pupils and slow respirations fit a medication cause.

options.text: Expected sleepiness after surgery
options.rationale: Expected sleepiness does not come with respirations of 8 and an SpO2 of 88%.

options.text: Abnormal posturing from brain injury
options.rationale: He moves all four limbs equally, which is not posturing.

options.text: Respiratory rate and SpO2
options.rationale: Shows whether breathing recovers and whether sedation returns as naloxone wears off.

options.text: Level of consciousness
options.rationale: Return to his alert, oriented baseline is the outcome.

options.text: Facial symmetry
options.rationale: Already symmetric and not affected by this problem.

options.text: Sensation in the feet
options.rationale: Not related to opioid sedation.

questions.takeaway: A global change with equal limbs points to a systemic cause such as a medication. A one sided change points to the brain.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Every line of the excerpt is a clue. The timing names the drug, the respirations name the danger, and the equal limbs rule out stroke.

steps.detail: Equal limbs and a symmetric face mean global.
Hydromorphone 30 minutes ago.
Airway and oxygen, reversal, then respirations and alertness.

elimination.verdict: Opioid sedation; airway with oxygen and naloxone; respirations with SpO2 and level of consciousness.

questions.stem: While passing a doorway, the nurse hears a patient who spoke clearly 30 minutes ago calling out in garbled words. Place the nurse's actions in order.

options.text: Check airway, breathing and vital signs
options.rationale: Fourth. With the change confirmed, check the ABCs and vital signs so the report is complete.

options.text: Enter the room and treat the speech as a new change
options.rationale: First. Recognize that this is different from 30 minutes ago and stop what you were doing.

options.text: Notify the provider or activate the rapid response
options.rationale: Fifth. Escalate with findings, baseline and vital signs in hand.

options.text: Assess alertness, speech, face and limb strength
options.rationale: Second. A focused neurologic check shows what has changed.

options.text: Compare the findings with the last documented assessment
options.rationale: Third. Findings only mean something against this patient's baseline.

questions.takeaway: New neurologic change: recognize, assess, compare with baseline, check ABCs and vital signs, then notify.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The step students drop is the comparison. It sits between the bedside check and the vital signs, before the call.

steps.detail: Clear speech 30 minutes ago, garbled now.
The focused check comes before the baseline comparison.

steps.action: Finish with ABCs and the call
steps.detail: Vital signs complete the picture you report.

elimination.verdict: Recognize, assess, compare, ABCs and vital signs, notify.

questions.scenario:
A patient with a head injury was treated for brain swelling.
0800: opens eyes to pain, says single words, pushes the nurse's hand away with either hand.
0800: pupils 3 mm, equal, brisk.
questions.stem: The nurse reassesses at 1200. For each finding, indicate whether it has improved, declined or is unchanged from 0800.

rows.text: Now opens eyes when his name is spoken
rows.rationale: Eye opening rose from pain to voice.

rows.text: Now speaks in confused sentences
rows.rationale: Verbal response rose from single words to confused conversation.

rows.text: Pupils 3 mm, equal, brisk
rows.rationale: Same as 0800.

rows.text: Right arm now extends rigidly to pain
rows.rationale: Extension is a lower motor response than pushing the stimulus away and needs immediate report.

rows.text: Left hand still pushes the nurse's hand away
rows.rationale: Localizing on the left is the same as 0800.

questions.takeaway: Trend each part of the assessment separately. One declining part needs action even when the others improve.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two better findings can hide one worse finding. Compare each row with its own 0800 line.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Match each row to its baseline line
steps.detail: Eyes, verbal and motor come from the first line. Pupils come from the second.
Pushing the hand away is localizing. Rigid extension is lower.
New extension on the right is reported at once.

elimination.verdict: Improved, improved, unchanged, declined, unchanged.

questions.stem: A patient admitted after a head injury was alert at 1900. At 2100 the nurse must call his name twice to wake him. Pupils and vital signs are unchanged. Which action is the priority?

options.text: Repeat the neuro check in 15 minutes to confirm a trend
options.rationale: Tempting because only one thing changed. The change is already confirmed against the 1900 baseline, so waiting only delays treatment.

options.text: Notify the provider now of the change from baseline
options.rationale: A drop in level of consciousness (LOC) is the earliest sign of decline after a head injury. It is reported before the pupils or vital signs change.

options.text: Continue hourly checks because the other findings are stable
options.rationale: Pupils and vital signs change late. Stable late signs do not cancel an early one.

options.text: Review the record for sedating drugs given this morning
options.rationale: A reasonable cause to look for, and it can be done after the call. After a head injury the change is treated as the brain first.

questions.takeaway: Level of consciousness changes first. Pupils and vital signs change late. A quiet drop in alertness after a head injury is reported now, not trended.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The stem gives one early sign and two normal late signs. Decide which of them carries more weight.

steps.detail: Alert at 1900 and hard to wake at 2100 is a completed comparison.
LOC falls first. Normal pupils and vital signs are not reassurance.
The chart review can follow the call.

elimination.verdict: Notify the provider now.

questions.stem: A patient with a severe headache, projectile vomiting and increasing drowsiness is scheduled for a lumbar puncture in 20 minutes. No brain imaging has been done. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Hold the preparation and call the provider
options.rationale: Headache, projectile vomiting and a falling level of consciousness suggest high intracranial pressure. A lumbar puncture without imaging risks herniation.

options.text: Have the patient empty the bladder before the procedure
options.rationale: Correct preparation for a lumbar puncture that should go ahead. This one should not, yet.

options.text: Position the patient side lying with knees drawn to chest
options.rationale: The right position for the procedure, and sharp flexion also raises intracranial pressure.

options.text: Give the prescribed antiemetic so the patient can lie still
options.rationale: Tempting because it treats the vomiting. It treats a cue as a nuisance and moves the procedure forward.

questions.takeaway: Before preparing a patient for a lumbar puncture, read the cues. Signs of high intracranial pressure without imaging mean stop and call.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Three options prepare for the procedure. Ask whether the procedure is safe before choosing how to prepare.

steps.detail: Headache, projectile vomiting and drowsiness point to high intracranial pressure.
No imaging has ruled out a mass.
Three move toward the procedure. One stops it.

elimination.verdict: Hold and call the provider.

questions.stem: The nurse receives report on four patients. Which patient does the nurse see first?

options.text: Severe brain injury with arms extended and turned inward, unchanged for 3 days
options.rationale: The most alarming picture of the four, and it is unchanged. Unchanged late findings do not outrank a new change.

options.text: Stroke 5 days ago with a limp left arm, crying and refusing breakfast
options.rationale: Needs support, and the limp arm dates from the stroke 5 days ago. Nothing here is described as new.

options.text: Diabetic neuropathy reporting burning pain and numbness in both feet
options.rationale: Uncomfortable and chronic. It is a safety teaching need, not an emergency.

options.text: Fall yesterday, oriented at the last check, now asking the same question for the third time
options.rationale: A subtle new change in mental status after a fall. It is the earliest sign of neuro decline and the only finding that is new.

questions.takeaway: New beats dramatic. A quiet change in thinking after a fall outranks severe findings that have not changed.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Sort each patient as changed or unchanged before you look at how severe the finding sounds.

steps.detail: Posturing for 3 days and a limp arm for 5 days are stable.
Neuropathy pain is long standing.
Repeating a question is a new thinking change in an oriented patient.

elimination.verdict: See the patient who fell and is now repeating questions.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old is seen for a routine visit. Which finding requires follow up?

options.text: Both pupils are equal and constrict slowly to light
options.rationale: Tempting because a slow pupil is a warning sign in a head injury. Equal, slower pupils are an expected change with age.

options.text: Loses track of conversations, new this week per daughter
options.rationale: A change in attention over days is not normal aging. Any subtle mental status change from baseline needs a cause found.

options.text: Ankle reflexes are weaker and equal on both sides
options.rationale: Weaker reflexes that are the same on both sides are expected with age.

options.text: Takes extra time but recalls a list of three words
options.rationale: Slower recall is expected with age when the patient still gets there.

questions.takeaway: Normal aging is slow and symmetric. A change that is new this week is a cue, however mild it looks.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Every option sounds like a deficit. Look for the one with a time stamp that makes it new.

steps.detail: Equal pupils and equal reflexes fit aging.
Slower is expected. Lost is not.
New this week, reported by family.

elimination.verdict: Follow up on the new loss of attention.

questions.stem: Four hours after a head injury a drowsy patient's blood pressure has gone from 118/76 to 164/70 and the pulse from 80 to 54. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give the prescribed as needed antihypertensive and recheck in 20 minutes
options.rationale: Tempting because the systolic pressure is high. The pressure is the brain's attempt to keep itself perfused, not the problem to treat.

options.text: Complete a full cranial nerve assessment before calling anyone
options.rationale: Tempting because assessment usually comes first. The stem already gives a late sign pattern, and more assessment costs time.

options.text: Call the rapid response team and report the findings now
options.rationale: Rising systolic pressure with a wider pulse pressure and a slow pulse in a drowsy patient is a late sign of high intracranial pressure. It is reported at once.

options.text: Recheck the blood pressure in the other arm in 10 minutes
options.rationale: Reasonable for one odd reading. Here the pressure and pulse changed together in a pattern.

questions.takeaway: Higher systolic pressure, wider pulse pressure and a slower pulse together are the brainstem's late alarm. Do not treat the number and do not keep assessing.
questions.coverage: Not in Lecture PPT. The Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Read the two vital signs as one pattern instead of two separate problems, then ask which option responds to the pattern.

steps.detail: Pulse pressure widened from 42 to 94 while the pulse slowed.
An antihypertensive and a recheck both treat a reading.
The decisive findings are already in hand.

elimination.verdict: Call the rapid response team now.

questions.stem: A drowsy patient squeezes the nurse's fingers with both hands when asked. Which action best confirms that the patient is following commands?

options.text: Ask the patient to let go of the fingers
options.rationale: Releasing on request cannot happen by reflex, so it shows the patient heard and understood.

options.text: Ask the patient to squeeze again, harder
options.rationale: Tempting because it repeats a command, but a grasp can be a reflex however strong it is.

options.text: Record that the patient follows commands
options.rationale: Premature. The squeeze alone may be a reflex grasp in a drowsy patient.

options.text: Apply nail bed pressure to each hand
options.rationale: Pain is used when voice and touch get no response. This patient is responding to voice.

questions.takeaway: A hand grasp can be a reflex. Letting go on command is what proves the patient understood.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Two options use a command. Ask which response a reflex could not produce.

steps.detail: Recording now skips the check.
The patient responds to voice.
Only release rules out a reflex.

elimination.verdict: Ask the patient to let go.

questions.stem: A patient with new dizziness is scheduled for a CT scan of the head with contrast in 1 hour. Which finding does the nurse report before the scan?

options.text: Has a permanent cardiac pacemaker
options.rationale: Tempting because it is a safety screen, but metal matters for MRI. CT does not use a magnet.

options.text: Serum creatinine of 2.6 mg/dL today
options.rationale: Contrast is cleared by the kidneys, so a high creatinine is reported before contrast is given.

options.text: Drank a cup of coffee at breakfast
options.rationale: Caffeine is held before an EEG. It does not change a CT.

options.text: Feels uneasy in small closed spaces
options.rationale: More of a concern in the long MRI tube. The CT is quick and open.

questions.takeaway: CT with contrast: check allergy and kidney function. Metal and claustrophobia belong to MRI, caffeine to EEG.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Each option is a real pre test check. Match each one to the test it belongs to.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: CT with contrast.
Pacemaker and closed spaces go with MRI, caffeine with EEG.
Creatinine shows whether the kidneys can clear contrast.

elimination.verdict: Report the creatinine.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old with a tumor in the left cerebellum is cleared to walk in the hall. Which plan is safest for the nurse to use?

options.text: Stand at the right side holding a gait belt
options.rationale: Tempting if you apply the crossed rule of the cerebrum. The cerebellum works on the same side.

options.text: Walk behind with a wheelchair, hands free
options.rationale: A chair nearby helps, but no one is guarding the side the patient will veer toward.

options.text: Stand at the left side holding a gait belt
options.rationale: A left cerebellar lesion causes left sided clumsiness, so the nurse guards the left.

options.text: Have the patient use the hallway handrail
options.rationale: Relies on the coordination that the lesion has taken away.

questions.takeaway: The cerebrum is crossed and the cerebellum is not. A left cerebellar lesion makes the left side unsteady.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Two options differ only by side. Decide which structure is injured before you pick a side.

steps.detail: Cerebellum, not cerebrum.
Same side coordination.
Left, with hands on a gait belt.

elimination.verdict: Stand at the left side with a gait belt.

questions.stem: The nurse teaches a patient who is scheduled for an EEG tomorrow morning. Which statement indicates the teaching was effective?

options.text: "I will take off my watch because of the magnet."
options.rationale: Describes MRI. An EEG records electrical activity and uses no magnet.

options.text: "I will lie curled on my side for the test."
options.rationale: Describes positioning for a lumbar puncture.

options.text: "I will have my usual coffee to stay alert."
options.rationale: Caffeine is often held because it changes brain electrical activity.

options.text: "I will wash my hair and skip the styling gel."
options.rationale: Clean hair with no gel lets the scalp electrodes make good contact.

questions.takeaway: EEG preparation is clean hair, no gels, and caffeine and sedatives often held.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Three statements belong to other tests or break a rule. Match each statement to its test.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Magnet is MRI. Curled on the side is lumbar puncture.
Caffeine is usually held.
Clean hair, no gel.

elimination.verdict: Wash the hair and skip the gel.

questions.stem: A patient diagnosed with Bell palsy 3 days ago has right facial paralysis that includes the forehead and cannot close the right eye. Which intervention does the nurse include?

options.text: Apply eye lubricant and cover the right eye at night
options.rationale: An eye that cannot close or blink dries out and is injured, so the nurse keeps it moist and covered.

options.text: Patch each eye in turn every 2 to 4 hours
options.rationale: Alternating patches treat double vision. This eye needs protection, not rest from double images.

options.text: Keep the patient NPO until a swallow screen
options.rationale: Tempting because droop suggests stroke. This is a diagnosed facial nerve problem and swallowing uses other nerves.

options.text: Place meal items on the left side of the tray
options.rationale: Used for a lost visual field. Bell palsy affects the facial nerve, not vision.

questions.takeaway: When the facial nerve cannot close the eye or the blink is absent, protect the eye.
questions.coverage: Not in Lecture PPT. The Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Name the nerve, name its job, then choose the action that covers the lost job.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Eyelid closure and blink.
Bell palsy does not cause double vision or field loss.
The diagnosis is known and swallowing is not a facial nerve job.

elimination.verdict: Lubricate and cover the right eye.

questions.stem: Three hours after a lumbar puncture, a patient reports a headache that worsens when sitting up and eases when lying down. Neurologic checks are unchanged. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Raise the head of the bed to 30 degrees
options.rationale: Tempting as the headache reflex from high pressure care. This headache is worse upright.

options.text: Help the patient lie flat and offer fluids
options.rationale: A positional headache is the expected effect of the procedure, and lying flat relieves it.

options.text: Prepare the patient for an urgent CT scan
options.rationale: Imaging fits a new neurologic change. The checks are unchanged.

options.text: Call the rapid response team to the bedside
options.rationale: Reserved for decline. This is an expected finding in a stable patient.

questions.takeaway: A headache after lumbar puncture that is worse upright and better flat is expected. Lie flat and give fluids, and keep checking the neuro status.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the finding is expected for this procedure. The position detail and the unchanged checks answer it.

steps.detail: Worse sitting, better lying.
Neuro checks are unchanged.
Flat with fluids.

elimination.verdict: Lie flat and offer fluids.

questions.stem: An 86-year-old is slow to answer orientation questions, so the nurse now waits longer after each question. Which finding indicates normal slowing and not deterioration?

options.text: Answers at once but gives the wrong year
options.rationale: A fast wrong answer is a thinking problem, not slow processing.

options.text: Looks to the daughter, who answers for him
options.rationale: Shows nothing about his own thinking.

options.text: Nods and smiles as each question is asked
options.rationale: Tempting because he seems engaged, but nodding is not an answer.

options.text: Gives correct answers after a longer pause
options.rationale: Accurate answers with extra time are the pattern of normal aging.

questions.takeaway: Give an older adult time to answer. Slow and correct is aging. Wrong or absent answers are a change to follow up.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The outcome to look for is accuracy, not speed and not friendliness.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Aging slows the answer and leaves it correct.

steps.action: Drop the answers that are not his
steps.detail: The daughter's answer and the nod.
Fast and wrong is not slowing.

elimination.verdict: Correct answers after a longer pause.

questions.stem: A patient is admitted unresponsive after being found on the floor at home. Which assessments does the nurse include in the focused neurologic assessment? Select all that apply.

options.text: Glasgow Coma Scale score
options.rationale: The standard measure of level of consciousness when it is altered.

options.text: Pupil size in millimeters and reaction to light
options.rationale: A cranial nerve check that does not need the patient's cooperation.

options.text: Motor response to voice, then to pain
options.rationale: Shows the best motor response and any posturing.

options.text: Vital signs
options.rationale: Part of every focused neurologic assessment.

options.text: Orientation to person, place, time and situation
options.rationale: Tempting because it is part of the alert patient's exam. An unresponsive patient cannot answer.

options.text: Swallowing with a small sip of water
options.rationale: Swallowing is never tested in a patient who cannot protect the airway.

questions.takeaway: With altered consciousness the focused assessment has 4 parts: level of consciousness by GCS, cranial nerves, motor response, vital signs.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Ask of each option whether it needs an awake, cooperative patient.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: GCS, pupils, motor response, vital signs.
Orientation questions.
Water by mouth.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D.

questions.nursesNote: Clinic visit: 67-year-old reports numbness and tingling in both feet for several months, worse at the toes. Hemoglobin A1c 9.4%. Has followed a strict vegan diet for 12 years and takes no supplements. Walks barefoot at home. Did not notice a blister on the left heel. Goes to bed and wakes earlier than he used to. Takes a moment longer to recall names, then remembers. Blood pressure 128/78.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings the nurse follows up in the plan of care for the numbness.

segments.text: Hemoglobin A1c 9.4%
segments.rationale: Poorly controlled diabetes is a common cause of numb feet.

segments.text: Has followed a strict vegan diet for 12 years and takes no supplements
segments.rationale: Vitamin B12 intake is part of the neurologic history, and a lack of it damages nerves.

segments.text: Walks barefoot at home
segments.rationale: A safety risk when the feet cannot feel injury.

segments.text: Did not notice a blister on the left heel
segments.rationale: Shows the lost sensation is already allowing injury.

segments.text: Goes to bed and wakes earlier than he used to
segments.rationale: An expected sleep change with aging.

segments.text: Takes a moment longer to recall names, then remembers
segments.rationale: Slower recall that still succeeds is expected with aging.

segments.text: Blood pressure 128/78
segments.rationale: Within normal limits and not related to the numbness.

questions.takeaway: Numbness in both feet, worse at the toes, points to the nerves. Look for diabetes and B12 intake, then protect feet that cannot feel.
questions.coverage: Not in Lecture PPT. The Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Sort each finding into cause, safety risk or normal aging. Highlight the first two groups.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: High A1c and no B12 source.
Barefoot and an unfelt blister.
Sleep timing and slow name recall.

elimination.verdict: A1c, vegan diet without supplements, barefoot, unnoticed blister.

questions.stem: At 1500 a patient with a brain bleed flexed both arms to the chest when the nurse applied pressure. Which response at 1600 indicates the patient is getting worse?

options.text: Arms straighten at the sides and turn inward, feet point down
options.rationale: Extension posturing means the brainstem is involved. It is more severe than flexion.

options.text: The pressed hand pulls back from the nurse's fingers
options.rationale: Withdrawal is a better motor response than abnormal flexion.

options.text: Arms flex to the chest again while the legs extend
options.rationale: This is the same flexion posturing seen at 1500. Legs may extend with it.

options.text: One hand reaches up and pushes the nurse away
options.rationale: Localizing is a clear improvement.

questions.takeaway: Flexion to the core is damage above the brainstem. Extension away from the body is brainstem involvement and is worse.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Rank the four responses from best to worst motor score. Only one sits below flexion.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Abnormal flexion at 1500.
Localizes, withdraws, flexion, extension.
Extension is the only step down.

elimination.verdict: Arms extended and rotated with feet pointed down.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old alert patient one day after surgery rates pain as 9 of 10. Both pupils are 6 mm and brisk, the pulse is 112 and the skin is cool and damp. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Start hourly neurologic checks because of the large pupils
options.rationale: 6 mm is the top of the normal range, and the pupils are equal and brisk in an alert patient.

options.text: Call the rapid response team for dilated pupils
options.rationale: Tempting, but equal brisk pupils with a fast pulse and damp skin fit a sympathetic response, not a brain problem.

options.text: Give the prescribed analgesic and recheck the pupils
options.rationale: Pain triggers fight or flight: pupils dilate, the pulse rises and the skin sweats. Treat the cause and confirm the findings settle.

options.text: Hold the prescribed opioid because the pupils are large
options.rationale: Opioids make pupils small, not large. Holding it leaves the cause untreated.

questions.takeaway: Fight or flight dilates the pupils and raises the heart rate. Equal, brisk pupils in an alert patient in pain are an autonomic response.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Three findings arrive together. Ask what single system produces all of them before you treat one of them as a brain sign.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Large pupils, fast pulse, damp skin, severe pain.
Sympathetic response.
Alert, equal, brisk. None present.

elimination.verdict: Treat the pain, then recheck.

questions.stem: A patient speaks in fluent sentences that make no sense and does not follow spoken requests. The nurse begins using gestures and demonstration. Which finding indicates the approach is effective?

options.text: He nods and says yes when asked if he understands
options.rationale: Tempting, but a nod from a patient who cannot understand words proves nothing.

options.text: He repeats the nurse's words back clearly
options.rationale: Repeating shows speech works. It does not show he understood.

options.text: He talks in longer sentences during care
options.rationale: His speech was already fluent. More words are not more understanding.

options.text: He brushes his teeth after the nurse mimes it
options.rationale: He acted on the meaning. That shows the message got through without words.

questions.takeaway: When a patient cannot understand language, judge your communication by what he does, not by what he says.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: The problem is understanding, so pick the option that proves understanding. Words and nods can be automatic.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Speech is fluent. Language comprehension is lost.
Repeating and longer sentences measure speech.
A yes can be automatic.

elimination.verdict: He carries out the mimed task.

questions.stem: A daughter says her 76-year-old mother has been "forgetting things since yesterday." The patient is alert and talkative. Which request best checks the patient's memory?

options.text: "Count backward from 100 by 7s."
options.rationale: This checks attention and calculation.

options.text: "Tell me how you got to the hospital today."
options.rationale: She has to recall a recent event the nurse can confirm with the daughter.

options.text: "Tell me your date of birth and where you were born."
options.rationale: Tempting, but long held facts stay intact when recent memory fails, so this misses the change.

options.text: "Copy this word onto the paper."
options.rationale: This checks the ability to see and reproduce, not to remember.

questions.takeaway: Check memory with a recent event you can verify, such as how the patient came to the hospital.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Match each request to what it measures. Only one asks her to recall something that happened today.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: New forgetting since yesterday, so recent memory.
Attention, recent memory, remote memory, copying.
Recent and verifiable.

elimination.verdict: Ask how she got to the hospital.

questions.stem: A patient admitted with a headache has a right pupil of 5 mm and a left pupil of 3 mm. Both react briskly. No baseline is charted. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Chart the pupils as reactive and recheck them again in 4 hours
options.rationale: Reactive is true, and equal is not. Unequal pupils with a headache cannot wait 4 hours.

options.text: Dim the lights and measure both pupils again
options.rationale: The sizes were already measured. Repeating adds time and no new information.

options.text: Check level of consciousness and strength in all limbs
options.rationale: With no baseline, the rest of the focused check tells the nurse whether this is a new problem and gives the provider a full picture.

options.text: Ask the provider to order a CT scan of the head
options.rationale: Tempting, but the nurse calls with a complete assessment, and that takes one minute.

questions.takeaway: One abnormal finding with no baseline is a cue to finish the focused neuro check: LOC, pupils, movement. Then report.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Two options delay and one skips ahead. Ask what the provider will want to know when you call.

steps.detail: Unequal pupils, headache, no baseline.
Rechecking later or remeasuring adds nothing.
Assess LOC and movement, then call.

elimination.verdict: Check LOC and limb strength first.

questions.stem: A nursing student plans to give sips of water to check swallowing in a patient who is NPO for surgery at 1300 and has clear speech and a symmetric face. Which direction does the nurse give?

options.text: "Leave out the swallow test and keep him NPO."
options.rationale: Swallowing is observed only when clinically appropriate and is not tested in a patient who is NPO.

options.text: "Use a single 5 mL sip so the risk stays small."
options.rationale: Tempting because it is small. Any water breaks the NPO order before anesthesia.

options.text: "Use ice chips in place of the water."
options.rationale: Ice chips are still oral intake.

options.text: "Ask the surgeon to move the surgery later."
options.rationale: Nothing in the patient calls for a swallow test, so there is no reason to delay surgery.

questions.takeaway: Do not test swallowing in a patient who is NPO. Check the face and speech, and note any signs of aspiration risk.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Three options still put something in the mouth or change the plan. One respects the order that is already there.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: NPO for surgery.

steps.action: Look for a reason to test
steps.detail: Speech clear, face symmetric. None.
Sips and ice chips are intake.

elimination.verdict: Omit the test and keep him NPO.

questions.stem: A patient newly diagnosed with seizures says her family sees the seizures as a spiritual matter and wants their healer to visit before she starts the medication. Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "Tell me what the visit involves so we can plan for it."
options.rationale: Asking about her beliefs lets the nurse fit them into the plan of care and keeps her involved in treatment.

options.text: "Seizures come from the brain, so the medication comes first."
options.rationale: True, and it dismisses the belief before the nurse has learned anything about it.

options.text: "The healer can come once the first dose is in."
options.rationale: Tempting as a compromise, but the nurse has set the terms without asking what the family needs.

options.text: "I will ask the hospital chaplain to see you."
options.rationale: The chaplain is not who she asked for.

questions.takeaway: Cultural and spiritual beliefs are part of the neurologic assessment. Ask about them first, then plan care around them.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Three responses decide for the patient. One asks her.

steps.detail: A visit from the family's healer.
Teaching and bargaining both skip the assessment.
A chaplain is a different person.

elimination.verdict: Ask what the visit involves.

questions.stem: A patient had a weak right hand grip and a right arm that drifted downward this morning. After treatment, which finding best indicates motor function has returned to baseline?

options.text: The right grip is firmer now than it was at the check this morning
options.rationale: Better is not the same as equal. It may still be weaker than the left.

options.text: The patient reports the right arm feels normal
options.rationale: Tempting, but a report is not a measured comparison of the two sides.

options.text: Grips are equal and both arms hold level for 20 seconds
options.rationale: Both sides now match on strength and on drift, which is how motor function is judged.

options.text: The right arm lifts off the bed against gravity
options.rationale: It can lift, but the nurse does not know how it compares with the left.

questions.takeaway: Motor recovery is measured by comparing right with left. Equal grips and no drift mean the asymmetry is gone.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Three options describe the right arm alone. Only one compares the two sides.

steps.detail: Weak grip and drift on the right.
Only one option tests both sides.
Grip and drift are both answered.

elimination.verdict: Equal grips, no drift.

questions.stem: A patient is going home after a mild head injury. The nurse taught his spouse what to watch for tonight. Which statement indicates the teaching was effective?

options.text: "I will let him sleep all night so his brain can rest."
options.rationale: Without waking him the spouse cannot tell sleep from a falling level of consciousness.

options.text: "If his pupils look equal, I will know he is fine."
options.rationale: Tempting, but pupils change late. He can be getting worse with equal pupils.

options.text: "I will call if he complains of feeling tired."
options.rationale: Tiredness is expected. The cue is being hard to wake or newly confused.

options.text: "I will wake him and call if he is hard to rouse."
options.rationale: Level of consciousness changes first, and the spouse has a clear action for it.

questions.takeaway: Level of consciousness is the earliest sign of neurologic change. Teach families to check that the patient wakes easily and makes sense.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Ask which statement lets the spouse catch the earliest change. Pupils and vital signs come late.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A drop in alertness.
Sleeping all night hides it.
Equal pupils do not rule out a decline.

elimination.verdict: Wake him, and call if he is hard to rouse.

questions.scenario: Four patients on a neurology unit are waiting for diagnostic tests.
questions.stem: For each patient, indicate the test the nurse expects to be prescribed.

rows.text: Brief staring spells with lip smacking and no memory of them
rows.rationale: The question is abnormal electrical activity in the brain.

rows.text: Weeks of weakness and muscle wasting in both hands
rows.rationale: The question is whether nerve or muscle is the source.

rows.text: Daily checks of blood flow in the brain arteries after a bleed
rows.rationale: It measures cerebral blood flow at the bedside and can be repeated.

rows.text: Unresponsive after a cardiac arrest; the team asks whether the brain is active
rows.rationale: Brain electrical activity is what an EEG records.

rows.text: Foot drop after a leg injury; the team asks if the nerve is working
rows.rationale: EMG evaluates nerve and muscle disorders.

questions.takeaway: Match the test to the question: EEG for brain electrical activity, EMG for nerve and muscle, transcranial Doppler for cerebral blood flow.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: For each patient ask what the team wants to know: electricity, nerve and muscle, or blood flow.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Staring spells and brain activity after arrest.

steps.action: Find the nerve and muscle questions
steps.detail: Hand wasting and foot drop.
Brain arteries after a bleed.

elimination.verdict: EEG, EMG, Doppler, EEG, EMG.

questions.stem: A patient eating breakfast says, "My face feels strange." Yesterday's cranial nerve check was normal. Which findings does the nurse report? Select all that apply.

options.text: The left corner of the mouth stays down during a smile
options.rationale: New facial asymmetry.

options.text: Both eyebrows rise evenly when the patient looks up
options.rationale: Equal movement of the upper face is a normal finding.

options.text: Pupils are 3 mm, equal and brisk
options.rationale: Normal size, equal and reactive.

options.text: The patient coughs after swallowing a sip of juice
options.rationale: A sign of aspiration risk. The patient also stays NPO.

options.text: Both eyes follow the nurse's finger in every direction
options.rationale: Normal eye movement.

options.text: The voice sounds wet and gurgly after drinking
options.rationale: Fluid is sitting at the airway. This is a swallowing problem.

questions.takeaway: A basic cranial nerve check covers pupils, eye movement, facial symmetry and swallowing. Report whatever differs from baseline.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Judge each finding alone against yesterday's normal check. Do not expect a set number of correct options.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Equal brisk pupils, full eye movement and even eyebrows.
The mouth is unequal. The eyebrows are even.
Cough and wet voice threaten the airway.

elimination.verdict: A, D, F.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old has a tumor pressing on the brainstem. Which assessment is the nurse's priority at each neurologic check?

options.text: Breathing rate and rhythm
options.rationale: The brainstem runs the vital functions. Pressure on it shows in breathing, which also ranks highest by the ABCs.

options.text: Orientation to time and place
options.rationale: Worth checking, but orientation is a thinking function of the cerebrum. It is not what the brainstem controls.

options.text: Recall of the trip to the hospital
options.rationale: Recent memory is a cerebral function. It does not show whether the vital centers are holding.

options.text: Light touch in both feet
options.rationale: Part of a full check, and the least urgent. A sensory change does not threaten life the way a breathing change does.

questions.takeaway: The brainstem controls vital functions. With a brainstem problem, watch breathing first.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: All four belong in a neurologic check. Match the injured part to its job, then pick the job that keeps the patient alive.

steps.action: Name the job of the part
steps.detail: Brainstem means vital functions.
Orientation and memory are both cerebral, so neither stands out.
Breathing outranks sensation in the feet.

elimination.verdict: Breathing rate and rhythm.

questions.stem: After a fall, a 66-year-old opens his eyes only to nail bed pressure, makes moaning sounds with no words and pulls his hand away from the pressure. Which Glasgow Coma Scale score does the nurse record?

options.rationale: The verbal part is off. Moaning with no words is sounds (2). A score of 3 needs actual words.
Eyes open to pain (2), sounds only (2) and withdrawing from the pressure (4) add up to 8.
The eye part is off. A score of 3 is opening to voice, and he opens only to pressure.
The motor part is off. Pulling away from the pressure is withdrawal (4). A score of 3 is abnormal flexion of the arms to the chest.

questions.takeaway: GCS: eyes 4 spontaneous, 3 voice, 2 pain, 1 none. Verbal 5 oriented, 4 confused, 3 words, 2 sounds, 1 none. Motor 6 obeys, 5 localizes, 4 withdraws, 3 flexion, 2 extension, 1 none.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Score each part on its own from the stem, then add. Do not start from the total.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Opens only to nail bed pressure is 2, which removes the option with E3.
Moans without words is sounds, 2, which removes V3.
Pulling away is withdrawal, 4, not flexion, 3.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old with diabetes has had tingling in both feet for 2 years. At a clinic visit, which report needs immediate follow up?

options.text: The tingling is worse at night in bed
options.rationale: A long standing pattern in both feet. It is uncomfortable and it is not new.

options.text: Cannot judge bath water temperature with the feet
options.rationale: A real safety problem that needs teaching. It fits the same chronic loss in both feet, so it is not the urgent one.

options.text: Numbness in the left arm and left leg since this morning
options.rationale: New since this morning and on one side only. A new sensory change with a difference between sides is reported now, and it does not fit the long standing pattern in both feet.

options.text: Numbness in both feet has slowly reached the ankles
options.rationale: Tempting because it is progressing. It is gradual and equal on both sides, so it fits the chronic pattern and is not a sudden change.

questions.takeaway: Compare right with left and now with baseline. Chronic and equal in both feet is this patient's baseline. New and one sided is a change that is reported now.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Sort each report by new or chronic, then by one side or both sides.

steps.detail: Three reports are long standing or gradual. One began this morning.
Three involve both feet. One involves an arm and a leg on the same side.
The bath water report needs teaching today, not an urgent workup.

elimination.verdict: Numbness in the left arm and left leg since this morning.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews Glasgow Coma Scale scores (range 3 to 15, 15 is fully alert) for four patients on a neurology unit. Which patient does the nurse report to the provider immediately?

options.text: Score of 11 yesterday and 11 today
options.rationale: Low but steady. No change from this patient's baseline.

options.text: Score of 15 one hour ago and 13 now
options.rationale: The only score that is falling. A declining score signals deterioration and calls for immediate action, and this drop happened within an hour.

options.text: Score of 13 this morning and 14 now
options.rationale: The score is rising, which is improvement.

options.text: Score of 9 for the past three days
options.rationale: The lowest number here, which is the trap. It is unchanged, so it is less urgent than a new drop.

questions.takeaway: Trend beats a single score. A declining GCS signals deterioration and is acted on immediately. A steady 9 is less urgent than 15 falling to 13 in an hour.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Read each option as a direction: steady, up or down. The lowest number is not the answer.

steps.detail: Two are steady, one is up, one is down.
15 to 13 in one hour is a falling trend.

elimination.verdict: 15 to 13. Call now.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old is admitted to the unit with new tingling in the right hand. No neurologic exam was charted in the emergency department. Which assessment does the nurse perform?

options.text: A complete neurologic exam to set the baseline
options.rationale: A new admission with a neurologic concern and nothing charted gets the comprehensive exam. Later checks have nothing to compare with unless a baseline exists.

options.text: A focused check of right hand sensation and grip
options.rationale: Tempting because a focused check targets the suspected problem. It is used to follow a known baseline, and this patient has none.

options.text: A Glasgow Coma Scale score each shift
options.rationale: The scale tracks level of consciousness. It does not measure sensation or strength, so it misses the reason for admission.

options.text: Orientation questions with different wording each shift
options.rationale: Good technique for one part of the exam. It leaves cranial nerves, movement and sensation unchecked.

questions.takeaway: Comprehensive on admission or with a new neurologic concern. Focused after that, to compare against the baseline.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two options are right at different times. The missing baseline in the stem tells you which time this is.

steps.detail: Nothing is charted, so no baseline exists.
The complete exam contains the hand check, the consciousness check and orientation.
It comes later, once there is something to compare with.

elimination.verdict: A complete neurologic exam to set the baseline.

questions.stem: The nurse checks the pupils of four patients admitted after head injuries. Which finding requires the nurse to intervene?

options.text: Both pupils 3 mm, round, constricting briskly to light
options.rationale: Inside the normal 2 to 6 mm range, equal, round and brisk.

options.text: Both pupils 4 mm, round, constricting briskly to light
options.rationale: Inside the normal range with a brisk reaction.

options.text: Both pupils 6 mm, round, constricting briskly to light
options.rationale: Large, which is the trap, but 6 mm is still inside the 2 to 6 mm range, and the pupils are equal and brisk.

options.text: Both pupils 5 mm, round, constricting sluggishly to light
options.rationale: The reaction is off. The size is inside 2 to 6 mm, but a sluggish reaction is an early warning of pressure on cranial nerve III.

questions.takeaway: Normal pupils are 2 to 6 mm, equal, round and brisk. Record size in millimeters. Sluggish is an early warning; fixed dilated or pinpoint is late.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Hold each option against two specifications: size within 2 to 6 mm and a brisk reaction. The largest pupil is not automatically the abnormal one.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 3, 4, 5 and 6 mm are all inside 2 to 6 mm, so size removes no one.
Three are brisk. One is sluggish.

elimination.verdict: 5 mm and sluggish. Report it.

questions.stem: A 77-year-old with diabetes ate little breakfast after her morning insulin. At 1100 she is suddenly confused. Oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. Which does the nurse check next?

options.text: Temperature
options.rationale: Infection is on the list of causes. It comes after glucose, and the stem points to glucose.

options.text: The list of medications given today
options.rationale: Tempting because insulin is the suspect. Reading the chart does not show what the insulin has done to her now.

options.text: Fingerstick blood glucose
options.rationale: Oxygen is already checked and normal. Insulin with little food makes low glucose the likely cause, and it takes seconds to check and is quick to treat.

options.text: This morning's electrolyte results
options.rationale: Electrolytes can cause confusion. Morning results do not show her state at 1100, and the stem does not point to them.

questions.takeaway: Sudden confusion: oxygen, then glucose, then infection, medications and electrolytes. Start where the stem leaves off.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The first check is already done in the stem. Do not repeat it. Take the next one, and let the insulin cue confirm it.

steps.detail: Saturation is 97%, so oxygen is answered.
Insulin given and little food eaten.
A fingerstick gives a current answer. A chart review and old results do not.

elimination.verdict: Fingerstick blood glucose.

questions.stem: After a head injury, a patient at 0800 opens his eyes to voice, says single words and pulls his hand away from pressure. Which finding at 1000 shows improvement?

options.text: Eyes open on their own, moaning sounds, pulls his hand away from pressure
options.rationale: Tempting because the eyes are better (4). The voice fell from words to sounds (2), so the total is still 10.

options.text: Eyes open to pressure, confused sentences, pulls his hand away from pressure
options.rationale: The voice is better (4), but the eyes now need pressure (2). The total is still 10.

options.text: Eyes open to voice, confused sentences, reaches to push the nurse's hand away
options.rationale: Eyes 3, confused speech 4 and localizing 5 make 12. At 0800 the total was 3 + 3 + 4 = 10, so the score has risen by 2.

options.text: Eyes open to voice, single words, both arms flex to the chest
options.rationale: Flexing the arms to the chest is abnormal flexion (3), lower than pulling away (4). The total fell to 9.

questions.takeaway: Score each part of the Glasgow Coma Scale at both times and compare totals. One part improving can hide another part falling.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Do not pick the option with the single best looking finding. Total each one and compare with 0800.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Eyes to voice 3, words 3, withdraws 4. Total 10.
Only one total is higher than 10.

elimination.verdict: Eyes to voice, confused sentences, pushes the nurse's hand away: 12.

questions.stem: A 73-year-old who speaks mainly Vietnamese answers the orientation questions incorrectly when his teenage grandson translates. He is awake and calm. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Chart that he is disoriented to place and time
options.rationale: Not yet. The wrong answers may come from the translation and not from his thinking.

options.text: Ask the grandson to repeat each question slowly
options.rationale: Tempting because it is quick. The same untrained translator leaves the same doubt about what was asked and answered.

options.text: Switch to yes or no questions in English with gestures
options.rationale: Gestures cannot test orientation in a patient whose main language is not English.

options.text: Repeat the questions through a qualified interpreter
options.rationale: Language is ruled out as the cause before a patient is called confused. A trained interpreter gives answers the nurse can trust as the baseline.

questions.takeaway: Before calling a patient confused, rule out a hearing, vision or language barrier. Use a qualified interpreter, not a family member.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the wrong answers measure his thinking or the way the question reached him.

steps.detail: Answers that pass through a teenager are not reliable data.
Charting disorientation draws a conclusion from that data.
