options.rationale: A rising pulse with lightheadedness is early blood loss, and a dry dressing does not rule out bleeding the nurse cannot see.

options.text: Lingering effect of the sedation
options.rationale: Sedation slows the pulse and makes a client drowsy. It does not raise the rate by 30.

options.text: Anxiety about the biopsy results
options.rationale: Possible, and never the first explanation for a new tachycardia after an invasive procedure.

questions.takeaway: After lung biopsy watch for two things: pneumothorax and bleeding. A climbing pulse with equal breath sounds points to bleeding.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides.
questions.strategy: Use the stem data to rule out. Equal breath sounds argue against one complication and leave the other.

steps.detail: Air or blood.
Equal sounds make collapsed lung unlikely.
Up 30 with lightheadedness is volume loss.

elimination.verdict: Internal bleeding.

questions.stem: A client on a simple face mask at 6 L/min keeps removing it to eat, and the SpO2 falls to 87% during each meal. Which plan is best?

options.text: Feed the client quickly so the mask is off for less time
options.rationale: Rushing a breathless client raises the risk of aspiration.

options.text: Hold solid food until the oxygen can be discontinued
options.rationale: Nutrition is part of recovery, and a device change solves the problem.

options.text: Lower the mask flow to 3 L/min and lift it between bites
options.rationale: A simple mask needs its minimum flow to flush exhaled carbon dioxide.

options.text: Request an order for a nasal cannula during meals
options.rationale: A cannula delivers oxygen while leaving the mouth free.

questions.takeaway: Match the device to the activity. A cannula lets a client eat and still receive oxygen. A mask run at low flow rebreathes carbon dioxide.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Reject any plan that gives up oxygen or food. One option keeps both.

steps.action: Cut the plan that drops flow
steps.detail: Low flow in a mask traps carbon dioxide.

steps.action: Cut the plans that trade one need for another
steps.detail: Rushing or holding food.
Cannula at meals.

elimination.verdict: Nasal cannula for meals.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old arrives at a clinic front desk with chills, a severe headache and body aches that began abruptly this morning. The waiting room is full. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Give the client a mask and seat him away from others
options.rationale: Source control comes first. It protects the room while the visit proceeds.

options.text: Obtain a nasal swab for rapid influenza testing
options.rationale: Needed, and it can follow once others are protected.

options.text: Ask whether he received this season's vaccine
options.rationale: Useful history that changes nothing in the first minute.

options.text: Offer acetaminophen for the headache and chills
options.rationale: Comfort comes after transmission is contained.

questions.takeaway: Abrupt fever, headache and myalgia is influenza until shown otherwise. It is highly contagious, so contain first, then test and treat.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides.
questions.strategy: The stem adds one detail on purpose: a full waiting room. Choose the action that answers it.

steps.detail: Other clients are at risk right now.
Testing, history and comfort all help him and can wait minutes.

elimination.verdict: Mask and separate.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old is one day past abdominal surgery, afebrile, breathing shallowly, with faint breath sounds at the bases. Which actions does the nurse include to prevent pneumonia? Select all that apply.

options.text: Give the prescribed analgesic before breathing exercises
options.rationale: Incisional pain after abdominal surgery commonly keeps breaths shallow. Treating it makes deep breathing possible.

options.text: Have the client splint the incision and cough every 2 hours
options.rationale: Coughing clears secretions before they become a place for infection.

options.text: Help the client walk in the hall three times today
options.rationale: Moving expands the lungs and mobilizes secretions.

options.text: Keep the client flat to protect the incision
options.rationale: Lying flat and still lets the bases collapse and secretions pool.

options.text: Request an antibiotic to prevent infection
options.rationale: The client is afebrile and no sign of infection is given. Prevention here is movement and airway clearance.

options.text: Limit oral fluids to keep secretions from increasing
options.rationale: Fluids thin secretions so they can be coughed out. The slides advise generous intake unless restricted.

questions.takeaway: Pneumonia prevention is cough, turn, move and deep breathe, with pain controlled and fluids adequate.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Judge each option by one test: does it open the bases or move secretions?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Analgesia, coughing with a splint, walking.

steps.action: Drop what keeps the client still
steps.detail: Flat positioning.

steps.action: Drop what treats a problem not present
steps.detail: Antibiotics, fluid limits.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C.

questions.stem: A resident with fever, cough and a roommate who has COVID 19 has a rapid antigen test result that is negative for COVID 19. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Stop the precautions and return her to group meals
options.rationale: A single negative antigen test in a symptomatic, exposed client does not rule out infection.

options.text: Repeat the same antigen test at once on the other nostril
options.rationale: Repeating the less sensitive test right away adds little.

options.text: Document the result and recheck her temperature tomorrow
options.rationale: Waiting leaves other residents exposed if the result is false.

options.text: Continue the precautions and obtain a PCR (nucleic acid) test
options.rationale: A nucleic acid test is more sensitive, and precautions stay until it results.

questions.takeaway: Symptoms plus exposure outweigh a negative antigen test. Keep precautions and confirm with NAAT or PCR.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides.
questions.strategy: Compare the test result with the clinical picture. When they disagree, protect others and get the better test.

steps.detail: Fever, cough and a known exposure.
Stopping or waiting.
PCR.

elimination.verdict: Keep precautions, send PCR.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old on day 5 of COVID 19 isolation says, "Staff rush in and out. I feel like I am being punished." Which response is best?

options.text: "The precautions protect other clients, so they must stay."
options.rationale: True, and it defends the rule instead of answering the feeling.

options.text: "Most people feel better once the first week is over."
options.rationale: Reassurance that dismisses what the client just said.

options.text: "I can ask the provider about medicine to help you relax."
options.rationale: Treats loneliness as a symptom to medicate before it has been explored.

options.text: "Being alone this long is hard. Let me sit and plan your day with you."
options.rationale: Names the feeling, gives time, and involves the client in a plan for contact and routine.

questions.takeaway: Isolation protects others and costs the client contact. Acknowledge it and build in presence, calls and a predictable routine.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides.
questions.strategy: Look for the response that stays with the client's words and offers the nurse's time.

strategies: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings

steps.detail: Correct facts do not answer a feeling.
It closes the conversation.
Acknowledge and plan together.

elimination.verdict: Acknowledge and sit down to plan.

questions.stem: An assistive personnel obtains pulse oximetry readings on a 79-year-old. Which action by the assistive personnel needs correction?

options.text: Removes nail polish from one finger before applying the sensor
options.rationale: Correct. Nail polish makes the reading inaccurate.

options.text: Moves the sensor to the warmer hand when one hand feels cool
options.rationale: Correct. A cool hand has less blood flow at the fingertip, and poor circulation makes the reading inaccurate.

options.text: Charts a reading from a cold finger while the client shivers
options.rationale: Cold extremities and movement both make the reading inaccurate. The number is not charted until it comes from a warm, still site.

options.text: Asks the client to rest the hand still on the bed
options.rationale: Correct. Movement distorts the reading.

questions.takeaway: Pulse oximetry is inaccurate with poor circulation, movement, cold extremities, nail polish or poor placement. Fix the site before trusting the number.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Run each action against the list of things that spoil a reading: poor circulation, cold, motion, polish, placement.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Check each action against the list
steps.detail: Polish removed, warmer hand chosen and hand held still all remove a source of error.

steps.action: Find the action that keeps two errors
steps.detail: A cold finger on a shivering client is both cold and moving.

elimination.verdict: Charting the reading from a cold finger on a shivering client.

questions.stem: An 86-year-old with pneumonia says his breathing feels fine. SpO2 is 87% on room air with a steady waveform and the respiratory rate is 28. Oxygen is prescribed for an SpO2 below 92%. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Apply the prescribed oxygen and stay to watch the response
options.rationale: Hypoxemia is treated promptly. The reading is reliable, the rate is fast, and an older adult has a weaker response to low oxygen, so feeling fine does not rule it out.

options.text: Move the sensor to another finger and compare the readings
options.rationale: Tempting because oximeters do misread. The steady waveform and the fast respiratory rate both say this number is real.

options.text: Ask him to rate his breathlessness and recheck in an hour
options.rationale: Dyspnea is subjective and worth asking about, but his report is already given and waiting leaves a saturation of 87% untreated.

options.text: Walk him in the hall to see how he tolerates activity
options.rationale: Activity raises oxygen demand in a client who is already hypoxemic at rest.

questions.takeaway: Aging blunts the response to hypoxia. When a reliable SpO2 is low, treat the number even if the older adult feels fine.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options check or recheck. The stem already tells you the reading is good, so the assessment is done and action is due.

steps.action: Decide whether the reading is trustworthy
steps.detail: Steady waveform and a rate of 28 agree with 87%.
An older adult may not feel short of breath when oxygen is low.
Rechecking later and walking him both leave the hypoxemia untreated.

elimination.verdict: Apply the prescribed oxygen and watch the response.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old who smokes a pack a day says, "I know it is bad for me, but with my job right now I am not ready to quit." Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "Let us pick a quit date within the next two weeks."
options.rationale: A quit date belongs to the assist step. He has just said he is not willing, so a date set for him will not hold.

options.text: "What would have to change for you to think about cutting back?"
options.rationale: He has said he is not ready. For a client who is not willing to try now, the nurse gives information, keeps the conversation open and listens for any wish to cut back.

options.text: "I will ask the provider to prescribe a nicotine patch for you today."
options.rationale: Medication works when paired with counseling in a client who is willing to try. He is not there yet.

options.text: "Your lungs will only get worse if you keep smoking."
options.rationale: Clear advice is one step of the 5 As, but he already says he knows it is bad for him. Repeating a warning after he has stated he is not ready closes the conversation.

questions.takeaway: Assess readiness before you assist. A client who is not ready gets information and an open question, and the nurse asks again at the next visit.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Three options push a plan or a warning onto him. One asks him a question. The stem's cue is "not ready".

steps.action: Find where he is in the 5 As
steps.detail: His own words answer the assess step: not willing now.
A quit date and a patch are for a client who is ready.
A repeated warning tells; the open question involves him.

elimination.verdict: Ask what would have to change. Keep the conversation open.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old with chronic bronchitis is seen for a routine visit. Which statement requires follow up by the nurse?

options.text: "I cough up white mucus most mornings, the same as always."
options.rationale: A long standing pattern that the client reports as unchanged.

options.text: "I have slept on two pillows for years."
options.rationale: Chronic and stable. A change in the number of pillows would matter.

options.text: "Since last month I sit down halfway through getting dressed."
options.rationale: A new limit on a daily activity. A change in what the client can do tells the nurse the disease is progressing.

options.text: "I still stop once on the stairs to my apartment, same as last year."
options.rationale: Limited, and no different from a year ago.

questions.takeaway: In a client with chronic lung disease, compare each report with the client's own baseline. A new limit in daily activities is the finding to pursue.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Every statement describes a symptom. Look for the time words: three say unchanged, one says since last month.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Mark each statement new or old
steps.detail: Same as always, for years, same as last year are all old.
Sitting down while dressing started last month.
Daily activities are shrinking, so the condition is worse.

elimination.verdict: The client who now sits down halfway through dressing.

questions.stem: After two liters of IV fluid, a client has new crackles at both lung bases that remain after coughing. The respiratory rate rose from 18 to 26. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Have the client cough again and listen once more
options.rationale: Coughing clears secretions in the large airways. These sounds already stayed after a cough, so repeating it adds nothing.

options.text: Encourage oral fluids to thin the secretions
options.rationale: Crackles that follow two liters of fluid point to fluid in the lungs. More fluid makes that worse.

options.text: Coach hourly deep breathing with an incentive spirometer at the bedside
options.rationale: Helps when small airways are collapsed. It does not remove fluid, and the rising rate needs attention now.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed and report the change
options.rationale: Crackles mean fluid. New crackles with a rising rate after a large fluid volume need upright positioning and a prompt report so the fluid plan can change.

questions.takeaway: Crackles mean fluid in the airways. When crackles are new, remain after a cough and come after a fluid load, sit the client up and report.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two options treat the sound as secretions. The stem says the sounds stayed after coughing, which rules secretions out.

steps.detail: Crackles mean fluid; secretions give rhonchi.
Sounds from secretions change with a cough. These did not.
Two liters went in and the rate is climbing.

elimination.verdict: Raise the head of the bed and report the change.

questions.stem: The nurse cares for a 72-year-old admitted this morning with pneumonia whose oxygen was just started. Which task does the nurse assign to the assistive personnel?

options.text: Measure the respiratory rate and SpO2 after the client walks
options.rationale: Collecting and reporting measurements is within the assistive personnel's role. The nurse interprets them.

options.text: Listen to the lung bases and report whether the crackles have cleared
options.rationale: Auscultation is assessment and stays with the nurse.

options.text: Decide whether the oxygen can come off while the client eats
options.rationale: Judging the response to oxygen and changing therapy is the nurse's decision under the prescription.

options.text: Explain to the client why smoking materials cannot be kept in the room
options.rationale: Initial teaching stays with the nurse.

questions.takeaway: Assistive personnel collect data and report it. Assessment, teaching and judging the response to oxygen stay with the nurse.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Look at the verb in each option: measure, listen, decide, explain. Only one is a task without judgment.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Listen, decide and explain are assessment, evaluation and teaching.
Counting respirations and reading an oximeter are routine measurements.
The assistive personnel reports the numbers and the nurse interprets them.

elimination.verdict: Measure the respiratory rate and SpO2 after the client walks.

questions.stem: An assistive personnel gives the nurse four reports at 1000. Which report does the nurse act on first?

options.text: "The client in 4 was winded after walking back from the bathroom and is resting now."
options.rationale: Shortness of breath with activity that settles with rest needs assessment soon, but the client is recovering.

options.text: "The client in 7 has lips that look blue gray."
options.rationale: Cyanosis is a concerning sign and a late one. This client is not oxygenating and needs the nurse now.

options.text: "The client in 9 coughed up yellow mucus into a tissue."
options.rationale: Sputum color is assessed and may need a specimen. It can wait a few minutes.

options.text: "The client in 12 says the cannula makes her nose feel dry."
options.rationale: A comfort problem with a simple fix after the urgent client is seen.

questions.takeaway: Cyanosis is a late sign of poor oxygenation. A report of blue or gray lips outranks reports of exertional breathlessness, sputum color or discomfort.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: None of the reports includes a number. Sort them into expected or settling findings and the one sign that oxygen is not reaching the tissues.

steps.action: Find the sign of failing oxygenation
steps.detail: Blue gray lips are cyanosis, which appears late.
Breathlessness after walking that is easing with rest is less urgent than cyanosis.
Sputum color and a dry nose are real and can wait a few minutes.

elimination.verdict: The client whose lips look blue gray.

questions.stem: A client is taught what to expect during a bedside thoracentesis. Which statement shows the teaching was effective?

options.text: "I will take slow deep breaths while the needle is in to help the fluid drain."
options.rationale: Deep breaths move the lung toward the needle. The client breathes quietly and holds still.

options.text: "If I need to cough, I will get it over with quickly."
options.rationale: A cough while the needle is in place can injure the lung.

options.text: "I will lie flat on my back so the doctor can reach my chest."
options.rationale: The client sits up and leans forward over a table.

options.text: "I will hold still, and tell you before I move if I feel a cough coming."
options.rationale: No moving, coughing or deep breathing while the needle is in. Warning the team lets the provider pause.

questions.takeaway: During thoracentesis the client stays still: no moving, coughing or deep breaths while the needle is in.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Three statements have the client doing something with the chest during the procedure. One has the client hold still and speak up.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Picture the needle next to the lung
steps.detail: Any chest movement brings the lung toward it.
Deep breaths and a quick cough both move the lung.
The position is upright, leaning forward.

elimination.verdict: Hold still and warn the team before a cough.

questions.stem: Forty minutes after a needle lung biopsy done with IV sedation, a client is asleep with snoring respirations. SpO2 has slipped from 97% to 91%. The chest rises equally on both sides. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Wake the client and lift the chin to open the airway
options.rationale: After a biopsy with sedation the nurse watches sedation and the airway. Snoring in a sleeping, sedated client means the airway is partly blocked, and rousing the client and opening the airway fixes the cause.

options.text: Apply the prescribed oxygen by nasal cannula
options.rationale: Tempting because the saturation is falling. Oxygen does not open a blocked airway, and the cause has to be addressed first.

options.text: Report a possible pneumothorax to the provider
options.rationale: Pneumothorax is watched for after a biopsy. Equal chest rise and a snoring sound point to the upper airway, and the airway is opened before any call.

options.text: Suction the mouth and throat to clear secretions
options.rationale: Snoring comes from a relaxed airway in a sedated client. Nothing in the stem describes secretions.

questions.takeaway: After a lung biopsy, monitor sedation and the airway, then watch for bleeding, pneumothorax and distress. Snoring in a sedated client is an airway problem: rouse the client and open the airway first.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two options treat the falling number and two treat a cause. Use the snoring and the sedation to name the cause before you pick.

steps.detail: Snoring in a sleeping client who was sedated 40 minutes ago is a partly blocked airway.
The chest rises equally, and airway comes before a call.

steps.action: Compare oxygen with opening the airway
steps.detail: Oxygen treats the number. Rousing the client and lifting the chin treats the cause.

elimination.verdict: Wake the client and lift the chin to open the airway.

questions.stem: A client was placed on a nonrebreather mask during an urgent episode last night. For six hours the client has breathed easily with an SpO2 above the prescribed goal. The prescription allows titration. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Keep the nonrebreather in place to hold a reserve in case of another episode
options.rationale: Tempting, since the client did well on it. More oxygen than the goal needs adds risk of oxygen toxicity and absorption atelectasis.

options.text: Remove the oxygen and observe the client on room air
options.rationale: Stopping all at once skips the step down and risks hypoxemia. The nurse lowers the oxygen in steps under the prescription.

options.text: Leave the mask on and check that the reservoir stays inflated
options.rationale: A correct check for this device, but it keeps a high concentration the client no longer needs.

options.text: Step the oxygen down as prescribed and watch the response
options.rationale: Oxygen is given at the lowest effective concentration that meets the prescribed goal, and the nurse monitors the response to each change.

questions.takeaway: A nonrebreather is for urgent needs. Once the goal is met and the client is stable, use the lowest effective oxygen and monitor the response.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Keeping everything and removing everything are opposite extremes. Look for the option that lowers oxygen in steps and checks the client.

steps.action: Compare the client with the goal
steps.detail: Above goal for six hours and breathing easily.
Do not keep a high concentration and do not stop it all at once.

steps.action: Pick the option with a check
steps.detail: Step down, then monitor the response.

elimination.verdict: Step the oxygen down as prescribed and watch the response.

questions.stem: A client has received IV antibiotics for pneumonia for three days. Which finding best indicates the treatment is not working?

options.text: She still coughs up thick yellow sputum each morning and after meals
options.rationale: A productive cough continues during recovery and helps clear the airways.

options.text: The respiratory rate rose from 22 to 30 and oxygen need is up
options.rationale: The pneumonia plan aims at gas exchange. A rising respiratory rate and a rising oxygen need show it is getting worse despite treatment.

options.text: She tires easily and naps after her bath
options.rationale: Fatigue is expected while recovering from pneumonia.

options.text: Crackles are still heard over the affected lobe on both shifts
options.rationale: Lung sounds take time to clear. Persistent crackles alone do not show failure.

questions.takeaway: Judge pneumonia treatment by gas exchange. A rising respiratory rate and a rising oxygen need mean it is failing, whatever the cough sounds like.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Three findings are things that linger in a recovering client. One is a trend moving the wrong way.

steps.detail: Adequate gas exchange.
Sputum, fatigue and crackles persist during recovery.
Rate up and oxygen need up.

elimination.verdict: Rising respiratory rate with a rising oxygen need.

questions.stem: A client with pneumonia is lying flat, with a weak, wet cough, a respiratory rate of 24 and an SpO2 of 90% on the prescribed oxygen. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Offer a glass of water to thin the secretions
options.rationale: Hydration thins secretions over hours. It does nothing for the airway in the next minute, and drinking while flat is unsafe.

options.text: Collect a sputum specimen now while the cough is still productive
options.rationale: Useful data, but the client needs help moving air before a specimen is collected.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed and coach deep breaths and a cough
options.rationale: The cues are complete: flat, retained secretions, borderline saturation. Positioning, deep breathing and coughing support ventilation and keep the airways clear right away.

options.text: Listen to all lung fields from apex to base
options.rationale: Assessment usually comes first, but the stem already gives enough to act, and auscultation is better done upright.

questions.takeaway: When the cues already show retained secretions and a low saturation, act: sit the client up and clear the airway. Positioning is fast and helps almost every breathing problem.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Assessment before intervention applies when data are missing. Here the stem hands you the data.

steps.action: Check whether more data are needed
steps.detail: Position, cough quality, rate and SpO2 are all given.
Upright position and a coached cough.
Specimen, fluids and a full auscultation follow.

elimination.verdict: Raise the head of the bed and coach deep breathing and coughing.

questions.stem: A client with COVID 19 is breathing easily at 18 breaths per minute with an SpO2 of 96% on room air. The temperature is 38.9 C, the client vomited twice today and feels dizzy on standing. Which problem does the nurse address first?

options.text: Impaired gas exchange
options.rationale: The usual first concern in a respiratory illness, but the rate, effort and saturation given are all normal.

options.text: Anxiety related to isolation
options.rationale: A real concern in COVID 19. Nothing in these cues points to it.

options.text: Activity intolerance
options.rationale: The dizziness comes on with standing and follows fluid loss, so it points to volume, not to oxygen demand.

options.text: Fluid volume deficit
options.rationale: Fever and vomiting are fluid losses, and dizziness on standing is the sign that volume is already low. It is also a fall risk.

questions.takeaway: Rank hypotheses by the cues in front of you. When breathing is stable in COVID 19, fever, vomiting and dizziness on standing make fluid loss the first problem.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The breathing option is the reflex pick. Check the stem's breathing data before choosing it.

steps.action: Clear the airway and breathing data
steps.detail: 18, easy and 96% on room air.
Fever, vomiting, dizzy on standing all point to low volume.
An actual fluid problem outranks problems with no cues.

elimination.verdict: Fluid volume deficit.

questions.stem: At the start of the shift the nurse receives report on four clients. Which client does the nurse see first?

options.text: Pneumonia, crackles in the right lower lobe and a temperature of 38.4 C
options.rationale: Expected findings in a client being treated for pneumonia.

options.text: Lung biopsy one hour ago, sudden sharp chest pain and a respiratory rate of 28
options.rationale: After a lung biopsy the nurse watches for pneumothorax and worsening distress. Sudden pain with rapid breathing is new and unstable.

options.text: Thoracentesis three hours ago, reporting soreness at the needle site
options.rationale: Mild soreness at the site is expected.

options.text: Bronchoscopy four hours ago, asking when the sore throat will ease
options.rationale: The procedure was hours ago and the complaint is a comfort question.

questions.takeaway: After a lung biopsy or thoracentesis, sudden pain, rapid breathing or worsening distress means pneumothorax until proven otherwise.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Three clients have what their condition or procedure normally brings. One has something sudden.

steps.detail: Crackles and fever in pneumonia, site soreness, sore throat.
Sudden sharp pain and a respiratory rate of 28.
A needle through the lung an hour ago.

elimination.verdict: The client one hour after lung biopsy.

questions.nursesNote: 1400: 69-year-old admitted this morning with cough and fever. Sitting upright in bed, alert and oriented. Pauses for breath after every 3 or 4 words; neck muscles tighten with each inspiration. Respiratory rate 18 and even. Left side of the chest rises less than the right. Loud, high pitched breath sounds over the trachea. Soft, low pitched breath sounds at the right base. New crackles at the left base.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that require follow up.

segments.text: Sitting upright in bed, alert and oriented
segments.rationale: Normal.

segments.text: Pauses for breath after every 3 or 4 words
segments.rationale: Short phrases show a high work of breathing.

segments.text: neck muscles tighten with each inspiration
segments.rationale: Accessory muscle use. Normal quiet breathing does not need them.

segments.text: Respiratory rate 18 and even
segments.rationale: Within normal limits.

segments.text: Left side of the chest rises less than the right
segments.rationale: Unequal expansion. Symmetry is part of every chest inspection, and a side that lags may not be moving air well.

segments.text: Loud, high pitched breath sounds over the trachea
segments.rationale: Bronchial sounds are normal over the trachea. They are abnormal only out over the lung fields.

segments.text: Soft, low pitched breath sounds at the right base
segments.rationale: Vesicular sounds, the expected finding at the bases.

segments.text: New crackles at the left base
segments.rationale: Crackles mean fluid in the airways, and these are new.

questions.takeaway: Know the normals so you do not over highlight: vesicular at the bases and bronchial over the trachea are expected. Short phrases, accessory muscles, unequal expansion and new crackles are not.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: One normal finding is written to sound alarming. Loud, high pitched sounds are expected over the trachea; location decides.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Start with how the client breathes
steps.detail: Short phrases and working neck muscles show effort, even with a rate of 18.
The left side lags and has new crackles.
Alert, rate 18, bronchial over the trachea, vesicular at the base.

elimination.verdict: Short phrases, neck muscle use, unequal expansion and new left base crackles.

chapters.title: Assessment of the Skin, Hair, and Nails

questions.stem: A client with a dark skin tone has a platelet count of 18,000/mm3. Which assessment best detects new petechiae in this client?

options.text: Inspect the shins and forearms under bright light
options.rationale: Tempting because petechiae often start on the legs, but they are often not visible on darkly pigmented skin even in good light.

options.text: Palpate the lower legs for raised spots
options.rationale: Petechiae are flat, so there is nothing to feel.

options.text: Inspect the oral mucosa and conjunctiva
options.rationale: These areas carry little pigment, so pinpoint bleeding shows there when the skin hides it.

options.text: Press a glass slide over the lower legs
options.rationale: Diascopy checks blanching of a lesion you can already see. It does not find hidden petechiae.

questions.takeaway: In dark skin, look for petechiae inside the mouth and on the conjunctiva.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options are inspection. The skin tone in the stem decides which site will actually show the finding.

steps.detail: Low platelets mean you are hunting for bleeding into the skin.
Petechiae are flat, and a slide needs a visible lesion.
Dark pigment hides petechiae on the legs. Mucosa does not.

elimination.verdict: Oral mucosa and conjunctiva.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old in a skilled nursing unit has hard, thick, overhanging toenails and asks the nurse to trim them today. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Soak both feet in warm water to soften the nails
options.rationale: Correct preparation for hard, thick nails, which makes it tempting. It is a step in trimming, and the nurse does not yet know that trimming is allowed.

options.text: Find out whether agency policy lets nurses trim them
options.rationale: Many agencies reserve thick toenails in older adults for a podiatrist. Scope is settled before any step of the procedure begins.

options.text: Cut the nails straight across at the toe tips
options.rationale: The right technique once trimming is approved. It is not the first step.

options.text: Request an antifungal for the thickened toenails
options.rationale: Thick, layered toenails are common with aging. Nail appearance alone does not establish a fungal infection.

questions.takeaway: Thick toenails in an older adult: agency policy decides who trims them. If approved, soak hard nails and cut straight across.
questions.coverage: Not in Lecture PPT. Covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Three options start the job or treat the nails. One asks whether the job is the nurse's to do.

steps.detail: Thick nails alone do not prove fungus.

steps.action: Notice the soak and the cut belong together
steps.detail: Both are steps of trimming.

steps.action: Ask what must be true before trimming
steps.detail: The agency has to allow it.

elimination.verdict: Confirm the policy first.

questions.stem: A client had a punch biopsy on the forearm this morning and plans to swim laps tonight. Which statement indicates the discharge teaching was effective?

options.text: "I will cover it with a waterproof bandage before I swim laps tonight."
options.rationale: The dressing stays in place and dry for at least 8 hours, so swimming tonight is out either way.

options.text: "Redness that spreads this week is part of normal healing."
options.rationale: Spreading redness or heavy drainage is reported, not expected.

options.text: "I will scrub off any crust with soap so it stays clean."
options.rationale: Crusts are loosened gently with tap water or saline after the dressing comes off.

options.text: "I will skip the pool and keep the dressing dry until tomorrow."
options.rationale: The dressing stays dry and in place for at least 8 hours, then the site is cleaned daily.

questions.takeaway: After a biopsy, keep the dressing dry and in place for at least 8 hours, then clean daily and report redness or drainage.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The swim plan is the cue. Look for the statement that changes that plan.

steps.detail: Swimming tonight would wet the dressing inside 8 hours.
Spreading redness is reported. Scrubbing a crust harms new tissue.
A covered dressing is still taken into the pool inside the 8 hours it must stay dry.

elimination.verdict: Skips the pool and keeps the dressing dry.

questions.stem: A hospitalized client with gel nail enhancements on every finger has a pulse oximeter that will not read reliably. Which plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Remove the enhancement from one nail for assessment
options.rationale: One bare nail gives a place to check color, capillary refill and the oximeter with the least loss to the client.

options.text: Ask the client to have all enhancements removed today
options.rationale: It would work, which makes it tempting. One nail is enough, so removing all of them is more than the assessment needs.

options.text: Estimate capillary refill through the enhancement
options.rationale: The coating hides the nail bed, so the result means nothing.

options.text: Record the nails as unable to assess
options.rationale: The nurse still needs perfusion data and has a simple way to get it.

questions.takeaway: For a hospitalized client with nail enhancements, remove the enhancement from one nail so the nail bed can be assessed.
questions.coverage: Not in Lecture PPT. Covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options solve the problem. Pick the one that solves it with the least cost to the client.

steps.action: Cut the options that give up the data
steps.detail: Guessing through gel and skipping the assessment both leave you blind.

steps.action: Compare one nail with all nails
steps.detail: Both give access to a nail bed.
One nail meets the need.

elimination.verdict: Remove one enhancement.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old reports an itchy rash since yesterday that began on the trunk and is spreading to the arms. The client first saw a cardiologist 12 days ago. Which question does the nurse ask first?

options.text: "Have you changed your soap or laundry detergent lately?"
options.rationale: A fair question, and a contact rash would be the runner up. Contact rashes stay where the product touched. This one started on the trunk and is spreading.

options.text: "Does anyone in your family have a skin condition?"
options.rationale: Part of a full history. It does not explain a rash that began yesterday.

options.text: "Have you started any new medicine or supplement recently?"
options.rationale: A new specialist visit often means a new drug, and a rash that starts on the trunk and spreads outward fits a drug reaction. This is the question that can change today's plan.

options.text: "How much time have you spent in the sun this week?"
options.rationale: Sun related rashes follow exposed skin. The trunk is usually covered.

questions.takeaway: When a new rash appears, ask what drug was started. A rash that begins on the trunk and spreads outward points to a drug, not a product on the skin.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Soap and medicine are both reasonable questions. The pattern of the rash and the recent specialist visit pick between them.

steps.detail: Family history and sun do not fit a one day course on the trunk.
Contact rashes sit where the product touched.
A cardiology visit 12 days ago suggests a new prescription.

elimination.verdict: Ask about a new medicine or supplement.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old found in a hot apartment has a temperature of 40 C, new confusion and dry skin. A coworker says the dry skin rules out overheating. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Recheck the temperature in one hour
options.rationale: A temperature this high with confusion cannot wait an hour.

options.text: Begin cooling measures and notify the provider
options.rationale: The temperature and confusion already show hyperthermia. Older adults sweat less, so dry skin does not argue against it.

options.text: Inspect the axillae and skinfolds for moisture
options.rationale: Looking for sweat feels like careful assessment, but sweating is not a reliable sign in older adults and the data needed are already in hand.

options.text: Offer oral fluids and reassess after the client drinks
options.rationale: A confused client may not swallow safely, and fluids alone do not cool.

questions.takeaway: Aging reduces sweat gland activity. Do not use sweating to decide whether an older adult is overheated.
questions.coverage: Not in Lecture PPT. Covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The assessment is already done. More looking only delays cooling.

steps.detail: High temperature, hot room, new confusion.
Less sweating is an aging change, so dry skin proves nothing.
Rechecking later, hunting for sweat and waiting on fluids all postpone treatment.

elimination.verdict: Cool the client and notify the provider.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman reports coarse, dark hair on her chin and chest that appeared over 3 months. The nurse also notes several bruises and a rounder face than in her last photograph. Which action is appropriate?

options.text: Document the hair growth as an expected change of aging
options.rationale: Facial hair can increase with aging, which makes this tempting. A 3 month onset at 44 with bruising and a rounder face is not an aging pattern.

options.text: Teach safe hair removal methods for the face
options.rationale: Treats the appearance and leaves the cause unexamined.

options.text: Ask how the hair growth affects her self-image
options.rationale: Body image matters and belongs in her care. It comes after the findings that suggest a hormone problem are reported.

options.text: Report the hair growth with the bruising and facial change
options.rationale: New hirsutism with easy bruising and a change in fat distribution suggests a hormone disorder and needs evaluation.

questions.takeaway: Hirsutism is a cue, not a diagnosis. Look for what travels with it: bruising, fat redistribution, voice change, acne. Then report the cluster.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Aging and self-image are both real considerations. The speed of onset and the two extra findings push this past either one.

steps.detail: Hair removal does not address why it grew.
Three months, age 44, plus bruising and a rounder face.
A possible hormone disorder is evaluated first.

elimination.verdict: Report the cluster of findings.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old with reduced sensation in the hands and feet had a scald burn last winter. Which statement shows the safety teaching was effective?

options.text: "I check the bath with a thermometer before I get in."
options.rationale: A thermometer does not depend on the client's sensation. Lowering the water heater setting is the other half of the plan.

options.text: "I dip one foot in first to feel how hot the water is."
options.rationale: The feet have reduced sensation, so they cannot judge the water.

options.text: "I test the water with my hand before I step in."
options.rationale: The usual advice for most adults, which makes it tempting. This client's hands have reduced sensation too.

options.text: "I add the hot water once I am sitting in the tub."
options.rationale: The client would be sitting in water that is heating up without being able to feel it.

questions.takeaway: When sensation is reduced, the client cannot be the thermometer. Measure the water and lower the water heater setting.
questions.coverage: Not in Lecture PPT. Covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Three statements rely on the client feeling the water. Reread the stem for which body parts can still feel.

steps.detail: Foot, hand and sitting in the tub all depend on sensation.
Sensation is reduced in the hands and the feet.
A thermometer reads the same for everyone.

elimination.verdict: The thermometer statement.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old with a long smoking history reports feeling well. Which nail finding requires follow up?

options.text: Longitudinal ridges on several fingernails
options.rationale: An expected aging change.

options.text: A 160 degree angle between nail plate and nail fold
options.rationale: This is the normal angle with a firm nail base.

options.text: A 180 degree nail angle with a spongy nail base
options.rationale: Early clubbing. It points to hypoxia, and with this smoking history lung disease has to be ruled out.

options.text: Thick, yellowish gray toenails
options.rationale: Common with aging. Worth watching for fungal infection, but not the finding tied to this client's risk.

questions.takeaway: A nail angle that straightens to 180 degrees with a spongy base is early clubbing, a sign of chronic hypoxia.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Sort expected aging from the one change that fits the smoking history.

steps.action: Link the history to the nails
steps.detail: Smoking raises the risk of chronic hypoxia and lung cancer.
Ridges and thick yellow gray toenails are expected.
160 degrees is normal. 180 degrees with a spongy base is not.

elimination.verdict: The 180 degree angle with a spongy base.

questions.stem: An 86-year-old on bed rest has paper thin skin, moist skinfolds under the breasts and reduced sensation in the feet. Which interventions does the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Position the client so air reaches the skinfolds
options.rationale: Air circulation keeps moisture from breaking down skin in the folds.

options.text: Assist with position changes at least every 2 hours
options.rationale: Thin subcutaneous tissue gives little padding over bone.

options.text: Secure dressings without adhesive tape when possible
options.rationale: Tape tears thin epidermis when it is removed.

options.text: Measure bath water temperature before bathing
options.rationale: Reduced sensation means the client will not feel water that is too hot.

options.text: Use warm water and limit soap to soiled areas
options.rationale: Hot water and full body soap dry aging skin. Warm water and less soap protect it.

options.text: Slide the client up in bed using the draw sheet edge
options.rationale: Sliding causes shear. A lift sheet is used to lift, not drag.

questions.takeaway: Aging skin: reposition at least every 2 hours, lift without sliding, let air reach skinfolds, avoid tape, bathe gently and measure water temperature when sensation is reduced.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Judge each option on its own against the three cues in the stem. Only the option that drags the skin fails.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Match each cue to an action
steps.detail: Thin skin: turn, avoid tape, gentle bathing. Moist folds: air. Reduced sensation: measure water temperature.

steps.action: Test the one about moving the client
steps.detail: Sliding on the sheet edge drags skin over linen and causes shear.

steps.action: Do not expect a fixed number
steps.detail: Five of six are supported here.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, E.

questions.stem: A client with thick, greasy scalp scales has been rubbing coconut oil into the scalp each night for "dryness." Which statement indicates the teaching was effective?

options.text: "I will wash my hair less often so that my scalp can recover."
options.rationale: Less washing leaves more oil on the scalp, which feeds the problem.

options.text: "I will stop the oil and see my provider about treatment."
options.rationale: Dandruff comes from excess oil, not dryness. Severe dandruff needs treatment because it can lead to hair loss.

options.text: "I will switch to a heavier moisturizing scalp cream."
options.rationale: Still treating dryness that is not there.

options.text: "I will pick the scales off gently before I shampoo."
options.rationale: Picking irritates the scalp and treats nothing.

questions.takeaway: Dandruff is caused by excess oil. Untreated severe dandruff can cause hair loss, so it is treated with the provider.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The client's own word, dryness, is the misunderstanding. Find the statement that drops it.

steps.detail: The client is adding oil to an oily scalp.

steps.action: Cut the options that keep the belief
steps.detail: Less washing and heavier cream both add oil.
Picking scales irritates the scalp.

elimination.verdict: Stop the oil and see the provider.

questions.stem: The nurse cleans a client's leg ulcer as prescribed. A foul odor is still present after cleaning. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Report the persistent odor as possible bioburden
options.rationale: Odor that remains after cleaning suggests organisms in the wound itself, so the provider needs to know.

options.text: Document the odor and reassess at the next dressing change
options.rationale: Documenting is correct and feels complete. The odor outlasting the cleaning makes this an unexpected finding that should not wait.

options.text: Apply an odor absorbing dressing over the ulcer
options.rationale: Covers the sign without addressing its cause.

options.text: Clean the ulcer a second time with more saline
options.rationale: The wound was already cleaned as prescribed. Repeating it delays reporting.

questions.takeaway: Odor that persists after a wound is cleaned suggests bioburden. Describe it and report it.
questions.coverage: Not in Lecture PPT. Covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The timing tips it. Odor before cleaning may be old drainage. Odor after cleaning belongs to the wound.

steps.detail: The odor is still there after cleaning.

steps.action: Cut the cover up and the repeat
steps.detail: A dressing hides it and more saline stalls.
An unexpected finding is reported now, not watched.

elimination.verdict: Report possible bioburden.

questions.stem: A client's nail beds look bluish. The nurse squeezes a fingertip, presses the nail bed and releases. The blue color does not change. The findings are most consistent with which problem?

options.text: Cyanosis from poor oxygenation
options.rationale: Color carried by blood fades with pressure and returns on release.

options.text: Venous stasis in the fingers
options.rationale: Also a blood flow color, so it would blanch.

options.text: Pigment in the nail bed
options.rationale: Pigment does not move with pressure, so the color stays the same through the blanch test.

options.text: Slow capillary refill from poor perfusion
options.rationale: Refill describes how fast color returns after blanching. Here nothing blanched.

questions.takeaway: Blanch test: color from blood changes with pressure and returns. Color from pigment does not change.
questions.coverage: Not in Lecture PPT. Covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Three options are blood flow problems and would all blanch. The unchanged color rules out all three together.

steps.detail: No change with pressure or release.
Cyanosis, stasis and slow refill all depend on blood in the nail bed.

steps.action: Keep the one that is not blood
steps.detail: Pigment stays put.

elimination.verdict: Pigment in the nail bed.

questions.scenario: A 78-year-old is seen for a yearly visit. The nurse notes: small cherry red papules on the trunk. Lengthwise ridges on the fingernails. Sparse hair on both lower legs for years. A round bald patch on the scalp that appeared this month. Soft, thin fingernails that bend easily. A brown spot on the forearm that the client says is larger than last year.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is an expected aging change or requires follow up.

rows.text: Cherry red papules on the trunk
rows.rationale: Cherry hemangiomas are benign. Reassure the client.

rows.text: Lengthwise ridges on the fingernails
rows.rationale: Reduced nail bed blood flow causes longitudinal ridges.

rows.text: Sparse hair on both lower legs for years
rows.rationale: Gradual, even hair loss on the lower legs is expected with aging.

rows.text: Round bald scalp patch that appeared this month
rows.rationale: Sudden patchy hair loss at any age is reported.

rows.text: Soft, thin fingernails that bend easily
rows.rationale: Soft, bending nails can mean malnutrition or other systemic disease.

rows.text: Brown forearm spot larger than last year
rows.rationale: A pigmented lesion that is changing needs evaluation for malignancy.

questions.takeaway: Gradual and symmetric is usually aging. Sudden, patchy or changing gets reported.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: For each row ask two things: did it come on slowly, and is it the same on both sides?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Cherry papules, nail ridges and thin leg hair.

steps.action: Mark the sudden or changing ones
steps.detail: A new bald patch and a growing pigmented spot.
Ridges are aging. Soft nails that bend are not.

elimination.verdict: Expected, expected, expected, follow up, follow up, follow up.

questions.stem: A new nurse collects fluid from an intact vesicle for a viral culture. Pickup by the lab courier is delayed. Which action by the new nurse shows the orientation was effective?

options.text: Places the swab in formalin until the courier arrives
options.rationale: Formalin is for pathology specimens and would ruin a culture.

options.text: Leaves the swab in a dry tube at the nurses' station
options.rationale: Without transport medium and cooling the virus will not survive.

options.text: Discards the swab and collects from a crusted lesion later
options.rationale: Intact vesicles give the best viral sample. Crusted lesions do not.

options.text: Keeps the swab in viral transport medium on ice
options.rationale: Viral specimens go in viral transport medium and stay cold until they reach the lab.

questions.takeaway: Viral culture: fluid from an intact vesicle, viral transport medium, kept cold, sent promptly.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The delay is the cue. Ask which choice keeps the specimen usable while it waits.

steps.detail: The specimen has to survive the wait.
Formalin fixes tissue for pathology.

steps.action: Cut the options that lose the sample
steps.detail: Room temperature and a crusted lesion both lower the yield.

elimination.verdict: Viral transport medium on ice.

questions.stem: A 77-year-old who was always well groomed arrives at the clinic with matted hair, body odor and soiled clothing. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Teach a daily bathing and hair care routine
options.rationale: Teaching assumes the client can learn and carry it out, which is not yet known.

options.text: Assess cognition and ability to perform self-care
options.rationale: A change from the client's usual grooming is a cue. The nurse needs to know why before choosing a response.

options.text: Arrange a home health aide to help with bathing
options.rationale: May turn out to be the right solution, which makes it tempting. It skips finding out whether the cause is cognitive, physical or something else.

options.text: Ask the family to supervise the client's hygiene
options.rationale: Hands the problem to others before the nurse knows what it is.

questions.takeaway: Poor hygiene that is new for an older adult calls for assessing cognition and self-care ability before teaching or referral.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The words always well groomed make this a change. A change is assessed before it is fixed.

steps.detail: Well groomed before, neglected now.
Three are interventions and one is assessment.
The stem gives the appearance only, not the cause.

elimination.verdict: Assess cognition and self-care ability.

questions.stem: Ten minutes after a shave biopsy on the back, blood is soaking steadily through the gauze. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Tape a second gauze pad over the first
options.rationale: Adds padding without stopping the bleeding.

options.text: Notify the provider that sutures may be needed
options.rationale: May be needed if bleeding continues, so it is tempting. The nurse controls the bleeding before making the call.

options.text: Apply direct pressure to the site
options.rationale: Pressure is the first measure for biopsy site bleeding. Topical agents and sutures follow only if it fails.

options.text: Remove the gauze to measure the wound
options.rationale: Measuring delays control of active bleeding.

questions.takeaway: Bleeding after a biopsy: direct pressure first, then a topical hemostatic agent or sutures if it continues.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The bleeding is already seen, so more assessment is not the answer. Pick the fastest action that is in the nurse's own hands.

steps.detail: Active bleeding, already observed.

steps.action: Cut what does not stop it
steps.detail: More gauze and measuring leave it bleeding.
Pressure works now. The call comes next if it fails.

elimination.verdict: Apply direct pressure.

questions.stem: A client with a dark skin tone is on day 3 of antibiotics for cellulitis of the lower leg. Which finding best indicates the treatment is effective?

options.text: The darkened area is smaller and cooler than on day 1
options.rationale: In dark skin inflammation shows as a darker area. Shrinking size and less warmth mean it is resolving.

options.text: No redness is visible on the lower leg
options.rationale: Sounds like improvement, but erythema is often not visible in dark skin, so its absence tells you nothing.

options.text: The client rates pain lower after the scheduled analgesic
options.rationale: The analgesic explains the relief, not the antibiotic.

options.text: The leg feels warm with firm edges at the border
options.rationale: Warmth and firmness are signs of ongoing inflammation.

questions.takeaway: In dark skin, inflammation looks darker than the surrounding skin. Track the size of the darkened area and its warmth, not redness.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options sound like less inflammation. Only one uses a sign that shows in this client's skin.

steps.detail: Redness may never have been visible.

steps.action: Cut the finding with another cause
steps.detail: Pain relief follows the analgesic.
Cooler and smaller is improving. Warm and firm is not.

elimination.verdict: Smaller, cooler darkened area.

questions.stem: A client is scheduled for a punch biopsy of a pigmented lesion on the shoulder. Place the nurse's actions in the order they are performed.

options.text: Confirm that informed consent was obtained
options.rationale: First. Nothing is opened or injected until consent is confirmed.

options.text: Set up the sterile field and supplies
options.rationale: The field is prepared once the procedure is cleared to go ahead.

options.text: Tell the client the anesthetic will sting briefly
options.rationale: The warning comes just before the provider injects the local anesthetic.

options.text: Place the specimen in 10% formalin
options.rationale: A pathology specimen goes into formalin as soon as it is removed.

options.text: Teach the client to keep the dressing dry for 8 hours
options.rationale: Aftercare teaching follows once the site is dressed.

questions.takeaway: Biopsy sequence: consent, sterile setup, prepare the client for the sting, specimen into formalin, aftercare teaching.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Anchor the two ends first. Consent opens the sequence and discharge teaching closes it.

steps.detail: Consent is confirmed before anything else.
Dressing teaching happens after the procedure.
Setup, then the anesthetic warning, then the specimen.

elimination.verdict: Consent, setup, warn, formalin, teach.

questions.stem: A nursing student is asked to establish a baseline skin tone for a client who works outdoors. Which action by the student shows the instruction was understood?

options.text: Inspects the face and neck in natural daylight
options.rationale: Good lighting, but these areas are darkened by sun exposure.

options.text: Compares the backs of both hands
options.rationale: Symmetry is checked, but the backs of the hands are among the most sun exposed skin.

options.text: Inspects the forearms after removing the client's watch
options.rationale: Removing the watch is a good thought, but the forearm is still sun exposed.

options.text: Inspects the inner upper arm
options.rationale: Skin less exposed to UV shows the genetically determined tone, which is the most accurate baseline.

questions.takeaway: Assess baseline skin tone in areas with little UV exposure, where sun has not changed the pigment.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The outdoor job is the cue. Three sites tan and one does not.

steps.detail: Sun adds pigment to exposed skin.
Face, hands and forearms are all exposed.
The inner upper arm sees little sun.

elimination.verdict: Inner upper arm.

questions.stem: Four clients with dark skin tones are on bed rest. Which finding does the nurse follow up first?

options.text: Yellow callused soles with white sclera next to the cornea
options.rationale: Calluses can look yellow without jaundice, and the clear sclera confirms it. Expected.

options.text: Gray lips and tongue in a client who is newly restless
options.rationale: Gray lips and tongue are cyanosis in dark skin, and new restlessness fits low oxygen. Breathing comes first.

options.text: One heel that is painful and cooler than the other heel
options.rationale: Tempting because it is real tissue damage, likely a deep tissue injury. It is offloaded and reported right after the client who may be short of oxygen.

options.text: A darker, warm patch on the forearm at an old IV site
options.rationale: Darker and warm is inflammation in dark skin. It is local and gets reported, after the oxygen problem.

questions.takeaway: In dark skin, cyanosis shows as gray lips and tongue. Gray lips with new restlessness is an oxygen problem and outranks local skin damage.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Three options are real problems. Ask which one is a whole body problem and which are local.

steps.detail: Yellow calluses with clear sclera are a normal variant.
The heel and the forearm are local tissue problems.
Gray lips and tongue plus new restlessness means low oxygen.

elimination.verdict: The gray lips and tongue with new restlessness. Breathing before skin.

questions.stem: An 85-year-old is receiving IV fluids for dehydration. Forearm skin still tents, pinched abdominal skin flattens at once, and the lung bases have new crackles. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Ask the provider to increase the fluid rate
options.rationale: Tempting because the forearm still tents. Forearm tenting in an older adult is lost elasticity, so it does not show dehydration.

options.text: Continue the current rate and reassess in 4 hours
options.rationale: Tempting because the abdominal turgor shows the fluids worked. The new crackles mean the fluid is now too much, so waiting is unsafe.

options.text: Recheck turgor over the radial wrist before deciding
options.rationale: The abdomen already gave a reliable turgor result. Another turgor check adds nothing and delays acting on the lungs.

options.text: Slow the infusion and report the new crackles
options.rationale: Abdominal turgor shows the dehydration is corrected, and new crackles show fluid moving into the lungs. Breathing decides it.

questions.takeaway: In older adults, read turgor on the abdomen or radial wrist. Once turgor is normal there, new crackles mean the fluids have gone too far.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Decide which turgor site counts in an 85-year-old, then ask which finding is new.

steps.detail: Forearm tenting is aging skin.
Abdominal skin flattens at once, so hydration is restored.
Crackles are a breathing problem and were not there before.

elimination.verdict: Slow the infusion and report the crackles.

questions.stem: A client with a dark skin tone has had brown vertical bands on every nail for years. Today the band on one thumbnail is wider and darker than last month. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Report the changed thumbnail band for evaluation
options.rationale: The bands are a common variant, and this one has changed. A changing pigmented band is treated as a new finding and evaluated for melanoma.

options.text: Document the bands as an expected normal variant
options.rationale: Tempting because about 75% of people with dark skin have these bands. That covers the stable ones and does not cover a band that is changing.

options.text: Press the thumbnail to see whether the color blanches
options.rationale: The blanch test separates blood from pigment. This is already known to be pigment, so the test does not answer the question of change.

options.text: Ask about thumb injury and recheck in one month
options.rationale: Tempting as assessment first. The change is already documented against last month, so waiting only delays the evaluation.

questions.takeaway: Pigmented nail bands are common and normal in dark skin when they are long standing and stable. A band that widens or darkens is evolving and gets reported.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The normal variant rule tempts you to stop. Look for the one word that says something changed.

steps.detail: Wider and darker than last month.

steps.action: Cut the test that answers a different question
steps.detail: Blanching separates blood from pigment only.
The comparison is already made, so more watching adds nothing.

elimination.verdict: Report the changed band. Stable is a variant. Changing is not.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old is 48 hours into antibiotics for forearm cellulitis. The redness is fainter than at admission. The warm area now extends past yesterday's marked border and is more tender. Which action is appropriate?

options.text: Continue the plan and recheck the arm tomorrow
options.rationale: Tempting because the redness has faded. In older adults redness does not track severity, and the warm area has grown.

options.text: Elevate the arm and recheck the border in 2 hours
options.rationale: Elevation is reasonable comfort care. The border has already been crossed, so another check only repeats what is known.

options.text: Report that the infection appears to be extending
options.rationale: Warmth past the marked border and more tenderness show the infection is spreading even though the color looks better.

options.text: Ask the provider to order a culture of the skin
options.rationale: A culture may follow. The provider first needs to hear that the infection is spreading on the current drug.

questions.takeaway: In older adults, do not judge infection by how red it looks. Track the border, the warmth and the pain.
questions.coverage: Not in Lecture PPT. Covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: One finding looks better and two look worse. Decide which findings can be trusted in a 67-year-old.

steps.detail: Faint redness underestimates infection in older adults.
Warmth past the mark and more tenderness.
The assessment is complete, so the next step is to tell the provider.

elimination.verdict: Report the spreading infection.

questions.stem: A 90-year-old whose skin tears easily has slid down in bed. She is comfortable and breathing easily. The AP is alone, and a second staff member will be free in 5 minutes. Which direction does the nurse give?

options.text: Pull her up now with a hand under each arm
options.rationale: Tempting because it fixes the position at once. Pulling under the arms drags thin skin across the sheet and tears it.

options.text: Wait for the second person and use the lift sheet
options.rationale: She is comfortable and breathing easily, so nothing is urgent. Five minutes costs nothing and a two person lift avoids shear.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed until the helper arrives
options.rationale: Raising the head makes her slide farther and adds shear over the sacrum.

options.text: Have her push with her heels while the AP helps
options.rationale: Tempting because it uses her own mobility. Digging the heels in adds friction to fragile heel skin, and one person still ends up dragging her.

questions.takeaway: Aging skin tears with shear. When the client is not in distress, wait for help and lift with a sheet.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Ask whether anything in the stem makes this urgent. If not, the safest method wins over the fastest.

steps.detail: Comfortable and breathing easily, so no reason to rush.

steps.action: Cut the moves that add shear
steps.detail: Pulling, raising the head and pushing with the heels all drag skin.
Two people and a lift sheet.

elimination.verdict: Wait 5 minutes and lift with the sheet.

questions.stem: A client with a dark skin tone and hepatitis C works as a bricklayer and has thick, yellow palms. Which assessment best confirms jaundice?

options.text: Inspect the hard palate
options.rationale: Bilirubin shows on the hard palate, where neither pigment nor callus hides it.

options.text: Inspect the outer edges of the sclera
options.rationale: Tempting because sclera is the classic site. In dark skin, normal fat deposits make the outer sclera look yellow, so you read the part closest to the cornea.

options.text: Compare the palms with the soles
options.rationale: Callused palms and soles can look yellow without jaundice.

options.text: Press a nail bed and watch the color
options.rationale: The blanch test separates blood from pigment. It does not confirm bilirubin.

questions.takeaway: Jaundice in dark skin: hard palate and the sclera closest to the cornea. Callused palms and the outer sclera mislead.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options name places where jaundice classically shows. Ask which of them has a normal reason to look yellow in this client.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A bricklayer has calluses, so yellow palms prove nothing.
Outer sclera has yellow fat deposits. Only the area near the cornea is reliable.

steps.action: Pick the site with no confounder
steps.detail: The hard palate.

elimination.verdict: Hard palate in bright light.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old on a juice diet has yellow-orange palms, soles and nose. The sclera and oral mucosa are their usual color. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Report the color change for liver testing
options.rationale: Tempting because yellow skin suggests jaundice. Bilirubin stains the sclera and mucous membranes, and this client's are clear.

options.text: Check the urine for a dark amber color
options.rationale: A reasonable jaundice follow up, and the clear sclera has already pointed away from bilirubin.

options.text: Ask how much carrot juice the client drinks
options.rationale: Carotene colors the palms, soles, nose and ears and spares the sclera and mucous membranes. Diet is the next cue to collect.

options.text: Document the finding as a sun tan
options.rationale: Tanning is brown and follows sun exposure. Soles do not tan.

questions.takeaway: Yellow with clear sclera and mucous membranes is carotene, not bilirubin. Ask about diet.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The stem tells you where the color is and where it is not. The clear sclera is the deciding detail.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Palms, soles, nose. Not sclera, not mouth.
Jaundice always reaches the sclera and mucosa.
A juice diet makes carotene the likely source.

elimination.verdict: Ask about carrot juice intake.

questions.stem: A client with heart failure has been on bed rest for 4 days. Weight is up 1.5 kg over those 4 days, and both ankles are free of edema. Which assessment does the nurse perform next?

options.text: Pinch the skin on the back of the hand
options.rationale: Turgor answers a dehydration question. The weight gain is asking about retained fluid.

options.text: Press a fingertip over the sacrum
options.rationale: Dependent edema collects at the lowest point. In a bedridden client that is the sacrum, buttocks and lower back.

options.text: Press over both shins for a full minute
options.rationale: The tibia is where nonpitting endocrine edema is checked. It is not the dependent area in bed.

options.text: Recheck the ankles after the legs hang down
options.rationale: Would move fluid to the ankles in time, but it delays finding fluid that is already pooled at the sacrum.

questions.takeaway: Edema is dependent. Walking clients pool at the ankles and feet; clients in bed pool at the sacrum, buttocks and lower back.
questions.coverage: Not in Lecture PPT. Covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Clear ankles look like good news. The weight gain says the fluid is somewhere, so ask where gravity puts it in a client lying down.

steps.detail: Weight up, ankles clear.

steps.action: Ask where fluid settles in bed
steps.detail: The sacrum and lower back.
It looks for too little fluid, and the scale says too much.

elimination.verdict: Check the sacrum and lower back for pitting.

questions.stem: During a bath, the assistive personnel (AP) tells the nurse that a client who started a new antibiotic yesterday has "red bumps" on the back. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Ask the AP to measure and describe the bumps
options.rationale: Tempting because the AP is already there. Describing and interpreting a new lesion is assessment, which is outside the AP's scope.

options.text: Document the AP's report in the skin assessment
options.rationale: Charting a secondhand description records a finding no nurse has assessed.

options.text: Tell the AP to apply moisturizer after the bath
options.rationale: Treats before anyone has assessed, and may cover what the nurse needs to see.

options.text: Go to the room and inspect the client's back
options.rationale: The AP reports, the nurse assesses. A new rash after a new drug needs the nurse's eyes and hands now.

questions.takeaway: The AP observes and reports skin changes during care. Assessing them is the nurse's job and is not delegated.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Three options keep the nurse out of the room. Decide who is allowed to assess a new finding.

steps.detail: Measuring and describing a new lesion is assessment.
A new drug yesterday makes this finding matter.

steps.action: Pick the option where the nurse assesses
steps.detail: Only one puts the nurse at the bedside.

elimination.verdict: Inspect the back personally.

questions.stem: A client scheduled for a Wood lamp examination of pale patches on the arms asks, "Will I get a numbing shot first?" Which plan is appropriate?

options.text: Obtain signed informed consent, then set up a sterile field
options.rationale: Tempting because that is how a biopsy is prepared. A Wood lamp exam is noninvasive.

options.text: Explain that the test is painless, then darken the room
options.rationale: A handheld ultraviolet light is shone on the skin in a darkened room. Nothing touches or enters the skin.

options.text: Apply a topical anesthetic to the patches as a comfort measure
options.rationale: There is nothing to numb, and a product on the skin can change what fluoresces.

options.text: Explain that a glass slide will be pressed on each patch
options.rationale: That describes diascopy, which checks whether a lesion blanches.

questions.takeaway: Wood lamp: ultraviolet light, darkened room, painless, noninvasive. Biopsy is the test that needs consent, a sterile field and local anesthetic.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The client's question shows they are picturing a biopsy. Match the preparation to the test that was actually ordered.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: It shines a light. Nothing is cut.
Consent form, sterile field and anesthetic belong to biopsy.
The glass slide is diascopy.

elimination.verdict: Explain it is painless and darken the room.

questions.stem: A bartender has had red, swollen, tender nail folds on several fingers for 5 months. Which statement indicates the teaching about chronic paronychia was effective?

options.text: "I will soak my fingers in warm water each night."
options.rationale: Tempting because soaks soothe an acute infection. Chronic paronychia is driven by repeated wetting, so soaking adds to the cause.

options.text: "I will push the cuticles back so the folds can drain."
options.rationale: Injuring the cuticle opens the fold to more irritation and infection.

options.text: "I will keep my hands as dry as I can at work."
options.rationale: Months of inflammation in someone whose hands are wet all shift points to moisture. Reducing exposure treats the cause.

options.text: "I will stop the treatment once the tenderness fades."
options.rationale: The condition has lasted months and recurs with exposure. Symptom relief is not the end point.

questions.takeaway: Acute paronychia follows a torn cuticle or ingrown nail. Chronic paronychia lasts months and comes from frequent wet exposure, so keep the hands dry.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
