questions.strategy: Use the occupation. A bartender's hands are wet for hours, and one statement removes that exposure.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Five months is chronic.
Constant water and detergent.
Soaking adds moisture. Keeping dry removes it.

elimination.verdict: Keeping the hands dry at work.

questions.stem: A client had a tattoo removed from the forearm by laser and plans a beach trip next week. Which statement indicates the teaching was effective?

options.text: "I will keep that arm covered while I am outside."
options.rationale: A tattoo removal site is very photosensitive. Clothing blocks ultraviolet light more reliably than any product.

options.text: "I will put SPF 15 lotion on it each morning."
options.rationale: Tempting because it shows intent to protect. The minimum taught is SPF 30, and one morning application does not last.

options.text: "I will save my beach time for right after lunch."
options.rationale: Midday sun is the strongest of the day.

options.text: "I will get a light base tan before the trip."
options.rationale: A tan is ultraviolet damage. It does not protect a photosensitive site.

questions.takeaway: Tattoo removal sites burn easily. Cover the area, use SPF 30 or higher on exposed skin, and stay out of midday sun.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two statements show a client trying to protect the skin. One uses too weak a product and too few applications.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Cut the two that add sun
steps.detail: Midday beach time and a base tan.
SPF 15 once a day against covering the arm.
SPF 30 is the floor, and a physical barrier is best for a photosensitive site.

elimination.verdict: Keeping the treated arm covered.

questions.stem: An 81-year-old reports 2 weeks of fatigue. Which nail findings does the nurse report as possible signs of a systemic problem? Select all that apply.

options.text: Thin dark red vertical lines under several nails, with a new fever
options.rationale: Splinter hemorrhages with fever raise concern for bacterial endocarditis.

options.text: Flattened, unusually smooth fingernails
options.rationale: Early koilonychia. A flat, smooth plate is linked to iron deficiency, which fits the fatigue. It is not an aging change.

options.text: A yellow gray tint to the toenails
options.rationale: A yellow gray color is a normal aging change.

options.text: White horizontal bands across the fingernails
options.rationale: White bands go with low albumin in chronic liver or kidney disease.

options.text: Nails that grow more slowly than they used to
options.rationale: Slower growth is expected with age. It raises fungal risk, so you keep inspecting.

options.text: Thick toenails that overhang the toes
options.rationale: Thickening is expected with age. It changes who trims them, not what you report.

questions.takeaway: Aging nails are slower, thicker and yellow gray. Splinter hemorrhages with fever, flattened or spoon shaped nails and white horizontal bands point to disease elsewhere.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Judge each finding alone. Ask whether age explains it or whether it points to the heart, the blood or the liver and kidneys.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Slow growth, thickening, yellow gray color.

steps.action: Pair each remaining finding with a system
steps.detail: Splinter lines and fever: heart. Flattened nails: iron. White bands: albumin.
Fatigue fits anemia and chronic disease.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D.

questions.scenario: A clinic nurse assists with several skin and nail procedures in one morning and prepares each specimen for the laboratory.
questions.stem: For each specimen, indicate the container the nurse uses.

rows.text: Excised mole going to pathology
rows.rationale: Tissue for pathology is fixed in formalin.

rows.text: Tissue from a draining ulcer going for bacterial culture
rows.rationale: Formalin kills organisms. Tissue for culture goes in sterile saline.

rows.text: Scales scraped from a foot rash with a tongue blade for a KOH test
rows.rationale: Scrapings for a fungal test are collected into a clean container.

rows.text: Shave biopsy taken to see whether a treatment is working
rows.rationale: Still a pathology specimen, whatever the reason for the biopsy.

rows.text: Clippings from a thick, layered toenail for a fungal test
rows.rationale: Nail clippings and hair are handled like scrapings.

questions.takeaway: Ask what the lab will do with it. Looking at cells: formalin. Growing organisms: sterile saline. Fungal scrapings and clippings: clean container.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The procedure name does not choose the container. The test does. A fixative in a culture specimen leaves nothing to grow.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Only one specimen has to stay alive.
Both biopsies are read under a microscope.
Scales and clippings go dry into a clean container.

elimination.verdict: Formalin, saline, clean container, formalin, clean container.

questions.stem: A florist has itchy, cracked skin on both hands. The rash cleared during 2 weeks off work spent at home and returned within days of going back to work. Which information is most important to obtain?

options.text: Products handled at work and glove use
options.rationale: The rash follows the work schedule and sits where the hands touch things, so occupational exposure is the history that explains it.

options.text: Relatives who have had eczema or skin cancer
options.rationale: Tempting because family history is part of every skin history. It does not explain a rash that comes and goes with work.

options.text: Soap and laundry products that are used at home
options.rationale: Tempting as a common allergen. The skin cleared while the client was at home using them.

options.text: Sun exposure and sunscreen use on the hands
options.rationale: Sun damage does not clear in 2 weeks and return in days.

questions.takeaway: The social history includes occupation. A rash that clears away from work and returns with it points to something handled on the job.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Follow the timing. Ask what changes when the rash changes.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Clear at home, back with work.
Home products and family history did not change.
What the hands touch at work.

elimination.verdict: Ask about products handled at work and glove use.

questions.stem: A client with a dark skin tone returned from a camping trip 9 days ago. A firm, darker, painless nodule on the lower leg has grown wider each day. Which question does the nurse ask first?

options.text: "Have you changed your laundry soap?"
options.rationale: A contact reaction itches and stays where the product touched. It does not expand day by day.

options.text: "Has anyone in your family ever been treated for skin cancer?"
options.rationale: Tempting because the lesion is changing. Growth over days after outdoor exposure points elsewhere first.

options.text: "Did you find a tick on you or notice a bite?"
options.rationale: An expanding lesion after outdoor exposure fits erythema migrans, the rash of early Lyme disease. In dark skin it can look like a darker nodule instead of a red ring.

options.text: "Do you use sunscreen on your legs?"
options.rationale: Useful teaching later. It does not explain this lesion.

questions.takeaway: Erythema migrans expands and means Lyme disease. In dark skin it may be a firm, darker nodule, so the exposure history is what gives it away.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides.
questions.strategy: Let the timing and the camping trip pick the question.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Days, not months.
Outdoors, lower leg.
A tick or bite.

elimination.verdict: Ask about a tick bite.

questions.stem: A provider presses a glass slide on a client's reddish purple forearm lesion. The color stays the same under pressure. Which assessment does the nurse add?

options.text: Inspect the gums and other skin for bleeding
options.rationale: A lesion that does not blanch is blood outside the vessels, so the nurse looks for bleeding elsewhere.

options.text: Compare the lesion's warmth with nearby skin
options.rationale: Tempting, since redness can mean inflammation. Inflamed vessels blanch with pressure, and this did not.

options.text: Measure the diameter against 6 mm
options.rationale: Diameter belongs to the check of a pigmented mole.

options.text: Ask about new soaps or lotions
options.rationale: A contact rash is red from dilated vessels and would blanch.

questions.takeaway: Diascopy: color that blanches is inside vessels. Color that stays is blood in the tissue.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Decide what a lesion that does not blanch is made of, then assess for more of it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: No blanching means blood has left the vessels.
Inflammation and contact rash blanch.
Gums, other skin.

elimination.verdict: Check the gums and other sites for bleeding.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old with scaly plaques on the face and hands has stopped attending class and says, "I look disgusting." Which response is best?

options.text: "Most plaques clear once treatment starts working."
options.rationale: Tempting and hopeful. It answers a feeling with a prediction and closes the topic.

options.text: "Tell me what has been hardest about how your skin looks."
options.rationale: Skin problems affect body image. An open question lets the client describe the effect before any plan is made.

options.text: "A support group could help you meet others living with this."
options.rationale: A reasonable later step. It moves to a solution before the concern is explored.

options.text: "Cover makeup hides plaques quite well."
options.rationale: Offers a fix and implies the skin should be hidden.

questions.takeaway: Visible skin conditions change how people see themselves. Explore the feeling before you offer fixes.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Three options solve or reassure. One asks.

strategies: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings

steps.detail: Withdrawal plus a harsh self description.
They skip the feeling.
It keeps the client talking.

elimination.verdict: Ask what has been hardest.

questions.stem: A client was treated 4 days ago for acute paronychia of one finger after a manicure. Which finding best indicates the treatment is effective?

options.text: The nail plate has a new horizontal ridge
options.rationale: A ridge records the injury to the nail. It says nothing about the infection.

options.text: The client keeps the finger covered at work
options.rationale: Describes behavior, not the tissue.

options.text: The other nail folds remain pink
options.rationale: Good, but acute paronychia usually involves one nail, so this was expected.

options.text: The nail fold is flat and no longer throbs
options.rationale: Acute paronychia is a tender, swollen nail fold. Less swelling and pain show it is resolving.

questions.takeaway: Judge a treatment by the signs the problem started with. For acute paronychia that is swelling and throbbing at the fold.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Evaluation questions want the original problem getting better at the original site.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Red, swollen, painful fold.

steps.action: Cut findings about other sites or behavior
steps.detail: They do not measure this infection.
Flat fold, no throbbing.

elimination.verdict: The fold is flat and no longer throbs.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old lifeguard completes teaching on skin self examination. Which statement indicates the teaching was effective?

options.text: "Once a month I will check all my skin, using a mirror for my back."
options.rationale: Monthly, all skin, including areas the client cannot see directly.

options.text: "Every week I will check the moles on my arms and face."
options.rationale: Tempting because it is more frequent. It leaves out skin that is hard to see, where changes are missed.

options.text: "My yearly physical will catch anything new."
options.rationale: A year is long enough for a lesion to change.

options.text: "I will check any mole that starts to hurt."
options.rationale: Pain is a late and unreliable sign. Change in shape, border, color or size comes first.

questions.takeaway: Self exam is monthly and covers all skin, with ABCDE as the checklist.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Check each statement for how often and how much skin.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Monthly is the standard.
All skin, including the back.
Pain comes late.

elimination.verdict: Monthly, all skin, with a mirror.

questions.stem: A client has open, draining lesions of unknown cause on both forearms. The nurse teaches the AP about care. Which action by the AP shows the teaching was effective?

options.text: Posts a contact isolation sign on the door
options.rationale: No organism or order supports isolation yet.

options.text: Wears a gown and mask to deliver the meal tray
options.rationale: Tempting as extra caution. Protection is matched to expected contact, and a tray involves none.

options.text: Wears gloves to bathe the arms and cleans hands after
options.rationale: Standard Precautions: gloves for contact with drainage or broken skin, then hand hygiene.

options.text: Bathes the arms with bare hands since the AP's skin is intact
options.rationale: Drainage from open lesions is a body fluid.

questions.takeaway: Impaired skin calls for hand hygiene and Standard Precautions: barrier for the contact you expect, no more and no less.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Match the protection to the contact in each option.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Bare hands on drainage.
Isolation and a mask without a reason.
Gloves for drainage, then hand hygiene.

elimination.verdict: Gloves for the bath and hand hygiene after.

questions.stem: A client arrives for a shave biopsy of a raised back lesion and mentions taking clopidogrel each morning. The drug is not on the chart's medication list. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Proceed with setup, since a shave biopsy is only skin deep
options.rationale: Tempting. Shallow sites still bleed, and a shave biopsy is not sutured.

options.text: Tell the client to skip tomorrow's dose
options.rationale: Changing a drug schedule is outside the nurse's scope.

options.text: Have extra gauze ready and document the drug
options.rationale: Tempting and useful preparation. It leaves the person doing the procedure unaware of a bleeding risk.

options.text: Tell the provider about the drug before the procedure
options.rationale: A drug that slows clotting changes bleeding risk, so the provider needs it before cutting.

questions.takeaway: Before any biopsy, the drug history that matters most is anything that affects bleeding.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The cue is new information that the person doing the procedure does not have yet.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: An antiplatelet drug.
Holding a dose.
The provider hears it first.

elimination.verdict: Tell the provider before the procedure.

questions.stem: A daughter cares for her 88-year-old mother, who has thin skin and little body fat. Which statement by the daughter indicates the teaching was effective?

options.text: "I will give her a hot bath daily to keep her warm."
options.rationale: Hot water and daily soap dry thin skin, and hot water can burn it.

options.text: "I will put a heating pad under her at night."
options.rationale: Thin skin with little fat under it burns easily, and older adults often sense heat poorly.

options.text: "Her cool hands are normal aging, so I will not change anything."
options.rationale: Tempting because less fat is expected. The expected change still needs a plan.

options.text: "I will add layers and keep her room warm."
options.rationale: Less subcutaneous fat means less insulation, so warmth is added safely from outside.

questions.takeaway: Subcutaneous fat insulates. When it thins with age, protect from cold with layers and room temperature, not direct heat.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Look for the option that adds warmth without adding a burn risk.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Little fat means poor insulation.
Hot baths and heating pads.
Expected does not mean ignored.

elimination.verdict: Layers and a warm room.

questions.nursesNote: 52-year-old seen for a skin check. Mole on the upper back measures 8 mm. One edge of the mole is notched. The mole is tan with a blue black area. Client says it was round and even last year. Flat tan freckles on both forearms, unchanged for years. Brown bands on all ten nails since childhood. Small smooth pink scar on the knee.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that require follow up.

segments.text: Mole on the upper back measures 8 mm
segments.rationale: Diameter over 6 mm.

segments.text: One edge of the mole is notched
segments.rationale: Border irregularity.

segments.text: The mole is tan with a blue black area
segments.rationale: Color variation within one lesion.

segments.text: Client says it was round and even last year
segments.rationale: Evolving. Change is the feature that most needs a referral.

segments.text: Flat tan freckles on both forearms, unchanged for years
segments.rationale: Even color and no change.

segments.text: Brown bands on all ten nails since childhood
segments.rationale: Long standing bands on every nail are a common variation.

segments.text: Small smooth pink scar on the knee
segments.rationale: A healed scar with no change.

questions.takeaway: ABCDE works one lesion at a time: shape, border, color, diameter over 6 mm, and change.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Ask of each line: is it uneven, large, or changing? Stable and uniform findings stay unmarked.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Size, border, color and change all flag.
Freckles, bands and scar are stable.

elimination.verdict: The four lines about the back mole.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A client with a dark skin tone reports soreness where a wrist splint has been rubbing for 2 days. The nurse expects irritated skin in this client to look [[1]].

To confirm the finding, the nurse [[2]].

options.text: bright red
options.rationale: Redness is often not visible through dark pigment.

options.text: darker than the surrounding skin
options.rationale: Irritation and inflammation show as hyperpigmentation in dark skin.

options.text: ash gray
options.rationale: Ash gray describes pallor.

options.text: yellow
options.rationale: Yellow suggests jaundice or callus.

options.text: inspects the sclera near the cornea
options.rationale: That is the check for jaundice.

options.text: looks inside the mouth
options.rationale: Mucosa is used for petechiae, pallor and cyanosis.

options.text: palpates for warmth and tenderness and compares both wrists
options.rationale: Inflammation can be subtle to the eye. Temperature, tenderness and the other side confirm it.

options.text: presses to see whether the area blanches
options.rationale: Blanching is hard to see in dark skin.

questions.takeaway: In dark skin, inflammation looks darker, not redder. Confirm with your hands and with the opposite side.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Match each color to its meaning, then choose the check that does not depend on color.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Gray is pallor, yellow is jaundice, darker is irritation.
Warmth, tenderness, comparison.

elimination.verdict: Darker than nearby skin, confirmed by palpation and comparison.

questions.stem: A client with a dark skin tone on bed rest reports new pain over one heel. The skin color looks unchanged. Which assessment does the nurse use to detect a deep tissue pressure injury?

options.text: Press the heel firmly for several seconds and watch for the skin to blanch
options.rationale: Blanching may not be visible in a dark skin tone, so this can miss the injury.

options.text: Ask when the pain began and feel the heel for a temperature change
options.rationale: In a dark skin tone the injury may not be easily visible, so the nurse assesses for preceding pain and a temperature change in the area.

options.text: Look for redness of the heel under bright overhead light
options.rationale: Erythema may be absent or hard to see through dark pigment.

options.text: Recheck the heel when purple discoloration can be seen
options.rationale: The color change may not be easily visible, and waiting lets the damage progress.

questions.takeaway: Deep tissue pressure injury in a dark skin tone may not be easily visible. Assess for preceding pain and a temperature change in the affected area.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Three options depend on seeing a color change. The stem tells you color is not helping in this client.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Blanching, redness and purple color may not show in a dark skin tone.

steps.action: Keep what can be felt and reported
steps.detail: Preceding pain and a temperature change.

elimination.verdict: Ask about the pain and feel for a temperature change.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old completes teaching on protecting the skin before a beach vacation. Which statement requires follow up by the nurse?

options.text: "I will wear a hat and long sleeves on the sand."
options.rationale: Correct. Covering the skin reduces exposure.

options.text: "I will look over all of my skin once a month."
options.rationale: Correct. All skin is examined monthly for new or changing lesions.

options.text: "With sunscreen on, I can stay on the beach all day."
options.rationale: Sunscreen is one part of the teaching. The other part is to reduce exposure to the sun and ultraviolet light, and a full day on the beach does the opposite.

options.text: "I will sit under an umbrella to cut down my time in the sun."
options.rationale: Correct. This reduces sun exposure.

questions.takeaway: Sun protection teaching has two parts: use sunscreen and reduce exposure to the sun and ultraviolet light. Sunscreen does not buy unlimited time in the sun.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Negative polarity. One statement uses a correct measure as a reason to add exposure.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Follow up means the wrong statement.
Clothing, monthly checks and shade all match the teaching.
All day in the sun is more exposure, even with sunscreen.

elimination.verdict: Staying on the beach all day because sunscreen is on.

questions.stem: Yesterday's note describes a flat rash on a client's chest. Today the color and area look the same, but the nurse's gloved fingertips feel that the spots are raised and firm. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Document the rash as unchanged because the color and area are the same
options.rationale: Tempting because it looks the same. Palpation is what confirms the size and consistency of lesions, and it shows a change.

options.text: Document a papular rash and pass on the change from yesterday
options.rationale: A flat rash is macular and a raised rash is papular. Palpation confirmed that the lesions have changed, so the record and the team need the new finding.

options.text: Pinch the skin over the chest to check turgor
options.rationale: Turgor shows skin elasticity. It does not describe the lesions.

options.text: Wait to see whether the spots look raised on inspection tomorrow
options.rationale: Palpation has already confirmed the change, so waiting for it to be visible adds nothing.

questions.takeaway: Palpation confirms the size and consistency of lesions. Macular means flat, papular means raised. A rash that goes from flat to raised has changed even if it looks the same.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Inspection and palpation disagree. Ask which one confirms whether a lesion is flat or raised.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: It confirms size and consistency.
Flat yesterday, raised today.

steps.action: Cut delay and the unrelated test
steps.detail: Waiting and turgor do not address the lesions.

elimination.verdict: Document a papular rash and pass on the change.

questions.stem: A client is going home after a shave biopsy on the shoulder covered with dry gauze. Which statement indicates a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I will leave the gauze on and dry for at least 8 hours."
options.rationale: Correct. The dressing stays dry and in place at least 8 hours.

options.text: "After the gauze is off, I will clean the site every day."
options.rationale: Correct. The site is cleaned daily once the dressing is removed.

options.text: "I will call the clinic if the site turns red or starts to drain a lot."
options.rationale: Correct. Redness, darkening or excessive drainage is reported.

options.text: "I will leave dried blood on the site so the scab protects it."
options.rationale: Dried blood and crusts are not left in place. They are removed with tap water or saline when the site is cleaned each day.

questions.takeaway: After a skin biopsy: keep the dressing dry at least 8 hours, then clean daily, remove dried blood and crusts with tap water or saline, and report redness or heavy drainage.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Negative polarity. Read each statement as true or false against the taught aftercare.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: More teaching means the wrong statement.
Dried blood and crusts are removed with tap water or saline, not left on.

elimination.verdict: Leaving dried blood on the site.

questions.stem: A client with a dark skin tone returns after 4 hours on a transport stretcher. The nurse presses on the sacrum and sees no color change: no redness and no visible blanching. Which action does the nurse take next?

options.text: Inspect and palpate the sacrum for other skin changes
options.rationale: In a dark skin tone a stage 1 pressure injury shows no visible blanching, and erythema may be absent or hard to see. The nurse inspects and palpates for other skin changes.

options.text: Document that the sacral skin shows no sign of pressure injury
options.rationale: Tempting because the usual signs are missing. In a dark skin tone those signs may not show, so their absence does not clear the skin.

options.text: Press on the sacrum for a longer time and watch again for blanching
options.rationale: Repeating the test relies on the same sign that is not visible in this client.

options.text: Ask the client to call when the sacral skin looks red
options.rationale: Erythema may be absent or hard to see, and the client cannot see the sacrum.

questions.takeaway: Stage 1 pressure injury in a dark skin tone: no visible blanching, erythema may be absent. Inspect and palpate for other skin changes.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The stem says the color signs are absent in a client where color signs are unreliable. Pick the option that does not depend on them.

steps.detail: Blanching and redness may not show in a dark skin tone.
No visible sign is not the same as no injury.
Inspect and palpate for other changes.

elimination.verdict: Inspect and palpate the sacrum for other skin changes.

questions.stem: A frail, underweight 83-year-old on bed rest sleeps soundly. The AP asks to turn her every 4 hours overnight so she can rest. Skin over the sacrum and hips is intact. Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: Keep turning her at least every 2 hours through the night
options.rationale: Clients are assisted to change position at least every 2 hours. Subcutaneous tissue cushions and protects, and an underweight client has little of it over the bony prominences.

options.text: Turn her every 4 hours and place pillows under the bony areas
options.rationale: Tempting because pillows reduce pressure. They do not replace position changes at least every 2 hours.

options.text: Turn her every 4 hours for as long as the skin stays intact
options.rationale: Intact skin now is the result of turning. Waiting for a change means the injury has already started.

options.text: Turn her every 4 hours and use a lift sheet each time
options.rationale: A lift sheet prevents shear during the move. It does not shorten the time spent on one area.

questions.takeaway: Reposition at least every 2 hours. Less subcutaneous tissue means less cushion over bone, so the interval is not stretched for sleep.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Three options accept the longer interval and add something. One keeps the interval.

steps.detail: Three options turn every 4 hours.
Position changes are at least every 2 hours.

steps.action: Keep the one that holds the interval
steps.detail: Every 2 hours through the night.

elimination.verdict: Keep turning her at least every 2 hours.

questions.stem: A client with brown skin reports fatigue and heavy menstrual periods. Her skin looks yellow-brown. The hard palate and the sclera near the cornea are not yellow. Which assessment does the nurse perform next?

options.text: Inspect the palms and soles for a yellow color
options.rationale: Callused palms and soles can look yellow without disease, and the reliable jaundice sites are already clear.

options.text: Inspect the conjunctivae and oral mucous membranes for an ash gray tone
options.rationale: Pallor in brown skin can look yellow-brown. With the jaundice sites clear and a history of blood loss, the nurse looks at the mucous membranes and conjunctivae for pallor.

options.text: Palpate the abdomen for liver tenderness
options.rationale: This follows a jaundice line that the hard palate and sclera have already made unlikely.

options.text: Ask how many carrots and how much vegetable juice she eats and drinks on a typical day
options.rationale: Tempting because carotene spares the sclera and mucous membranes. It collects on the palms, soles and face, and it does not explain fatigue with heavy bleeding.

questions.takeaway: In brown skin, pallor can look yellow-brown. If the hard palate and the sclera near the cornea are clear, check the mucous membranes and conjunctivae for an ash gray tone.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The stem has already answered the jaundice question. Use the history to decide which color change is left to confirm.

steps.detail: Hard palate and sclera are not yellow.
Fatigue with heavy periods points to blood loss.
Conjunctivae and mucous membranes.

elimination.verdict: Inspect the conjunctivae and mucous membranes for an ash gray tone.

questions.stem: A client who scratches itchy forearms during sleep has new open scratch marks. The fingernails are long with debris under them. Which teaching is the priority?

options.text: Examine all skin monthly for new or changing lesions
options.rationale: True teaching for every adult, but it does not stop the injury happening now.

options.text: Apply sunscreen to the forearms before going outdoors
options.rationale: Sun protection is sound teaching. It does not address skin being opened by the nails.

options.text: Wrap the forearms in gauze and tape at night
options.rationale: Tempting as a barrier. It leaves the long, soiled nails in place, and tape adds another source of skin trauma.

options.text: Keep the fingernails clean and trimmed short
options.rationale: Clients are encouraged to keep the fingernails clean and trimmed. Short, clean nails remove the cause of the open areas and the debris that can enter them.

questions.takeaway: Keeping fingernails clean and trimmed is basic skin protection. Long, dirty nails turn an itch into open skin.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The stem gives an actual injury and its cause. Pick the teaching that removes the cause.

steps.detail: Open scratch marks from long, soiled nails.
Monthly checks and sunscreen prevent other problems.
Gauze and tape do not change the nails.

elimination.verdict: Keep the fingernails clean and trimmed short.

questions.stem: A client with a scaly, itchy rash on the trunk has a potassium hydroxide (KOH) test read as positive in the clinic. The client asks whether treatment must wait for a culture. Which response is accurate?

options.text: "Yes. The culture has to finish growing before any treatment for the rash can be started."
options.rationale: Waiting for culture results delays treatment, which the point of care test is meant to avoid.

options.text: "A biopsy is the next step to confirm what the test showed."
options.rationale: A punch biopsy is used for deeper fungal infection. A positive test on surface scales does not need it.

options.text: "A positive test can confirm fungus today, so a culture may not be needed."
options.rationale: The test is read at the point of care, and a positive result may eliminate the need for a culture, so treatment is not delayed.

options.text: "This test only rules out bacteria, so a culture comes next."
options.rationale: The test looks for fungal elements in the scales. It is not a test for bacteria.

questions.takeaway: A positive KOH test confirms a fungal infection at the point of care and may remove the need for a culture and its delay.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Ask what the positive result has already answered. If the cause is confirmed, more testing only adds waiting.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The test detects fungus and is read in the clinic.
A required culture or biopsy adds waiting the result does not call for.
A culture may not be needed.

elimination.verdict: A positive test can confirm fungus today.

questions.stem: A client with a dark skin tone is admitted with pneumonia. Which finding does the nurse follow up first?

options.text: Brown lengthwise bands on several fingernails
options.rationale: Hyperpigmented nail bands are common in people with dark skin tones, so this is an expected variation.

options.text: Yellow, callused skin on both heels
options.rationale: Callused palms and soles may look yellow even without jaundice.

options.text: A bluish tinge of the palms and soles
options.rationale: Cyanosis in a dark skin tone may show as a bluish tinge of the palms, soles, conjunctiva and nail beds. In a client with pneumonia this is a breathing problem and comes first.

options.text: A darker patch on the shin where a rash cleared
options.rationale: Skin that was irritated can stay darker than the surrounding skin afterward. It is not an acute change.

questions.takeaway: Cyanosis in a dark skin tone: lips and tongue gray or white, with a bluish tinge of the palms, soles, conjunctiva and nail beds. Nail bands, yellow calluses and darker healed patches are expected.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Sort the four into expected variations and one sign of poor oxygenation. Breathing comes first.

steps.detail: Nail bands, yellow calluses, a darker healed patch.
Bluish palms and soles in a client with pneumonia.

elimination.verdict: The bluish tinge of the palms and soles.

questions.stem: A mail carrier with a dark skin tone says her face and forearms grow darker each summer. Her upper inner arms and trunk are unchanged, and she has started no new drugs. Which action is appropriate?

options.text: Teach sunscreen use and ways to reduce sun exposure
options.rationale: Darkening limited to exposed skin is facultative pigmentation, which develops from ultraviolet exposure. Adults are taught to use sunscreen and reduce exposure to sun and ultraviolet light.

options.text: Explain that skin tone is set by genetics and is not changed by the sun
options.rationale: Only constitutive pigmentation is genetically determined. Facultative pigmentation changes with ultraviolet exposure.

options.text: Inspect the hard palate and sclera for yellowing
options.rationale: Those sites are checked for jaundice. Her change is darker skin on sun exposed areas, not a yellow color.

options.text: Ask about new soaps, detergents and cosmetics
options.rationale: Tempting because allergens are part of the skin history. The change follows sun exposure each summer and spares the covered skin.

questions.takeaway: Constitutive pigmentation is genetic. Facultative pigmentation comes from ultraviolet exposure, so darkening of exposed skin only calls for sun protection teaching in every skin tone.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Compare the exposed skin with the covered skin. The pattern names the cause, and the cause names the teaching.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Exposed skin darker, covered skin unchanged, worse in summer.
Sun does change pigmentation.
Ultraviolet exposure calls for sunscreen and less sun.

elimination.verdict: Teach sunscreen use and less sun exposure.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old has had diarrhea for 3 days. Which findings does the nurse interpret as fluid loss rather than aging skin? Select all that apply.

options.text: Dry buccal mucosa
options.rationale: Decreased moisture from fluid loss shows first in the buccal mucosa, so a dry mouth lining after 3 days of diarrhea counts as fluid loss.

options.text: Skin on the back of the hand returns slowly after a pinch
options.rationale: Elastic fibers degenerate with age, so the back of the hand can return slowly in an older adult who is not dehydrated.

options.text: Skin over the abdomen stays tented after a pinch
options.rationale: The abdomen is a site used in older adults so that dry aging skin is not mistaken for dehydration. Tenting here means fluid loss.

options.text: Dry, flaking skin on the lower legs
options.rationale: Dryness and flaking of the feet and lower legs are common with aging and dry air.

options.text: Little sweating in a warm room
options.rationale: Sweat gland activity falls with age, so reduced sweating is not a reliable sign.

questions.takeaway: In an older adult, judge hydration from the buccal mucosa and from turgor on the abdomen or radial wrist. Dry legs, slow hand skin and little sweat can all be aging.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: For each finding ask whether a well hydrated older adult could show it. If yes, it does not count as fluid loss.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Dry lower legs, slow return on the hand, little sweating.

steps.action: Keep what aging does not explain
steps.detail: Dry mouth lining and tenting over the abdomen.

elimination.verdict: Dry buccal mucosa and abdominal tenting.

questions.stem: A client with a dark skin tone who takes warfarin bumped a thigh on the bed rail yesterday. The area is now darker than the surrounding skin, tender and raised. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Apply a warm compress to the area to ease inflammation
options.rationale: Tempting because inflamed skin can also look darker. A bump in a client on an anticoagulant with a raised, tender area points to bleeding, and heat can increase bleeding.

options.text: Record the area as darkening left behind by old skin irritation
options.rationale: Darkening after irritation is flat and not tender, and it does not appear the day after an injury.

options.text: Treat the area as a pressure injury and keep the client off that side
options.rationale: The cause given is a bump in a client taking warfarin, not pressure.

options.text: Outline and measure the area to track bleeding into the tissue
options.rationale: In a dark skin tone an ecchymosis appears darker than the normal skin tone and may be tender or palpable when a hematoma is present. Marking and measuring shows whether the bleeding is growing.

questions.takeaway: In a dark skin tone, ecchymosis looks darker than the surrounding skin and may be tender or palpable if there is a hematoma.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Several things look darker in a dark skin tone. Use the trauma, the anticoagulant and the raised, tender feel to choose among them.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Inflammation, old irritation or bleeding.
A bump, warfarin, tender and raised fit ecchymosis with a hematoma.
Heat does not belong on a bleeding site.

elimination.verdict: Outline and measure the area.

questions.stem: A client with obesity sits in a recliner most of the day. Skin under both breasts and in the abdominal fold is intact but damp. Skin over the sacrum and heels is intact and its usual color. Which addition to the plan addresses this?

options.text: Use a lift sheet for every move in the chair or bed
options.rationale: A lift sheet prevents shear. The finding is moisture trapped in folds.

options.text: Help the client change position at least every 2 hours
options.rationale: Tempting because it belongs in the plan. It relieves pressure over bony prominences, and those areas show no damage.

options.text: Apply an emollient to the folds while the skin is still damp
options.rationale: An emollient holds moisture in, and these folds are already damp.

options.text: Position the client so air circulates to the skinfolds
options.rationale: Clients are positioned to promote air circulation to skinfolds. Air lets the trapped moisture dry before the skin breaks down.

questions.takeaway: Match the intervention to the mechanism: lift sheets for shear, turning for pressure, air circulation for moisture in skinfolds.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: All four protect skin. Ask what is harming this skin: pressure, shear or moisture.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Damp folds, bony areas undamaged, so moisture.
Lift sheet and turning answer other problems.
Emollient on damp folds.

elimination.verdict: Position the client so air reaches the skinfolds.

questions.stem: A client with a dark skin tone has had yellow outer sclerae for years. Today the sclera next to the cornea and the hard palate are also yellow. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Report the new yellowing as possible jaundice
options.rationale: In a dark skin tone, jaundice is checked at the hard palate and the sclera closest to the cornea. New yellow at both sites is a real change.

options.text: Document the yellow sclerae as the client's baseline
options.rationale: Tempting because the outer yellow is longstanding. The new yellow is at the sites that are accurate for jaundice.

options.text: Look at the sclerae again in daylight tomorrow
options.rationale: Delays a finding already seen at two accurate sites.

options.text: Check the palms and soles for a matching yellow color
options.rationale: Palms and soles can look yellow without jaundice when callused, so they neither confirm nor rule it out.

questions.takeaway: Jaundice in a dark skin tone: trust the oral mucosa and hard palate and the sclera closest to the cornea, not the outer sclera or the palms and soles.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Separate the old finding from the new one. Then ask whether the new one sits at a site you can trust.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Outer sclera yellow for years. Sclera next to the cornea and hard palate yellow today.
Those two are the accurate sites for jaundice.

steps.action: Cut delay and the unreliable site
steps.detail: Waiting a day, and palms and soles.

elimination.verdict: Report the new yellowing as possible jaundice.

chapters.title: Care of Clients with Conditions of the Skin, Hair, and Nails

questions.stem: A client with a reddened sacrum and a Braden score of 12 (high risk) receives continuous tube feeding. Which positioning plan does the nurse choose?

options.text: Lower the head of the bed flat between turns
options.rationale: Tempting because flat removes shear. The continuous feeding tips it away, since lying flat risks aspiration.

options.text: Keep the head of the bed at 30 degrees with side tilts
options.rationale: Thirty degrees is the lowest safe angle for the feeding and the highest angle that limits shear. The side tilt takes weight off the sacrum.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed to 45 degrees during the feeding
options.rationale: Protects the airway but the client slides, and shear builds on a sacrum that is already red.

options.text: Turn the client fully onto the side at 90 degrees
options.rationale: Moves the pressure from the sacrum to the hip bone.

questions.takeaway: Two risks, one angle. Thirty degrees protects the airway during feeding and limits shear, and a 30 degree tilt offloads the sacrum.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options protect one thing and harm another. Pick the option that covers both the airway and the skin.

steps.detail: Aspiration from the feeding and shear on the sacrum.
Flat fails the airway. 45 degrees fails the skin.
It loads the trochanter.

elimination.verdict: 30 degrees up and 30 degrees tilted.

questions.stem: Five days after abdominal surgery, a client's dressing is suddenly soaked with pink, watery drainage. The incision edges are closed without redness. Which complication does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Wound infection
options.rationale: Tempting because any new drainage suggests infection. The drainage is pink and watery, not purulent, and there is no redness.

options.text: Hemorrhage from the incision
options.rationale: Bleeding would be frank red blood, not blood tinged serum.

options.text: Wound dehiscence
options.rationale: A sudden increase in serosanguineous drainage in a closed incision often comes just before the edges separate.

options.text: Delayed inflammatory phase
options.rationale: Serosanguineous drainage is expected in the first 48 hours. A sudden increase on day 5 is a change.

questions.takeaway: A sudden rise in serosanguineous drainage from a closed incision warns of dehiscence, even when the edges still look closed.
questions.coverage: Not in Lecture PPT. Covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Read the drainage color and the timing. Pink and watery plus sudden on day 5 points away from infection and toward separation.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pink and watery is serosanguineous, not purulent and not frank blood.
Normal for 48 hours. A sudden increase on day 5 is new.
Sudden serosanguineous increase comes before dehiscence.

elimination.verdict: Dehiscence.

questions.stem: A client with toxic epidermal necrolysis had the causative drug stopped yesterday. The client now has a hoarse voice and is drooling. Which action is the priority?

options.text: Call the rapid response team for airway evaluation
options.rationale: Hoarseness and drooling mean the airway mucosa is sloughing. Airway comes before everything else.

options.text: Increase the IV fluid rate as prescribed
options.rationale: Tempting because detached skin loses fluid like a burn. Circulation comes after an airway that is closing.

options.text: Apply lubricant to both eyes
options.rationale: Eye care prevents scarring and belongs in the plan after the airway is secured.

options.text: Give the prescribed IV analgesic
options.rationale: Pain control matters and it does not come before the airway.

questions.takeaway: In SJS or TEN, stop the drug first. Once that is done, the airway leads the supportive care, ahead of fluids, pain and eyes.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The stem says the drug is already stopped, so the usual first step is gone. Rank what is left with the ABCs.

steps.detail: The drug was stopped yesterday.
Hoarse voice and drooling are airway cues.
Fluids are circulation. Pain and eyes follow.

elimination.verdict: Airway evaluation now.

questions.stem: The day after surgery, the assistive personnel (AP) reports a red heel. The nurse finds intact maroon skin that feels boggy and does not blanch. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Document a stage 1 injury and recheck next shift
options.rationale: Tempting because the skin is intact and does not blanch. The maroon color and boggy feel tip it to deeper damage.

options.text: Cover the heel with a hydrocolloid and continue the turning schedule
options.rationale: A dressing does not remove the pressure, and the turning schedule alone leaves the heel on the bed.

options.text: Ask the AP to recheck the heel after the next turn
options.rationale: Assessment of a changing area stays with the nurse.

options.text: Float the heel and report a suspected deep tissue injury
options.rationale: Maroon, boggy, nonblanchable intact skin is deep tissue damage that can open quickly. Offload it and report.

questions.takeaway: Stage 1 is red. Purple or maroon intact skin is a deep tissue injury, so offload it at once and report.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Intact skin does not mean minor. Color is the detail that separates stage 1 from deep tissue injury.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Maroon and boggy means deep damage, not stage 1.
Only floating the heel takes weight off it.
The AP reports. The nurse assesses.

elimination.verdict: Float the heel and report.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old reports 36 hours of deep, burning pain on the left side of the chest. Today the nurse sees grouped vesicles in a band that stops at the midline. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Apply calamine lotion and recheck the rash next week
options.rationale: Calamine is a real comfort measure for these lesions. Used alone, it lets the window for antiviral treatment close.

options.text: Arrange provider evaluation today for antiviral treatment
options.rationale: One sided vesicles in a band after deep pain fit herpes zoster. Antivirals work best within 72 hours of the rash, and these vesicles appeared today.

options.text: Teach that the blisters will crust and clear without treatment
options.rationale: The lesions do crust in time. Early treatment is what limits the course and lasting nerve pain in older adults.

options.text: Schedule the shingles vaccine for later this week
options.rationale: The vaccine prevents zoster. It does not treat an active outbreak.

questions.takeaway: Pain first, then one sided vesicles along a dermatome: think herpes zoster and get antivirals started within 72 hours of the rash.
questions.coverage: Not in Lecture PPT. Covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Calamine and antivirals are both part of zoster care. The rash is new today, which makes one of them time sensitive.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Deep pain, then grouped vesicles in a band on one side.
A vaccine is not treatment.
Antivirals work best within 72 hours of the rash. Calamine can be added.

elimination.verdict: Same day evaluation for antiviral treatment.

questions.stem: A client with a stage 2 coccyx injury rates pain 7 of 10 with movement and refuses to turn. The dressing change is due. Which action comes first?

options.text: Give the prescribed analgesic before repositioning
options.rationale: Pain is treated before repositioning and dressing changes. Once it is controlled, the turn and the dressing change can go ahead.

options.text: Ask the client to describe the pain location and quality
options.rationale: Tempting because assessment usually comes first. The stem already gives the rating and the trigger, so action is due.

options.text: Explain that turning is needed to heal the wound
options.rationale: True, and teaching does not work on a client in pain.

options.text: Postpone the dressing change until the next shift
options.rationale: Leaves the pain untreated and the client on the wound.

questions.takeaway: Give pain medication before repositioning and dressing changes. Controlled pain is what lets the client move.
questions.coverage: Not in Lecture PPT. Covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Check whether the stem already assessed. When it has, the assessment option is a stall.

steps.action: Find the assessment in the stem
steps.detail: Pain 7 with movement, refusing to turn.
Turning and wound care.
Medicate, then do the care.

elimination.verdict: Analgesic first, then turn and dress.

questions.nursesNote: 1000: 82-year-old with dark skin, bed rest day 4 after a stroke. Sacral skin same color as surrounding skin but warmer and firm, and client winces when it is touched. Weight down 6% in one month. Hair sparse and nails dull. Oxygen tubing in place with red grooves behind both ears. Heels same temperature and firmness as surrounding skin, nontender. Voiding by scheduled toileting, skin dry.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that require follow up for tissue integrity.

segments.text: bed rest day 4 after a stroke
segments.rationale: Immobility is the leading risk factor and calls for a pressure reduction plan.

segments.text: Sacral skin same color as surrounding skin but warmer and firm, and client winces when it is touched
segments.rationale: In dark skin, warmth, firmness and pain signal early damage before any color change.

segments.text: Weight down 6% in one month
segments.rationale: More than 5% weight loss is a nutrition cue. Request a dietitian consult.

segments.text: Hair sparse and nails dull
segments.rationale: Both suggest undernutrition, which slows healing.

segments.text: Oxygen tubing in place with red grooves behind both ears
segments.rationale: A device related injury is starting. Pad or reposition the tubing.

segments.text: Heels same temperature and firmness as surrounding skin, nontender
segments.rationale: No temperature change, firmness change or pain. Nothing here needs follow up.

segments.text: Voiding by scheduled toileting, skin dry
segments.rationale: Moisture is controlled. Nothing to act on.

questions.takeaway: In dark skin, use your hands: warmth, firmness and pain come before color. Check under every device and read the nutrition cues.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The sacrum is the trap because the color is normal. Normal color does not clear dark skin.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Warm, firm and painful means early damage.
Grooves behind the ears are pressure.
Weight loss, sparse hair, dull nails.

questions.stem: A long term care resident has intense itching at night and thin raised lines between the fingers. The roommate has begun itching too. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Apply moisturizer after bathing and add a room humidifier
options.rationale: Tempting because dry skin is the usual cause of itching in older adults. The burrows and the roommate tip it away.

options.text: Request a bedtime antihistamine for the resident
options.rationale: Eases the itch and leaves the mites and the spread untreated.

options.text: Start contact precautions and have the roommate examined
options.rationale: Burrows in the finger webs with night itching and an itching contact point to scabies, which spreads by contact and bedding.

options.text: Inspect the hair shafts near the scalp for nits
options.rationale: Nits fit lice. The finger web lines fit mite burrows.

questions.takeaway: Night itching, finger web burrows and an itching contact mean scabies: contact precautions, examine and treat contacts, hot water laundry.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two cues separate this from simple dry skin: the lines between the fingers and the second person itching.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Raised lines in the finger webs are burrows.
A second itching person means spread.
Precautions and contact examination come before comfort care.

elimination.verdict: Contact precautions and check the roommate.

questions.stem: Two days after sharp debridement, a stage 3 injury measures larger than last week. The bed is moist and red with no odor, and the surrounding skin is intact and its usual color. Which conclusion is correct?

options.text: The wound is deteriorating, so the provider needs a report today
options.rationale: Tempting because a larger wound is normally reported. The recent debridement and the healthy bed tip it away.

options.text: The wound is infected, so an antimicrobial dressing is needed
options.rationale: No purulent drainage, odor or spreading redness supports infection.

options.text: The debridement failed, so mechanical debridement should be added
options.rationale: Mechanical debridement is avoided when the bed is mostly granulation.

options.text: The change is expected, so continue the current plan
options.rationale: Wound size increases after dead tissue is removed. A red moist bed, no odor and calm margins show a healthy wound.

questions.takeaway: Wounds measure larger right after debridement. Judge the bed, the drainage and the margins before calling it deterioration.
questions.coverage: Not in Lecture PPT. Covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The size alone misleads. The timing of the debridement is the detail that changes the meaning.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Debridement was 2 days ago.
Red, moist, no odor.
Intact skin of the usual color means no spreading infection.

elimination.verdict: Expected. Continue the plan.

questions.stem: Six days after surgery, a client taking long term prednisone has a pale incision with closed edges and normal temperature. Which finding requires follow up?

options.text: Absence of redness along the incision line
options.rationale: Tempting to read as slow healing. With steroids, a calm looking incision neither confirms nor rules out a problem.

options.text: Incision pain that has increased since yesterday
options.rationale: Steroids blunt redness, warmth and fever. Rising pain may be the only sign of infection in this client.

options.text: Scant dried serosanguineous drainage on the dressing
options.rationale: Old, dried and scant. Nothing new is draining.

options.text: Oral temperature of 37.1 C
options.rationale: Expected, and not reliable in a client whose inflammatory response is suppressed.

questions.takeaway: Immunosuppressed clients may not show typical inflammation. A change in pain counts even when the wound looks quiet.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The drug in the stem tells you which cues you cannot trust. Look for the cue steroids do not hide.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Prednisone mutes redness, warmth and fever.
Pain is increasing.
They are unreliable here, not reassuring.

elimination.verdict: Increasing incision pain.

questions.stem: A client receiving heparin has negative pressure wound therapy on a sacral wound. The canister is filling quickly with bright red blood. Which action comes first?

options.text: Stop the suction and apply direct pressure to the wound
options.rationale: The suction is pulling blood from an anticoagulated wound. Stop the source and control the bleeding.

options.text: Notify the provider of the bleeding
options.rationale: Needed right away, and tempting as the first step. The client is actively bleeding, so the nurse stops it before calling.

options.text: Check the most recent clotting time result
options.rationale: Useful for the provider and it delays control of visible bleeding.

options.text: Replace the canister and continue to monitor output
options.rationale: Leaves the suction running on a bleeding wound.

questions.takeaway: Clients on anticoagulants need close watching during negative pressure therapy. Bright red blood in the canister: stop suction, apply pressure, then notify.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The finding is already clear, so more data is not the first step. Do the thing that stops the harm.

steps.detail: Bright red blood filling quickly is active bleeding.
Suction on a wound in a client on heparin.
Stop and press, then call.

elimination.verdict: Stop suction and apply pressure.

questions.stem: A client with hives from a new food is going home on an antihistamine. Which statement indicates a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I will skip my evening run until the hives are gone."
options.rationale: Correct. Overexertion dilates vessels.

options.text: "I will not have wine with dinner this week."
options.rationale: Correct. Alcohol dilates vessels.

options.text: "A long hot bath tonight should calm the itching."
options.rationale: Heat dilates vessels and makes hives worse. Cool or tepid water is the choice.

options.text: "I will not drive after I take the medicine."
options.rationale: Correct. Antihistamines cause drowsiness.

questions.takeaway: With urticaria, remove the trigger, take the antihistamine, and avoid heat, alcohol and overexertion because all three dilate vessels.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: You are looking for the wrong statement. Three statements avoid something and one adds heat.

steps.detail: Find the statement that is wrong.
Three avoid a vessel dilator or a safety risk.
A hot bath adds heat.

elimination.verdict: The hot bath statement.

questions.stem: A stage 3 injury has stayed the same size for 3 weeks. The bed is red and moist with no odor, turning is documented, and the client eats about a third of each meal. Which addition is the priority?

options.text: Request a wound culture
options.rationale: Open pressure injuries are colonized, and there are no clinical signs of infection here.

options.text: Ask the wound nurse for a different dressing
options.rationale: A reasonable thought when a wound stalls. The bed is red and moist, so the dressing is doing its job.

options.text: Increase the turning schedule to every hour
options.rationale: Pressure relief is already documented, and more turning does not supply what the wound lacks.

options.text: Request a dietitian consult for protein and calories
options.rationale: A wound cannot build tissue without protein and calories. Poor intake is the one unmet need in the stem.

questions.takeaway: When a clean, moist, offloaded wound stops progressing, look at intake. Severe protein deficiency stops healing.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Each option fixes a different cause of a stalled wound. Match each cause to the stem and see which one is actually present.

steps.detail: No odor, no change in the bed. A culture is not supported.
Red, moist bed and documented turning.
A third of each meal is not enough protein to heal.

elimination.verdict: The dietitian consult.

questions.scenario: A client with a Braden score of 14 (moderate risk; lower scores mean higher risk) has had a prevention plan for one week: turning every 2 hours, heel pillows, barrier cream and a protein supplement.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether the plan is effective or needs revision.

rows.text: Sacral redness fades and blanches within 20 minutes of turning
rows.rationale: Blanching means the capillaries refill and the turning plan is relieving pressure.

rows.text: Heel shows redness that stays when pressed
rows.rationale: Nonblanchable redness is new damage. The heel pillows are not keeping pressure off this heel.

rows.text: Client eats all of the protein supplement and weight is stable
rows.rationale: Protein and calorie goals are being met.

rows.text: Perineal skin is moist and macerated at the 2 hour checks
rows.rationale: Moisture is not controlled by barrier cream alone. Add prompt cleansing and a toileting schedule.

rows.text: Client is found slid down with the head of the bed at 50 degrees
rows.rationale: Sliding at that angle causes shear. Keep the head at or below 30 degrees.

rows.text: A hand slides easily between the heels and the mattress
rows.rationale: The heels are floated.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate each part of the plan against its own target: blanching skin, floated heels, dry skin, met protein goals, head at or below 30 degrees.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Match each finding to the intervention it tests. A plan can work in one area and fail in another.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Blanching and floated heels are good. Nonblanching is not.
Macerated skin means moisture is winning.
Sliding at 50 degrees fails. Supplement taken passes.

elimination.verdict: Effective, revise, effective, revise, revise, effective.

questions.stem: A stage 3 injury has a hydrocolloid dressing changed every 3 days. At each change drainage has leaked past the edges, and the skin around the wound is white and wrinkled. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Apply barrier cream to the wound edges and keep the dressing
options.rationale: Barrier cream protects the edges, which makes it tempting. The dressing would still be overwhelmed by the drainage.

options.text: Ask the wound nurse about an alginate dressing
options.rationale: White, wrinkled skin is maceration from drainage the dressing cannot hold. An alginate absorbs exudate in a draining stage 3 injury.

options.text: Ask the wound nurse about a hydrogel dressing
options.rationale: Hydrogel adds moisture and suits wounds with minimal exudate. This wound has too much.

options.text: Leave the wound uncovered for part of each day
options.rationale: Wounds heal in a moist, covered environment. An open wound dries and is exposed to contamination.

questions.takeaway: Match the dressing to the exudate. Leaking drainage with macerated edges means the wound needs absorption: alginate or foam.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options change the dressing type. One adds moisture and one absorbs it, so read the wound edges.

steps.detail: White and wrinkled means too wet.
Hydrogel adds moisture. Alginate absorbs it.
Cream shields the skin. Absorption removes the cause. Open air dries the bed.

elimination.verdict: An alginate dressing.

questions.stem: At a skin screening, four clients need follow up. Which client does the nurse refer first?

options.text: A client with a pearly bump on the nose that bleeds and crusts
options.rationale: Tempting because it is actively bleeding. This pattern fits a slow growing cancer that rarely spreads.

options.text: A farmer with rough, scaly patches on the forehead
options.rationale: Sun damaged skin that can progress and needs referral, though not first.

options.text: A client whose mole now has three colors and a ragged border
options.rationale: Color variation, an irregular border and change point to melanoma, the skin cancer most likely to spread.

options.text: A client with a round, even brown mole unchanged in photographs
options.rationale: Stable and symmetric. Continue monthly self examination.

questions.takeaway: All changing lesions are referred. A multicolored, irregular, changing mole goes first because melanoma spreads.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides.
questions.strategy: Bleeding draws the eye. Rank by which lesion can spread fastest, not by which looks worst today.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Unchanged in photos.
Scaly patches and a pearly bump progress slowly.
A changing multicolored mole.

elimination.verdict: The changing mole.

questions.stem: A client with a Braden score of 15 (mild risk) sits in a chair most of the day and can stand with one person assisting. Which plan is best?

options.text: Assist the client to stand and march in place every hour
options.rationale: A client who can stand relieves pressure by standing and stepping about 5 times each hour.

options.text: Return the client to bed after one hour in the chair
options.rationale: Tempting because it limits sitting time. The client can stand, so bed rest gives up mobility without need.

options.text: Place a ring shaped cushion under the buttocks
options.rationale: Ring cushions press on the surrounding tissue and reduce blood flow.

options.text: Reposition the client in the chair every 2 hours
options.rationale: Two hours is the bed schedule. Sitting loads a smaller area and needs hourly relief.

questions.takeaway: Chair clients who are able stand and march in place 5 steps every hour. Use the client's own mobility before limiting activity.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Use the detail that the client can stand. The best plan relieves pressure and keeps the client moving.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Can stand with one assist.
Bed rest relieves pressure and costs mobility.
It damages capillaries.

elimination.verdict: Stand and march every hour.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old with dry, itchy skin and nightly scratching completes teaching. Which statement indicates the plan is understood?

options.text: "I will take a warm shower each morning with deodorant soap."
options.rationale: Daily full bathing and deodorant soap both strip oil from dry skin.

options.text: "I will rub my legs dry and put my lotion on at bedtime."
options.rationale: Lotion is right. Rubbing irritates the skin, and moisturizer goes on right after the bath.

options.text: "I will keep my bedroom warmer so my skin does not dry out."
options.rationale: Warmth makes itching worse. A cool room with a humidifier is the advice.

options.text: "I will bathe every other day in lukewarm water."
options.rationale: A full bath every other day in tepid water limits drying. Soap is used daily only on the face, axillae and perineum.

questions.takeaway: Dry, itchy skin: bathe every other day in tepid water, mild soap, pat dry, moisturize, sleep in a cool room.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Every statement contains something that sounds like skin care. Look for the one with no drying or warming step in it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Daily deodorant soap, rubbing dry.
A warm bedroom increases itch.
Every other day, lukewarm water.

elimination.verdict: Bathing every other day in lukewarm water.

questions.stem: A son asks for a swab culture of his mother's open stage 3 injury. The wound is smaller with no odor, redness or fever. Which response is most appropriate?

options.text: Request a culture order so that treatment can start early
options.rationale: Tempting as the cautious choice. With a shrinking wound and no signs, a positive swab would lead to unneeded antibiotics.

options.text: Explain that infection is identified by clinical signs
options.rationale: Open pressure injuries are always colonized, so a swab grows bacteria anyway. Infection is judged by the wound and the client.

options.text: Request an antimicrobial dressing as a precaution
options.rationale: Antimicrobial dressings are for infected wounds. This one is healing.

options.text: Tell him a culture is unnecessary because the wound is healing
options.rationale: Dismisses the concern and gives him nothing to watch for.

questions.takeaway: Wound cultures are not routine for pressure injuries. Watch for spreading redness, a change in drainage, a larger wound, fever or a high white count.
questions.coverage: Not in Lecture PPT. Covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The assessment in the stem is already complete and reassuring. The right response uses it and still answers the son.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Smaller, no odor, no redness, no fever.
A colonized wound grows bacteria without being infected.
Explain what is being watched.

elimination.verdict: Explain clinical monitoring.

questions.stem: A husband will care for his wife's stage 4 sacral injury at home. Which statements by the husband indicate the discharge teaching was effective? Select all that apply.

options.text: "I will show you how I take off the old dressing, clean the wound and put on a new one before we leave."
options.rationale: A return demonstration before discharge confirms the caregiver can do the care.

options.text: "I will rub the red skin near the wound to bring the blood back."
options.rationale: Massage damages the capillaries in reddened skin.

options.text: "I will call if the drainage changes color, smells bad or the skin around it gets redder."
options.rationale: These are the changes that are reported.

options.text: "I will keep the wound open to air so it dries out."
options.rationale: Wounds heal in a moist, covered environment. Drying slows healing.

options.text: "I will give the pain medicine about half an hour before I change the dressing."
options.rationale: Pain is treated before dressing changes and repositioning.

questions.takeaway: Home wound care teaching is effective when the caregiver demonstrates the dressing change, knows what to report and treats pain first.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two statements sound caring and harm the wound. Rubbing red skin and drying the wound both slow healing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Return demonstration, reporting changes, pain control before the dressing change.
It injures reddened skin.
A moist wound bed heals.

elimination.verdict: A, C, E.

questions.stem: The nurse receives report on four clients with pressure injuries. Which client does the nurse see first?

options.text: Stage 4 sacral injury with tunneling and moderate drainage, unchanged this week
options.rationale: Looks the worst, and it is unchanged. A stable chronic wound can wait.

options.text: Unstageable heel injury covered with dry, intact eschar
options.rationale: Dry, stable eschar on a heel is left alone and offloaded. Expected.

options.text: Stage 2 sacral injury, new foul tan drainage, temperature 38.7 C
options.rationale: The stage is not the cue. A new change in the color and odor of drainage with a fever suggests infection that may be reaching the blood.

options.text: Heel deep tissue injury that opened to a shallow ulcer overnight
options.rationale: Tempting because it is a real change. Deep tissue injuries often open as they evolve, and the change described is local. No fever or drainage change is reported.

questions.takeaway: Do not rank pressure injuries by stage. New foul drainage with a fever means infection and outranks a deeper wound that is stable.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Do not rank by stage. Look for the client with a new change plus a whole body sign.

steps.detail: Unchanged stage 4 and dry intact eschar.
One wound opened as expected. One has new foul drainage and a fever.
Fever with a drainage change points to infection that can spread.

elimination.verdict: The stage 2 injury with foul drainage and a fever.

questions.stem: A male client was turned off a reddened left hip 30 minutes ago. The skin is intact, and the redness does not blanch. The AP asks whether the left side can stay in the turning schedule. Which response is correct?

options.text: "No. Keep him off that hip, and I will report it."
options.rationale: Redness that does not blanch after 30 minutes off the area is a stage 1 pressure injury. It is offloaded and reported.

options.text: "Yes. The skin is intact, so keep the 2 hour schedule."
options.rationale: Tempting because the skin is unbroken. Intact skin that does not blanch is already damaged, and more pressure deepens it.

options.text: "Not yet. I will check the blanching again in 30 minutes."
options.rationale: Tempting as assessment first. The blanch test is already done and gave the answer.

options.text: "Yes, but limit his time on that side to 1 hour."
options.rationale: Shorter time sounds like a fair compromise. Nonblanchable redness is tissue damage, and any more pressure on it adds to the injury.

questions.takeaway: Blanchable redness means perfusion is intact. Intact skin with nonblanchable redness is stage 1, so it stays offloaded.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Intact skin sounds reassuring. The deciding word is in the blanch test.

steps.detail: Does not blanch after 30 minutes off the area.
Intact skin that does not blanch is already injured, so it takes no more pressure.

steps.action: Choose action over a repeat test
steps.detail: The assessment is complete.

elimination.verdict: Keep him off the hip and report it.

questions.stem: A stage 3 sacral injury is slightly smaller than two weeks ago. The wound bed was beefy red and moist two weeks ago and is now pale and dry with no drainage or odor. How does the nurse interpret these findings?

options.text: The wound is healing well, so continue the plan
options.rationale: Tempting because the wound is smaller and clean. Healthy granulation is beefy red and moist, and this bed has lost both.

options.text: The wound is infected, so request a wound culture
options.rationale: There is no odor, drainage change or redness, and cultures are not routine for pressure injuries.

options.text: The wound is ready to be left open to the air
options.rationale: A dry bed is the problem here. Open wounds heal in a moist environment.

options.text: Healing has stalled, so report the change
options.rationale: Granulation that turns from beefy red to pale and dry means poor healing despite the smaller size. The change is reported so the plan can be reviewed.
