questions.takeaway: Size alone does not prove healing. Healthy granulation is beefy red and moist. A bed that turns pale and dry is reported.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: One finding looks better. Check the wound bed against what healthy granulation looks like before you accept it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Beefy red, moist, slightly spongy.
This bed has gone from beefy red and moist to pale and dry.
No odor, drainage or redness.

elimination.verdict: Healing has stalled. Report the change.

questions.stem: A client has two lesions. One is 7 mm, round and evenly tan, unchanged in photos for 10 years. The other is 3 mm and in 2 months has darkened and developed two colors. Which conclusion guides the referral?

options.text: The 7 mm lesion is the greater concern because of its size
options.rationale: Tempting because it passes the 6 mm mark, and it is still checked. Ten years without change makes it the lesser concern.

options.text: The 3 mm lesion is the greater concern because it is changing
options.rationale: Evolving outranks the other ABCDE features. A small lesion that darkens and gains colors is the one referred first.

options.text: Both can wait for the next yearly skin examination
options.rationale: Any ABCDE feature is checked now, and a changing lesion does not wait a year.

options.text: Neither needs referral until a border becomes irregular
options.rationale: Each ABCDE feature counts by itself. Waiting for a second feature delays care.

questions.takeaway: Any one ABCDE feature gets a lesion checked. When features compete, evolving outranks diameter.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides.
questions.strategy: Both lesions meet one ABCDE feature. Decide which feature carries more weight.

steps.action: Match each lesion to a letter
steps.detail: 7 mm is diameter. Darkening with two colors is color and evolving.
A changing lesion is not watched for a year.
Change beats size.

elimination.verdict: The small changing lesion goes first.

questions.stem: A heel injury was covered with dry, intact eschar last week. Today the eschar edge is soft and lifting, and the skin around it is red and warm. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Leave the eschar alone and keep the heel floated
options.rationale: Tempting because that is the rule for stable heel eschar. Soft edges with redness and warmth mean it is no longer stable.

options.text: Apply a hydrogel to soften the rest of the eschar
options.rationale: Softening eschar is a debridement decision that belongs to the provider.

options.text: Trim the loose eschar edge with sterile scissors
options.rationale: Sharp debridement is outside the nurse's role here and could cause bleeding.

options.text: Report the change for possible debridement
options.rationale: The eschar is unstable and there are signs of infection, so the leave it alone rule no longer applies.

questions.takeaway: Heel eschar is left intact only while it is dry, stable and free of infection. Softening, lifting, redness or warmth gets reported.
questions.coverage: Not in Lecture PPT. Covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The familiar rule has conditions. Check whether this heel still meets them.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Dry, intact, no infection.
Soft, lifting, red and warm fail all three.
The nurse reports. The provider decides on debridement.

elimination.verdict: Report it. The eschar is no longer stable.

questions.stem: After surgery for a ruptured appendix, a client's abdominal wound is left open and packed, with closure planned later this week. The spouse asks whether the surgeon forgot to close it. Which response is accurate?

options.text: "It will fill in by itself from the bottom up."
options.rationale: Tempting because the wound is open now. That describes second intention, and this wound is planned for closure.

options.text: "It stays open until the infection risk clears, then it is closed."
options.rationale: Delayed primary closure, or third intention. A contaminated wound is closed once it is clean.

options.text: "I will page the surgeon and ask whether the closure step was missed."
options.rationale: Treats a planned approach as an error and leaves the spouse more worried.

options.text: "The edges were brought together under the packing."
options.rationale: Closed edges describe first intention, and packing means the wound is open.

questions.takeaway: First intention: edges closed. Second: left open to granulate. Third: left open until infection risk clears, then closed.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: A ruptured appendix means contamination. Ask which healing pattern is chosen on purpose for a dirty wound.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A rupture contaminates the wound.
Second intention never gets closed. Third intention does.
It was not forgotten. It is planned.

elimination.verdict: Open until infection risk clears, then closed.

questions.stem: Three days after a knee incision, the edges are together with about 5 mm of redness, slight warmth and swelling. There is no drainage. How does the nurse evaluate these findings?

options.text: Early cellulitis that should be reported
options.rationale: Tempting because redness and warmth are infection signs. Cellulitis is redness spreading more than 1 cm from the edge.

options.text: Early dehiscence that needs a binder
options.rationale: Dehiscence is warned by separating edges or a sudden rise in drainage. Neither is present.

options.text: Delayed healing that needs a nutrition consult today
options.rationale: Day 3 is too early to call healing delayed, and nothing here is off schedule.

options.text: Normal inflammatory phase, so continue monitoring
options.rationale: Days 1 to 5 bring redness, warmth, edema and pain as white cells arrive. Narrow, non spreading redness with closed edges is expected.

questions.takeaway: Redness, warmth and swelling are expected in days 1 to 5. Redness wider than 1 cm, purulent drainage or separating edges are not.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Every finding in the stem can mean infection or normal healing. The day and the width of the redness decide which.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Day 3 is inside the inflammatory phase.
5 mm is well under 1 cm.
No drainage, edges together.

elimination.verdict: Normal inflammatory phase. Keep monitoring.

questions.stem: An unstageable sacral injury covered with tan slough has had a prescribed enzymatic agent for 1 week. Which finding best indicates the treatment is working?

options.text: Less slough covers the base, and red tissue shows
options.rationale: The agent loosens the collagen that holds dead tissue. Thinner slough with red tissue showing is the goal, and the wound can then be staged.

options.text: The skin around the wound is no longer red
options.rationale: Tempting because it sounds like healing. It reports on the surrounding skin, and the agent is there to clear dead tissue from the base.

options.text: A dry, dark crust now covers the wound bed
options.rationale: That is eschar. There is more dead tissue, not less.

options.text: The client reports no discomfort with application
options.rationale: Enzymatic agents can sting. Comfort does not show that slough is clearing.

questions.takeaway: Debridement is judged by how much dead tissue is left. Once the base is visible, an unstageable injury can be staged. Stable, dry heel eschar is the exception: leave it alone.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Ask what the treatment is for. An enzymatic agent removes slough, so look for the option that reports on slough.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Clear the dead tissue.
Calmer surrounding skin is welcome and says nothing about the slough.
A dark crust is the opposite of the goal.

elimination.verdict: Less slough with red tissue showing.

questions.stem: A client with a stage 4 sacral injury lies on the right side. The nurse probes a 2.5 cm tunnel that points straight toward the client's feet. How is this documented?

options.text: 2.5 cm tunnel at 3:00, toward the mattress side
options.rationale: Uses the bed as the reference. The clock is fixed to the client's body, not to the room.

options.text: 2.5 cm of undermining along the lower edge
options.rationale: Undermining is skin separating from tissue at the wound margin. A tunnel is a track extending from the wound.

options.text: 2.5 cm tunnel at 6:00, with the head as 12:00
options.rationale: The clock is anchored to the client. Head is 12:00 and feet are 6:00 in any position.

options.text: 2.5 cm added to the recorded wound depth
options.rationale: Depth is measured straight down at the base. A tunnel is recorded separately, with its direction.

questions.takeaway: Tunneling is recorded by length and clock position. The head is 12:00 and the feet are 6:00, whatever position the client is in.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The side lying position is there to pull you toward the room's up and down. Anchor the clock to the client.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Head 12:00, feet 6:00.
A track into tissue, not a lip under the edge.
Depth and tunnel length are two measurements.

elimination.verdict: 2.5 cm tunnel at 6:00.

questions.stem: A client who uses a wheelchair about 10 hours a day has a stage 3 ischial injury. Dressing and protein plans are in place and followed. Which referral does the nurse request?

options.text: Physical therapy for seating and offloading
options.rationale: The source of pressure is the chair. Physical therapy addresses offloading, cushions and tilt in space seating.

options.text: The wound nurse for a different type of dressing
options.rationale: Tempting because the wound is deep. The dressing plan is already in place and followed, and no dressing removes the pressure.

options.text: The dietitian for a higher protein goal
options.rationale: Nutrition is already planned and followed.

options.text: The surgeon for a muscle flap closure
options.rationale: A flap placed over an area still under 10 hours of pressure will break down.

questions.takeaway: Find the source of the pressure and send the problem to the team member who owns it. Seating and offloading belong to physical therapy.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The stem closes two doors for you: dressings and protein are covered. Ask what is still causing the injury.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Cross off what is in place
steps.detail: Dressing and nutrition.
Ten hours a day on the ischium.
Offloading and seating: physical therapy.

elimination.verdict: Physical therapy for seating and offloading.

questions.stem: An 83-year-old who takes six daily medications is prescribed diphenhydramine at bedtime for itching. Which addition to the plan of care is the priority?

options.text: Cotton mittens to wear during sleep
options.rationale: Protects the skin from scratching. Broken skin is a smaller risk than a fall.

options.text: A cool bedroom with a light blanket
options.rationale: A real comfort measure for itching that does nothing about the new drug's risk.

options.text: Fall precautions with assistance to the bathroom
options.rationale: A sedating antihistamine added to polypharmacy in an older adult raises fall risk. Safety comes before comfort.

options.text: A tepid bath with moisturizer at bedtime
options.rationale: Treats dry skin. It does nothing about the new drug's risk.

questions.takeaway: Sedating antihistamines plus polypharmacy in an older adult means falls. Add fall precautions when the drug is added.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: All four belong in a pruritus plan. The priority word asks which one prevents injury.

steps.detail: A sedating drug was added.
Age 83 and six medications.
Three options ease itching. One prevents a fall.

elimination.verdict: Fall precautions.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old had a basal cell carcinoma removed 4 years ago. An old burn scar on the shoulder now itches and has a scaly crust. Its color and size are unchanged. Which action is appropriate?

options.text: Recheck the scar at the monthly self examination
options.rationale: Tempting because nothing on the ABCDE list has changed. New itching and crusting are reportable changes by themselves.

options.text: Suggest a moisturizer for the dry, scaly area
options.rationale: Treats a warning sign as dry skin.

options.text: Photograph the scar to compare in 3 months
options.rationale: Photos track stable lesions. This one has already changed.

options.text: Arrange a skin evaluation for the scar
options.rationale: A changing scar with new itching, scaling or crusting is reported, and a history of skin cancer raises the concern.

questions.takeaway: Report more than color, size and shape. New itching, tenderness, bleeding, oozing, crusting or scaling in a mole, wart, birthmark or scar gets evaluated.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The unchanged color and size are there to reassure you. Ask whether anything about the lesion is new.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Itching and a scaly crust.
Prior skin cancer and chronically damaged skin.
Three options wait or treat. One gets it examined.

elimination.verdict: Arrange a skin evaluation.

questions.stem: A client with a stage 3 injury has taken protein supplements for a month. Which finding best indicates the nutrition plan is supporting healing?

options.text: Weight is up 2 kg, with new ankle edema
options.rationale: Tempting because weight gain looks like better nutrition. Weight that arrives with edema is fluid.

options.text: Prealbumin has risen, and the bed shows new granulation
options.rationale: A rising protein marker together with new tissue in the wound shows the protein is reaching the wound.

options.text: The client finishes the dessert on every tray
options.rationale: Dessert adds calories and says little about protein intake.

options.text: Serum sodium is within the normal range
options.rationale: Sodium reflects hydration, not protein stores.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate nutrition with a protein marker and the wound itself: prealbumin, albumin or total protein rising, with granulation appearing.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Ask what each finding measures. Only one measures protein, and it comes with a change in the wound.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Fluid, protein, calories, hydration.
Edema explains it.
A marker and the tissue it is meant to build.

elimination.verdict: Rising prealbumin with new granulation.

questions.stem: A chair bound client with fecal incontinence has blanchable redness over the coccyx. The AP offers several ideas. Which does the nurse approve? Select all that apply.

options.text: Rub lotion into the reddened area at each turn
options.rationale: Massaging reddened skin damages capillaries in tissue that is already stressed.

options.text: Check under the brief at least every 2 hours
options.rationale: Stool left on the skin breaks it down. Frequent checks keep contact time short.

options.text: Seat the client on a donut cushion
options.rationale: A donut relieves the center and squeezes the ring around it, cutting off blood flow.

options.text: Scrub the skin with warm soapy water after each stool
options.rationale: Prompt cleaning is right. Scrubbing adds friction. Use mild soap, warm water and pat dry.

options.text: Apply a zinc oxide barrier cream after cleaning
options.rationale: A barrier keeps moisture and stool off the skin.

questions.takeaway: Protect at risk skin: clean promptly without scrubbing, pat dry, apply a barrier, check every 2 hours. Never massage reddened areas or use donut cushions.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Three of these ideas feel caring and add force to fragile skin: rubbing, scrubbing and a ring of pressure.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Massage, scrubbing and the donut.
Frequent checks and a barrier cream.
Two remain, and that is acceptable.

elimination.verdict: B and E.

questions.scenario: A 41-year-old started allopurinol 2 weeks ago. Today the skin is dusky red and painful, with blisters and sheets of peeling over about 35% of the body surface. The mouth has erosions. The next allopurinol dose is due now.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the client is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Withhold the allopurinol and notify the provider
options.rationale: Stopping the causative drug is the first step. Nothing else works while it continues.

options.text: Anticipate transfer to a burn unit or ICU
options.rationale: Skin loss over 30% behaves like a major burn and is usually managed in a burn unit or ICU.

options.text: Give the dose with an antihistamine
options.rationale: Treats it as hives and keeps giving the trigger.

options.text: Open the blisters to relieve pressure
options.rationale: Breaks the remaining barrier and raises infection risk.

options.text: Apply warm compresses to the red areas
options.rationale: Heat dilates vessels and adds fluid loss and pain.

options.text: Toxic epidermal necrolysis
options.rationale: A drug triggered reaction with mucosal erosions and more than 30% of the body surface involved.

options.text: Stevens-Johnson syndrome
options.rationale: The same process, involving less than 10% of the body surface.

options.text: Urticaria
options.rationale: Hives are raised, itchy wheals. They do not blister, peel or erode the mouth.

options.text: Contact dermatitis
options.rationale: Follows the shape of what touched the skin and spares the mouth.

options.text: Intake and urine output
options.rationale: Open skin loses fluid and electrolytes the way a burn does.

options.text: Body temperature
options.rationale: Lost skin cannot hold heat, and fever may signal infection.

options.text: Serum uric acid
options.rationale: Tracks the gout the drug was treating, which is not the current threat.

options.text: Blood glucose
options.rationale: Nothing in this picture points to a glucose problem. Fluid and heat loss are the threats.

options.text: Pupil size
options.rationale: Eye care matters here, and it means lubricating and protecting the surface, not checking pupils.

questions.takeaway: SJS and TEN are the same drug reaction sorted by body surface: under 10% is SJS, over 30% is TEN. Stop the drug first, then support like a burn.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Let the percentage name the condition. Then treat the skin as a lost barrier: fluid leaves, heat leaves, organisms enter.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 35% is over 30%.
A new drug 2 weeks ago, and a dose due now.

steps.action: Monitor what a lost barrier costs
steps.detail: Fluid and temperature.

elimination.verdict: Withhold the drug, notify the provider and anticipate burn level care; TEN; intake and output, temperature.

questions.stem: A restless client on bed rest shifts position often without help. Both elbows and heels have shiny, abraded skin from rubbing against the sheets. Which plan addresses the cause?

options.text: Cover elbows and heels with foam dressings
options.rationale: The damage is friction from rubbing, so a protective layer between skin and linen removes the cause.

options.text: Increase turning to every hour
options.rationale: Tempting. Turning relieves pressure, and this client already moves a great deal.

options.text: Apply zinc oxide to both areas
options.rationale: Barrier cream protects from moisture, which is not the problem here.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed to 45 degrees for comfort
options.rationale: A higher head of bed adds sliding and shear.

questions.takeaway: Name the force before you pick the fix: friction needs a protective surface, pressure needs offloading, moisture needs a barrier.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Each option treats a different force. Find the one in the stem.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Rubbing is friction.

steps.action: Cut the pressure and moisture fixes
steps.detail: Turning, zinc oxide.
Head of bed at 45.

elimination.verdict: Foam dressings over elbows and heels.

questions.stem: A client on a nasal cannula for 3 days says the tops of both ears are sore. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Apply moisturizer behind both ears
options.rationale: Treats before looking, and lotion does not relieve pressure.

options.text: Lift the tubing and inspect the skin under it
options.rationale: Devices cause pressure injuries, and soreness is an early cue. The nurse must see the skin before choosing padding or repositioning.

options.text: Change to a face mask
options.rationale: Tempting because it moves the tubing. It changes oxygen delivery, needs a prescription, and puts straps on new skin.

options.text: Explain that soreness from the tubing is expected at first
options.rationale: Dismisses an early warning of tissue damage.

questions.takeaway: Oxygen tubing, tubes, stockings and collars all cause pressure injuries. Soreness under a device means look under it.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The stem gives a symptom and no skin findings yet.

steps.detail: Only a report of soreness.
Lotion, mask.
Lift and inspect.

elimination.verdict: Lift the tubing and inspect the skin.

questions.stem: A sacral pressure injury is completely covered by yellow slough. A student plans to chart it as stage 3 because no bone is visible. Which response by the nurse is correct?

options.text: "Agreed. No bone means it cannot be stage 4."
options.rationale: Bone could lie under the slough.

options.text: "Chart it as stage 2 until the base is seen."
options.rationale: Slough is not present in stage 2, so this is already full thickness.

options.text: "Probe through the slough with an applicator to find the depth."
options.rationale: Tempting as a way to get the answer. Forcing through necrotic tissue causes harm and still does not show the base.

options.text: "The base is hidden, so the depth cannot be confirmed yet."
options.rationale: When slough or eschar obscures the wound bed, the extent of tissue loss cannot be determined until it is removed.

questions.takeaway: You stage what you can see. A covered base is unstageable until the slough or eschar is gone.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Ask whether anyone can see the wound bed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The base is fully covered.
Stage 2 and stage 3 both assume a depth.
Probing through slough.

elimination.verdict: The depth cannot be confirmed yet.

questions.stem: A client with toxic epidermal necrolysis over 35% of the body is receiving IV fluids. Which finding best indicates fluid replacement is adequate?

options.text: The open areas look moist and shiny
options.rationale: Moist wound surfaces reflect the skin loss, not the client's volume.

options.text: Urine output is 50 mL per hour
options.rationale: Large skin loss means large fluid loss. Steady urine output shows the kidneys are being perfused.

options.text: The client asks for water less often
options.rationale: Thirst is subjective and does not measure circulating volume.

options.text: Weight is 2 kg above admission
options.rationale: Tempting as proof fluid went in. A rapid gain suggests excess, not balance.

questions.takeaway: Skin is the barrier against fluid loss. When a large area is lost, urine output tells you whether replacement is keeping up.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides.
questions.strategy: Pick the measure of perfusion, not of comfort or of fluid given.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Fluid loss through open skin.
Thirst.
Rapid weight gain.

elimination.verdict: Urine output of 50 mL per hour.

questions.stem: A client in a group home was treated for head lice this morning. Which statement by the client indicates the teaching was effective?

options.text: "The itching will stop tonight, so I will know it worked."
options.rationale: Itching can last after treatment and does not prove success.

options.text: "I can share my brush again once my hair is dry."
options.rationale: Lice spread on shared combs, brushes and hats.

options.text: "I will comb out the nits with a fine comb and wash my bedding in hot water."
options.rationale: Nits stay glued to the hair shaft after treatment, and lice survive off the host for about 2 days, so combing and hot laundering finish the job.

options.text: "I will shampoo with it every day this week to be sure."
options.rationale: Tempting thoroughness. Overuse irritates the scalp and is not how the product is prescribed.

questions.takeaway: Lice treatment has three parts: the product, combing out the nits, and hot washing of linens and clothing. Nothing that touches the hair is shared.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Look for the statement that deals with what the product leaves behind: nits and linens.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: It spreads lice.

steps.action: Cut symptom based proof and overuse
steps.detail: Itch lingers, and daily treatment irritates the scalp.
Nits combed out, bedding washed hot.

elimination.verdict: Comb out the nits and wash bedding in hot water.

questions.stem: A client who walks independently has a Braden score of 17 (mild risk). The lowest subscale is moisture, from urinary incontinence several times a day. Which plan best targets this client's risk?

options.text: Order a powered pressure redistributing overlay for the bed
options.rationale: Tempting for any at risk score. Mobility and activity are good, so pressure is not the main driver.

options.text: Start a toileting schedule and apply a barrier cream
options.rationale: The subscale shows moisture is the problem. Keeping skin dry and protected addresses it directly.

options.text: Turn the client every 2 hours in bed
options.rationale: A walking client already shifts weight.

options.text: Request a dietitian consult for protein
options.rationale: Useful if nutrition were the low subscale.

questions.takeaway: The Braden total tells you who is at risk. The subscales tell you what to do about it.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Match the intervention to the lowest subscale.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Moisture.
Overlay, turning.
Nutrition.

elimination.verdict: Toileting schedule and barrier cream.

questions.stem: The nurse teaches the AP to protect a bedbound client's heels. Which action by the AP indicates the teaching was effective?

options.text: Places a folded pillow directly under both heels
options.rationale: The heels still bear weight on the pillow.

options.text: Rubs lotion into both heels with each turn
options.rationale: Rubbing over a bony prominence damages capillaries.

options.text: Places a pillow under the calves so the heels hang free
options.rationale: Floating the heels removes pressure from them completely.

options.text: Puts thick socks on and tucks the top sheet tightly
options.rationale: Socks do not relieve pressure, and a tight sheet presses the heels down.

questions.takeaway: Float heels: support the calf so the heel touches nothing.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Ask where the weight rests in each option.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Under the heel still means pressure.
It harms fragile vessels.
Pillow under the calves.

elimination.verdict: Pillow under the calves, heels free.

questions.stem: A client with a stage 4 sacral injury is newly confused. Temperature is 38.9 C, heart rate 118/min and blood pressure 88/52 mm Hg. Which action is the priority?

options.text: Give the prescribed acetaminophen and recheck in 1 hour
options.rationale: Treats the number and delays recognition of the cause.

options.text: Change the dressing and measure the wound
options.rationale: Tempting because the wound is the likely source. Wound care can wait behind an unstable client.

options.text: Offer oral fluids every 15 minutes
options.rationale: A confused, hypotensive client needs more than sips.

options.text: Report the findings as possible sepsis now
options.rationale: Fever, tachycardia, hypotension and new confusion with a deep wound point to sepsis, a known complication that needs rapid treatment.

questions.takeaway: Pressure injuries can seed sepsis. Fever with low pressure and new confusion is unstable, and that outranks wound care.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Unstable beats stable. Find the option that responds to the whole picture.

steps.detail: Fever, fast heart rate, low pressure, confusion.
Acetaminophen, sips.

steps.action: Cut the task that can wait
steps.detail: Dressing change.

elimination.verdict: Report possible sepsis now.

questions.stem: A client with diabetes has itchy lower legs with scratch marks. Fingernails and toenails are long and jagged. Which plan is best?

options.text: File the fingernails and refer to podiatry for toenails
options.rationale: Short, filed nails limit scratch injury. Toenails in diabetes go to podiatry because a small cut can become a serious wound.

options.text: Trim the fingernails and toenails straight across at the bedside
options.rationale: Tempting and efficient. Toenail cutting in diabetes is referred.

options.text: Teach the client to clip the toenails after a warm soak
options.rationale: Clients with diabetes should avoid cutting their own toenails.

options.text: Place mitts on both hands at night
options.rationale: More restrictive than needed when nail care solves the problem.

questions.takeaway: For itching, keep nails short and filed. For diabetes, toenails belong to podiatry.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two different nails, two different rules. Find the option that respects both.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Fingers can be filed.
Toenails are referred.
Mitts.

elimination.verdict: File fingernails and refer toenails to podiatry.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a sacral pressure injury at a scheduled dressing change. Place the nurse's actions in the order they are performed.

options.text: Perform hand hygiene and apply gloves
options.rationale: First. Standard Precautions come before any contact with the wound.

options.text: Remove the old dressing and note the drainage on it
options.rationale: Second. The dressing shows the amount and type of exudate.

options.text: Clean the wound as prescribed
options.rationale: Third. The bed and edges must be visible before measuring.

options.text: Measure length and width, then depth with a cotton tipped applicator
options.rationale: Fourth. Surface first, then depth marked at skin level.

options.text: Probe gently for tunneling and note its clock position
options.rationale: Fifth. Hidden extension is checked after the open wound is measured.

options.text: Apply the new dressing and document, comparing with the last entry
options.rationale: Last. Cover the wound, then record so the trend is clear.

questions.takeaway: Protect, expose, clean, measure what you see, probe what you cannot, then cover and compare.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: You cannot measure what you have not cleaned, and you cannot document a trend until you have numbers.

steps.detail: Hand hygiene and gloves.
Old dressing off, wound cleaned.
Surface, depth, tunnels, then dress and document.

elimination.verdict: Hand hygiene, remove, clean, measure, probe, dress and document.

questions.stem: A client with diabetes has a stage 3 heel injury unchanged for 4 weeks. The heel is floated and intake meets protein goals. The foot is cool with a faint pedal pulse. Which prescription does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Arterial blood flow studies of the leg
options.rationale: A heel injury that will not heal despite offloading and nutrition, in a cool foot with a faint pulse, points to poor arterial supply. Flow studies check it.

options.text: Duplex ultrasound of the leg veins
options.rationale: Tempting because it is also a blood flow test. It looks for venous disease or a clot, and a cool foot with a faint pulse is an arterial finding.

options.text: A larger protein supplement
options.rationale: Tempting because protein drives healing, but intake already meets the goal. The cool foot and faint pulse are the unexplained cues.

options.text: A transparent film dressing
options.rationale: Film is for noninfected stage 2 injuries, and no dressing fixes a wound that lacks blood flow.

questions.takeaway: When pressure and nutrition are already handled and a heel or ankle wound still will not heal, look at perfusion. Poor circulation is a leading cause of slow healing.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Cross off what the stem says is already done. The cue left over tells you what is missing.

steps.detail: Offloading and protein are in place.
A cool foot with a faint pulse is a perfusion finding.
Arterial flow studies, not a venous ultrasound, evaluate a heel injury that is not healing.

elimination.verdict: Arterial blood flow studies.

questions.stem: An 86-year-old woman has a small skin tear on the shin that looks unchanged after 7 days of the same dressing. The AP says it is minor and can wait for weekly skin rounds. Which response does the nurse give?

options.text: "It is small, so we will measure it again at weekly rounds."
options.rationale: Size does not make it safe to wait. In an older adult a minor wound that is not improving is acted on right away.

options.text: "Older skin heals slowly, so no change at one week is what we expect to see."
options.rationale: Tempting because aging does slow healing. That is the reason to act early, not a reason to wait.

options.text: "Keep the same dressing a second week before we change anything."
options.rationale: Repeats a plan that has produced no progress.

options.text: "At her age a stalled wound can turn chronic. I will look at it today."
options.rationale: Any wound in an older adult can become chronic, so even a minor problem is acted on right away.

questions.takeaway: In an older adult, any wound can become chronic. A minor wound that is not improving gets attention now, not at the next routine check.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options use the client's age. Decide whether age is a reason to wait or a reason to move sooner.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Weekly rounds and a second week of the same dressing both delay.
One uses age to excuse the stall. The other uses age as the reason to act today.

elimination.verdict: Reassess the wound today.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old is admitted for bowel surgery. Which history findings does the nurse report to the surgical team as raising the risk of slow wound healing? Select all that apply.

options.text: Radiation to the abdomen last year
options.rationale: Radiation damages circulation in the treated tissue, and poor circulation slows healing.

options.text: Cytotoxic drug therapy for cancer
options.rationale: Cytotoxic drugs slow healing.

options.text: One small meal a day with recent weight loss
options.rationale: Poor nutrition slows healing.

options.text: A steroid nasal spray used each spring for allergies
options.rationale: Tempting because steroids slow healing. That applies to high dose steroids, and a seasonal nasal spray is a small local dose.

options.text: Type 2 diabetes for 15 years
options.rationale: Diabetes causes poor circulation, a leading reason wounds heal slowly.

options.text: A healed appendectomy scar from age 20
options.rationale: An old wound that healed normally does not predict a problem now.

questions.takeaway: Healing slows with poor circulation (diabetes, arteriosclerosis, venous insufficiency, radiation), high dose steroids and cytotoxic drugs, infection or dead tissue, aging, stress, poor nutrition and poor oxygenation.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Judge each finding alone: does it cut blood supply, blunt the body's repair work or starve the wound of building material?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Radiation and diabetes both reduce blood flow to tissue.
Cytotoxic drugs and poor intake both slow repair.
A nasal spray is not high dose steroid therapy, and an old healed scar does not slow healing.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C and E.

questions.stem: A hip wound has full thickness skin loss. Fat is visible, the edges are rolled, and a thin strip of slough lies at one edge. No muscle, tendon or bone is seen or felt. How does the nurse stage it?

options.text: Stage 2
options.rationale: Stage 2 is partial thickness with exposed dermis. Fat and slough are not visible.

options.text: Stage 3
options.rationale: Full thickness skin loss with visible fat and no exposed muscle, tendon or bone. Slough may be present.

options.text: Stage 4
options.rationale: Stage 4 needs exposed or palpable fascia, muscle, tendon, ligament, cartilage or bone.

options.text: Unstageable
options.rationale: Unstageable means slough or eschar hides the base. Here the fat is seen.

questions.takeaway: Stage by the deepest visible tissue: dermis is stage 2, fat is stage 3, muscle, tendon or bone is stage 4. Unstageable only when slough or eschar hides the base.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Name the deepest tissue you can see, then ask whether the slough hides the base.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Fat.
A thin strip at one edge does not obscure the base.

elimination.verdict: Stage 3.

questions.stem: A client on bed rest has an unbroken blister on one heel filled with clear, straw colored fluid. The skin around it is its usual color. How does the nurse document this finding?

options.text: Deep tissue pressure injury
options.rationale: That is a blood filled blister or persistent deep red, maroon or purple skin.

options.text: Stage 1 pressure injury
options.rationale: Stage 1 is intact skin with nonblanchable erythema and no blister.

options.text: Unstageable pressure injury
options.rationale: No slough or eschar is hiding a wound bed.

options.text: Stage 2 pressure injury
options.rationale: Stage 2 may look like an intact or ruptured serum filled blister.

questions.takeaway: Serum filled blister is stage 2. Blood filled blister or maroon or purple skin is a deep tissue pressure injury.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The fluid in the blister decides. Clear serum and blood point to different injuries.

steps.detail: Clear and straw colored is serum.
Serum is stage 2. Blood would be deep tissue injury.

elimination.verdict: Stage 2.

questions.stem: A client's stage 3 sacral injury is clean and will heal by second intention. Which statement by the daughter shows she understands what to expect?

options.text: "The edges will knit together in a thin line, like her hip incision did."
options.rationale: Tempting because it describes normal healing. It is first intention, where the edges are brought together. An open cavity cannot heal that way.

options.text: "It will fill in slowly from the base and leave more of a scar."
options.rationale: Second intention: the open cavity fills with granulation tissue. It is slower and scars more.

options.text: "Once the infection risk passes, it will be stitched closed."
options.rationale: That is third intention, or delayed primary closure.

options.text: "It should be closed over in about 5 days, like a scrape."
options.rationale: A full thickness cavity takes weeks to fill and contract.

questions.takeaway: Pressure injuries heal by second intention: the cavity fills with granulation, slowly, with more scarring. First intention is closed edges and a thin scar. Third intention is left open, then closed later.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Match each statement to a healing pattern, then ask which pattern fits an open pressure injury.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Thin line is first intention. Stitched later is third intention.
An open cavity fills from the base.
Days is too fast for a full thickness wound.

elimination.verdict: It fills in slowly from the base and scars more.

questions.stem: The nurse and an assistive personnel (AP) share care of a newly admitted client with a Braden score of 11 (high risk) who wears a rigid cervical collar. Which task does the nurse keep?

options.text: Turning the client every 2 hours with a 30 degree side tilt
options.rationale: Routine repositioning is a task the AP carries out under supervision.

options.text: Cleaning the skin and applying barrier cream after incontinence
options.rationale: Hygiene and barrier cream are within the AP role.

options.text: Inspecting the skin under the collar and over bony prominences
options.rationale: Skin assessment is beyond the AP's scope. A new admission with a device needs the nurse's baseline inspection, including under the collar.

options.text: Checking under the incontinence brief every 2 hours for wetness
options.rationale: Tempting because it is a check. Looking for wetness on a schedule is an observation the AP makes and reports, not a skin assessment.

questions.takeaway: Delegate the doing, keep the assessing. Skin assessment, including under devices, is never delegated to the AP.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Sort each option into a task, a simple observation or a judgment. The nurse keeps the one that requires judgment.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Two are care tasks with a fixed method. Two involve looking at the client.
Checking a brief for wetness is a scheduled observation. Inspecting skin under a device and over bone is assessment.
Assessment is not delegated to the AP.

elimination.verdict: The nurse inspects the skin, including under the collar.

questions.stem: At 1500 the AP gives the nurse four reports about clients on turning schedules. Which report does the nurse act on first?

options.text: "He refused his turns and has been on his back since 1100."
options.rationale: Turning is due at least every 2 hours, and this client has gone 4 hours with the sacrum and heels unrelieved and the pressure is continuing. The nurse goes now to inspect the skin and find a position the client will accept.

options.text: "She ate half of her lunch and did not want the supplement."
options.rationale: Nutrition affects skin over days. It needs follow up later in the shift, after the client whose pressure is still unrelieved.

options.text: "His brief was wet at the 1400 check, so I cleaned him and changed it."
options.rationale: The moisture was found on schedule and handled correctly.

options.text: "The red spot on her hip faded a few minutes after I turned her."
options.rationale: Redness that fades after pressure is relieved shows the capillaries refill. It is an early sign to keep watching, and the turn has already relieved it.

questions.takeaway: Rank reports by what is still going on. Pressure left unrelieved past the 2 hour turning limit is a risk that continues until the nurse acts. A problem already handled or one that builds over days can wait.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Ask of each report: is the problem still going on, already handled, or slow to build?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The wet brief was changed, and the redness faded after the turn.
A missed supplement acts over days. Four hours on the back is twice the turning limit, and the pressure is still there.

elimination.verdict: The client who has been on his back since 1100.

questions.stem: A client with a Braden score of 13 (moderate risk) has a prevention plan that sets fluids at 2500 mL/day and a protein goal. Which finding shows the plan needs revision?

options.text: Weight is unchanged over the past 2 weeks
options.rationale: Stable weight suggests intake is holding.

options.text: The Braden score is still 13 on reassessment
options.rationale: Tempting because the risk has not improved. The score describes the client's risk, and an unchanged score means the same plan continues.

options.text: Serum sodium has risen from 140 to 149 mEq/L with scant, dark urine
options.rationale: Sodium and urine output are monitored to judge hydration. A rising sodium with low, dark urine shows the fluid goal is not being met.

options.text: Reddened skin over the sacrum blanches when pressed and fades after turning
options.rationale: Blanching and fading show blood flow returns. Keep turning and keep watching.

questions.takeaway: A prevention plan includes fluids of 2000 to 3000 mL/day. Judge it by weight, skin turgor, urine output, renal function and sodium, not by the Braden score alone.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Ask which finding measures whether the plan is being met, not whether the client is still at risk.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Stable weight and blanching skin are what you hope to see.
An unchanged Braden score restates the risk. Rising sodium with scant urine shows too little fluid is getting in.

elimination.verdict: The rising sodium with scant, dark urine.

questions.stem: A client with dark brown skin has been supine for 3 hours. The AP reports no sacral redness. The nurse finds one sacral area warmer, firmer and more tender than nearby skin. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Apply barrier cream to the area and keep the current turning schedule
options.rationale: Barrier cream protects from moisture. It does nothing for pressure, and the area needs relief now.

options.text: Have the AP look for redness again at the next turn
options.rationale: Tempting because redness is the usual early sign. In darker skin redness may never show, so waiting for it misses the injury.

options.text: Rub the area gently to bring blood flow back to the skin
options.rationale: Reddened or suspect areas are never massaged. It damages capillaries.

options.text: Turn the client off the sacrum and document suspected stage 1
options.rationale: In darker skin, changes in temperature, firmness and pain mark early pressure damage. Relieve the pressure and record it.

questions.takeaway: In darker skin redness is less visible. Compare temperature, edema, pain and firmness with nearby skin. A warm, firm, tender spot over bone is treated as early pressure injury.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Decide whether the absence of redness rules out injury in this client. Then pick the option that removes the cause.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Warm, firm and tender over a bony prominence after 3 hours of pressure.

steps.action: Cut what does not relieve pressure
steps.detail: Barrier cream and waiting leave the client on the sacrum.
Rubbing damages capillaries.

elimination.verdict: Turn the client off the sacrum and document it.

questions.stem: The nurse changes wound dressings for four clients on a surgical unit. Which finding does the nurse report now?

options.text: Blood tinged amber drainage on an abdominal incision 36 hours after surgery
options.rationale: Serosanguineous drainage is normal in the first 48 hours.

options.text: A beefy red, moist, slightly spongy base in a stage 3 injury
options.rationale: This is healthy granulation tissue.

options.text: New greenish blue staining on the dressing with a fruity odor
options.rationale: A change in the color and odor of exudate is reported. This pattern suggests Pseudomonas infection.

options.text: A stage 3 injury that measures slightly larger the day after sharp debridement
options.rationale: Removing dead tissue makes the wound larger at first. This is expected.

questions.takeaway: Report a change in the amount, color or odor of wound drainage. Greenish blue with a fruity odor suggests Pseudomonas. Blood tinged drainage is normal for the first 48 hours.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Sort each finding as expected for its timing or unexpected. Report the unexpected one.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Blood tinged drainage at 36 hours and a larger wound after debridement both fit their timing.
Beefy red and moist is healthy.
New color and odor in the drainage is the infection cue.

elimination.verdict: The greenish blue drainage with a fruity odor.

questions.stem: A stage 3 hip injury measured 4 x 3 x 0.5 cm (length x width x depth) last week. Today, without debridement, it is 4 x 3 x 1.5 cm and the applicator slides 2 cm under the edge. How does the nurse interpret this?

options.text: Stable, since length and width are unchanged
options.rationale: Tempting because the surface looks the same. Depth is the third measurement, and it has tripled.

options.text: Deteriorating, with deeper tissue loss and new undermining
options.rationale: Greater depth and skin separating from the tissue at the wound edge both show the wound is getting worse under an unchanged surface.

options.text: Expected, since a healing wound deepens before it fills in
options.rationale: A healing wound fills in and gets shallower. With no debridement to explain it, a deeper wound with undermining is not an expected change.

options.text: Now a stage 4 injury, since the depth has tripled
options.rationale: Stage depends on the tissue exposed, such as muscle or bone, not on centimeters.

questions.takeaway: Compare length, width and depth every time. A wound can hold the same surface size and still deteriorate through depth and undermining.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Compare all three measurements, then name what the applicator found at the edge.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Depth went from 0.5 to 1.5 cm.
Skin separated from the tissue beneath it is undermining.
No muscle, tendon or bone is described.

elimination.verdict: Deteriorating, with deeper loss and undermining.

questions.stem: A stage 3 sacral injury has thick yellow drainage, new warmth and redness spreading past the wound edge. Which dressing does the nurse discuss with the wound nurse?

options.text: Hydrocolloid dressing
options.rationale: For noninfected stage 2 injuries. It would seal in an infected wound.

options.text: Antimicrobial dressing with silver
options.rationale: Antimicrobial dressings such as silver, honey or chlorhexidine are for infected pressure injuries.

options.text: Alginate dressing
options.rationale: Tempting because alginate suits a stage 3 injury with moderate drainage. It absorbs fluid and does nothing for the infection cues.

options.text: Hydrogel dressing
options.rationale: For noninfected wounds with minimal exudate, and it adds moisture.

questions.takeaway: Infected pressure injury: antimicrobial dressing (silver, honey, chlorhexidine). Hydrocolloid and hydrogel are for noninfected wounds, and alginate only absorbs.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Name the problem the stem describes before matching a dressing. Drainage alone and infection call for different dressings.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Thick yellow drainage, new warmth and spreading redness point to infection.
Hydrocolloid and hydrogel are for noninfected wounds.
Alginate handles drainage. Silver handles the infection.

elimination.verdict: Antimicrobial dressing with silver.

questions.stem: A client's stage 4 sacral injury has had negative pressure wound therapy for 2 weeks. Which finding best shows the therapy is working?

options.text: The canister collects more drainage each day
options.rationale: More drainage shows fluid is being removed. Rising drainage can also mean the wound is worse.

options.text: The foam stays collapsed and the seal holds without leaks
options.rationale: Tempting because it shows the device is working. It says nothing about how the wound is responding.

options.text: The client sleeps through the night without waking
options.rationale: Comfort matters and is not the purpose of this therapy.

options.text: Less swelling, and red tissue is filling the bed
options.rationale: Negative pressure increases blood flow, minimizes edema and enhances granulation. These are the results it is meant to produce.

questions.takeaway: Negative pressure wound therapy increases blood flow, minimizes edema and enhances granulation. Judge it by the wound, not by the machine.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Separate signs that the device is running from signs that the wound is responding.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Two describe the equipment, one describes comfort and one describes the wound.
Less edema and more granulation are what the therapy is for.

elimination.verdict: Less swelling and red tissue filling the bed.

questions.stem: A client who started phenytoin 3 weeks ago for seizures has painful red skin on the chest with new blisters. The next dose is due now. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Hold the dose and report the findings to the provider
options.rationale: Anticonvulsants are high risk drugs for Stevens-Johnson syndrome. The first step is to stop the drug, and a possibly life threatening reaction is reported at once.

options.text: Give the dose to prevent a seizure, then report the rash
options.rationale: Tempting because a missed dose risks a seizure. Painful blistering skin after a new high risk drug is a possible life threatening reaction, and each dose continues it.

options.text: Give the dose and apply cool compresses to the chest
options.rationale: Comforts the skin while the trigger keeps being given.

options.text: Hold the dose and recheck the skin next shift
options.rationale: Holding is right. Waiting a shift to report leaves a reaction that can be life threatening without evaluation or supportive care.

questions.takeaway: Painful, blistering skin after a new anticonvulsant, allopurinol, sulfonamide or NSAID: stop the drug first and report. Nothing else works while the trigger continues.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two risks compete here. Decide which one is already happening, then ask whether the action can wait.

steps.detail: Giving the drug continues the reaction, so both give options go.
Reporting now gets the reaction evaluated. Waiting until next shift does not.

elimination.verdict: Hold the phenytoin and report now.

questions.stem: A client on a medical unit has a drug reaction with skin detachment that has spread from 8% to 34% of the body surface since admission. Which change in the plan does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: An oral antihistamine for comfort, as for hives
options.rationale: This is a life threatening skin reaction, not hives.

options.text: Continued care on the unit with skin checks every shift
options.rationale: Tempting because that fit the reaction at 8%. Above 30% it is toxic epidermal necrolysis and needs a higher level of care.

options.text: Transfer to a burn unit or intensive care
options.rationale: More than 30% of body surface is toxic epidermal necrolysis, which is often managed in an ICU or burn unit for airway, fluid, temperature, pain and infection support.

options.text: Contact precautions for the skin lesions
options.rationale: The reaction is not contagious. Infection prevention protects the client's open skin.

questions.takeaway: Stevens-Johnson syndrome is under 10% of body surface, toxic epidermal necrolysis is over 30%, and 10 to 30% is overlap. Toxic epidermal necrolysis is often cared for in an ICU or burn unit.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The percentage changed. Ask what that change means for where the client can be cared for safely.

steps.detail: From 8% to 34% moves the client past the 30% line.
Antihistamines and contact precautions treat a different problem.
Unit care fit the earlier extent. The current extent needs a burn unit or ICU.

elimination.verdict: Transfer to a burn unit or intensive care.

questions.stem: A client with hives takes the antihistamine as prescribed. The hives fade by morning and flare each evening after a hard run followed by a beer. The client asks for a stronger drug. Which response is best?

options.text: "I will ask the provider about a higher antihistamine dose."
options.rationale: Tempting because the hives keep returning. The stem shows a trigger that has not been removed, so more drug is not the first answer.

options.text: "Take the antihistamine right before your run instead."
options.rationale: Changing the timing leaves the trigger in place.

options.text: "Evening flares are common and will settle on their own."
options.rationale: Dismisses a pattern the client can change.

options.text: "Skip hard runs and alcohol until the hives clear."
options.rationale: Heat, alcohol and overexertion dilate blood vessels and worsen hives. Removing them comes before adding drug.

questions.takeaway: Hives: remove the trigger, give antihistamines, and avoid heat, alcohol and overexertion, which dilate blood vessels.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Look for a pattern in when the hives return. Fix the pattern before changing the drug.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Flares follow a hard run and a beer.
A higher dose and new timing leave the cause in place.
Waiting ignores a cause the client controls.

elimination.verdict: Skip hard runs and alcohol until the hives clear.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old with fair skin whose father was treated for melanoma completes prevention teaching. Which statement requires follow up?

options.text: "A few tanning bed sessions first will keep me from burning."
options.rationale: Tanning beds are a source of ultraviolet exposure and are avoided. A tan is skin damage and does not protect.

options.text: "I will photograph my moles and compare them each month."
options.rationale: Correct. Monthly self examination with photos or a body map tracks change.

options.text: "I will move my runs to early morning."
options.rationale: Correct. Midday sun is avoided.

options.text: "I will call if a mole starts to itch or bleed."
options.rationale: Correct. New itching, tenderness or bleeding in a lesion is reported.

questions.takeaway: Skin cancer prevention: avoid midday sun and tanning beds, use sunscreen and protective clothing, check the skin monthly, and report any new or changing lesion.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Look for the statement that sounds protective and still adds ultraviolet exposure.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: You are looking for the statement that is wrong.
Three statements match the teaching.
A tanning bed is ultraviolet light.

elimination.verdict: The tanning bed statement.

skills.title: FSBS/Insulin Administration Check-Off
skills.subtitle: Interpreting the value, recognizing hypoglycemia, insulin types and timing, and injection technique

questions.stem: A 61-year-old's premeal fingerstick reads 312 mg/dL after a week of readings near 150 mg/dL. He has just peeled an orange and his hands were not washed. Sliding scale insulin is ordered. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give the sliding scale dose listed for 312 mg/dL
options.rationale: Tempting because the order covers this value. Sugar on the skin can raise the reading, and insulin dosed from a false high can cause a low.

options.text: Wash and dry his hands, then repeat the fingerstick
options.rationale: The value does not fit his trend and the finger was not clean. A clean, dry finger gives a result the dose can be based on.

options.text: Notify the provider of the sudden rise in glucose
options.rationale: Reasonable if a repeat on a clean finger is still high. The nurse confirms the value before reporting it.

options.text: Hold the insulin and recheck before the next meal
options.rationale: This leaves a possible high untreated for hours when a repeat takes one minute.

questions.takeaway: Wash and dry the hands before every fingerstick. A reading that does not fit the client is repeated on a clean, dry finger before insulin is dosed from it.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: The stem gives a number and a reason to doubt it. Settle the doubt before you treat or report.

steps.action: Compare the value with the trend
steps.detail: 312 mg/dL after a week near 150 mg/dL does not fit.
Orange juice on unwashed fingers.

steps.action: Cut the actions that trust the number
steps.detail: Dosing and calling both act on a doubtful value.
Waiting until the next meal answers nothing now.

elimination.verdict: Wash, dry and repeat the fingerstick.

questions.stem: A student's first fingerstick on a 76-year-old with cold hands gave too small a drop. After coaching, which action on the second attempt shows the coaching was effective?

options.text: Warms the hand, then punctures the center pad
options.rationale: Tempting because gentle warming is correct. The center pad is more painful, and the side of the fingertip is the taught site.

options.text: Lowers the hand, then squeezes the fingertip for a drop
options.rationale: Lowering the hand is correct. Squeezing is the error to avoid.

options.text: Rewashes the hand, then punctures while it is damp
options.rationale: Washing is correct. The finger must be dry, because water dilutes the sample.

options.text: Lowers the hand, then punctures the side of the fingertip
options.rationale: Letting the hand hang down improves flow, and the side of the fingertip gives a good sample.

questions.takeaway: Poor flow from a cold hand: warm gently or lower the hand, use the side of a dry fingertip, avoid squeezing.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Each option has two parts. One wrong half spoils the option, so check both.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Warming, lowering and washing are all correct first halves.
Center pad, squeezing and a damp finger are each errors.

steps.action: Keep the option with two correct halves
steps.detail: Lowered hand, side of the fingertip.

elimination.verdict: Lowers the hand and punctures the side of the fingertip.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old received regular and NPH insulin in one syringe at 0800. She missed her afternoon snack and is shaky and sweating at 1630. Which explanation guides the nurse's follow-up?

options.text: The NPH is still within its peak
options.rationale: NPH peaks 4 to 12 hours after the dose. At 1630 she is 8.5 hours in, with no snack to cover it.

options.text: The regular insulin is reaching its peak
options.rationale: Tempting because regular insulin is the mealtime insulin. Its peak was 2 to 4 hours after the dose, which ended at 1200.

options.text: The two insulins cancelled each other in the syringe
options.rationale: Mixing regular and NPH is a prescribed practice. It does not cancel either dose.

options.text: The morning dose has worn off entirely
options.rationale: A dose that has worn off would produce a high, not signs of a low.

questions.takeaway: Count the hours from the dose. Regular peaks at 2 to 4 hours. NPH peaks at 4 to 12 hours, so an afternoon low after a morning mix belongs to the NPH.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Do the clock math for each insulin before you choose. 0800 to 1630 is 8.5 hours.

steps.detail: 0800 to 1630 is 8.5 hours.
Regular peaked from 1000 to 1200. NPH peaks from 1200 to 2000.
Reduced intake at the peak sets up the low.

elimination.verdict: The NPH is still within its peak.

questions.stem: At 0730 a 63-year-old who is eating normally is due regular insulin 6 units before breakfast. His tray comes at 0800. Which actions does the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Check his fingerstick glucose before preparing the dose
options.rationale: The current value decides whether insulin is safe to give now.

options.text: Confirm the solution in the vial is clear
options.rationale: Regular insulin is clear. A cloudy vial is not used.

options.text: Roll the vial between the palms before drawing
options.rationale: Rolling is for NPH, a cloudy suspension. Regular insulin is a clear solution that does not need mixing.

options.text: Give the dose now, 30 minutes before the tray
options.rationale: Regular insulin has an onset of 30 to 60 minutes, so half an hour ahead matches it to the meal.

options.text: Pinch up the skin and insert the needle at 90 degrees
options.rationale: Correct technique that keeps the dose in the subcutaneous tissue.

options.text: Pull back on the plunger to check for blood
options.rationale: Aspiration is not required for subcutaneous insulin.

questions.takeaway: Before regular insulin: check the glucose, confirm the vial is clear, give it 30 minutes before the meal, pinch and insert at 90 degrees without aspirating. Rolling is for NPH.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Two options are correct habits for a different insulin or a different injection. Judge each against regular insulin given subcutaneously.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Glucose check, clear vial, timing and a pinched 90 degree insertion are all correct.
Rolling mixes a cloudy suspension. Regular insulin is a clear solution.
Not done for subcutaneous insulin.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D and E.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old with erratic glucose readings was taught site rotation last week. Which report at today's visit shows the teaching was effective?

options.text: "I use my abdomen in the morning and my thigh at night."
options.rationale: Tempting because it sounds organized. Moving between regions makes each dose absorb at a different rate.

options.text: "I use the exact same spot so the dose stays predictable."
options.rationale: One region is right, but one spot is not. Rotation within the region protects the tissue.

options.text: "I stay in my abdomen and pick a different spot each time."
options.rationale: One anatomical region with rotation inside it keeps absorption consistent.

options.text: "I move from abdomen to arm to thigh through the week."
options.rationale: This is rotation between regions, which varies absorption dose to dose.

questions.takeaway: One region, a new spot within it each time. Rotating between regions changes absorption and makes readings erratic.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Three options change something that should stay fixed or fix something that should change. Find the one that keeps the region and moves the spot.

steps.detail: Two options move between regions. They say the same thing.
It keeps the region but never rotates.
Same region, different spot.

elimination.verdict: Stays in the abdomen and picks a different spot each time.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old with type 1 diabetes and influenza calls the clinic. She has taken her insulin and is sipping fluids often. Her glucose has stayed near 270 mg/dL since morning. What does the nurse tell her to do next?

options.text: Test for ketones
options.rationale: A glucose that stays over 240 mg/dL during illness calls for a ketone test, which shows whether ketoacidosis is developing.

options.text: Keep sipping fluids and recheck in four hours
options.rationale: Tempting because both are sick day rules. She is already doing them. The sustained value over 240 mg/dL adds a step.

options.text: Skip the next insulin dose until she can eat
options.rationale: Illness raises glucose. Stopping insulin leads to ketoacidosis.

options.text: Drink a glass of juice to keep her strength up
options.rationale: Her glucose is high. Fast-acting carbohydrate is for a low.

questions.takeaway: Sick days: keep taking insulin, check glucose every three to four hours, keep fluids going, test ketones when glucose stays over 240 mg/dL.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Ask what the stem says she is already doing. The answer is the sick day rule she has not yet followed.

steps.detail: Insulin taken, fluids going.

steps.action: Find the trigger in the stem
steps.detail: Glucose staying over 240 mg/dL.

steps.action: Match the trigger to its rule
steps.detail: Over 240 mg/dL means ketones.

elimination.verdict: Test for ketones.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old going home on regular 5 units and NPH 15 units in one syringe gives a return demonstration. Which sequence shows the teaching was effective?

options.text: Rolls the NPH, draws NPH to the 15 unit mark, then regular to the 20 unit mark
options.rationale: Right total, wrong order. A syringe holding NPH should not enter the regular vial.

options.text: Rolls the NPH, draws regular to the 5 unit mark, then NPH to the 20 unit mark
options.rationale: Clear before cloudy, with the second insulin drawn to the total of both doses.

options.text: Rolls the NPH, draws regular to the 5 unit mark, then NPH to the 15 unit mark
options.rationale: Right order, but stopping at the 15 unit mark gives only 10 units of NPH.

options.text: Rolls the regular, draws regular to the 5 unit mark, then NPH to the 20 unit mark
options.rationale: The vial that needs rolling is the cloudy NPH. Drawing it unmixed gives an uneven dose.

questions.takeaway: Roll the NPH, draw regular first, then draw NPH to the total of both doses.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Check three things in each option: which vial is rolled, which is drawn first, where the plunger stops.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: NPH first is out.
5 plus 15 is 20, so stopping at 15 is out.
The cloudy vial is rolled.

elimination.verdict: Rolls the NPH, draws regular to the 5 unit mark, then NPH to the 20 unit mark.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old with an insulin pump is admitted. Her glucose has climbed from 150 to 320 mg/dL in four hours with ketones present. Lunch was normal. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Have her deliver a correction dose through the pump
options.rationale: Tempting because the glucose is high. If the pump is not delivering, a dose sent through it will not reach her.

options.text: Ask what she ate for lunch
options.rationale: The stem already says lunch was normal. A meal does not explain ketones.

options.text: Inspect the infusion site and tubing
options.rationale: A fast rise with ketones in a pump user points to interrupted delivery, since there is no long-acting insulin on board.

options.text: Recheck the glucose in one hour
options.rationale: Waiting lets ketones build in a client who may be getting no insulin.

questions.takeaway: A pump holds only rapid-acting insulin. Rising glucose with ketones means look for an interruption at the site or in the tubing first.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Two options treat the high. Ask whether the route for that treatment can be trusted yet.

steps.detail: Fast rise plus ketones means no insulin is arriving.
Lunch was normal.

steps.action: Check the delivery before using it
steps.detail: A correction through a blocked line does nothing.

elimination.verdict: Inspect the infusion site and tubing.

questions.stem: At 1500 a 73-year-old who received NPH at 0700 has a fingerstick glucose of 56 mg/dL. He is alert, shaky and able to swallow. Place the nurse's actions in order.

options.text: Give 15 to 20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate
options.rationale: First. The glucose is known and under 70 mg/dL, so treatment comes before anything else.

options.text: Recheck the fingerstick glucose in 15 minutes
options.rationale: The recheck number, not how he feels, shows whether the low has resolved.

options.text: Give another 15 to 20 g if the recheck is under 70 mg/dL
options.rationale: Treatment repeats until the glucose is at least 70 mg/dL.

options.text: Review his intake and insulin timing to find the cause
options.rationale: Once he is safe, work out why it happened. He is in the NPH peak.

questions.takeaway: Treat first, recheck in 15 minutes, repeat if still under 70 mg/dL, then work out why it happened.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: The assessment is already in the stem. Start with treatment and leave the search for a cause until he is above 70 mg/dL.

steps.detail: 56 mg/dL, alert, able to swallow.
No further assessment is needed to act.
Finding the reason does not raise his glucose.

elimination.verdict: Treat, recheck, repeat if needed, then find the cause.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old has sliding scale NovoLog ordered with meals. Her fingerstick at 1100 was 204 mg/dL. Lunch was delayed and the tray is set down at 1235. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Repeat the fingerstick and dose from the new value
options.rationale: The 1100 value is over 90 minutes old. A sliding scale dose is based on the glucose at the time the insulin is given.

options.text: Give the dose listed for the 1100 value now
options.rationale: Tempting because the food is here and the check was done. Her glucose may have changed since 1100, so the dose could be wrong.

options.text: Hold the mealtime dose since the check is outdated
options.rationale: The check is outdated, but the fix is a new check. Holding leaves the meal uncovered.

options.text: Ask the provider for a dose based on the 1100 value
options.rationale: The order already tells the nurse what to give. What is missing is a current value.

questions.takeaway: A sliding scale dose needs a current glucose. If the meal is delayed, repeat the fingerstick when the food arrives and dose from that value.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Look at the two times in the stem. Ask whether the number still describes the client.

steps.detail: 1100 to 1235 is 95 minutes.

steps.action: Cut the options that use the old value
steps.detail: Dosing from it or calling about it.
Holding skips the meal coverage. A new fingerstick takes a minute.

elimination.verdict: Repeat the fingerstick, then dose.

questions.stem: The nurse gave a 65-year-old Humulin R 8 units at 1130 for a 1200 lunch. At 1200 the kitchen says trays will be 45 minutes late. He is alert with no symptoms. Which action is best?

options.text: Notify the provider that the tray is late
options.rationale: Tempting because a delay that affects the regimen is reported. Calling does not protect him from insulin that is already working.

options.text: Document the delay and check him at 1245
options.rationale: Regular insulin has started working. Waiting until the tray comes leaves him uncovered.

options.text: Give his next dose 45 minutes later
options.rationale: This addresses the next meal, not the insulin already given.

options.text: Check his glucose and get food to him now
options.rationale: Regular insulin starts in 30 to 60 minutes, so he needs food now and a glucose check while intake is delayed.

questions.takeaway: Insulin already given cannot wait for a late tray. Recheck the glucose and bring food to the client.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: The insulin is in. Pick the action that deals with this dose in this client right now.

steps.detail: Given at 1130, regular insulin is active by 1200.
Next dose and a 1245 check do not help now.
Food and a glucose check protect him first. The call can follow.

elimination.verdict: Check his glucose and get food to him now.

questions.stem: A new nurse had a near miss with look-alike insulins last week. Today the order reads Novolin R 4 units before lunch. Which action by the new nurse shows the review was effective?

options.text: Takes the Novolin vial from the client's usual bin
options.rationale: Tempting because the bin is labeled for the client. Location does not confirm which Novolin is in the hand.

options.text: Selects a cloudy Novolin vial and rolls it gently
options.rationale: Rolling is right for NPH. A cloudy vial means this is Novolin N, or a regular vial that should not be used.

options.text: Reads the label for R and confirms the vial is clear
options.rationale: The letter and the appearance are the two checks that separate regular from NPH under one brand name.

options.text: Matches the brand name on the vial to the order
options.rationale: The brand is shared by both insulins. Matching it is how the near miss happened.

questions.takeaway: A shared brand name does not mean a shared insulin. Read the letter and check the appearance: regular is clear, NPH is cloudy.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Ask which option would catch the wrong vial. Brand and bin location would both let Novolin N through.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Novolin N given for Novolin R.

steps.action: Cut checks that both vials would pass
steps.detail: Brand name and bin location.
Cloudy is not regular insulin.

steps.action: Keep the two checks that differ
steps.detail: The letter R and a clear solution.
