elimination.verdict: Reads the label for R and confirms the vial is clear.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old's sliding scale lists regular insulin doses for 151 to 400 mg/dL and gives no instruction above 400 mg/dL. His 1130 fingerstick is 418 mg/dL. He is alert and thirsty. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give the dose listed for 351 to 400 mg/dL
options.rationale: Tempting because it is the closest dose on the scale. His value is outside the order, so no listed dose applies.

options.text: Report the value to the provider and get a dose
options.rationale: The order does not cover 418 mg/dL. The nurse assesses him and gets a prescribed dose instead of choosing one.

options.text: Give the top listed dose plus 2 more units
options.rationale: The nurse does not add units without an order.

options.text: Recheck the fingerstick at 1230 before acting
options.rationale: Waiting an hour leaves a high glucose with symptoms untreated and unreported.

questions.takeaway: A sliding scale covers only the values written on it. A glucose outside the scale is reported, and the nurse gives only a prescribed dose.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Read the order as written. Ask whether it covers this number before you ask which dose is closest.

steps.action: Place the value on the scale
steps.detail: 418 mg/dL is above the last range.

steps.action: Cut the doses the nurse invents
steps.detail: The top dose and the top dose plus 2 units both lack an order.
He is thirsty and high now.

elimination.verdict: Report the value and get a dose.

questions.stem: At 2100 the nurse prepares insulin glargine for a 75-year-old and sees the solution is cloudy. The client says it looked the same last night and the dose was given. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Discard the vial and obtain a new one for tonight's dose
options.rationale: Glargine is a clear solution. Cloudiness means contamination or degradation, and the basal dose is still due.

options.text: Roll the vial gently and draw up tonight's dose
options.rationale: Tempting because rolling a cloudy vial is correct for NPH. Glargine should never look cloudy.

options.text: Hold tonight's dose and report the vial in the morning
options.rationale: Tempting because it avoids the bad vial. Basal insulin is not skipped, and a new vial solves the problem tonight.

options.text: Draw the dose, since last night's caused no problem
options.rationale: A dose from a degraded vial is unpredictable. One uneventful night does not make it safe.

questions.takeaway: Only NPH and premixes that contain it look cloudy. Glargine is always clear, so a cloudy vial is discarded and replaced.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Two options reject the vial. Ask which one still gets the client the basal dose.

steps.detail: Glargine is clear.

steps.action: Cut the options that use the vial
steps.detail: Rolling it or drawing from it.

steps.action: Compare the two that reject it
steps.detail: Holding leaves the client without basal insulin. Replacing does not.

elimination.verdict: Discard the vial and get a new one.

questions.scenario: A 64-year-old is going home on Lantus at bedtime and NovoLog with meals. The nurse evaluates his statements after teaching.
questions.stem: For each statement, indicate whether the teaching was understood or needs reinforcement.

rows.text: "I take the NovoLog when my plate is in front of me."
rows.rationale: Rapid-acting insulin starts in 10 to 30 minutes, so it is given with the food.

rows.text: "Lantus has no big peak, so I take it whether or not I eat."
rows.rationale: Lantus is basal insulin with no pronounced peak. It is not matched to meals.

rows.text: "To save a shot, I draw the Lantus and NovoLog in one syringe."
rows.rationale: Lantus is never mixed with other insulins.

rows.text: "If my sugar is 62 mg/dL, I take glucose and check again in 15 minutes."
rows.rationale: Under 70 mg/dL is treated with fast-acting carbohydrate and rechecked in 15 minutes.

rows.text: "I pull back on the plunger to look for blood before I inject."
rows.rationale: Aspiration is not required for subcutaneous insulin.

questions.takeaway: NovoLog follows food. Lantus does not, and it is never mixed. A low is treated and rechecked in 15 minutes. Subcutaneous insulin is not aspirated.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Judge each statement alone. Two of them sound careful or efficient and are still wrong.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Mealtime insulin follows food. Basal insulin does not.
Long-acting insulin goes in its own syringe.
No aspiration for a subcutaneous injection.

elimination.verdict: Rows 1, 2 and 4 are understood. Rows 3 and 5 need reinforcement.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old jogs after dinner and takes regular insulin before that meal. He has had two evening lows this week after injecting his thigh. Which plan does the nurse suggest for the dinner dose?

options.text: Keep the thigh and inject deeper
options.rationale: Depth is not the issue. The working muscle speeds absorption.

options.text: Use the thigh and massage it before the jog
options.rationale: Massage and exercise both speed absorption, which would add to the lows.

options.text: Inject the abdomen at dinner
options.rationale: The abdomen is not the working limb during a jog, so absorption is not sped by the exercise.

options.text: Skip the dinner dose on jogging days
options.rationale: Tempting because it stops the low. Omitting a prescribed dose is not the nurse's or client's call. The site is the cause.

questions.takeaway: Exercise speeds absorption from the injected limb. Do not inject a limb that is about to work.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: The lows have a pattern in the stem: thigh plus jog. Change the site, not the prescription.

steps.detail: Lows follow thigh injections before a jog.
Massage and a working thigh.
Skipping a dose is not a site fix.

elimination.verdict: Inject the abdomen at dinner.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old had a 0300 glucose of 46 mg/dL followed by a 0700 glucose of 250 mg/dL, so the provider lowered her bedtime NPH. Which result shows the change was effective?

options.text: 0700 glucose 122 mg/dL, no overnight check done
options.rationale: Tempting because the morning value is in range. Without the 0300 value the overnight low could still be there.

options.text: 0300 glucose 58 mg/dL, 0700 glucose 204 mg/dL
options.rationale: Both improved slightly, but she is still low overnight and still rebounding.

options.text: 0300 glucose 52 mg/dL, 0700 glucose 148 mg/dL
options.rationale: The morning value is in range, but the overnight value is still a low.

options.text: 0300 glucose 102 mg/dL, 0700 glucose 136 mg/dL
options.rationale: The overnight low is gone and the morning value is in range, so the rebound has stopped.

questions.takeaway: The problem was the overnight low. The change worked only when the 0300 value is above 70 mg/dL and the morning value is in range.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Evaluate the problem that was treated. The dose was lowered to stop a 0300 low, so the 0300 value must be in the answer.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A low at 0300 that rebounded.

steps.action: Cut any option with a 0300 value under 70 mg/dL
steps.detail: 52 and 58 mg/dL are still lows.

steps.action: Cut the option with no 0300 value
steps.detail: It cannot show the low is gone.

elimination.verdict: 0300 glucose 102 mg/dL, 0700 glucose 136 mg/dL.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old's home list shows Lantus 20 units at bedtime. Tonight's medication record reads Humalog 20 units at bedtime. He ate dinner at 1730. Which action does the nurse take at 2100?

options.text: Give the Humalog with a snack to cover it
options.rationale: Tempting because food makes rapid-acting insulin safer. A snack does not make a questionable order correct.

options.text: Hold the dose and verify the order with the provider
options.rationale: Humalog is rapid acting and given with meals. Twenty units at bedtime that matches his Lantus dose suggests a transcription error, so it is verified first.

options.text: Give the Humalog as written on the record
options.rationale: A large rapid-acting dose with no meal can cause a severe low overnight.

options.text: Give Lantus 20 units, since that matches his home list
options.rationale: Tempting because it is probably what was meant. The nurse does not substitute one insulin for another without an order.

questions.takeaway: Check the insulin type against its usual timing. A rapid-acting insulin ordered at bedtime with no meal is verified before it is given, and the nurse does not substitute.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Two options give the insulin as written and one swaps it. Ask which option fixes the order itself.

steps.action: Match the insulin to its timing
steps.detail: Humalog follows food. Lantus is the bedtime basal insulin.

steps.action: Cut the options that give Humalog
steps.detail: With or without a snack, the order is still in doubt.
Changing the insulin needs an order.

elimination.verdict: Hold and verify with the provider.

questions.stem: At 0930 a 72-year-old who received regular insulin at 0645 and ate little breakfast snaps at the nurse and refuses his bath. He is awake and answering questions. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Check his fingerstick glucose
options.rationale: New irritability at the peak of regular insulin after a small meal suggests a low. The check takes seconds and directs treatment.

options.text: Give 4 ounces of juice
options.rationale: Tempting because a low is likely. He is awake and stable enough for a quick check. The value has not been measured.

options.text: Return in an hour to offer the bath again
options.rationale: This treats a behavior change in a client on insulin as a mood problem.

options.text: Ask the provider about a sleep aid
options.rationale: Nothing in the stem points to a sleep problem.

questions.takeaway: A behavior change in a client on insulin is a glucose check first, most of all at the insulin's peak with reduced intake.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: No glucose value is in the stem. When the assessment is missing and the client is awake, get the number before you treat.

steps.detail: 0645 to 0930 is inside the 2 to 4 hour peak.
None is given.
A fingerstick is fast and tells you whether juice is needed.

elimination.verdict: Check his fingerstick glucose.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old with type 1 diabetes has a stomach virus and cannot keep food down. Which statement shows the sick day teaching needs to be repeated?

options.text: "I will skip my Levemir until I can eat again."
options.rationale: Basal insulin is not matched to food and is never stopped on sick days. This is the statement that needs correcting.

options.text: "I will hold my Humalog when I cannot eat a meal."
options.rationale: Sounds like skipping insulin, which tempts. Mealtime insulin follows food, so holding it without a meal is correct.

options.text: "I will test for ketones if I stay over 240 mg/dL."
options.rationale: Correct sick day rule.

options.text: "I will check my glucose every four hours tonight."
options.rationale: Correct. Glucose is checked every three to four hours during illness.

questions.takeaway: Rapid acting insulin follows food. Basal insulin does not, and it continues through illness.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Two statements involve holding insulin. Sort them by which insulin depends on a meal.

steps.detail: You are looking for the wrong statement.
Ketones over 240 mg/dL and checks every three to four hours are right.
Humalog follows food. Levemir does not.

elimination.verdict: Skipping the Levemir is the error.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old's glucose readings are still erratic two weeks after site teaching. Which report best explains the readings?

options.text: "I stay in my abdomen and use a new spot each time."
options.rationale: Correct rotation within one region. It keeps absorption steady.

options.text: "I pinch the skin and go straight in at 90 degrees."
options.rationale: Correct technique.

options.text: "I rub the spot afterward so it will not bruise."
options.rationale: Massaging the site changes how fast the insulin is absorbed, which makes the readings swing.

options.text: "I skip the bruised spot from last week's injection."
options.rationale: Correct. Bruised tissue is avoided.

questions.takeaway: Do not massage an insulin site. Rubbing changes absorption even when the rotation is correct.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: The rotation sounds fixed. Look for the other habit that changes absorption.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: One region, new spot. Correct.
Pinch and 90 degrees. Correct.
Rubbing the site.

elimination.verdict: Rubbing the site explains the swings.

questions.stem: At 1030 the nurse reviews four clients. Which client does the nurse check first?

options.text: Regular insulin at 0715, ate all of breakfast, no symptoms
options.rationale: Tempting because regular insulin is at its peak. A full breakfast and no symptoms make a low less likely.

options.text: Basal insulin at 0800, ate 25% of breakfast, no symptoms
options.rationale: Tempting because of the poor intake. Basal insulin has no pronounced peak and is not matched to meals.

options.text: Rapid-acting insulin with breakfast, glucose 226 mg/dL, reports thirst
options.rationale: A high with thirst is assessed next, after a possible low.

options.text: Regular insulin at 0730, ate half of breakfast, asks for a snack
options.rationale: Regular insulin peaks 2 to 4 hours after the dose, so this client is at the peak with reduced intake. Hunger is an early sign of a low.

questions.takeaway: Reduced intake at the insulin's peak is the setup for a low. Hunger is a warning sign, so check the glucose before treating it as a food request.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Each client has a risk on paper. Find the one with a peak, reduced intake and a symptom together.

steps.detail: A high with thirst follows a possible low.

steps.action: Cut the insulin with no peak
steps.detail: Basal insulin is not matched to meals.

steps.action: Compare the two regular insulin clients
steps.detail: Both are at the peak. One ate fully and has no symptoms. One ate half and is hungry.

elimination.verdict: The client on regular insulin who ate half and asks for a snack.

questions.stem: A client on bedtime NPH has a 0200 glucose of 128 mg/dL and a 0700 glucose of 234 mg/dL. A coworker suggests asking the provider to lower the bedtime NPH. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Agree and request a lower bedtime NPH dose
options.rationale: Tempting because a lower dose fixes a rebound high. A rebound needs an overnight low, and 128 mg/dL is not low.

options.text: Report both values and that no overnight low occurred
options.rationale: The glucose rose without a low, which is the dawn pattern. The provider needs both values to choose the change.

options.text: Ask for another 0200 check before reporting anything
options.rationale: The overnight value is already in hand. Repeating it delays the report.

options.text: Give a bedtime snack tonight and recheck at 0700
options.rationale: A snack treats an overnight low that did not happen and would raise the morning value.

questions.takeaway: Somogyi is an overnight low that rebounds to a morning high. Dawn rises without a low. The overnight value tells them apart.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Decide what the 0200 number rules out before you choose what to ask for.

steps.detail: 128 mg/dL is not a low.
A rise without a low is dawn, so lowering the dose does not fit.
The needed assessment is already done.

elimination.verdict: Report both values. There was no overnight low.

questions.stem: At 1100 a client with a glucose of 262 mg/dL received correction insulin. At 1300 his glucose is 66 mg/dL. He reports no symptoms and says, "Finally, it is down." Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give 15 to 20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate
options.rationale: 66 mg/dL is under 70 mg/dL, so it is treated now even without symptoms. The correction went too far.

options.text: Document the result as an effective treatment
options.rationale: Tempting because the number fell and he has no symptoms. Effective means 70 to 180 mg/dL, and lower is not better.

options.text: Recheck the glucose in 15 minutes before acting
options.rationale: Tempting because a recheck is part of the rule. The recheck comes after the carbohydrate.

options.text: Hold his next mealtime insulin and notify the provider
options.rationale: Reporting the low is reasonable later. It does not raise his glucose now.

questions.takeaway: Effective glucose treatment lands between 70 and 180 mg/dL. Under 70 mg/dL is treated first, with or without symptoms.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: The number moved the right way. Check where it stopped.

steps.detail: 66 mg/dL is below the 70 mg/dL line.
No symptoms does not cancel the rule.
Treat, then recheck, then report.

elimination.verdict: Treat the low with fast-acting carbohydrate.

questions.stem: After teaching, a 54-year-old stopped injecting into a firm raised area on her abdomen. On unchanged doses her prelunch readings fell from the 230s to the low 70s mg/dL within a week. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Report the trend so the doses can be reviewed
options.rationale: Insulin absorbs better from healthy tissue, so the same dose now does more. Readings heading toward 70 mg/dL mean the dose needs review before a low happens.

options.text: Advise going back to the old site for now
options.rationale: The thickened tissue absorbs poorly and unpredictably. It was the cause of the high readings.

options.text: Praise the change and continue the same plan
options.rationale: Tempting because the teaching clearly worked. The plan was built on poor absorption and the trend is still falling.

options.text: Suggest a larger breakfast to offset the insulin
options.rationale: Adjusting food to chase a dose is not the nurse's fix. The dose itself needs review.

questions.takeaway: Thickened injection sites absorb insulin poorly. When a client moves to healthy tissue the same dose works harder, so watch for lows and have the dose reviewed.
questions.coverage: Not in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: The teaching worked. The question is what the falling numbers mean for a dose that has not changed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: From the 230s to the low 70s mg/dL on the same dose.
The lump caused the problem.
The trend is one step from a low, so someone must review the dose.

elimination.verdict: Report the trend for a dose review.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old on insulin is found unresponsive with a fingerstick glucose of 41 mg/dL. A saline lock is in place. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Squeeze glucose gel inside the cheek
options.rationale: Tempting because it is fast and at hand. An unresponsive client cannot protect the airway, so nothing goes in the mouth.

options.text: Give IV dextrose per the hypoglycemia protocol
options.rationale: Oral treatment is for a client who is alert and can swallow. With IV access in place, dextrose treats the low without an aspiration risk.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed and offer juice
options.rationale: Positioning does not make swallowing safe in a client who does not respond.

options.text: Repeat the fingerstick on the other hand
options.rationale: The value fits the client. Repeating it delays treatment.

questions.takeaway: The rule of 15 by mouth is for a client who is alert and can swallow. An unresponsive client gets a route that does not involve the mouth.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Two options treat the low. The word "unresponsive" decides the route.

steps.detail: An unresponsive client cannot swallow safely.
Gel and juice share the same flaw.
A reading of 41 mg/dL in an unresponsive client fits.

elimination.verdict: IV dextrose per protocol.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old has NovoLog 4 units scheduled with meals plus a correction scale that starts at 150 mg/dL. Her prelunch glucose is 139 mg/dL and her tray has arrived. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Hold all insulin because the glucose is in range
options.rationale: Tempting because 139 mg/dL is in range. The scheduled dose covers the meal she is about to eat, not the current number.

options.text: Give 4 units plus the lowest correction dose
options.rationale: The scale does not start until 150 mg/dL, so no correction is ordered for 139 mg/dL.

options.text: Wait and recheck the glucose after she eats
options.rationale: Rapid acting insulin is given as the food arrives. A reading after the meal cannot be used for a premeal order.

options.text: Give the scheduled 4 units with no correction
options.rationale: The mealtime dose covers the food. The correction dose is added only when the glucose reaches the scale.

questions.takeaway: Scheduled mealtime insulin and correction insulin are two separate orders. A glucose below the scale cancels the correction, not the meal dose.
questions.coverage: Not in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Read the order as two parts and answer each part separately.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The tray has arrived, so the scheduled dose is due.
139 mg/dL is under 150 mg/dL, so no correction.

steps.action: Cut the all or nothing options
steps.detail: Holding everything and adding a correction both ignore one part.

elimination.verdict: Give the scheduled 4 units with no correction.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old on insulin is alert and shaky with a glucose of 60 mg/dL. Lunch is due in 20 minutes. Which does the nurse give?

options.text: Half a cup of regular apple juice
options.rationale: About 15 g of simple sugar with nothing to slow it, so the glucose rises within minutes.

options.text: Peanut butter on whole grain crackers
options.rationale: Tempting because it has carbohydrate and staying power. Fat and protein slow absorption, so it suits the follow up, not the first treatment.

options.text: A small bar of milk chocolate
options.rationale: The fat in chocolate slows the sugar.

options.text: The lunch tray as soon as it arrives
options.rationale: A glucose under 70 mg/dL with symptoms is treated now, not in 20 minutes.

questions.takeaway: Fast-acting means simple sugar without fat or protein: juice, regular soda or glucose tablets. Fat slows the rise.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: All four contain carbohydrate. Ask which one reaches the blood fastest.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Twenty minutes is too long for a symptomatic low.
Peanut butter and chocolate both carry it.
Juice has nothing to slow it.

elimination.verdict: Half a cup of regular juice.

questions.stem: At 0740 four insulin doses are coming due on the unit. Which dose does the nurse give first?

options.text: Lantus due at 0800 for a client still asleep
options.rationale: Basal insulin is not matched to food, so a few minutes do not matter.

options.text: Novolin R for a client whose tray comes at 0830
options.rationale: Regular insulin goes about 30 minutes before the meal, so this one is due at 0800.

options.text: Humalog for a client whose tray comes at 0815
options.rationale: Rapid acting insulin waits for the food. Given now, it would act before the client eats.

options.text: Humalog for a client whose tray was just set down
options.rationale: Rapid acting insulin is given as the meal arrives. The food is here, so the dose is due this minute.

questions.takeaway: Insulin timing follows the food: rapid acting as the tray arrives, regular about 30 minutes before, basal on the clock.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: For each dose, find the tray. Only one client has a tray at the bedside.

steps.detail: Lantus does not depend on a meal.
Thirty minutes before 0830 is 0800.
Same insulin; only one tray has arrived.

elimination.verdict: Humalog for the client whose tray is here.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old who tests four times a day has sore, calloused finger pads. After teaching, which statement shows it was effective?

options.text: "I skip the bedtime test to rest my fingers."
options.rationale: Dropping a check hides a reading the insulin plan depends on.

options.text: "I use the sides and switch fingers each time."
options.rationale: The sides of the fingertips have fewer nerve endings, and rotating fingers lets each site heal.

options.text: "I keep to one finger so the others can heal up."
options.rationale: Tempting because it spares most fingers. Repeated sticks in one place are what build the callus and soreness.

options.text: "I squeeze the tip hard to get a bigger drop."
options.rationale: Squeezing hurts more and can alter the reading.

questions.takeaway: Puncture the side of the fingertip and rotate fingers. It hurts less and keeps the skin intact for the next check.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Look for the statement that keeps every scheduled test and spreads the punctures out.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Skipping a test is not a comfort measure.
It adds pain and can spoil the result.
One finger concentrates the damage. Sides and rotation spread it.

elimination.verdict: Sides of the fingertips, a different finger each time.

questions.stem: The nurse asked an assistive personnel to report any fingerstick under 70 mg/dL at once. Which action by the assistive personnel shows the direction was understood?

options.text: Gives juice for a reading of 63 mg/dL, then tells the nurse
options.rationale: Tempting because the low gets treated. Deciding on treatment belongs to the nurse, who must assess the client first.

options.text: Charts a reading of 63 mg/dL and reports it after rounds
options.rationale: A low reported late is a low left untreated.

options.text: Uses the call light to report a reading of 63 mg/dL now
options.rationale: The value reaches the nurse at once and the assistive personnel stays with the client.

options.text: Repeats a reading of 63 mg/dL twice before telling the nurse
options.rationale: Extra checks delay the report the nurse asked for.

questions.takeaway: An assistive personnel can obtain the fingerstick. The nurse assesses and decides treatment, so a low value is reported immediately.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: The direction had two parts: under 70 mg/dL, and at once. Find the action that meets both without adding anything.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Charting first and repeating first both slow the report.
Giving juice is a treatment decision.
Call light, now, staying with the client.

elimination.verdict: Reports the 63 mg/dL right away by call light.

questions.stem: At 1100 a 77-year-old who received regular insulin at 0700, before breakfast, has a glucose of 57 mg/dL. After treating him, the nurse reviews the morning. Which findings could explain the low? Select all that apply.

options.text: He left most of his breakfast on the tray
options.rationale: The dose was sized for a full meal that he did not eat.

options.text: He walked the hall for 30 minutes at 0930
options.rationale: Exercise uses glucose, and 0930 is 2.5 hours after the dose, inside the 2 to 4 hour peak.

options.text: The dose was injected into his abdomen
options.rationale: The abdomen is a standard site with steady absorption. It does not explain a low.

options.text: The dose was given 30 minutes before the tray came
options.rationale: That is the correct timing for regular insulin.

options.text: He has had a low grade fever since 0600
options.rationale: Illness tends to raise glucose, not lower it.

options.text: The syringe was drawn 2 units past the ordered mark
options.rationale: More insulin than ordered lowers the glucose further.

questions.takeaway: After a low, work out why: less food, more activity or too much insulin, most of all at the peak of the insulin.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: For each finding ask one question: does this add insulin effect or remove glucose? If neither, leave it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Less eaten than the dose was meant for.
A walk that fell inside the peak of regular insulin.
Two extra units.
A usual site, correct timing and fever do not cause a low.

elimination.verdict: Poor intake, the walk and the overdrawn dose.

questions.stem: A 51-year-old has a fingerstick glucose due before lunch. Place the nurse's actions in order.

options.text: Verify the client's identity with two identifiers
options.rationale: First. The result and any insulin that follows must belong to the right client.

options.text: Check the strip date and have the client wash and dry hands
options.rationale: Supplies and skin are made ready before the puncture so the reading can be trusted.

options.text: Hold the hand below the heart and puncture the fingertip
options.rationale: Lowering the hand improves blood flow so one puncture gives an adequate drop.

options.text: Touch the drop to the strip without squeezing the finger
options.rationale: Squeezing can alter the sample.

options.text: Compare the result with the client and the insulin order
options.rationale: Last. The number is judged against how the client looks and what is ordered.

questions.takeaway: Fingerstick: right client, valid strip, clean dry finger, hand lowered, no squeezing, then interpret the number against the client and the order.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Anchor the ends first. Identity opens the sequence and interpreting the result closes it.

steps.detail: Nothing is done to an unverified client.
Strip date and clean dry hands.
Hand lowered, no squeezing, then read it against the client.

elimination.verdict: Identify, prepare, puncture, sample, interpret.

questions.scenario: A 29-year-old with type 1 diabetes missed two days of insulin. Her fingerstick glucose is 436 mg/dL. She is drowsy and very thirsty, with dry mucous membranes, deep rapid breathing and abdominal pain.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the client is most likely experiencing and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Test for ketones
options.rationale: High glucose with deep rapid breathing and abdominal pain means ketones are likely, and the result guides treatment.

options.text: Give the prescribed insulin and IV fluids
options.rationale: She lacks insulin and is dry. Both are replaced together.

options.text: Give 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate
options.rationale: That treats a low. Her drowsiness comes from a very high glucose.

options.text: Encourage a walk to bring the glucose down
options.rationale: Her signs point to ketones, and exercise with ketones makes the ketosis worse.

options.text: Hyperglycemia with ketoacidosis
options.rationale: No insulin for two days, a glucose of 436, deep rapid breathing and abdominal pain.

options.text: Hypoglycemia
options.rationale: A low gives sweating and shakiness with a low reading.

options.text: Dawn phenomenon
options.rationale: That is a mild early morning rise in a client who is taking insulin.

options.text: Rebound after a night time low
options.rationale: A rebound follows a low in a client who is taking insulin. She has had no insulin for two days.

options.text: Glucose at the prescribed intervals
options.rationale: Shows the insulin is working and catches a fall that is too fast or too far.

options.text: Level of consciousness and breathing pattern
options.rationale: Drowsiness and deep rapid breathing should ease as the acidosis clears.

options.text: Injection site for bruising
options.rationale: Not the concern in this emergency.

options.text: Appetite at the next meal
options.rationale: Intake matters later, once she is stable.

questions.takeaway: Very high glucose with deep rapid breathing and abdominal pain is ketoacidosis. Check ketones, replace insulin and fluid, and watch the glucose and the brain.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Drowsiness can come with a high or a low. The number, the dryness and the breathing pattern say which.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 436 mg/dL with dry membranes is high.
Carbohydrate does not belong.
Glucose and mental status.

elimination.verdict: Ketones and insulin with fluids, ketoacidosis, glucose and level of consciousness.

questions.scenario: At 1130 a 59-year-old had a glucose of 318 mg/dL with thirst and frequent urination. The nurse gave the prescribed correction dose of rapid-acting insulin and he ate lunch.
questions.stem: For each finding at 1400, indicate whether it shows the expected response or requires follow up.

rows.text: Glucose is 182 mg/dL
rows.rationale: The glucose has come down and is nowhere near low.

rows.text: Glucose is 326 mg/dL
rows.rationale: No change after the dose. Recheck the technique and the order, and report it.

rows.text: He is sweating and his hands shake
rows.rationale: Rapid-acting insulin is at its peak. Check the glucose now.

rows.text: He reports less thirst and has not voided since noon
rows.rationale: Less glucose is spilling into the urine, so the water loss has slowed.

rows.text: Glucose is 244 mg/dL and he says the thirst is easing
rows.rationale: The value is falling and the symptoms are easing. Rapid-acting insulin is still working, so the nurse keeps monitoring.

questions.takeaway: A correction dose has worked when the glucose falls toward range and the symptoms ease. No change and an overshoot both need action.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: There are two ways to miss: the number did not move, or it moved too far. Anything else is the goal.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sweating and shaking hands at the peak of the dose.
326 mg/dL.
182 and 244 mg/dL are both lower than 318 mg/dL and neither is low.

elimination.verdict: Expected, follow up, follow up, expected, expected.

questions.stem: The nurse must give regular insulin 8 units. The supply drawer has no insulin syringes, only 1 mL tuberculin syringes. The client's tray arrives in 30 minutes. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Draw 0.8 mL in the tuberculin syringe
options.rationale: A tenfold overdose. That volume holds 80 units of U-100 insulin.

options.text: Get an insulin syringe from another unit or pharmacy
options.rationale: Insulin is measured in units on a syringe marked in units. A short delay is safer than converting.

options.text: Draw 0.08 mL in the tuberculin syringe
options.rationale: The arithmetic is right. Measuring units in a syringe marked in mL is the error that causes insulin overdoses.

options.text: Hold the dose and chart that supplies were unavailable
options.rationale: An omitted dose leaves the meal uncovered when the right syringe can be found.

questions.takeaway: Insulin is drawn up only in an insulin syringe marked in units. Never convert a dose to mL at the bedside.
questions.coverage: Not in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Two options convert the dose and one skips it. Only one keeps both the dose and the safeguard.

steps.detail: Either volume relies on a decimal point.
The dose is still due.
Use the right syringe.

elimination.verdict: Get an insulin syringe.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old on insulin is found unresponsive with a fingerstick glucose of 38 mg/dL. She has no IV access. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Pour apple juice slowly into her mouth
options.rationale: She cannot protect her airway, so anything by mouth can be aspirated.

options.text: Place glucose gel inside her cheek and wait
options.rationale: Still an oral route in a client who cannot swallow.

options.text: Start an IV line first, then give dextrose by that route
options.rationale: Access may take several attempts while her brain goes without glucose.

options.text: Give glucagon by injection and turn her on her side
options.rationale: It works without a vein or a swallow, and vomiting is common afterward, so she is positioned to protect the airway.

questions.takeaway: Unresponsive and low: nothing by mouth. With no IV, give glucagon by injection and position on the side.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: First rule out every option that needs her to swallow. Then choose the fastest route that remains.

steps.detail: Juice and gel both risk aspiration.
An IV start delays treatment.
Side lying after glucagon.

elimination.verdict: Glucagon and side lying.

questions.stem: A 53-year-old takes glargine at bedtime and aspart with meals. For 4 days the fasting readings were 196 to 214 mg/dL with no night time lows, and readings after meals were at goal. What does the nurse conclude?

options.text: The aspart doses are too small for the meals he eats
options.rationale: Readings after meals are at goal, so the mealtime insulin is doing its job.

options.text: The glargine dose is not covering him overnight
options.rationale: The fasting value reflects basal insulin, and it is the only reading out of range.

questions.stem: The nurse watches an assistive personnel do morning fingersticks. Which action requires the nurse to step in?

options.text: Carries the meter from one room to the next without wiping it
options.rationale: A shared meter carries blood between clients. It is disinfected after every use.

options.rationale: Correct practice.

options.rationale: Correct practice.

questions.stem: At 1100 the nurse has four tasks waiting. Which one does the nurse give to an experienced assistive personnel?

options.text: Decide whether a client at 148 mg/dL needs correction insulin
options.rationale: Interpreting a value against an order is nursing judgment.

options.text: Show a new client how to rotate injection sites
options.rationale: Teaching stays with the nurse.

options.text: Recheck a client who was treated for a low 15 minutes ago
options.rationale: This client is not yet stable, and the recheck is an evaluation of treatment.

options.text: Obtain the prelunch fingerstick on a stable client
options.rationale: A routine procedure with a predictable result on a stable client, reported back to the nurse.

questions.takeaway: Delegate the routine fingerstick on a stable client. Keep assessment, teaching, evaluation and the unstable client.

Site rotation.
The recent low.

questions.stem: The nurse draws up regular insulin 6 units and sees a large air bubble in the barrel with the plunger at the 6 unit line. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Give the dose, since a little air under the skin is harmless
options.rationale: The air is harmless. The problem is that it takes the place of insulin, so the dose is short.

options.text: Add 1 more unit to make up for the bubble
options.rationale: Guessing at the lost volume makes the dose inaccurate.

options.text: Tap the bubble out, then correct the dose to 6 units
options.rationale: Removing the air and redrawing to the line gives the exact dose.

options.text: Discard the vial and open a new one
options.rationale: The vial is not the problem.

questions.takeaway: An air bubble in an insulin syringe means less insulin than the line shows. Clear it and recheck the dose.
questions.coverage: Not in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Ask what the bubble changes. It changes the amount of drug, so the fix must restore the exact amount.

steps.detail: Underdose, not air injury.
Adding a unit is a guess.
Expel air, redraw to 6.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old's readings rose from the 140s to the 260s mg/dL over 5 days on unchanged doses, meals and sites. Which report best explains the rise?

options.text: "I leave the vial on the dashboard between visits to my daughter."
options.rationale: Heat breaks insulin down, so each dose delivers less effect.

options.text: "I keep the vial I am using in the refrigerator door."
options.rationale: Proper storage.

options.text: "I opened this vial about 2 weeks ago."
options.rationale: Within the usual use period after opening.

options.text: "I let the dose warm in my hand before I inject."
options.rationale: Comfort measure that does not weaken the insulin.

questions.takeaway: Insulin exposed to heat or freezing loses strength. When doses and habits are unchanged and glucose rises, check storage.
questions.coverage: Not in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Doses, food and sites are ruled out by the stem. Look for the habit that damages the drug itself.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Use what the stem rules out
steps.detail: Dose, meals and sites.
Refrigerator, 2 weeks open and hand warming are fine.
Heat in a car.

elimination.verdict: The dashboard.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old on sliding scale insulin with a prelunch glucose of 296 mg/dL says she will skip lunch to bring it down. After teaching, which statement shows she understood?

options.text: "I will skip lunch and still take my usual insulin."
options.rationale: Mealtime insulin without the meal sets up a low.

options.text: "I will skip both lunch and insulin, then recheck at dinner."
options.rationale: With no insulin the glucose stays high through the afternoon.

options.text: "I will drink juice in place of lunch so I do not go low."
options.rationale: Juice raises a glucose that is already high.

options.text: "I will eat lunch and take the insulin my scale calls for."
options.rationale: Insulin lowers a high glucose. Regular meals with the ordered dose keep it steady.

questions.takeaway: A high reading is treated with the ordered insulin, not by skipping a meal. Skipping meals leads to swings.
questions.coverage: Not in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Find the statement that keeps food and insulin together. The others separate them or add sugar.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Insulin alone and food alone both fail.
Juice at 296 mg/dL.
Meal plus the scale dose.

elimination.verdict: Eat and dose by the scale.

questions.stem: At 1700 a student has glargine 16 units and aspart 5 units to give, and plans to draw both into one syringe to spare the client a second injection. What does the nurse tell the student?

options.text: Draw the aspart first, then the glargine
options.rationale: That order is for mixing a short-acting insulin with NPH. Glargine is not mixed at all.

options.text: Draw the glargine first, then the aspart
options.rationale: Order does not matter because the two cannot share a syringe.

options.text: Use two syringes and two separate sites
options.rationale: Glargine cannot be mixed with any other insulin, since mixing changes how it is absorbed.

options.text: Give the aspart now and hold the glargine until 2100
options.rationale: The glargine is due now. The fix is a second syringe, not a new time.

questions.takeaway: Long-acting insulin is never mixed in a syringe with another insulin. Two insulins, two syringes, two sites.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Two options argue about drawing order. If the mix itself is wrong, both go.

steps.detail: The shared error is one syringe.
The dose is due.
Two injections.

elimination.verdict: Two syringes, two sites.

questions.stem: At 0730 a new nurse explains the insulin plan for four clients whose breakfast trays come at 0800. Which statement needs correction?

options.text: "The Humulin N I give now will cover this breakfast."
options.rationale: NPH has an onset of 1 to 2 hours and peaks at 4 to 12 hours. It will not be working at 0800, so it does not cover this meal.

options.text: "The Novolin R I give now will be working when the tray comes."
options.rationale: Correct. Regular insulin starts in 30 to 60 minutes and is given about 30 minutes before the meal.

options.text: "The NovoLog waits until the tray is in front of the client."
options.rationale: Correct. Rapid acting insulin starts in 10 to 30 minutes and is given with the food.

options.text: "The Lantus is not timed to the tray."
options.rationale: Correct. Long-acting basal insulin has no pronounced peak and is not matched to meals.

questions.takeaway: NPH: onset 1 to 2 hours, peak 4 to 12 hours, duration 14 to 24 hours. It covers the hours after a meal, not the meal that comes 30 minutes after the dose.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Put each insulin's onset next to the 30 minutes before the tray. One of them has not started by then.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Rapid 10 to 30 minutes, regular 30 to 60 minutes, NPH 1 to 2 hours, long-acting no peak.
NPH has not started at 0800.

elimination.verdict: The Humulin N statement.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews new insulin prescriptions for four clients who are eating normally. Which prescription does the nurse question?

options.text: NovoLog 4 units with each meal, three times daily
options.rationale: Correct. Rapid acting insulin is given with meals.

options.text: Humulin R 6 units 30 minutes before breakfast
options.rationale: Correct. Regular insulin is given about 30 minutes before the meal.

options.text: Lantus 14 units with each meal
options.rationale: Lantus is a long-acting basal insulin that lasts 20 to 24 hours and is not timed to food. A dose with every meal reads like a mealtime insulin order written for the wrong drug, so it is verified.

options.text: Humulin N 18 units once every morning
options.rationale: A usual NPH schedule. It lasts 14 to 24 hours.

questions.takeaway: Check the insulin type against its usual timing. Long-acting insulin lasts 20 to 24 hours and is given on the clock, not with each meal.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Put each drug's duration next to how often it is ordered. One order repeats a 24 hour insulin at every meal.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: NovoLog with meals and regular 30 minutes before are correct.
NPH once a morning fits. Lantus with every meal does not.

elimination.verdict: Lantus with each meal.

questions.stem: A client has NovoLog 5 units with each meal plus a NovoLog correction scale: 151 to 200 mg/dL, 2 units; 201 to 250 mg/dL, 4 units. The tray is here and the fingerstick is 236 mg/dL. Which dose does the nurse give?

options.text: 4 units
options.rationale: This is the correction alone. The scheduled dose that covers the meal is left out.

options.text: 5 units
options.rationale: This is the scheduled dose alone. The glucose is on the scale, so the correction is also due.

options.text: 7 units
options.rationale: This adds the correction for 151 to 200 mg/dL. A value of 236 mg/dL is in the next row.

options.text: 9 units
options.rationale: The scheduled 5 units cover the meal and the 4 units from the 201 to 250 mg/dL row correct the glucose. Both are the same insulin and both are due now.

questions.takeaway: Scheduled mealtime insulin and correction insulin are two orders. When the glucose is on the scale and the meal is present, give both: here 5 plus 4 is 9 units.
questions.coverage: Not in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Work the two orders one at a time, then add.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 5 units, because the tray is here.
236 mg/dL sits in the 201 to 250 mg/dL row: 4 units.
9 units.

elimination.verdict: 9 units.

questions.stem: An 83-year-old received NPH insulin at 0730. His fingersticks were 122 mg/dL at 0730, 98 mg/dL at 1130 and 74 mg/dL at 1530. His afternoon snack has not come. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Record 74 mg/dL as within target and recheck before dinner
options.rationale: Tempting because 74 mg/dL is inside the 70 to 180 mg/dL target. The steady fall during the NPH peak with no snack yet is what makes waiting unsafe.

options.text: Give 15 to 20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate per the hypoglycemia protocol
options.rationale: The protocol is for a glucose under 70 mg/dL. He is not there yet.

options.text: Get his snack to him now and recheck the fingerstick
options.rationale: The value is falling toward 70 mg/dL at eight hours after NPH, inside its 4 to 12 hour peak. Food now and a recheck keep him from becoming low.

options.text: Hold his next NPH dose
options.rationale: The nurse does not withhold a later dose without an order for a value that is still in range.

questions.takeaway: Read the trend, not only the number. A glucose that keeps falling toward 70 mg/dL during an insulin's peak needs food and a recheck before it becomes a low.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: 74 mg/dL is in range, so ask where it is heading. Count the hours since the NPH and look at the three values together.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 122, then 98, then 74 mg/dL, eight hours after NPH.
The protocol starts under 70 mg/dL.
Holding a later dose is not the nurse's decision here.
Waiting until dinner leaves a falling value alone at the peak.

elimination.verdict: C: feed him now and recheck.

questions.stem: The nurse is mixing regular insulin 6 units with NPH 11 units. Regular was drawn first. While drawing the NPH, the plunger slips to the 19 unit line. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Push 2 units back into the NPH vial
options.rationale: The syringe now holds a mix. Pushing it back puts regular insulin into the NPH vial.

options.text: Discard the syringe and prepare the dose again
options.rationale: No one can tell how much of each insulin the extra 2 units contain, and the mix cannot go back into a vial. Starting over is the only way to a known dose.

options.text: Expel 2 units into the sink, then give the dose
options.rationale: The total would read 17, but the amount of each insulin in it would be unknown.

options.text: Give the 19 units and check the glucose more often
options.rationale: A known overdose is not given. Too much insulin is a main cause of a low.

questions.takeaway: Once two insulins share a syringe, an overdrawn dose cannot be fixed. Discard it and start again: regular first, then NPH to the total.
questions.coverage: Not in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: The syringe already holds two insulins. Ask what each option does to the vial or to the dose.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 6 plus 11 is 17 units. The syringe holds 19.
It gives 2 units too many.
It contaminates the NPH vial with regular.
It leaves an unknown mix.

elimination.verdict: B: discard and prepare a new syringe.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old has Humalog 5 units ordered with meals. His prelunch fingerstick is 158 mg/dL. The tray is in front of him, and he says he is too nauseated to eat anything. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Hold the Humalog and report that he is not eating
options.rationale: Mealtime insulin covers food. With no food going in, the dose would drop his glucose with nothing to work on, so it is held and the reduced intake is reported.

options.text: Give the Humalog now because the tray is present
options.rationale: A tray on the table is not intake. The dose is matched to food he actually eats.

options.text: Give half of the Humalog dose
options.rationale: Changing a dose is a prescriber decision. The nurse gives the ordered dose or holds it.

options.text: Give the Humalog and urge him to eat within 15 minutes
options.rationale: Tempting because rapid-acting insulin is given with the meal. He has said he cannot eat, so the insulin would act with no food.

questions.takeaway: Rapid-acting mealtime insulin follows food that is eaten, not a tray that is delivered. No intake: hold the dose and report it.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: The glucose is in range and the tray is here. The cue that decides it is that he will not eat.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: He is too nauseated to eat.
The nurse does not choose a new dose.
Both give insulin with no food going in.

elimination.verdict: A: hold the Humalog and report the reduced intake.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old with a fingerstick glucose of 49 mg/dL was sipping juice. She is now drowsy and coughs with each swallow. A saline lock is in place. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Sit her upright and keep giving small sips of juice
options.rationale: Oral treatment is for a client who is alert and can swallow. Coughing with each swallow means she no longer can.

options.text: Stop the juice and give IV dextrose
options.rationale: She can no longer swallow safely and she has IV access, so glucose goes in by vein.

options.text: Give glucagon by injection
options.rationale: A correct route when there is no IV access. She has a saline lock, so IV dextrose is used.

options.text: Recheck the fingerstick in 15 minutes
options.rationale: The recheck follows a treatment. She has not received an effective one yet and is getting worse.

questions.takeaway: When a client with a low glucose stops being able to swallow safely, stop oral treatment. IV access present means IV dextrose. No IV access means glucagon by injection.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Two cues changed: she is drowsy and she coughs when swallowing. Then look for what access she has.

steps.detail: Coughing with each swallow rules out more juice.
Waiting is not treatment.
Both avoid the mouth. The saline lock tips it to IV dextrose.

elimination.verdict: B: stop oral intake and give IV dextrose.

questions.stem: At 1500 the nurse hears about four clients who take insulin. Which client does the nurse see first?

options.text: Glucose 58 mg/dL, alert, drinking juice the nurse just gave
options.rationale: A real low, but it is known and treatment is under way. The recheck is due in 15 minutes.

options.text: Glucose 288 mg/dL, alert and thirsty, sliding scale dose due at dinner
options.rationale: High and needs follow up, but this client is alert and it is not an immediate threat.

options.text: Asks for help planning site rotation before discharge
options.rationale: Teaching can wait.

options.text: NPH at 0700, now sweaty and confused, no reading yet
options.rationale: Sweating and new confusion during the NPH peak point to a low that nobody has measured or treated.

questions.takeaway: New confusion and sweating in a client on insulin is a low until a fingerstick says otherwise. An unmeasured, untreated change comes before a low that is already being treated.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Sort by what is unknown and getting worse. One client has a change in thinking and no number yet.

steps.detail: Teaching is not urgent.
High, alert, and a dose is already planned.
A is alert and treated. D is confused with no reading.

elimination.verdict: D: the confused, sweaty client with no reading.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old who started insulin had a low at home last week. After teaching about treating a low, which statement needs follow up?

options.text: "I take 15 grams of fast sugar as soon as I am under 70 mg/dL."
options.rationale: Correct. Under 70 mg/dL is treated right away.

options.text: "I test again 15 minutes after I treat it."
options.rationale: Correct. The recheck is at 15 minutes.

options.text: "Once the shaking stops, I know my sugar is back up."
options.rationale: Feeling better does not show that the glucose has recovered. Only the recheck does.

options.text: "If I am still under 70 mg/dL when I retest, I treat again."
options.rationale: Correct. Treatment is repeated while the value stays under 70 mg/dL.

questions.takeaway: Symptoms easing does not mean the glucose is back over 70 mg/dL. The 15 minute recheck decides whether to treat again.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: You are hunting the unsafe statement. Three follow the rule of 15. One replaces the recheck with a feeling.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the statement that is wrong.
Treat under 70 mg/dL, recheck in 15 minutes, repeat if still low.
C skips the recheck.

elimination.verdict: C: symptoms are not a substitute for the recheck.

questions.stem: At 1645 the nurse prepares regular insulin 8 units, ordered before dinner, for a 68-year-old. Which findings lead the nurse to hold the dose and clarify it? Select all that apply.

options.text: His fingerstick is 59 mg/dL
options.rationale: Insulin is never given to a client whose glucose is under 70 mg/dL. The low is treated first.

options.text: He vomited lunch and says he will not eat dinner
options.rationale: Premeal insulin with no meal coming in sets up a low.

options.text: The solution in the vial is clear
options.rationale: Regular insulin is clear. This is the expected appearance.

options.text: His fingerstick is 172 mg/dL
options.rationale: This is inside the 70 to 180 mg/dL target and does not stop a scheduled premeal dose.

options.text: Yesterday's abdominal site has a bruise
options.rationale: The nurse picks an intact spot away from the bruise. The dose is still given.

options.text: His dinner tray is due at 1715
options.rationale: Regular insulin is given about 30 minutes before the meal, so this timing is correct.

questions.takeaway: Hold insulin and clarify when the glucose is under 70 mg/dL or the client will not be eating. A bruise changes the spot, not the decision to give.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Ask of each finding: does this make the dose unsafe, or is it a normal part of giving it?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A glucose of 59 mg/dL and no intake both make the dose dangerous.
Clear vial, 172 mg/dL and a tray in 30 minutes are all as they should be.
Choose a different spot in the same region.

elimination.verdict: A and B.

questions.stem: A client's sliding scale dose depends on the prelunch fingerstick. The meter passed its control check and the tray is on the unit. The nurse sees that the strip vial expired last month. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Test with these strips because the meter passed its check
options.rationale: The control check shows the meter works. It says nothing about strips past their date.

options.text: Get in-date strips before the fingerstick
options.rationale: An expired strip can give a false number, and the insulin dose is taken from that number.

options.text: Test now and repeat only if the value looks abnormal
options.rationale: Tempting with the tray waiting. A false value can look normal, and the client gets a second puncture either way.

options.text: Give the dose he received at lunch yesterday
options.rationale: A sliding scale dose needs a current glucose.

questions.takeaway: The insulin dose is only as good as the number. Check the strips as well as the meter before the puncture.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: The tray is waiting and that is the pressure. Ask whether the number that sets the dose can be trusted.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

No current glucose, no sliding scale dose.
Both produce a number that cannot be trusted.

questions.stem: The nurse has drawn up NPH 20 units as written on the medication record. As she pinches the skin, the 59-year-old says, "I only take 10 at home." Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Stop and verify the dose before giving it
options.rationale: A wrong dose is a main cause of a low, and the client knows the usual home dose. The nurse checks before the insulin is in.

options.text: Explain that hospital doses often differ, then give the 20 units
options.rationale: Tempting because it can be true. Without checking, the nurse is guessing which number is right.

options.text: Give the dose, then check the order afterward
options.rationale: Insulin cannot be taken back once it is injected.

options.text: Give 10 units now and clarify the rest later
options.rationale: The nurse does not choose a new dose. She gives the ordered dose or holds it.

questions.takeaway: When a client questions an insulin dose, stop and verify before injecting. Insulin given cannot be taken back.
questions.coverage: Not in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: The client has given new information at the last second. Decide whether to act on the record or check it.

steps.detail: The usual home dose is half of what is drawn up.
Checking after the injection is too late.
The nurse does not set the dose.
B answers the client without checking.

elimination.verdict: A: stop and verify the dose first.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old takes Humulin R at 0700 before breakfast and wants to add a hard 45 minute swim to his day. Which swim time carries the highest risk of a low?

options.rationale: The insulin has barely begun to work. Onset is 30 to 60 minutes and the peak is hours away.
This is 3 hours after the dose, inside the 2 to 4 hour peak of regular insulin. Exercise on top of the peak drops the glucose furthest.
By now the dose is past the end of its 5 to 8 hour duration.
The morning dose has worn off.

questions.takeaway: Exercise lowers glucose most when it lands on the insulin's peak. Regular insulin peaks 2 to 4 hours after the dose.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Count the hours from 0700 to each swim time and place each on the regular insulin curve.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 0700 plus 2 to 4 hours is 0900 to 1100.
Both fall after the end of the dose.
0715 is before onset. 1000 is in the peak.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old's NPH has gone into his abdomen all week. Today the nurse finds a red, tender area at yesterday's spot. The rest of the abdomen is intact. Where does the nurse give this morning's dose?

options.text: The same spot, to keep absorption consistent
options.rationale: Inflamed tissue is avoided. Rotation means a new spot each time.

options.text: The buttock, the farthest site from the redness
options.rationale: The buttock absorbs slowest. A new region changes how the dose acts.

options.text: The thigh, to rest the abdomen
options.rationale: Tempting because it avoids the red area. Moving to another region changes absorption and makes readings harder to predict.

options.text: An intact abdominal spot away from the red area
options.rationale: He stays in the same region so absorption stays the same, and the inflamed spot is avoided.

questions.takeaway: Stay in one region and move the spot. Skip any area that is red, bruised, scarred or damaged.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Two rules apply at once: avoid damaged tissue and keep the same region. Find the option that keeps both.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: It injects inflamed tissue.
Both change the region, which changes absorption.
Same region, different spot, intact skin.

elimination.verdict: D: an intact spot on the abdomen.

questions.stem: The nurse gave an 82-year-old Humalog 4 units as her lunch tray was set down. She eats two bites, pushes the tray away and refuses the rest. She is alert. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Record the amount eaten and recheck before dinner
options.rationale: The insulin is already working with almost no food. Waiting until dinner leaves her uncovered.

options.text: Give 15 to 20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate per the hypoglycemia protocol
options.rationale: The protocol treats a glucose under 70 mg/dL. No value shows she is low yet.

options.text: Offer other carbohydrate she will accept and monitor her glucose
options.rationale: The dose cannot be taken back, so the food has to catch up. Something she will eat or drink now plus glucose checks keeps a low from developing.

options.text: Hold her dinner Humalog
options.rationale: That decision belongs to dinner and to her intake then. It does nothing for the dose already given.

questions.takeaway: Insulin already given needs food behind it. If the client stops eating, find carbohydrate she will take and watch the glucose.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: The insulin is in. The question is how to cover it now, not what to do at dinner.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Rapid-acting insulin on board and two bites eaten.
Both leave the present dose uncovered.
The protocol needs a low value. Preventing the low comes first.

elimination.verdict: C: get carbohydrate into her and monitor.

questions.stem: At 1230 an assistive personnel tells the nurse, "His fingerstick was 67 mg/dL at 1100. He had no symptoms, and he ate all of his lunch at 1130." He is on insulin. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Assess him and repeat the fingerstick now
options.rationale: The value is 90 minutes old and he has eaten a full meal since. The nurse needs his condition and a current number before choosing a treatment.

options.text: Give 15 to 20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate
options.rationale: Tempting because 67 mg/dL is under 70 mg/dL and should have been treated at 1100. A full meal has gone in since, so the nurse confirms where he is now before treating.

options.text: Give his lunch insulin now since he has eaten
options.rationale: Insulin is not given until the nurse knows his glucose is no longer low.

options.text: Have the assistive personnel recheck him in 15 minutes
options.rationale: The 15 minute recheck follows a treatment. A low that was never treated or assessed needs the nurse now.

questions.takeaway: A low reported late is old data. Assess the client and get a current fingerstick first, then treat what you find. A low under 70 mg/dL is reported and treated when it is found.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Check the clock. Ninety minutes and a full meal have passed since the number was taken.

steps.detail: 67 mg/dL was taken at 1100. Lunch was eaten at 1130. It is now 1230.
No insulin until the glucose is known.
Waiting 15 more minutes delays the nurse assessment.
Treatment follows a current value.

elimination.verdict: A: assess him and repeat the fingerstick.
